Apple iPhone Duo review: Two screens, two experiences, two thousand dollars

Ars Technica Long form October 27, 2026

I respect Apple’s first crack at a foldable phone, but I’m not sure I like it.

I understand the appeal of foldable phones—they let manufacturers keep expanding screen sizes while still producing devices that can reasonably fit in a pocket. In practice, though, every foldable Android phone I’ve seen in public has had a ridiculously visible seam between the two halves of the screen, often with what looks like delamination from the underlying surface, giving the display an ugly, bubbly appearance.

Back when Android phones began shipping with bigger and bigger screens and the iPhone was stuck at a miserly four inches, I was jealous. But I’ve never looked at anyone using a chunky, fragile-looking foldable phone in public and pined for Apple’s take on the idea.

Nevertheless, that take has arrived, in the form of the iPhone Duo. This $1,999-and-up foldable is the biggest change to the iPhone in years, with both hardware and software updates that dramatically change how you interact with the device.

Like most Apple products, it looks and feels solid, and Apple has managed to engineer its way around at least some of the problems that have bedeviled other foldables (in particular, it has wrangled the between-screen crease so close to invisibility that I rarely thought about it while using the phone unfolded).

But like most first-generation Apple products, it has some odd rough edges and costs more than most people will want to spend. Some aspects of its design feel like steps backward from the standard iPhone design, as exemplified by the current iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro.

The result is something that is technically impressive but not always enjoyable to use. As a little iPad, it’s surprisingly good. As an iPhone, though, I struggle to think of a single way I prefer it to a regular old iPhone.

The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone I’ve used in a long time that comes with a learning curve. It’s the first time since 2018’s iPhone X that a hardware update has fundamentally changed how you interact with the software.

For the first day or two, I found this pretty off-putting. I kept losing track of the iPad-style button-mounted Touch ID sensor and flipping the phone around with the camera upside down. When fully opened, the phone acts like an iPad: It’s orientation-agnostic, and it will work in portrait or landscape, regardless of which end is up. But in its folded one-handed mode, the Duo still has a right-side-up and an upside-down just like any iPhone, and it took a couple of days of retraining my muscle memory before I was consistently pulling it out of my pocket and looking at it the right way without thinking about it.

When folded up, the iPhone Duo has a more compact footprint than Apple’s other phones and a screen that’s both shorter and wider. The titanium frame looks and feels a lot like last year’s iPhone Air, which plenty of people (us included) pegged as a half-step toward a foldable design. The outer screen looks and feels like a typical glassy iPhone screen, and the “back” of the phone where the camera is (the only quadrant of the phone that isn’t a screen) uses familiar-looking and -feeling Ceramic Shield glass.

Despite having a familiar-looking camera cutout and Dynamic Island on the front screen, the Duo totally lacks a Face ID scanner, which is a pretty big behavioral change following years of face-scanning phones. The Touch ID button has been migrated to the power button, iPad-style, which is in the upper-right corner of the phone when it’s folded (when unfolded, the positioning depends on which direction is “up” because the phone flips its screen orientation no matter which way you’re holding it).

In general, the Duo’s button positioning is strange. The power button’s position is… fine. It’s the only placement that makes Touch ID authentication even remotely possible with one hand, even though I felt like I was about to drop the phone every time I tried. But the volume buttons are on the top of the phone in this mode. The left button is volume down and the right button is volume up in this orientation, like on a landscape iPad, even though the volume indicator itself is a tiny bar that lives in the Dynamic Island and travels up and down vertically.

The Duo’s other physical button is the Camera Control button. I would vastly prefer it be a customizable Action Button, which I use constantly on my iPhone 17 Pro. For a phone with this many acres of edge, it feels like the Action Button should have room to exist somewhere, but it doesn’t.

That shorter, wider screen leads to the biggest and most noticeable of the iPhone Duo’s software design changes, at least in folded-phone mode: Your dock moves to the right edge of the screen, and that’s where most app controls move, too. Controls for apps that normally appear on the top or the bottom of the screen are now generally relocated to the right side of the screen, which is still something I’m still getting used to, even after nearly a week of daily use.

These side-mounted controls feel like they’re swimming upstream against almost two decades of smartphone app design—and they don’t even really solve the “lack of vertical space” problem because as soon as the iOS keyboard pops up, the viewable area still shrinks to just a few lines of text.

This right-hand navigation area also feels weirdly underutilized, given the percentage of the front screen it takes up. Your dock is there, but Apple still limits it to four icons, leaving a ton of unused space above and below it. The nav area feels too wide, with too much negative space.

In the end, I only really liked the Duo in folded-down phone mode when it was sitting on a desk, couch, or table next to my laptop, serving as a separate compact notification screen—in other words, when I was not actively holding or touching it. And this isn’t something no other phone can do; it’s just a regular phone thing that the Duo doesn’t make worse.

While folded, the Duo is fundamentally designed for right-handed use. Controls throughout iOS and Duo-optimized apps have been scooted to the screen’s right edge to make up for the loss of vertical screen area. The screen is wide enough that any attempt by lefties to reach across with their thumbs to tab that part of the screen will be difficult to impossible, and I say this as someone with fairly large hands.

The Touch ID sensor—integrated, iPad-style, into the phone’s long, flat power button—is also mounted on the right side. Even if iOS did flip around the other way when you hold the Duo with the rounded edge on the left (and it doesn’t, to be clear), the camera would then be on the bottom of the phone, blocked by your fingers.

But even as a right-hander, I don’t find the Duo to be especially comfortable to use one-handed. Sure, I can reach everything, but the phone is so heavy and thick that the standard “rest the phone on my pinkie and use it with my thumb” move is fatiguing. A left-handed friend who held and tested the Duo found it extremely uncomfortable, particularly the stretch you need to do to hit any app icon in the side-mounted dock.

As frustrating as the Duo is when it’s folded, I genuinely enjoy it when it’s unfolded. Think of an iPad Nano, and you’ll be pretty close to what the experience is.

To answer the biggest question first: Yes, you can see and feel the seam between the screens if you’re looking for it. But most of the time, if you’re just holding it and watching video or reading a webpage and using a thumb to scroll in the corner of the screen, you just don’t notice it. Apple has gotten very close to making it invisible.

Frankly, I’m much more bothered by the under-screen camera, which is visible pretty much constantly. The seam is visible from some angles if you go looking for them. The under-screen camera pinhole is only invisible from some angles if you go looking for it. It’s out of the way enough not to be experience-ruining, but I did find it distracting, and I don’t know that I find it to be a net improvement over the actual-pinhole-with-Dynamic-Island solution that Apple has used for the last few iPhone generations.

When unfolded, the Duo’s screen expands from a squat 5.4 inches to a more comfortable 7.6 inches, which isn’t so far off from the new iPad mini’s 8.5-inch screen. The dock is still limited to four app icons, like a regular iPhone, but it moves back to a familiar place at the bottom of the screen, and apps have more room to breathe.

In landscape, apps usually retain the same side-mounted controls you see on the phone’s front screen, but when you pivot to portrait mode, they revert to more familiar positioning at the top and bottom of the screen—portrait mode looks pretty much like an iPad, while landscape mode looks more like a pair of iPhone home screens next to each other (more on that in a minute).

The inner screen has a matte nano-texture finish, which shares a name with the technology used in some Macs and iPads. But Apple says that both the materials used and the actual nano-texture pattern are both different, changes that were necessitated by the fact that this is a foldable phone and not an inert glass slab. A slightly raised rim around the edge of the screen keeps it from resting directly on a table or desk and leaves room for tiny bits of dust or crud to get trapped without grinding into the screen. If the inner screen does get damaged, this cover layer can apparently be removed and replaced without too much trouble.

I find the screen mostly pleasant to look at and interact with, and I really appreciate the lack of glare. My only gripes are that it picks up smudges that are slightly harder to wipe off than they are on regular glass and that contrast (particularly for dark/black elements) is visibly worse than on the front glassy screen. The inner screen does use OLED display panels, the same as the front screen, but this specific benefit of OLED is missing from the inner screen.

While an unfolded Duo is decidedly iPad-like, it’s still running iOS, not iPadOS, and Apple has gone back to the drawing board for yet another take on split-screen iDevice multitasking. What the company landed on is most similar to the iPad’s old Split View interface, but with some limitations and benefits that help it feel somewhat more at home on the Duo.

To enter split-screen multitasking, open an app and swipe up from the bottom of the screen, then drag the window to the areas that appear on the left and right of the screen. Once you’ve anchored an app in this way, the unused half of the screen simply becomes a standard iPhone home screen, with all your icons, widgets, and the side-mounted dock (which can appear on the left side of the screen when the phone is unfolded).

Launch another app from that home screen, and it will take up the other half of the screen. Both apps can be used and dismissed independently, as though you were using two separate iPhones next to each other; you can even launch the same app twice if you really want to.

The center of the screen, where the fold is, is mostly treated as a dead zone by default, but drag it one way or the other to resize one of the apps to full screen, and tap the divider to lock two apps together so they always appear and are dismissed in tandem. If you close the phone’s screen, what you were doing on the right half of the inner screen is preserved on the outer screen, giving the transition a seamless feel.

The hardware’s design makes sense when you look at multitasking mode. Half of an unfolded iPhone Duo is exactly the same as using the iPhone Duo in its folded-down phone mode. The side-nav is pinned to the left side of the screen instead of the right side, but it otherwise feels very similar to having a pair of iPhones you can use in tandem (I would say “two iPhones for the price of one,” but that doesn’t work when the base Duo model is even more expensive than buying two regular iPhones).

Third-party apps need to be updated in one way or another to support the Duo, with baseline support granted at least partly for “free” to apps that target the Xcode 27.1 SDK. Apps that haven’t been updated look mostly OK on the outer screen, since its strip of usable space is roughly the same width as a regular iPhone. Apps that haven’t been updated look like iPhone apps running on an iPad when the screen is unfolded, though: little phone-sized windows with black borders all around, with an option to expand them so they take up the entire screen.

I’ve been surprised how many apps have added Duo support in the few days since the device came out, given that Apple didn’t even make these tools available to developers until just a few weeks ago. But early adopters will run into tons of apps that don’t know what to make of the Duo’s larger inner screen, and I suspect it will be a while before you can assume that any given app will work properly on it.

The Duo can be a phone. The Duo can be a tablet. But it also supports several liminal states that exist somewhere in between the two (nomenclature mine):

Not all apps that support the Duo do different things in every one of its modes, but apps can treat them all as their own unique views if they want to. (I asked a developer from the New York Times Cooking team at an Apple-hosted developer showcase how many distinct views they needed to support to cover every possible position that an app can appear in on the Duo. “Seven. It’s seven,” he replied without hesitation.)

But we’ve already seen a few examples of developers doing things that wouldn’t be at home on a regular iPhone or an iPad. The Headroom app uses a remote desktop connection to connect to a remote Mac and simulate a tiny MacBook; the Delta emulator app has been updated with a Nintendo DS mode; and the Tiny Computers app will change it into arguably copyright-safe facsimiles of distinctive classic computers. I can’t vouch for the quality of any of these apps, and Headroom and Tiny Computers in particular have a distinct air of “quickly vibe-coded to catch the wave of early adopter interest” to them. But the ideas are interesting, and they wouldn’t work as well on different hardware.

Along with the review unit, Apple included a $79 iPhone Duo Case and a $129 iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand. The case provides a basic level of protection without really changing anything about how the Duo works (though the fact that it sticks to the phone using adhesive raises concerns about its longevity).

The Folio is more interesting. It attaches with magnets, and it has a retractable strip between its two halves that stretches to cover the hinge when the phone is folded and retreats into the case when it’s opened. The kickstand that props the phone up in tablet mode is genuinely useful; in phone mode, it solves one problem while creating another.

Here’s the problem it solves: By default, if you’re using the Duo in tablet mode and you fold it closed, the phone transitions your current app to the outer screen rather than putting the phone to sleep. Flipping the Folio cover open and closed does put the phone to sleep and wake it up. It makes the question of “is my phone awake or isn’t it” easier to answer.

The problem it creates is that this cover is opaque, and when you fold it around to the back of the phone, it covers both the camera and the flashlight. These are two things I regularly need fast access to when I pull my phone out of my pocket, and the Folio case asks you to leave the cover flopping around, remove the case temporarily, or snap the phone open into tablet mode instead of using it in phone mode.

The chip and the camera in the iPhone Duo are way less interesting than the brand-new hardware and software changes, so apologies if this section feels like an afterthought. But it kind of is.

The Apple A20 Pro is Apple’s first 2 nm phone chip, and its second 2 nm chip overall after the M6 that debuted in the new Mac mini. It still uses two large CPU cores and four efficiency cores, the same as the last few generations of A-series chips, but it’s the first phone chip to include “super” cores instead of performance cores. Unlike the M6, which ships all three kinds of cores, the A20 Pro just uses super and efficiency cores.

The A20 Pro does ship with 7 GPU cores, up from the 5-6 cores in the A19 Pro, plus Apple’s upgraded 32-core Neural Engine (Apple usually refers to this as a “dual Neural Engine” with 16 cores each). The A20 Pro still includes 12GB of RAM, the same as the A19 Pro (both upgraded from the 8GB of RAM in the A18 Pro—either chip would be a solid upgrade option for a future MacBook Neo).

In the benchmarks I ran, Apple’s performance promises for the A20 Pro end up in the ballpark of the figures Apple has published: around 20 to 30 percent better single- and multi-core CPU performance compared to A19 Pro, and between 40 and 50 percent faster GPU performance (the 73 percent performance improvement for the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme test is an outlier). If you own any iPhone made within the last three or four years, the chip isn’t the reason to buy the phone, but it’s a respectable upgrade.

The Duo’s camera system is fine. Like the iPhone Air, this hardware is priced well into iPhone Pro territory while lacking the camera system that makes the Pro my default iPhone choice.

The Duo uses the same basic camera configuration as the basic iPhone. It has one 48 MP main sensor and one 48 MP ultrawide sensor, both of which enable a 2x optical zoom feature by cropping a 12 MP patch out of the middle. (Apple’s tech specs page also claims that the ultrawide lens can zoom out by 2x, giving it a “4x optical-quality zoom range,” which feels hand-wavy even if you accept “optical-quality zoom” as an accurate description of what Apple’s cameras are doing).

What keeps me away from the standard iPhone these days is that I find the ultrawide lens to be by far the least useful one Apple ships and the telephoto lens to be the most useful. The Duo’s camera asks you to make the same kind of downgrade from a Pro iPhone, though it at least improves on the one-camera setups Apple ships in the iPhone 17e and iPhone Air.

Once you get past the lack of a telephoto lens, the Duo’s camera system is perfectly competent. Apple’s year-to-year camera quality improvements generally happen around the margins—a little less noise here, a little better low-light performance there—and that’s what I observed while comparing it to my iPhone 17 Pro. To my eye, the differences between the 17 Pro and Duo in good lighting were minimal, but the Duo did capture marginally better detail in low light (see the cat pictures). Of course, when you try comparing the Duo’s digitally zoomed 4x and 8x photos to the 17 Pro’s telephoto lens, there’s zero contest.

The front cameras, like Face ID, are another casualty of the Duo’s design changes. There are technically two front-facing cameras: a typical-ish pinhole cutout on the front of the outer screen and the one hidden underneath the inner screen (as we discussed before, “hidden” is generous; the camera is almost always visible underneath whatever you’re looking at).

The outer camera is lower-resolution than most other iPhones (12 MP, down from 18 MP), but it’s in the ballpark when you’re on a FaceTime call or taking a selfie. The under-screen inner camera is noticeably worse, capturing noisier video and photos that look excessively digitally sharpened to try to cover for its reduced quality and lack of detail. Apple doesn’t list a resolution for the inner camera, but its 2432 x 1824 resolution works out to around 4.4 megapixels, just one-third the resolution of the outer camera.

That the inner camera is so much worse than the outer camera is made even more obvious by the fact that the inner screen is twice as large; when you fire up a FaceTime call, you’re looking at a lower-resolution image on a larger screen. This isn’t a dealbreaker; the bi-directional FaceTime call that shows the person on the other end of the line on both the outer and inner screens remains genuinely cool, even with the potato-esque quality of the inner camera. But it’s yet another place where the core/traditional iPhone experience is degraded to make room for the Duo’s hero features.

In some ways, foldable phones remind me of the PC industry’s push toward convertible tablet PCs in the early 2010s. In the wake of Apple’s original iPad, Microsoft and its partners clearly thought that they had to figure out tablets or get left behind, but even the designs with staying power (mainly Microsoft’s Surface and Lenovo’s Yoga) aren’t as good at being laptops as a purpose-built laptop or as good at being tablets as a purpose-built tablet.

For me, the iPhone Duo straddles a similar line between the iPhone and the iPad. As a regular one-handed iPhone, it feels deeply compromised—too thick and heavy to comfortably hold in one hand for long, no Face ID, no action button, and power/volume/camera button positioning that feels like it was dictated by “where the buttons can physically fit on the phone” rather than ergonomics. It costs nearly twice as much as the iPhone Pro but has an inferior camera system.

I do really like the Duo as a Kindle-sized iPad. But if that’s what I want, I can buy something like it for less money without saddling myself with a regular phone I don’t particularly like using.

I see the promise of the Duo. It feels well-built—some users have had problems with screen breakage, but it’s not something we ran into. Its hardware and software are cleverly designed. It mostly solves the visible-seam problem that most Android foldables come with. An updated version of the Duo with Face ID support would be just about the best possible version of this form factor, given the limits of battery technology and physics. But for me personally—and for many happy iPhone users—it requires too many compromises to enable features I don’t want badly enough.

Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production

Ars Technica Long form October 20, 2026

Slate’s first showroom sells the promise. Mass production will determine the rest.

As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips.

Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even preorder a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit.

Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is a bare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950. It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Ars went for a ride in a Slate Truck over the summer, but we haven’t had a chance to shop for one. So I stopped by the Slate Experience Center so I could, er, experience the Slate.

Upon walking into the showroom on a Monday morning, the first thing I noticed was a marquee-style sign on the wall boldly and brightly serving as a price tag for the black truck parked in the middle of the showroom. The vibe was industrial-barn-chic-meets-SoHo-loft. Three other people were there, and another shopper entered as I left. One man alternated between sitting in the cab, peering at the truck as he walked around it, and peppering Manager of Customer Experience Steve Purdy with questions.

The showroom has been open since October 15, launching with a three-day event that offered ridealongs. Interest has been strong, Purdy told me, and while he couldn’t provide sales numbers, he said the response has been “incredible.”

“We’re really happy with the number of [$300] deposits we’ve gotten since we opened,” Purdy said.

I was hoping there would be at least two Slate Trucks on site so I could compare build quality between trucks and check things like panel gaps, window operation, and chassis creaks. But only one truck was on display. And it wasn’t close to a production model; rather, the black Slate Truck was a hand-built older prototype with a black wrap (the Slate Truck base color is gray). The bed and passenger sides were cordoned off, but the driver-side door was open so shoppers could hop in and check out the interior.

It was bigger than I expected—to my eye, roughly the size of a Hyundai Santa Cruz. The tailgate was down, and it felt reassuringly sturdy when I pressed down on it. The 5-foot-long (152.4 cm) bed floor looked and felt durable, not much different from any other pickup on the market.

The exterior passed the eye test, with the panels appearing well-fitted. The doors sat flush with the surrounding body panels when closed. Of course, I was looking at a prototype carefully built to be poked and prodded by automotive reporters and the general public, so the level of fit and finish was no surprise. The challenge for Slate will be getting consistent build quality with minimal panel gaps, watertight seals, consistent door-to-fender transitions, and hood/frunk alignment. The Slate assembly line in Warsaw, Indiana, is still making prototyping runs at this point, Purdy told me, and the company is hoping to start on production models “soon.”

I hopped inside the cab once I got the opportunity, and the door closed with a solid-sounding “thunk.” It’s spartan inside, with a small screen for the instrument panel, a phone holder, physical climate controls, and window winders. The seats were both supportive and comfortable, and, after moving my seat, I had ample legroom. While the seat slid back and forth smoothly, the seatback recline lever on the side didn’t work.

Beyond the default Blank Slate body style, Slate offers two SUV options—the Squareback SUV and Fastback SUV—and an open-air kit. I asked Purdy if they were selling any of the SUVs. “Most customers are going with the truck configuration,” he said. “And then they’re customizing their trucks in the Slate Garage.”

Being able to order online and have the truck delivered is a major attraction for those who can’t stand “the kabuki dance of f***ery at a dealership,” as one of my colleagues put it. But if you want to do all that at the Slate Experience Center, staffers will sit down and help you configure your customized Slate. There is a wall with removable dashboard panels across the color spectrum and a couple of miniature models of the cab with tiny, colored panels to help customers decide on the details.

Purdy told me that Slate is staying the course with the $24,950 sticker price. But will customers actually get their Slate Trucks this year as the company promised? “We will ship some trucks by the end of the year,” Purdy said. “Those will go to investors and employees, with early orderers receiving their Slate Trucks in early 2027.

For service, Slate will be using RepairPal. Owners will be able to choose from 4,000 shops, some of which can service the high-voltage electrical systems and others limited to body damage, Purdy said. For scratches or minor dings from fender benders, owners can replace the exterior body panels themselves. Pricing for replacement parts has yet to be finalized. And Slate is confident the plastic body panels will weather climate extremes without a hitch. “We’re a Michigan company,” Purdy reminded me.

Monday morning is not exactly prime time for dealership traffic, but a handful of prospective customers were in the showroom, which is a promising sign. While there is no shortage of electrified pickup trucks on the market, there is a shortage of affordable ones. At $25,000, the Slate Truck costs far less than a Rivian R1T, Tesla Cybertruck, Chevy Silverado EV, or any currently shipping battery-electric truck. It could be a breakout hit—especially if Slate can beat Ford’s sub-$30,000 Fathom pickup to market.

But the sleek-looking showroom and an attractive prototype still face a production reality check. Tesla had significant quality-control problems with early Model Ys, with customers receiving cars with loose seats and broken seatbelts, and some Cybertrucks have shipped with misaligned panel gaps. A new player is entering the game, but production is still on the (near) horizon, and no one knows if the Slate Trucks delivered to customers will live up to the promise of the carefully hand-built prototypes. People are definitely very interested in Slate. Now it’s time to deliver.

Trump wanted to give No Kings no air. Then, Meta suspended its Instagram.

Ars Technica Long form November 03, 2026

Meta faces pressure to protect No Kings Instagram on election day.

Over the weekend, the No Kings Coalition said Meta declined to commit to taking steps to prevent automated systems from suspending one of Instagram’s most prominent pro-democracy accounts if activity surged around the page during the midterm elections.

A demand for action came after Meta apologized for temporarily suspending the No Kings Instagram account and disabling access for four hours at the peak of an early voting push from the group. In a post on X, Meta’s Andy Stone said the account had been using a Claude AI tool in a way that made it appear to be a bot. But even though automated review detected the error within an hour, Stone acknowledged that additional hurdles kept admins locked out. State and federal lawmakers—as well as a coalition of 14 attorneys general—have asked Meta to further explain its actions.

In a letter to No Kings, Meta offered to arrange a meeting with a technical expert who could better explain the mistake. But No Kings rejected the response, saying it failed to address any of the group’s ongoing concerns and requesting a meeting with Meta senior leadership instead. The group stressed that the issue goes beyond its Instagram account, saying that Americans who rely on Meta’s platforms need assurance that voting content won’t be suppressed ahead of or on election day. Among eight questions, the coalition asked Meta to publicly disclose any communications with the Trump administration about the No Kings account or the historic early voting day event.

On October 30, Meta executives met with No Kings. According to the coalition’s account of the meeting, Meta said it has “no plans” to change policies that lead to harmful over-enforcement, a problem that even the independent Oversight Board, which reviews Meta’s content decisions, worries could result in suppression or censorship of No Kings and other pro-democracy content during this critical period.

“Meta acknowledged that it made a mistake, but an apology without action does nothing to ensure that this kind of censorship won’t happen again,” No Kings said, calling Meta’s laissez-faire attitude “unacceptable.”

Ars has found no evidence that the Trump administration asked Meta to restrict the No Kings account or that anyone at Meta intentionally targeted the account for political reasons. Meta told No Kings that it planned to post a public reply to the coalition’s demands, but the company did not respond to Ars’ request for comment, and Stone has yet to post an update on X. His account did, however, apologize for another accidental enforcement action impacting a Republican-controlled account the day before the No Kings meeting. “We automatically removed the @MOSenateGOP Facebook account because our systems mistakenly assessed the account was impersonating another one,” Stone said.

“This was never simply about a technical glitch or one Instagram account,” No Kings’ press release said. “It’s about whether millions of Americans can rely on these platforms to organize, communicate, and access critical voting information without disruption.”

Formed in 2025 after Donald Trump returned to office for a second term, the No Kings Coalition is best known for organizing some of the largest coordinated protests in recent US history. Using social media channels to coordinate nationwide demonstrations against Trump policies viewed as anti-democratic, organizers estimated that more than 5 million people participated in its first protests in June 2025 and say attendance has only increased since. No Kings estimates 7 million people attended the second protests in October 2025, and more than 8 million showed up for the third demonstration last March.

For the fourth event, however, No Kings sought to get more than 9 million people into the streets, and then directly to the polls, by organizing an early voting event on October 17. Unlike the family-friendly protests where Americans held up signs demanding “No Kings in America,” this event focused on driving voter turnout. Although No Kings describes itself as a pro-democracy coalition with no interest in building up the Democratic Party, turnout for its events is driven by those who oppose Trump’s most controversial policies—including domestic ICE enforcement and US military involvement in Iran.

Hundreds of civil rights organizations, including Black Voters Matter and the American Civil Liberties Union, make up the No Kings Coalition. Initially, there was no centralized Instagram account where the groups could coordinate their social media messaging. But as the November 3 election approached, the coalition got more organized, hoping that an official No Kings account with a large following would help it identify and amplify content ahead of the fourth event.

That’s when No Kings decided to use Claude as a “keyword and hashtag search tool to track conversations across social media platforms,” the group’s social media team told Ars.

According to Stone, the Claude tool was “reading profiles, posts, and hashtags,” which “sharply” increased the account’s activity in “intense bursts” that “resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems.”

Ars could not determine what specific Claude-powered tool the coalition was using, how it accessed Instagram, or whether it was an Anthropic service or a third-party integration built using Claude. Ars asked both Anthropic and Meta whether there was anything unusual about the way No Kings was using Claude, but neither company responded.

Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, a progressive nonprofit in the No Kings Coalition, told Ars that the volume of posting increases because organizers understand a basic principle of advertising: “You’ve got to reach people seven different times in seven different ways, and it’s the seventh time that they hear, and they’re like, ‘Oh right, there is an early vote action going on. I should get out there.’”

The high volume shouldn’t matter, though, Levin said, emphasizing that “it seems pretty absurd that a social media company that doesn’t go down during the Super Bowl or during the World Series or during the Oscars shuts our account down during an early vote push.”

“We’re not using any boutique tools that nobody has developed before,” Levin said. “These are all nonprofits. We’re putting things together with popsicle sticks and glue. We’re not developing our own sophisticated apparatus. So there is nothing that I’m aware of that is unique about how we were using the social media platform that day.”

Levin pointed to a series of episodes dating back to at least 2016 that raised questions about Meta’s role in protecting democratic processes. That year, Facebook acknowledged that it sold election-related ads to a shadowy Russian company. More recently, Meta faced questions from Congress in 2021 after turning off election-related safeguards and failing to detect “Stop the Steal” groups from gaming its algorithm to spread disinformation. After Trump’s 2024 election and shortly before his inauguration, Meta announced that it would end its US third-party fact-checking program. Zuckerberg also said Meta would work with Trump to push back against what he characterized as censorship by foreign governments. Critics warned that the move amounted to Meta declaring that “the truth doesn’t matter.”

To Levin, Meta’s playbook for handling controversies like the No Kings Instagram suspension is to lawyer up, offer technical explanations, and issue “empty apologies.”

Levin also pointed to Meta’s decision to donate $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and later $5 million for Trump’s ballroom project, which Levin said were blatant efforts to curry favor with the president.

Given what Levin sees as Zuckerberg’s alignment with Trump, he said it’s difficult for No Kings to accept that a technical glitch, rather than deliberate action by someone at Meta, was behind the suspension. Levin acknowledged that some posts that appear to be suppressed on Meta platforms may simply fail to get traction. But given Meta’s history with election content and its failure to make changes to protect pro-democracy content, he said, it’s difficult for outsiders to not be skeptical.

For example, Levin said Meta never acknowledged that at least one No Kings creator’s account was also suspended on the day the No Kings account was disabled. Other No Kings creators have reported that some Instagram posts seemingly receive no views.

“This is why the history does matter,” Levin said. “The context matters here because if I believed Meta to be a corporation that was operating above-board and was stridently pro-democracy and always erred in the defense of people organizing, I would say, ‘Look, it’s Meta. You know Meta, they wouldn’t do that. Probably there’s something else going on.’ But you would have to not have your head screwed on straight to believe that based on the publicly available information.”

Levin told Ars that one of his biggest remaining questions is whether Meta had any interactions with the Trump administration ahead of the suspension.

To No Kings, the Trump administration had been vocal in its opposition to the protests during the coalition’s first two events. Last October, Trump controversially posted an AI-generated video of a jet labeled “King Trump” flying over protesters while blasting the Kenny Loggins song “Danger Zone.” He has also directly dismissed protesters as an “ineffective” “joke,” echoing comments from others in his administration.

But Trump may have realized that such comments were only drawing more attention to the movement, and there has since been a “notable tactical shift,” Levin suggested. Trump and his supporters now seem to pointedly refuse to discuss No Kings, perhaps hoping to deny the movement oxygen, he said.

“It’s not absurd to think they were also talking to their friends in social media and asking them to not cover this as much or tilt the algorithm a certain way,” Levin said.

Although four hours may not seem like a long time, any disruption that makes it harder for No Kings to reach people has a significant impact, Levin said.

“We are forced to use these platforms that are privately owned in order to reach these folks,” Levin said. “And in using the platforms, we are vulnerable to this kind of pressure, and that directly undermines our ability to reach these people.”

If the same thing happened “in the middle of election day, where pro-democracy accounts are suppressed or shut down,” that could be “cataclysmic,” Levin said.

David Greene, senior counsel for the digital rights group the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), told Ars that the timing of the No Kings Instagram suspension is “suspicious” and that Meta’s technical excuse is “a really incomplete answer.”

As No Kings continues to demand that Meta release any communications with Trump, Meta also faces increased pressure from lawmakers and state officials to make changes to support accounts like No Kings during election day.

Last week, a coalition of 14 state attorneys general sent a letter to Meta demanding a more transparent explanation of the suspension. By October 29, they asked Meta to “detail its plans to ensure that legitimate election activity on Meta platforms is not disrupted.”

“This is particularly concerning given the proliferation of AI agents marketed to consumers, including by Meta, as compatible with social media accounts,” the attorneys general wrote.

Ars could not confirm whether the coalition’s deadline was met, but the attorneys general weren’t alone in expressing concern that Meta may be “unable to differentiate between legitimate political activity and bot activity that harms users” in the age of AI.

Democratic Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen sent a similar request, The New Republic reported, specifically asking why it took so long for Meta to help admins regain access. In Congress, Robert Garcia and Jamie Raskin, members of the House Oversight Committee and House Judiciary Committee, also probed Meta for answers. Levin noted that these lawmakers could become future chairs of those committees if the elections swing No Kings’ way.

In Levin’s ideal world, “the next Congress” would “take a very different approach” to regulating the tech industry. He believes that could have significant consequences ahead of the next presidential election. Rather than seeing tech CEOs aligned with the executive branch, there could finally be a more “healthy” public debate, where “different presidential candidates” may adopt “different positions of their orientation towards Silicon Valley,” Levin said.

Greene suggested that Meta could take steps such as requiring human review of election-related content or creating emergency support channels to quickly address automated throttling, inadvertent suspensions, or content removals.

Although Meta has no legal obligation to do so, Greene said, “they certainly have an obligation to their users to anticipate these things and to be ready for them.”

Greene told Ars that he agreed with Meta’s Oversight Board, which directed Meta to take proactive steps to protect election-related content rather than simply waiting to fix problems after an account is automatically suspended. One possible solution, Greene suggested, would be a notification system allowing No Kings to notify Meta when major events are planned so the company can prepare.

“Clearly if it was a technical problem, it’s a technical problem that should have been expected and thought about ahead of time and anticipated and addressed ahead of time,” Greene said. “The No Kings stuff was not secret in any way.”

Like Levin, Greene pointed to Meta’s history of mishandling election content, not just in the US but around the world. Levin noted that No Kings worked with election organizers in Brazil, where Meta also recently faced allegations of electoral interference.

“These are technical glitches that happen around elections all the time, and Meta just needs to have an affirmative plan for this and not just try to respond as they happen,” Greene said. “And I think until they do that, they’re not going to dispel suspicion that things are politically motivated.”

The EFF believes the Trump administration should disclose all its communications with Meta, but so far neither side is clarifying whether Trump may be influencing how Meta handles election-related content, Greene said.

Greene said it’s difficult to determine whether Meta was engaged in “jawboning,” with the Trump administration pressuring the platform to silence dissidents. However, “the explanation they’ve given is so inadequate that it’s hard to discount the [idea] that there was political influence,” he said.

And he agreed that a four-hour admin lockout was too long.

“Because as we know, when you’re organizing a protest, even if you shorten this to a three-minute delay from a three-hour delay, that could be consequential,” Greene said. “And so, the idea is to avoid these things in the first place.”

Kate Ruane, director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s Free Expression Project, told Ars that Meta must explain not only why its automated systems flagged accounts like the No Kings Instagram account but also why the “mistake prevention systems” it designed to avoid such situations “were not triggered in this circumstance.”

Ruane noted that the CDT supports the JAWBONE Act, which “would require the government to be transparent with the public about communications from the government to online speech intermediaries related to the constitutionally protected speech they distribute.” If the next Congress passes that law, Meta could face greater scrutiny if questions about the No Kings suspension remain unanswered. Levin suggested that “a pro-democracy Congress” would send subpoenas, hold hearings, and use legislative processes to hold Meta accountable.

“Large-scale political speech events are frequently organized using Meta’s services,” Ruane said. “It is critical for users engaged in those activities to understand exactly what happened and how they and Meta can avoid it in the future.”

SpaceX no longer needs NASA, and that’s a problem for America’s space agency

Ars Technica Long form October 29, 2026

“NASA desperately needs SpaceX, and SpaceX knows it, and Elon knows it.”

For nearly a quarter of a century, Elon Musk and his essential partner at SpaceX, Gwynne Shotwell, viewed the United States government as El Dorado, the mythical city of gold.

Like machete-wielding treasure hunters, Musk and Shotwell hacked through a tangled jungle filled with lurking carnivores such as Boeing and Lockheed Martin, as well as bean counters and regulators. Over time, against long odds, the pair cleared a path for SpaceX to contracts at NASA and the US military. They sued when things did not go their way. They hollered about unfair playing fields. Most importantly, they delivered quality space products to the US government for less.

And so, after a while, SpaceX found El Dorado and a city of contracts.

Then they started winning everything. So much so that the relationship between the customer and contractor began to change. Slowly at first, but ever more quickly, SpaceX went from needing the US government as an indispensable customer to becoming an indispensable contractor for the nation.

The pendulum has swung so far now that SpaceX seems increasingly disinterested in the US government for most contracts outside of data services, such as Starshield for military communications and observations.

“I guess I am still in denial that there is a divorce pending,” said Lori Garver, a deputy NASA administrator during the Obama White House years who was instrumental in expanding the agency’s use of commercial contracts with companies like SpaceX. “I literally cannot wrap my head around a future yet where SpaceX stops flying Dragon and Falcon. Not yet.”

But the signs point to at least a partial breakup. Consider the following data points:

To be clear, SpaceX is still fulfilling its existing contracts with NASA, the US Space Force, and other government entities. And it continues to do so at a lower cost and generally higher level of reliability than pretty much anyone else.

But the company is no longer signing many large new contracts for spaceflight services, at least in the traditional launch and in-space flight domains. The shift comes after 15 years in which the US government has grown accustomed to lower costs and rapid innovation that has revitalized the nation’s access to space.

For SpaceX and its shareholders, as shocking as it may seem for a US company to leave billions of dollars on the table in government contracts, this may be the right decision. SpaceX sees the vast bulk of its future revenue coming from artificial intelligence. However, SpaceX’s retreat from the public square comes as both NASA and the Space Force confront growing challenges from a rising space program in China and an aging but still dangerous Russia in space.

So what does it mean if the halcyon days of SpaceX riding to the rescue for America in space—such as in the saga of Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams—seem to be ending?

In the early days, Musk and Shotwell sought revenue from various sources as SpaceX developed the scrappy Falcon 1 rocket. But it was NASA that stepped in at two crucial moments in the company’s first decade.

The first came in 2006, with a $278 million award to develop a cargo delivery spacecraft for the International Space Station. It helped SpaceX expand rapidly when it was struggling to develop the Falcon 1 rocket. An even more consequential award arrived in December 2008, $1.6 billion for a dozen Dragon cargo flights to the space station. The funding arrived as SpaceX struggled to meet payroll. Both Musk and Shotwell have said this award probably saved SpaceX from bankruptcy.

NASA and SpaceX then fell into an increasingly warm and mutually beneficial relationship. During the last two decades, NASA has awarded contracts to SpaceX worth approximately $20 billion, and Musk has been deeply appreciative. In 2017, he revealed that the online password for some of his accounts was “ILoveNASA.” In return, NASA got reliable cargo, eventually crew services into low-Earth orbit, and a revolution in US spaceflight capabilities.

Musk and Shotwell fought to extend their relationship with the federal government in the mid-2010s. In 2014, they filed a lawsuit against the US Air Force for the right to bid for national security launch contracts. Musk contended that United Launch Alliance had a monopoly and said SpaceX should be eligible to bid. “We’re just protesting and saying these launches should be competed,” he said at the time. “And if we compete and lose, that’s fine, but why were they not even competed?”

The effort proved successful. SpaceX won national security contracts, and launch costs for the military plunged. Over time, SpaceX became the dominant player. Even today, with United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin struggling to bring their large Vulcan and New Glenn rockets into service, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets have become a single-point failure for national security launches. If the US military needed to get a dozen large satellites into orbit during the next 12 to 18 months, there is only one company that could credibly pull that off.

The bottom line is that SpaceX, far more often than any other competitor over the last 15 years, delivered spaceflight services to the US government when other contractors were late or overbudget or simply failed. That no other commercial space company has risen alongside SpaceX during this period is a problem. NASA, certainly, sought to support competitors such as Blue Origin, Sierra Space, Rocket Lab, Orbital Sciences, Boeing, and others. The US military supported development of United Launch Alliance’s rocket with $2 billion in funding as an alternative to Falcon.

And still, none have yet come remotely close to matching what SpaceX has done in launch, spacecraft, and in-space data services.

The relationship dynamic began to change about half a decade ago.

At the height of the pandemic, in mid-2020, SpaceX delivered a huge win for NASA by safely flying astronauts Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken to the space station. It is difficult to overstate the importance of this achievement for NASA. Since 2011, the space agency had swallowed its pride and gone, hat in hand, to Russia for transportation to the space station. Its astronauts spent months in Russia learning the language and training to ride the Soyuz spacecraft into orbit. With a single successful 64-day mission, SpaceX ended all of that.

Less than a year later, NASA again turned to SpaceX. The space agency needed a Moon lander. But Congress had only appropriated beer money for a champagne project. NASA had three options for a privately developed lunar lander. None were ideal. SpaceX’s $2.89 billion proposal to develop Starship as a lunar lander and fly two missions was the only bid that fit NASA’s budget profile. Yes, Starship presented a complicated, oversized, and technically demanding solution. But in 2021, SpaceX was NASA’s only spaceflight contractor consistently delivering big results.

Almost overnight, then, NASA’s two most important and costly programs, the Artemis Program to land humans on the Moon and the International Space Station, became utterly dependent on SpaceX.

This power imbalance continued to grow, breaking into wider public view in June 2025 amid a temporary falling out between Musk and the president he helped elect. After Trump threatened to “terminate” SpaceX’s governmental contracts and subsidies, Musk’s response was essentially so what? In return, Musk threatened to decommission the Dragon spacecraft. He knew—correctly, it turns out—that SpaceX’s role in US government space programs could not be easily replaced. A Pentagon review in July 2025 found most of the company’s contracts with the US Department of Defense were essential.

Trump could still have hurt Musk’s businesses through regulatory review, particularly with the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Aviation Administration. And the two made up. But one indisputable takeaway from this brouhaha is that the US government now needed SpaceX more than SpaceX needed the US government.

“The dust-up with President Trump, when Musk threatened to take away Dragon, was utterly irresponsible,” said Chris Davenport, a professor at Arizona State University and author of Rocket Dreams. “If Falcon and Dragon go away, that is a huge disservice to the US government. NASA desperately needs SpaceX, and SpaceX knows it, and Elon knows it.”

This represented a truly remarkable shift for everyone who watched SpaceX fight so hard, for so long, to get its foot in the door at NASA and the Space Force. But as jarring as it is, this shift is no longer deniable.

Around the time of his dispute with Trump, Musk came to fully believe that artificial intelligence was not just the next big thing. Rather, it was the industrial revolution of his lifetime. He began vectoring his two biggest companies, Tesla and SpaceX, toward dominating AI software, AI hardware, and computing power on the ground and in space to run it all.

This largely explains SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI and its subsequent IPO. It is also behind the potential merger of SpaceX and Tesla. This will give Musk more direct control over Tesla, something he values. But more critically, it gives him an immense pool of assets to deploy toward building data centers terrestrially and in space, autonomous vehicles, robots, massive rockets, and more.

No other company on Earth has the potential, at least in the near term, to own an entire stack of artificial intelligence. Elon Musk wants to manufacture the chips and electricity infrastructure for data centers, he wants to build the data centers that will power the AI revolution, he wants to develop and train the AI models that will provide its intelligence, and he wants to build physical products that he believes will become the shaping force of the 21st century.

He wants it all.

Such a future, in his mind, does not include a dead-end technology like the Dragon spacecraft—even though Dragon is the only reliable way to get humans into space outside of China and Russia, and only took flight with humans six years ago. He does not want to fly the partially reusable Falcon 9 rocket—even though it is the best, cheapest, and only Western vehicle capable of expanding to meet the growing demand from government and commercial customers for access to space right now.

Musk believes the government moves too slowly and simply isn’t ambitious enough when it comes to space. Often, in meetings at SpaceX, he will describe working with the US government as “like wearing lead shoes and walking through molasses.”

Instead, Musk wants to build bigger things, like Starship. He wants to move fast and break things when necessary. This explains why he has invested something like $15 billion in the development of the Starship rocket, from its engines to a growing number of launch sites in Texas and Florida, to get the massive, fully reusable vehicle off the ground.

For a time, this looked like a win-win situation for the US government and a growing commercial space industry counting on frequent, low-cost access to space. NASA built its Artemis Program around Starships landing on the Moon. The commercial space industry looked forward to abundant, cheap launches. The general sense was that pulling Dragon and Falcon 9 off the market would cause temporary upheaval, but these problems would soon be ameliorated by Starship and its promise of lower cost and even greater capability.

That was the hope, at least.

In March 2020, SpaceX published its first “Starship Users Guide,” which included a 9-meter payload fairing with a “clamshell” structure that would open once in space to deploy payloads. The company said it would support Falcon-compatible payload adapters.

But in recent years, there has been little evidence that SpaceX is actually developing such a deployment mechanism. Rather, the company has implemented a Pez-like dispenser that releases flattish satellites from a narrow door in the middle of the Starship vehicle. This serves SpaceX’s internal payloads of Starlink and future Starmind (data center) satellites. But it’s unsuitable for deploying more traditional satellites or big NASA payloads, such as large space telescopes.

Multiple people Ars spoke with for this story said it would be incredibly beneficial if SpaceX publicly committed to developing a large payload door and provided a timeline for its readiness. Ars offered SpaceX the opportunity to make such a commitment, but the company didn’t take it.

And it doesn’t have to. The reality is straightforward. This year’s IPO gave SpaceX a laser-like focus on its core business plan. Reaching stratospheric financial targets requires launching incredible numbers of Starlink and Starmind satellites, all of which can be dispensed like Pez candy into space. Launch services for third parties, which include NASA and other Moon Base customers, represent a rounding error in SpaceX’s revenue in the post-IPO world.

In its recent third-quarter 10-Q financial filing, the company references these launch priorities for Starlink and artificial intelligence: “We allocate a significant amount of launch capacity to our Connectivity segment and expect to allocate a significant amount to our SI segment in the future.”

An argument often made about SpaceX’s decision to end the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rocket is that these programs—which operate with unprecedented efficiency in the history of launch—consume valuable engineering time. This talented team pushed Falcon 9 above 150 launches a year and helped make SpaceX globally dominant. Musk has said he would like to redirect these talented engineers to bring similar launch-operation efficiency to the Starship program.

Great engineers are certainly a finite resource. And SpaceX faces fierce competition in the US space industry for talented engineers, with higher salaries offered by Blue Origin, and attractive alternatives such as Stoke Space, Rocket Lab, Firefly, and Relativity Space all recruiting.

The question is whether Musk would devote his Falcon engineering team solely to Starship. Perhaps not. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call in October, Musk made a striking comment while musing about how the company aimed to deploy 10 GW of compute (on Earth) in 2027.

“What we’ve done at SpaceX is we’ve taken a team that has been able to achieve a market share in mass to orbit that is almost 90 percent,” Musk said. That team, he added, “has been able to achieve results that are an order of magnitude greater than the rest of all competitors in space combined.” Now, he said, SpaceX was applying that same team to the deployment of terrestrial compute. They would not be sent to Starbase for Starship, in other words, but to places like Memphis, Tennessee.

“This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League,” Musk said. “It’s not fair. But the net result is being able to deploy power, cooling, and infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than anyone else and may at some point be faster than everyone else combined.”

So yeah.

SpaceX can do what it wants. But there are consequences, and some people at NASA are starting to wonder how serious SpaceX is about the Human Landing System contract it won from NASA in 2021. Landing on the Moon is wholly tangential to the company’s near-term AI future, and fulfilling the contract will almost certainly be a net negative from a financial perspective.

SpaceX, of course, says it is working assiduously on a lunar lander. And publicly, NASA officials say the company is a good partner. In an interview with Ars last week, the manager of the Artemis Program for NASA, Jeremy Parsons, said he regularly visits SpaceX facilities in Hawthorne, California, and Starbase, Texas. “Their management team is definitely committed to the lunar missions,” he said. Parsons credited the SpaceX engineers working on Starship as “some of the smartest individuals” he had ever met.

No one I have spoken to at NASA, both on and off the record, says SpaceX has given them a reason to believe the company will not eventually meet its Human Landing System commitments. And to date, SpaceX has had a remarkably good track record of delivering for NASA on its contracts. Nevertheless, the road ahead may be rocky in an era when SpaceX is pulling back from government involvement.

SpaceX has consistently told NASA it must get Starship flying orbital missions regularly. It has to get to full reusability, or nothing else matters. It has to do propellant transfer. All of that must come before finalizing the lander. And sure, it’s totally fair to say that the most important thing SpaceX can do for NASA right now is getting Starship to a very high flight rate. In SpaceX’s view, in a few years, Starship will be flying so often—the company recently told the Federal Aviation Administration it plans to launch 10,000 Starships a year by the 2030s—that fueling depots for missions to the Moon and Mars will be trivial.

Such a launch cadence surely would change everything, but nothing in aerospace ever happens as fast as one thinks or wants. And for now, the real issue is just how committed SpaceX is to the lander project and NASA’s competition with China. At SpaceX, projects deemed most important by leadership get the most resources. That is, the best engineers, the most software support, the most funding, and so on. Those projects are currently things like Starmind, the Colossus data center project in Memphis, and Starship engineering. It’s not the Human Landing System, multiple sources told Ars.

As SpaceX has struggled through the Starship test flight program, NASA has been waiting for an in-space fueling test, which has slipped its schedule many times. Testing propellant transfer and storage at a large scale is critical, and it has never been done in space. Successfully completing this test would reduce much of the risk for the kinds of refueling operations needed to send a fully loaded Starship to the Moon.

The latest target for such a test is “early” 2027, according to NASA and SpaceX. But this date seems aspirational. According to Parsons, the test requires one Starship to launch from Starbase in Texas and another to launch from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Starship has not yet flown from there. Presently, a debut Florida launch is not expected until at least January. According to Parsons, the in-orbit fueling test is the third launch planned from Florida.

Once SpaceX demonstrates in-orbit refueling, it could begin planning a campaign to send an uncrewed Starship to land on the Moon as a demonstration. How many tanker launches would this take? The internal estimate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center is “about 22” Starship launches, Ars reported last week. Musk followed that up by saying the actual number “will be more like 6 to 8.”

So what’s the truth? In the near term, given Starship’s lift capacity, a lunar landing will probably require about 20 launches, which is the most current publicly disclosed government planning figure. With improvements to Starship and Raptor engine performance, and as SpaceX gets a better handle on in-space refueling operations, that number will assuredly come down. So at some point in the future, it could be as low as six. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman appeared to confirm this last week when he characterized Musk’s estimate of six to eight refueling flights as the “ultimate potential end state” of Starship.

Unfortunately, to beat China back to the Moon by 2030, NASA can’t wait for Starship to reach its final form. If SpaceX were to fly a lunar demonstration in the next year or two, a necessary precursor to human landings, it probably would take something like 20 Starship launches. Starship has flown 14 times in the last three and a half years. Its flight rate will undoubtedly accelerate in the coming months, but even at a weekly launch cadence, fueling a Starship for a lunar landing would still require more than four months of dedicated launches.

Frankly, it’s difficult to envision SpaceX dedicating 20 Starships to a NASA mission anytime soon. The opportunity cost is enormous. Those same rockets could launch hundreds of revenue-generating Starlink V3 satellites into orbit. A single Starlink launch on Starship delivers the same amount of bandwidth as 10 Falcon 9 launches—bandwidth SpaceX can sell to customers for years to come. And as SpaceX expands into artificial intelligence, the company has even greater incentives to reserve Starship’s capacity for its own growing constellation of satellites.

And then there’s the financial burden. Let’s assume an unoptimized launch cost of $100 million for early Starship flights—still a phenomenally low number for a super heavy lift vehicle. At that price, a lunar landing campaign requiring 20 launches would cost approximately $2 billion in launch expenses alone. Recall that SpaceX’s original Human Landing System contract was valued at $2.89 billion and included both an uncrewed demo and crewed landing.

The actual cost of a single lunar landing mission remains uncertain, and some of the investments needed to fulfill the contract will benefit Starship more broadly. But the larger point is clear: NASA is asking SpaceX to devote substantial resources to a program that offers comparatively little financial upside at a time when the company’s own commercial ambitions are growing exponentially.

Imagine a world where SpaceX had gone all in on developing a lunar lander. Would the company be taking a different approach to the immense technical challenges of getting Starship to the Moon, perhaps with a stubby Starship variant? Would it be devoting more of its best engineers to the program? Would it consider using an expendable tanker Starship to reduce the total needed?

SpaceX very well might still get to the Moon in the next five years, and the company has enormous technical capacity. Its history suggests that when Musk makes something an overriding priority, things happen quickly. All it would take for SpaceX to go full throttle on a lunar Starship would be for Musk to text a technical leader at the company something like, “Do HLS.”

Last year, Ars asked Musk if it mattered to him that China gets back to the Moon before NASA with the Artemis Program.

“I think the United States should be aiming for Mars, because we’ve already actually been to the Moon several times,” he replied. “Yeah, if China sort of equals that, I’m like, OK, sure, but that’s something that America did 56 years ago.”

In November of last year, Ars posed a similar question to Blue Origin’s chief executive, Dave Limp. “We just want to help the US get to the Moon,” he said. “If NASA wants to go quicker, we would move heaven and Earth, pun intended, to try to get to the Moon sooner.”

Multiple NASA sources said Blue really is doing whatever it takes to help NASA and that what once appeared as a rocky relationship is now flourishing.

After SpaceX won a sole-source contract for the Human Landing System in 2021, Blue Origin sued NASA. This pressure, along with NASA’s desire for a second provider, led Congress to eventually add funding for a second lander. As with Starship, Blue Origin’s original design under this new contract also involved refueling operations in low-Earth orbit for the large Blue Moon Mark 2 vehicle.

As it became increasingly clear that China was on course to land humans on the Moon by or before 2030, Blue Origin’s large and ambitious Blue Moon lander did not serve NASA’s more immediate needs. It would take too long.

In 2025, Ars was first to report that Blue Origin might be able to develop a lunar landing system that involved a smaller version of the Blue Moon Mark 2 vehicle and multiple transfer stages based on the existing Mark 1 lander. This involved a significant redesign to the Blue Moon program, but critically, it removed the need for in-space refueling. Eventually, this became the new plan. Blue Origin, without any guarantee of new funding, changed its design when NASA needed something faster.

“I will tell you, they are absolutely fantastic partners,” Parsons, NASA’s Artemis manager, said of Blue Origin. “They have leaned forward at every step, and they are all in on the mission.”

NASA’s upcoming Artemis III mission is illustrative of the differences.

The mission is intended to test both Blue Origin and SpaceX’s lunar landers in space. Blue Origin is building a special “test” version of its Blue Moon lander to demonstrate a host of capabilities for NASA. After docking, the crew will exit the Orion spacecraft and spend time aboard the Blue Moon vehicle. By contrast, SpaceX is pulling a “ship off the line” of its Starship program for the flight. Orion will rendezvous and dock with Starship, but there will be no ingress into the vehicle and hence no life support equipment.

Earlier this year, NASA revealed a major new initiative to develop a Moon Base. Not long after, New Glenn exploded on its launch pad. In the aftermath, Blue Origin has moved with uncharacteristic speed to repair its launch pad to get New Glenn flying again, while investing $3 billion in Florida facilities to support a much higher launch cadence.

This matters because New Glenn is superseding Starship as the essential rocket powering NASA’s lunar ambitions.

Beyond the Human Landing System, there are myriad robotic elements of the Moon Base that need to get to the surface, and NASA has contracted with a host of US space companies to develop smaller cargo landers. Some of these providers are growing nervous about launch. At least two of these companies had “rough order of magnitude” estimates and other types of launch agreements with SpaceX for Falcon 9s to deliver elements of NASA’s Moon base later this decade. But in the last several weeks, SpaceX, the only company that can offer reliable launch dates, has told them it will no longer sell rides to the Moon.

This has sent shockwaves through the Artemis community. It is not the behavior of a partner being broadly supportive of NASA’s lunar efforts. These smaller lander companies now must hope that New Glenn can pick up the slack or a company like Relativity Space can bring its Terran R rocket to readiness quickly.

Ars pressed Parsons on how committed SpaceX really was to NASA’s lunar activities. For example, did he really believe SpaceX would be willing to sideline its profitable Starlink and Starmind launches for the extended period to support an Artemis landing? “It’s a fair question, especially as they have gone public,” he acknowledged.

For more than a decade, NASA more or less turned its spaceflight fortunes over to one billionaire. That partnership now appears to be unraveling, and there seems to be a growing sense that if the space agency is to achieve its considerable lunar ambitions in the next decade, it may need another billionaire to bail it out.

“This could end up being a very big opportunity for Blue Origin and Jeff Bezos, who would absolutely relish the role of coming to the country in its time of need,” said Davenport, the author who has written about the rocket billionaires. “Bezos has been public in saying he wanted to serve his country, particularly if it meant in doing it instead of SpaceX and Elon.”

Bezos, of course, is not doing this out of the goodness of his heart or because he bleeds red, white, and blue. He stands to gain Artemis customers, national security launch contracts, and commercial business. He is chasing SpaceX’s enormous valuation with his own space company. But no one thinks Bezos would pull his rockets off the market if NASA were desperate to get to the Moon.

The real question is whether Blue Origin can succeed. The company has a long, long list of things to achieve to make Artemis a reality, from rockets to landers to in-space operations. And for all the many billions of dollars Bezos has invested, Blue Origin has a short track record of execution. It has only ever launched three orbital missions.

Now it is being called on to spearhead the landing of humans on the Moon. On a rocket that recently blew up. Aboard a lander that doesn’t yet exist. At the 11th hour.
