Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

BBC News Thu, 05 Nov 2026 03:47:56 GMT

Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.

In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.

But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.

Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.

Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.

It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.

"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."

Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.

That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.

Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."

The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.

The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.

Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.

It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.

Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.

The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.

The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).

Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.

Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

Would you take a test to see if your life will be cut short? I did - and it changed me

BBC News Thu, 05 Nov 2026 00:32:09 GMT

If you could find out if you had a gene that would cut your life short, would you?

This is the dilemma Laura Sides faced when she was offered a test for the rare form of early onset dementia that her dad was diagnosed with in his 40s.

Laura spoke to Dr Sian Williams, host of BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, about her decision to take the test and how it has shaped the rest of her life.

Growing up, Laura says she always felt close to her dad as they had a "similar nature". He was a GP and "the most amazing doting father," she says. When his Alzheimer's symptoms became more severe, Laura dropped out of university to care for him.

"We did have a really lovely time," she says, remembering trips to a lighthouse and collecting coasters. "I'd run him baths and just play music and pour jugs of hot water over his head and he loved it."

It was at a hospital appointment with her dad when a doctor told Laura she had a 50/50 chance of developing the same type of early onset Alzheimer's known as the "London variant".

"All I could think was, that's a toss of a coin," she says. "I was still so involved with what was going on with him [her dad]. I just pushed it really, really deep down."

Laura's dad died in 2009, just a year after her mum had died.

"All of a sudden I got such an overwhelming urge to leave," she says. So she booked a solo around-the-world trip, eventually settling in Melbourne, Australia.

It was there that thoughts of inheriting her dad's condition "started creeping in" and she went to see a specialist in 2013.

He told her a test could determine with 99.999% certainty if she would inherit early onset dementia. If she had the gene, her expected age of decline would be 46 to 48, he said.

"I just thought, I'm not there yet. I don't want to do that."

As Laura entered her 30s she found herself thinking about the test more and more and decided she wanted to know. But first, she had to undergo six months of genetic counselling.

"There's not many realms in life where you find out your fate and it can be very difficult information to process," she says.

After a six-week wait for the test results to come through, the day finally arrived. Laura says she felt "extremely nervous".

She had booked a table for lunch with a friend afterwards - but went into the appointment alone.

"I said, 'Let's cut straight to it.' They said, 'We're really sorry, it's not good news, and you have inherited the gene.'"

She remembers "almost a white blurry noise of just sitting there".

"I came out of that room and my friend burst into hysterical tears." But Laura didn't react. "We went for our lunch and it was lovely. I don't know if it'd sunk in."

The reality hit later. "I was angry. I felt it was so unjust. I was just too confused at how I was meant to live now. How do you live with that knowledge?"

Laura began to feel a pull back home to the UK, especially as her sister was pregnant. "It doesn't make sense... to live on the other side of the world when she's going to have a baby."

However, her around-the-world travels continued as she took part in medical trials before and after her diagnosis.

"It felt like such a positive to be involved in something out of such a negative situation."

Laura is now 43 - three years away from the age doctors predicted she will begin to notice symptoms.

"I keep waiting for something to sort of hit home. I guess one day I'll start declining but that doesn't keep me up at night."

She is "grateful and so lucky for the people in her life". But meeting anyone new is hard.

"Do I tell them? Do I not tell them? At what point do I tell them?

"And more often than not, when I have told them, it ends."

However she says she has been "proven wrong".

"I have been shown I can be loved despite this. It fills my heart with reassurance and joy".

Laura says she had always "naively assumed" she would be a mother.

"[Its] one of the very few things that I never questioned that I'd be good at and I wanted to do. That's hard... but it doesn't make sense to do it. It wouldn't be fair."

For Laura, life is now about tapping in to things that "make her happy".

"It's not about huge aspirations. It's not like I want to see the Grand Canyon... I want to have time now around the people that I adore and make me feel safe.

"I love nature. I love being outside. I'm obsessed with being submerged in water. It sounds so corny, but... I believe it really is actually the little things are the big things.

"I hope I just have a wonderful few years in this world... drinking champagne and eating oysters - two of my favourite things."

If you or someone you know has been affected by dementia, you can access support from the BBC Action Line.

Toothbrush that emits electricity may more effectively prevent gum disease

New Scientist November 04, 2026

A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes. When put to the test, it led to more than twice the reduction of plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding as conventional toothbrushes.

“The concept is great,” says Nicholas Jakubovics at Newcastle University, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.”

How regrowing your own teeth could replace dentures and implants

Oral diseases, such as tooth decay, affect nearly half the global population. Brushing regularly can help remove plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria that forms on teeth. These bacteria can produce acids that cause cavities and irritate gums, sometimes leading to tooth loss.

Advertisement

But even thorough brushing can leave behind bacteria deep in plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to grow back within hours. Researchers have previously developed toothbrushes with antibacterial metal nanoparticles, including silver and zinc, embedded in their bristles, although their long-term effectiveness is uncertain. Others have designed ionic toothbrushes that use electric currents to help loosen plaque, but they are dependent on batteries.

Now, Yanhui Lu at Peking University in China and her colleagues have turned to studies showing that so-called piezoelectric materials fight bacteria in infected wounds and medical implants. These generate electric charges under pressure, prompting Lu’s team to develop toothbrush bristles made from piezoelectric plastic.

Free newsletter

The idea was that, as the bristles bend during brushing, they would generate electricity, triggering chemical reactions that produce molecules called reactive-oxygen species that damage bacteria, while the bristles physically remove plaque.

The researchers made two sets of bristles of different thicknesses, both of which met Chinese national standards for softness and strength. Laboratory tests confirmed the bristles generated electricity under pressure, particularly the thicker ones. The team also detected reactive-oxygen species on the brushes, which remained soft and retained their electrical properties after three months of use.

Next, the researchers exposed two common oral bacteria to their bristles and nylon ones, which are used in standard toothbrushes, in laboratory experiments, including simulated brushing movements. The thicker piezoelectric bristles were particularly effective, killing about 53 per cent of Streptococcus mutans, which causes cavities, and 78 per cent of Porphyromonas gingivalis, which contributes to gum disease, compared with just 9 and 8 per cent, respectively, for nylon bristles.

The team also grew plaque from human mouths on pieces of cow enamel and brushed them for 3 minutes. The new toothbrushes removed more than 99 per cent of the plaque, compared with about 80 per cent for conventional nylon brushes.

Finally, the team tested the toothbrushes in 109 adults with dental plaque and gum inflammation, who were randomly assigned to use either a piezoelectric or nylon toothbrush twice daily for three months. Dental examinations revealed reductions of roughly 40 per cent in plaque build-up, gum inflammation and bleeding among those using the piezoelectric brushes, compared with around 15 per cent for those using conventional brushes.

Genetic sequencing of the dental plaque from the piezoelectric group also revealed a decline in the relative abundance of harmful bacteria and an increase in some potentially beneficial bacteria.

Larger studies now need to establish whether the toothbrush actually prevents issues like cavities and tooth loss, says Jakubovics.

The economic benefits of the covid vaccines may be double what we thought

New Scientist November 05, 2026

The covid-19 vaccines may have provided health and economic benefits worth up to $64.3 trillion in the first year alone – almost double an earlier estimate. Previously, researchers calculated that the $79.4 billion invested in developing covid-19 vaccines saw a return of between $4.8 trillion and $37.9 trillion globally in the first 12 months after their rollout. But now, a reanalysis of the data suggests it is actually between $6.43 trillion and $64.3 trillion.

This means that for every $1 spent on the vaccines’ development, between $59.70 and $809 was gained in that year. “It is great to finally see this research published to demonstrate the enormous health and financial benefits gained from covid-19 vaccines, in comparison to the costs that went into their development and delivery,” says Hallie Benjamin at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.

Does each new covid-19 variant pose a significant threat?

The $6.43 trillion figure is based on a cost-effectiveness analysis that is generally used in the health sector and factors in quality of life, while the $64.3 trillion figure is based on a cost-benefit analysis used in the public sector.

Advertisement

Both include data from 173 countries on averted hospitalisations, productivity losses and lives saved. For instance, one of the estimates Benjamin and her colleagues used came from modelling that suggested the vaccines prevented 14 million to 20 million deaths in their first year.

The initial $4.8 trillion and $37.9 trillion figures were released when the research was in a preprint stage, before it had been peer-reviewed. “We made many changes throughout the peer-review process that strengthened the quality of our findings,” says Benjamin.

The researchers originally used the Value of Statistical Life Years, which considers how many years a person would be likely to live because of the vaccine, a figure that would be lower if someone was older. As part of the peer-review process, they were advised to use the Value of Statistical Life. Team member Mark Jit at New York University says this treats life spans more equally and is aligned with recommendations for valuing mortality-risk reductions.

Free newsletter

The cost-benefit analysis figure also increased significantly due to a change from calculating the economic value of avoiding a death, says Jit.

But the returns weren’t equally distributed. The researchers found that the vaccines had the highest returns in richer countries. This was probably because poorer countries accessed them later, so fewer lives were saved and fewer productivity and healthcare costs were averted, says Jit. The results are “a message about the need for being able to distribute the vaccines fairly to the people most in need around the world”, he says.

Getting covid-19 for the first time slightly increased the risk of heart inflammation, blood clots and bleeding disorders among children, whereas being vaccinated against the virus was much safer and sometimes protective

Richard Carpiano at the University of California, Riverside, says we already knew the covid-19 vaccines were a “life-saving success”, but this study reinforces that “protecting the public’s health is protecting the economy”.

This challenges the “black-and-white” thinking during the covid-19 pandemic on the trade-off between protecting public health through lockdowns and protecting the economy, says Carpiano.

He also hopes these understandings will be used for future infectious outbreaks, or pandemics. “We are in a historical period that has been labelled as ‘a new pandemic age’,” says Carpiano. “The probability of another pandemic in the next 10 years is significant, as are the chances of smaller regional disease outbreaks from existing or new pathogens.” This analysis is “fundamental” to informing policy-making decisions, he says.

Tomb in Siberia reveals humans were using cannabis 2800 years ago

New Scientist November 05, 2026

A hair found in a 2800-year-old tomb in Siberia has yielded the earliest definitive evidence of cannabis being used as a psychoactive drug. But the history of such use is likely to go back much further.

Genomic studies suggest that the domestication of cannabis plants (Cannabis sativa) was happening in China about 12,000 years ago, with people potentially exploiting it for oil and hemp fibre. Archaeological sites with artefacts made from hemp dating to 7500 years ago have been found in China and Japan. The earliest firm evidence of the plant’s use as a drug had been chemical traces on wooden braziers in China that implied humans were “smoking” cannabis 2500 years ago as part of funeral rites.

How a surge in ancient plagues 5000 years ago shaped humanity

Now, Gino Caspari at the University of Bern in Switzerland and his colleagues have pushed the date back another 300 years with a find at the Tunnug 1 burial mound in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia.

Advertisement

The royal burial mound dates to the time of the Scythians, nomads renowned for their military skills and horseback archery who spread across a huge swathe of Eurasia.

In an excavation trench at the centre of the mound, Caspari and his colleagues recovered almost 1000 whole cannabis seeds. Radiocarbon dating indicated that they were deposited around the start of the 8th century BC, some 2800 years ago.

Subscriber-only newsletter

They also found a preserved human hair dating to the same time, and chemical analysis of it detected cannabinol, a compound produced when THC, the psychoactive compound found in cannabis, oxidises, alongside chemical signatures of THC itself, so the person is likely to have felt psychoactive effects.

“It’s not often as an archaeologist that you get to drug test a person who has been dead for almost 3000 years,” says Caspari.

He says we can’t say how the person consumed the drug – it might have been smoked or the seeds could have just been ingested.

Given its presence in the burial mound, Caspari says the use of cannabis was probably related to a ritual funerary process. That could have been for a religious high, but he suggests there might have been a more sinister use.

Claims that a small-brained hominin called Homo naledi buried its dead raise intriguing questions about ancient minds and why we engage in this peculiar practice

The burial mound also contains the remains of dozens of sacrificed horses and some scattered human bones, which could be indications of human sacrifice. “If you’re trying to sacrifice a human, it might be easier if they’re not quite as resisting. And cannabis could be used to sedate people quite heavily,” says Caspari.

“The suggestion that cannabis may have been used to calm individuals selected for ritual sacrifice is intriguing, but remains highly speculative,” says Adam Brumm, an archaeologist at Griffith University in Australia, who recently showed that people were sucking betel nuts to extract a pain-relieving compound up to 25,000 years ago in Indonesia.

There is also evidence that people chewed coca leaves in Peru 8000 years ago, and brewed beer in Israel 13,000 years ago. The use of cannabis as a drug may extend much further back into prehistory than the archaeological record currently allows us to document, says Brumm. Long before people deliberately cultivated cannabis, the plants may have been familiar “camp followers” thriving in the disturbed, nutrient-rich soils around human settlements, giving people ample opportunities to experiment with their properties, he says.

Google shouldn’t be pressuring schools to use its AI

New Scientist November 05, 2026

When I was at school, a new technology launched in the form of a magic box that could answer any question you wanted. It was called Google, and my teachers cautioned that we shouldn’t trust everything it spat out, because anyone could put anything on the internet. Three decades later, history is repeating – with a twist. Schools are now begging Google to allow students to access its search engine, but the tech giant says that is only possible if teachers also accept a new kind of magic box, AI.

Google is far more integrated into education than it was in my day, with its Classroom and Workspace products providing teachers and students with a range of tools from email to lesson planning. More recently, Google has incorporated its Gemini AI chatbot into Classroom, to the chagrin of some US school districts that want to be able to decide whether or not students have access to AI. Sure, said Google, you can switch off AI, but then you lose search. “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Google’s Chris Phillips told The New York Times.

Why I have changed my mind about AI and you should too

At first, I thought this must be a misunderstanding about what we call AI. For most people today, AI means a large language model (LLM) of the type that powers Gemini or ChatGPT. But Google’s search engine has long used AI in the historical sense of machine learning, starting in 2015 with a system called RankBrain that helped relate words to concepts in order to produce search results. The AI Overviews you often see at the top of a search today, which launched in 2024, are the only part of the search results produced by Gemini.

Advertisement

Surely, I thought, what’s happening here is that school districts saying “no AI” simply mean no AI Overviews, while Google is quite reasonably saying it isn’t possible to rip out elements of its search engine that have been operating for over a decade in order to comply with a strict “no AI” request. This can easily be solved by making sure everyone is talking about the same thing, right?

Wrong. Google really is presenting schools with an all-or-nothing choice. “If a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have search on at all,” Phillips told education news outlet Chalkbeat. This is a product decision, not a technical one. AI Overviews do not appear on every search, and they can be disabled for every search by adding a short code to the URL. Google could surely provide schools with this option, if it wished. When asked to comment, a Google spokesperson sent New Scientist a link to a blog post on AI tutoring with its Gemini product.

We have seen a tech giant use this playbook before. Around the same time that Google was launching its young, upstart search engine in the late 1990s, Microsoft was facing legal action for forcing people to install the Internet Explorer (IE) browser as part of its Windows operating system, in an effort to fight off competitor browsers. At the time, Microsoft claimed that the files for IE were an “integral part” of Windows and could not be removed “without impairing the performance of the operating system”. In 2001, a US court ruled that this integration served to illegally maintain a monopoly, and Microsoft was obliged to make other browsers more accessible. By 2010, Microsoft was forced to offer users a range of browsers, following a European Commission ruling.

Around one-third of AI search tool answers make unsupported claims

There is no suggestion that Google is doing anything illegal in its approach to schools, although the company is currently appealing a US antitrust ruling that found it illegally maintains a monopoly in online search, and commentators have accused it of exploiting that monopoly. “Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools”, wrote New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on X. Following the backlash, Google posted on X that for schools, Gemini and search will be off by default and schools can choose to turn on either at their discretion. That doesn’t actually address the issue of having search without AI Overviews, however.

Ultimately, it will probably be for the courts to decide whether Google should be made to offer search without AI, but I am more interested in the question of how and when children should begin to use AI. Google has a 90 per cent market share in search, so it would be naive to think that children aren’t being exposed to AI Overviews, even if they do end up banned in schools. Personally, I know that AI Overviews can be heavily flawed and provide incorrect information, and yet I still find it hard to ignore them at the top of my search results, even while knowing that I should be clicking links to provide websites with revenue if I want them to continue existing.

Research on how LLMs affect learning is still in early days, but the evidence we have is worrying. One study of around 10,000 adults found that people who used an LLM summary rather than a list of links gained a shallower understanding of a topic, seemingly because having the results predigested by an AI required less cognitive effort. Another study of more than 26,000 students in China found that allowing them to use AI drastically improved homework performance, but saw exam results fall – suggesting that the children were letting AI do their homework for them without really learning anything.

Google’s answer to these concerns is its Guided Learning product, which it is adding to search for student accounts. It says the system will pick up when children are looking for help with homework, and walk them through it step by step, rather than simply providing an answer. In tests conducted with around 1800 students in Sierra Leone, Google says this approach provided more than a year of typical learning progress in just eight weeks.

In principle, I am not against the use of AI in schools – it is a modern, useful technology that will surely be part of students’ lives in the future, and they should learn to understand it just as I learned the pros and cons of using Google back in the 90s. The question of how to handle homework assignments in the age of AI, when an essay can be produced in seconds, is thorny and ongoing. One option is to simply scrap homework and require more in-classroom testing, but if Google gets its way and AI ends up being unavoidable there as well, it seems like teachers will have little control. That, to me, is the most objectionable point, as it should not be down to tech giants to set education policy.

Ordering takeaway food, writing emails, reworking presentations: AI assistants are promoted as a way of outsourcing mundane tasks to free up your time for more interesting pursuits. So, what are they actually good for – and what are the risks?

They were able to link recent, narrow fissures in the Alba Mons region of Mars to the HCl emissions, providing strong evidence of underground lava flow.

To assess whether the HCl could have come from the fissures, the team modelled the wind direction at the time the measurements were taken.

“We have 2 kilometres of wind between them, and in this season there are a lot of dust devils. So, the atmosphere is turbulent. It’s an enormous mess,” says Mège.

Nicolas Thomas at the University of Bern, Switzerland, another team member, stresses that until the area is investigated up-close, there will always be doubt about the source of the gas. But, he argues, this finding makes the case for further surface exploration of Mars.

Thomas thinks the finding makes the prospects for life on Mars more likely. “We know that Mars, even at the equator, can be −70°C, −80°C at night. It’s a very harsh environment,” he says. “If this thermal source were constant and continuous, then you have to admit it’s improving the situation [in terms of the hunt for life].”

“This is definitely a highly interesting finding,” says Lena Noack at the Free University of Berlin. “Many scientists working on Mars will not be too surprised, as the picture of a ‘dead’ Mars was inconsistent with many recent research findings.”

The sea around the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is changing colour, and microplastics may be to blame.

The Great Pacific Garbage Patch (GPGP), located roughly midway between Hawaii and California, covers around 1.6 million square kilometres and is thought to contain nearly 80,000 tonnes of plastic debris, carried there by ocean currents.

How worried should you be about microplastics?

Near the surface of the ocean in parts of the garbage patch, microplastic densities may reach up to 17 milligrams per cubic litre.

Advertisement

While most concern about the vast patch has focused on its impact on sea life and environmental health, three separate datasets have shown distinct colour changes in the ocean itself.

Other recent research has found that the world’s oceans are generally darkening for a variety of reasons, including agricultural runoff and phytoplankton growth.

Free newsletter

“The ocean’s colour is created from the interaction of sunlight with seawater and all the things contained in it, and therefore the colour is indicative of the ocean’s content,” says Shea Cheatham at the University of Bergen, Norway.

The unique circulation patterns that have created the garbage patch have also created an area much more likely to experience the kind of microplastic accumulation needed to be detectable from space, she says.

Cheatham and her colleagues analysed three satellite datasets collected between 2002 and 2022. The data showed that parts of the GPGP saw an approximately 10 per cent increase in blue light and a 2 to 4 per cent increase in green light over the 20-year period.

Not all of the satellites agreed on the extent of the blue and green brightening, which together create the colour cyan, but all found that some brightening had occurred.

They also simulated how the ocean’s colour would change from natural things, like more or different micro-algae and other material.

Globally, only 14 per cent of the plastic we use is recycled – but some countries achieve higher rates and new technologies could change the picture drastically

“We found that brightening of the water in both blue and green light is rarely produced by natural changes,” says Cheatham. “When we included microplastic particles in our simulations, this pattern we saw near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch of brightening in both blue and green light became more than four times as likely.”

Microplastic particles, in contrast to most natural contributors to ocean colour, do not absorb very much light, she says, but scatter light strongly. “This means that as their quantities increase in the ocean, they cause the ocean to brighten, and this brightening happens most strongly at blue-green wavelengths.”

“In short, this is compelling evidence for a potential satellite signature of microplastic accumulation, rather than evidence that satellites have actually detected the microplastics themselves,” says Smyth.

Marginal oil and gas wells have outsized pollution impact

New Scientist November 05, 2026

Satellite imagery has revealed that most of the methane pollution from oil and gas infrastructure in the US comes from hundreds of thousands of small wells scattered across the country – prompting calls for tougher climate regulation of low-producing oil and gas wells.

“We view the emissions from marginal wells as a major underappreciated mitigation opportunity,” says Mark Omara at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit organisation in the US.

How incredibly simple tech can supercharge the race to net zero

Last month, the administration of President Donald Trump moved to relax laws governing how methane emissions from oil and gas wells are managed, including lowering standards for emissions from marginal wells.

Advertisement

But Omara’s research suggests these marginal wells should be the highest priority for methane reduction efforts, a key global climate challenge.

Together with colleagues, Omara collated methane emissions data covering more than 80 per cent of US onshore oil and gas production, sourced from the methane-spotting satellite MethaneSat, for the period May 2024 to June 2025.

Free newsletter

The researchers then extrapolated to estimate methane emissions from oil and gas infrastructure across the contiguous US, establishing emissions rates across different production sites.

They found that marginal wells, which produce less than 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day, collectively contribute about 5 per cent to US oil and gas production. But they are responsible for about 58 per cent of all methane emissions from well sites, and 40 per cent of methane emissions across the oil and gas supply chain.

Compared with high-producing wells, these marginal wells are 10 times more polluting per unit of fuel extracted. “That is a significant contribution from a large population of very low-producing well sites across the country,” says Omara.

The study is the largest and most comprehensive of its kind and bridges a gap between top-level global emissions mapping and point-source emissions tracking from satellites, which wouldn’t pick up the low-level but constant emissions from these marginal wells.

This state’s power prices are plummeting as it nears 100% renewables

Methane is the second most important greenhouse gas to address, behind carbon dioxide. Globally, the world is far off track to meeting an industry target to reduce methane intensity – how much methane is emitted for each unit of marketed gas – to 0.2 per cent by 2030, a promise unveiled at the COP28 climate summit in Dubai in 2023. Current methane intensity levels are about 2.9 per cent, but in some regions such as in Turkmenistan and Venezuela, methane intensity can exceed 100 per cent, new research shows. For marginal wells in the US, the emissions intensity is estimated by Omara and colleagues at 60 per cent – 300 times larger than the industry target.

Tougher regulation of these marginal wells – or even shutting the sites down altogether – offers a quick route to reducing methane emissions in the short term, without significantly denting oil and gas production overall. But Daniel Jacob at Harvard University warns this will be a difficult challenge to address because there are so many emissions sources to deal with. “The methane emissions are not coming from a few super-emitters or high-producing wells; they’re just coming from all these pieces of infrastructure littered around the landscape,” he says.

Robin Lamboll at Imperial College London says global progress towards meeting methane targets has been “very disappointing”. “Reducing methane leaks is an extremely cheap, sometimes revenue-generating form of climate action,” he points out.

“We had very much hoped that the US, as a major gas producer signed up to the methane accords, would be bringing down their wasteful gas leakage problem. Under Trump this hasn’t happened, and regulatory rollback and personnel cuts have meant that the trends are both harder to track and likely going the wrong way,” says Lamboll.

Stunning collection of prehistoric engravings found in Spanish cave

A gallery of hundreds of engraved motifs and dozens of prehistoric animal images has been found in a cave in Spain, where they had gone unnoticed despite the cave being a popular tourist attraction.

Josep Maria Vergès at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology stumbled on the rock art at Cova de la Font Major, west of Barcelona, after a tourist group caught his attention.

The visitors, wearing wetsuits, were taking part in an adventure activity and had emerged from a nearby opening that led into a small side gallery. “Since it was my first time working at the site and I was unfamiliar with this side gallery, I went to take a look,” says Vergès.

Advertisement

Before the Stone Age: Were the first tools made from plants not rocks?

Upon entering, he saw that the walls were covered with names and dates engraved by people who had passed through the gallery since 1957. To examine them more closely, he removed his helmet and used the headlamp to illuminate the wall with raking light – a technique used to observe engravings because it creates shadows in the incised grooves.

“Almost immediately, among the modern graffiti, I noticed a series of vertical lines that appeared ancient,” says Vergès. “I moved slightly and spotted another one. Then, as I turned toward the opposite wall and shone the light across its surface, the horse appeared and I realised it was executed in a Palaeolithic style.”

He also immediately discovered that there were “many more engravings, many of them figurative representations of different animals”, he says.

So far, 280 motifs have been discovered in the gallery, including 55 animal figures, making the cave one of the richest and most important archaeological finds along the Iberian coast between the Pyrenees and Gibraltar.

One challenge for archaeologists is that it is extremely difficult to date the engravings themselves, but human occupation in the cave has been dated to between 26,000 and 41,000 years ago and, based on the style, the art is likely to be over 19,000 years old.

Team member Míriam Salas-Altès, also at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution, says one of the most outstanding figures is a hind, or adult female deer, depicted with its head lowered, its muzzle extending across a natural fissure.

The crack appears to have been deliberately incorporated into the composition as the surface of a body of water from which the hind is drinking. “If this hypothesis is correct, the scene would constitute one of the earliest known representations of water in human artistic expression,” she says.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Among the non-figurative engravings, the team identified groups of lines arranged in twos, threes or fours and, in some cases, series of up to 40 straight, parallel lines, as well as Y-shaped signs and circular or semicircular shapes. “As for what they represent, that question has led to dozens of different theories,” says Vergès. “Unfortunately, the code needed to understand its message has not fossilised.”

Paul Taçon at Griffith University in Australia says the discovery fills a large gap in our knowledge of the distribution of Palaeolithic art in western Europe. While the exact age of the rock art is yet to be determined, it is “obvious” that it was made by a Palaeolithic culture, he says.

“It is exciting that new discoveries at long-visited sites are revealing ancient evidence of a very early painting tradition,” says Taçon.

British Iron Age ‘king’ who prompted Roman invasion was probably a woman

New Scientist November 05, 2026

King Verica is one of the central figures in early British history. Verica convinced the Roman emperor Claudius to launch an invasion, setting in motion the Roman Empire’s conquest of Britain.

A pivotal king – except Verica was probably a queen. A new analysis suggests we have long misread Verica’s gender and she was actually female.

The surprising origins of Britain’s Bronze Age immigrants revealed

“Verica is probably the most important person at the end of the Iron Age, at that point where Britain gets dragged kicking and screaming into history,” says Miles Russell, an archaeologist at Bournemouth University in the UK and author of the forthcoming book Caratacus: Great king of Britain.

Advertisement

Our knowledge of Verica comes from two main sources. The first is Iron Age coins from the southern English counties of Hampshire and West Sussex, which bear the name “Verica”. It appears Verica was a ruler of the Atrebates: a group that originated in what is now northern France, some of whom made their home in southern Britain.

The other is the Roman historian Cassius Dio, who in the early 200s AD wrote a history of Rome. Cassius Dio records that a Briton called Berikos fled the island following an uprising and went to the Emperor Claudius to ask for help. Most historians agree that this was Verica and that Cassius Dio slightly mangled the name.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Previous Roman invasions of Britain, like those led by Julius Caesar in 55 and 54 BC, had been unsuccessful. But Claudius’s expedition in AD 43 succeeded and much of Britain became a Roman province for several centuries.

In his book, and in a summary article published in Current Archaeology, Russell presents several lines of argument that Verica was a woman.

The first point is Verica’s name. In Iron Age Britain, names that end with “a” are usually female, while names that end in “os” or “us” are typically male. The two other known female British rulers of this time, Boudica of the Iceni and Cartimandua of the Brigantes, both follow this pattern. “It’s not a clear-cut rule,” says Russell, but it applies to “about 95 per cent of Iron Age British names”.

Secondly, coins bearing Verica’s name tend to show images of female warriors on horseback, says Russell. “It is odd that Verica’s images are all female warriors,” he says. “Other coin-producing leaders don’t have that. They have male characters.”

Meanwhile, there is little or nothing specifying that Verica was male. Verica’s coins sometimes have the inscription “COM F” or “COMMI F”, which has been interpreted as Commios filus or “son of Commios”. However, argues Russell, it could just as easily be Commios filia or “daughter of Commios”. Likewise, the inscription “rex” meant ruler, but wasn’t gender-specific.

Astonishing new archaeological finds and ancient DNA analysis leave no doubt that throughout prehistory women were rulers, warriors, hunters and shamans

Furthermore, if Verica was female, Cassius Dio’s account of her interactions with the Roman emperor makes more sense. “Claudius is always demonised by Roman writers because they say he’s weak-minded,” says Russell. “He’s governed by ex-slaves and he’s governed by women. He makes no decisions of his own.” A female British ruler persuading him to invade would fit that narrative.

“It’s a highly compelling argument,” says Katharina Rebay-Salisbury, a prehistoric archaeologist at the University of Vienna. However, she is sceptical of the imagery on the coins, because they aren’t anatomically exact: “I find it a bit difficult to differentiate a naked female body from a naked male body in these very stylised images.” However, Russell has “multiple lines of evidence”, she says.

The idea also fits our emerging understanding of the northern European Iron Age, says Rebay-Salisbury. While the preceding Bronze Age was “highly gendered” and “people differentiated a lot between women and men”, she says, in the Iron Age, there was more emphasis on social status rather than gender, so women sometimes held power.

In 2025, Russell co-authored a study of ancient DNA from Iron Age cemeteries in southern Britain, which found that, for several centuries, women remained in their ancestral homes while men moved around – indicating that women held significant status. Similar patterns have been found in central Europe.

“There are by now so many of these instances,” says Rebay-Salisbury, yet “people keep being surprised”. She wonders: “When do we just accept that this happens on a more or less regular basis?”

Still on the fence this election? Compare all the big policies to decide how you'll vote.

Who'll govern if the election ends in a deadlock? The Front Page breaks it down.

With just one sleep to go until election day, a new poll out this morning shows Labour edging ahead of National, but with Opportunity still in kingmaker position.

The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll puts Labour on 30.7%, climbing two points since late October.

National is down to 26.4%, dropping 1.2 points in a fortnight.

The Opportunity Party makes it over the line - just - on 5.1% (-0.3% on October).

The Green Party sits on 13.0% (-1.3%), New Zealand First is 12.0% (+0.2%), Act is on 9.8% (+0.8%) with Te Pāti Māori on 2.0% (+0.1%).

According to these numbers, National, Act and NZ First would win a combined 59 seats, two short of the 61 needed to govern.

The Post's analysis of the poll results says Labour's late momentum has been propelled by women and youth, with Hipkins holding an 11.7-point lead among female voters, and under-35s voting heavily towards the left.

The analysis also says support for National has held up in Auckland, but has "suffered a collapse" in Wellington, with the capital becoming a "stronghold for Opportunity".

Freshwater Strategy interviewed 1044 eligible voters between October 29 - November 3 for the poll. The margin of error is +/-3%.

Beginning in Rotorua, Luxon's campaign bus is working its way to Hamilton before making the final push to Auckland, where he'll spend the night at home before election day tomorrow.

He started the day cleaning Rotorua MP Todd McClay's car, which had been half muddied – another visual metaphor of National's "get the job done" message.

Luxon joked that he is a bit of a clean freak and a perfectionist. He said his Instagram algorithm fed him water-blasting content.

"You meet incredible people along the way who come and tell you their story."

Act party candidate Paul Henry says it will be easier for the right wing to form a government if the Opportunity Party falls short of 5%.

"It's not all roads closed, but it would be a little harder [if Opportunity were elected]," Henry told Ryan Bridge TODAY.

The majority of polls have Opportunity meeting the threshold to get elected to Parliament.

Bridge asked if Act were "prepared to swallow the rat", to which Henry responded: "It's quite a big rat to swallow, but yeah, it is a rat. We're capable of eating rats of that size."

It's always been hard to know with much certainty about an incoming government's agenda under MMP, given the rarity of single party majorities.

It has been a fair assumption, though, that the agenda would be dominated by either National or Labour.

But this next Government will be unlike any before it in the MMP era, because the biggest party will be so weak, possibly below 30%.

NZ Media Council Upholds Complaint Against NZ Herald over election security story

New Zealand Herald November 05, 2026

The Media Council has upheld a complaint against the Herald.

The NZ Media Council has upheld a complaint by Jeremy Verity against the NZ Herald over an article about security concerns at election campaign events, finding breaches of Principles (1) Accuracy, Fairness and Balance and (12) Corrections. The complaint arose from a report on a candidates’ meeting in Wadestown involving Labour MP Ayesha Verrall, which described Mr Verity and John Ansell as “agitators” and referred to police and a protective barrier being used around Dr Verrall.

Mr Verity said the article exaggerated events; wrongly implied police intervention was required because of his conduct, inaccurately described his involvement with the Stop Tiaki Wai movement, and relied solely on Dr Verrall’s account.

The NZ Herald rejected those claims, maintaining its reporting was accurate, that both Mr Verity and Mr Ansell publicly supported Stop Tiaki Wai, and that the description of Mr Verity as an “agitator” was justified. The newspaper also said it removed the word “frenzied” from the article to avoid confusion, although it was not intended to refer to Mr Verity.

After reviewing video footage, the Media Council found that descriptions of Dr Verrall being “accosted” and Mr Verity being an “agitator” were not inaccurate and that the newspaper was entitled to report Dr Verrall’s perception of the incident. However, it noted that there was an implication that those who approached Dr Verrall were “frenzied” was unsupported by evidence. It concluded the NZ Herald acted unfairly by identifying Mr Verity in a story about threats and intimidation of politicians without seeking his comment or providing an opportunity to respond, breaching Principle (1).

The Council also upheld the complaint under Principle (12), finding the newspaper was too slow to deal with concerns about the word “frenzied”, despite eventually amending the article and removing the word. The complaint was not upheld under the Privacy or Headlines and Captions Principles.

Four Media Council members dissented, considering there was insufficient evidence to support findings against the newspaper and that its response to the complaint was adequate.

The full Media Council ruling can be found here.

WARNING: This story details the death of a young girl and may be distressing for some readers.

While an infant’s death remains unexplained, a coroner has examined the possibility the child’s older sibling may have played a role in the tragedy.

Today, Coroner Heather McKenzie released findings saying the girl’s death may have resulted from accidental or deliberate smothering, a sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI), or a medical event.

The child was the youngest of several children. The findings detail a series of interactions with Oranga Tamariki, health services and support agencies in the days before her death.

Coroner McKenzie said those events provided important context.

The mother told police and other agencies that her preschool-aged son had been showing violent behaviour towards her, the infant and an older sister.

She said she was scared he would try to harm the infant and that when he became angry or frustrated, he would shout, hit out and throw or slam objects.

The woman’s mother told police her grandson had been acting differently and had been aggressive before his sister’s death.

Kindergarten staff, family members and other witnesses also described challenging and unusual behaviour from the boy.

The mother called emergency services five days before the girl’s death after waking to find the boy lying on top of the infant.

She was found active and responsive.

The mother told police that about two hours later she heard muffled screaming and ran into a room to find her son on top of the infant again, wriggling.

She pulled him off and found her daughter “pale blue, just lethargic”.

Emergency services were called again, reporting the infant appeared less interactive and paler than earlier.

The girl was taken to hospital where she was assessed and appeared normal.

An emergency social worker was consulted before discharge amid allegations the brother had lain on the infant, causing her to turn blue, and that her mother had reported similar incidents on multiple occasions.

The hospital emergency department and Hato Hone St John filed a report of concern with Oranga Tamariki when the infant was discharged.

The mother met with Oranga Tamariki and whānau support workers that day to develop an interim safety plan.

It was agreed the boy would stay overnight with his grandmother until a face-to-face meeting the following day.

The mother called emergency services again the next day after the infant failed to wake for a feed and was difficult to rouse.

She was taken to hospital, where examinations returned results within normal limits.

Meanwhile, an Oranga Tamariki social worker contacted the mother and a whānau services worker to arrange a face-to-face meeting to review the safety plan.

The mother said her sister was staying with her and updated the social worker about the hospital admission.

They agreed to meet after the infant was discharged.

Three days later, the social worker contacted the mother again and was told the infant had been discharged from hospital that day.

A friend who looked after the infant early that afternoon noticed bruising around her nose and beneath her eyes, which she believed she had first seen at the hospital four days earlier.

The mother told police she was at home with the infant and the boy that night and put the girl in her bassinet in the lounge about 10.30pm.

She slept on the sofa and the boy slept in a bedroom. She later told police she chose the sofa because she was worried about the infant, and it was warmer near the fire.

At 2.30am, she fed the girl, returned her to the bassinet and went back to sleep.

When she next awoke, the infant was asleep but looked pale.

The mother told police she thought nothing of it and instead interacted with her son, who had been playing in his room, giving him breakfast and doing “what I needed to do”.

She said she was not aware of her son having been in the lounge and that no one else had been at the house that day.

The mother later went back to sleep.

When she woke again, she noticed the girl was not breathing. She phoned an ambulance and her friend.

The infant could not be revived and was pronounced dead.

Coroner McKenzie said a forensic pathologist found no infectious, traumatic, toxicological or underlying natural cause of death during the autopsy.

However, two possibilities warranted consideration, she said.

The first was sudden cardiac death associated with underlying cardiac conduction abnormalities.

Those abnormalities can be present from birth and may cause a sudden, potentially fatal heart rhythm disturbance at any age.

Many leave no signs that would allow a diagnosis at autopsy.

The second possibility was the death resulted from asphyxiation or smothering by a sibling or another person.

Contact the Open Justice team

Given the incidents described in the days before the tragedy, the pathologist advised the possibility the sibling was in the same room at the time of death could not be ruled out.

“Similarly, the scenario that someone other than this young sibling was involved in any smothering attempts should also not be discounted,” the pathologist said, as reported in the findings.

“However, it should be reiterated that no injuries or other positive findings to support this mechanism were found at autopsy.”

On the available evidence, Coroner McKenzie said she could not make a finding on the cause or immediate circumstances of the infant’s death.

“This is because of the various open possibilities, as well as because on the evidence before me, the death was not witnessed.

“This second factor fundamentally means that even if other possibilities had not been brought to light by the evidence, I still could not make safe findings about the cause and circumstances of the death because no one saw, or has told police, what happened.”

Al Williams is an Open Justice reporter for the New Zealand Herald, based in Christchurch. He has worked in daily and community titles in New Zealand and overseas for the last 16 years. Most recently he was editor of the Hauraki-Coromandel Post, based in Whangamatā. He was previously deputy editor of the Cook Islands News.

Christchurch's highest rooftop bar at the Sheraton Hotel is due to open late July, 2027. Photo / Anna Heath.

Christchurch’s newest and highest rooftop bar might still be 10 months from opening, but champagne was poured on the 14th floor of the Sheraton Hotel as it celebrated a significant milestone this week.

The still-under-construction Sheraton on Oxford Terrace, formerly Rydges and before that Noah’s, is a refurbished, enlarged and improved hotel that will bring five-star accommodation to the doorstep of Te Pae – the Christchurch convention centre.

The $150m development overlooks the city’s river precinct, with views from the rooftop taking in everything from the Port Hills to the Southern Alps, looking south. The penthouse Presidential suite looks back over the city with floor-to-ceiling windows offering unobstructed views.

The hotel is owned by Emmons Developments New Zealand, a consortium of New Zealand investors, led by a joint venture between Mainland Capital and Russell Property Group.

The 240-room hotel will be under the management of Marriott International, Inc. and its Sheraton Hotels and Resorts brand.

The building that survived the 2011 earthquake has required significant strengthening, along with the addition of rooms and rooftop hospitality. Wednesday marked the “roof shout” for the hundreds of workers who have brought the project to its current point. The structural work is done.

Mainland Capital executive director Ben Bridge says a huge amount of work was done researching the job before the building was purchased - but the job has been challenging.

“This is the most complex project I’ve been involved with, and I’d say second only maybe to the Art Centre, it’d be the most complex renovation post-quake, in New Zealand.

“We’ve had a great team working on it, and I have to pinch myself that I can tell you in all honesty, we’re running on time and on budget, which is pretty weird for most projects, let alone a renovation of this scale.”

Bridge credits the Russell Property Group’s experience in projects like this – and the commitment from the “United Nations” of workers involved.

“Today is all about the 300 or 400 guys and girls downstairs that have been working on the site. It’s a big crew, it’s a difficult job and yet they’re kicking the goals,” Bridge said.

Russell Property Group managing director Brett Russell thanked his workers for their efforts so far and asked for a big push before the Christmas break as they aim for a late July 2027 completion.

Russell points out that the hotel will attract visitors and locals alike.

“Adding another 40 rooms on made the feasibility work a lot better. Made the property look a lot better from the back of it. And also, moving the driveway from the riverside around to Worcester Street makes a big difference as well,” he said.

“So that means that people can walk along that riverside and hopefully we get people into that restaurant, not just [those who are] staying, it’s all the locals. This bar up here is about the locals and so is down there.

“When we did the QT in Auckland, 70% of the people are locals. There’s only 30% of the people in the bar or the restaurants that are actually staying in it.”

One of the major benefactors of the Sheraton’s arrival will be the neighbouring convention centre, Te Pae. General manager Ross Steele says the hotel will add to their attraction for high-end events such as medical conferences.

“I think when Te Pae was built, people that had the foresight to build it were hoping that this sort of product would come into Christchurch, and the foresight that Ben and Brett have to bring this online, and to reinvigorate a building that was existing, it’s just amazing.

“It’ll really help us when we go internationally to try and bring international conferences to Christchurch, to have a quality hotel like this right next door, like a game changer for us.”

The rooftop bar is the brightest jewel in the hotel’s already sparkling crown. It’s becoming a Brett Russell trademark.

“I’ve got a bit of a thing with rooftop bars. Obviously did the QT in Auckland and then the Sheraton Four Points, we’ve got the Churchill bar there and it was the same sort of feeling when you came up here,” Russell said.

Bridge says the show-stopping additions that the Sheraton will offer took some consideration.

“We had a fork in the road early - before we committed to an operator - as to whether this was going to be a 4- or 5-star offering, and we jumped the way of Sheraton, which was elevating the offering.

“With that came additional cost, therefore additional risk, but the result was we were able to invest with more confidence in the nice-to-haves like the rooftop, the Presidential suite, the restaurant and dialling up things like furniture or artwork.

“It allows you to invest with confidence having a partner like Sheraton beside you.”

Mike Thorpe is a senior multimedia journalist for the Herald, based in Christchurch. He has been a broadcast journalist across television and radio for 20 years and joined the Herald in August 2024.

Flash flooding and slips could hit parts of Auckland and Northland today, with severe thunderstorms threatening intense downpours of up to 40mm an hour.

Auckland Emergency Management last night warned of flooding in low-lying areas as unsettled weather threatens the upper North Island.

MetService has issued a severe thunderstorm watch for Auckland and southwestern parts of Northland from noon until 9pm, with a moderate risk of severe thunderstorms bringing hazardous driving conditions, surface flooding and poor visibility.

The threat extends beyond the watch areas, with a moderate risk of thunderstorms bringing heavy rain of 10 to 25mm per hour from Northland through to parts of Hawke’s Bay this afternoon and evening.

The heightened thunderstorm risk comes as warm, moisture-laden tropical air sweeps across the country before tomorrow’s election day.

A complex trough of low pressure is expected to move slowly eastwards across New Zealand tomorrow, bringing periods of northerly rain to the central and upper North Island, “along with possible thunderstorms and localised downpours”, according to the MetService’s severe weather outlook.

MetService meteorologist Alanna Burrows said the risk of thunderstorms would increase today and “further increase on Saturday”, as voters head to the polls.

“With rain and the risk of thunderstorms over the next few days, it’s worth keeping an eye on our rain radar and latest forecasts if you’re heading out to vote.”

The unsettled conditions could extend into parts of the South Island over the weekend, Burrows said.

Heading out to enjoy a warm spring evening or joining in on some Guy Fawkes festivities and wondering what's the forecast? 🌅🎆Cloudy periods continuing in the north and west, with sunnier spells in the south and east. A few showers here and there, mainly inland and away from… pic. twitter. com/lXchsXXn6W

El Niño continues to make its presence felt in Northland, with the region experiencing widespread “meteorological drought” conditions.

Northland Regional Council monitoring manager Jason Donaghy said the region’s average rainfall for October was 32mm, about 36% of the usual monthly total.

“Most groundwater levels are ‘below normal’ to ‘extremely low’ for most of the region for this time of year.”

MetService meteorologist Lewis Ferris said the forecast rain was unlikely to provide significant relief given how dry the region had become.

“There’s some rain around, but it’s not really going to be meaningful rain for that sort of soil mush in the ground. They might have a little bit more luck through Friday and Saturday, but they’re not big rainmakers.”

Over the next 7-10 days, high pressure east of New Zealand (🔴) and low pressure (🔵) in the Tasman Sea will act like cogs pulling moisture-rich air south from the tropics.⛈️ This will result in rounds of moderate to heavy rain and thunderstorms, especially in the North Island. pic. twitter. com/qIlpjyAO7l

OCD: Mount Maunganui teenager experiences life-changing results after Bergen treatment

New Zealand Herald November 05, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Teenager Bailey Moore has gone from living in fear to living life on his own terms. After being “bedridden” for a year, he is reaching milestones he never thought he could.

Mount Maunganui teenager Bailey Moore’s life “shut down” last year.

He could not see his friends, go to school or be in the same room as his family.

“Every time I’d go out or even just touch something that’s not my bed … I’d have to wash my hands using a full block of soap.”

He had 45-minute showers, three or four times a day.

Bailey, 16, was diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) at intermediate school.

It reached its “worst point” last year when he caught a cold and cough.

“That’s where my whole life pretty much shut down.

“My OCD said I need to continue coughing … every single moment I was awake, I was coughing … non-stop.”

Bailey was in and out of hospital, consistently thinking he was going to die.

When he got a sore throat, his OCD manifested in him only whispering and only eating ice blocks for “months”.

He was “pretty much bedridden” all last year.

Bailey saw psychologists, publicly and privately, “but nothing was working”.

His “last hope” became the Bergen four-day treatment his mother found.

The intensive, Norway-developed treatment was delivered in New Zealand for the first time this year by Open Closed Doors – a charity established in 2025 to address OCD treatment gaps.

Early results showed half of those treated were in remission.

Bailey is one of them.

Bailey said his OCD began at age 7 and heightened during Covid-19.

Before biking home from school, he would use “a whole bottle” of hand sanitiser, then wash his hands at home.

“I just couldn’t live my life ... I was just having to follow what these things in my head were saying.”

This included thinking he would get sick or die if he did not clean his hands.

Bailey had been doing exposure and response prevention before the Bergen treatment, but “wasn’t leaning in”.

“I would do it, but then I’d wash my hands afterwards.”

He went to Christchurch in April for his scholarship-funded Bergen treatment.

He said each participant was supported one-to-one by a therapist, who would assist them in completing tasks.

Under their guidance, Bailey went to shopping malls, paid with cash and used public restrooms, drinking fountains and Ubers.

He said at the end of each day, the group would celebrate their successes.

“That is probably one of the best things because you felt so good hearing about other people’s successes and you could tell yours …

“The treatment was phenomenal.”

He attributed its success to his willingness and the positive group environment.

Pre-treatment, he scored 38 out of 40 on the children’s Yale-Brown obsessive-compulsive scale.

Two weeks post-treatment, he scored 12, classified as “mild OCD”.

A score of five three months later indicated “full remission”.

“I feel free, I feel open, I’m forever grateful to the Bergen and Open Closed Doors team. I just do whatever I want whenever I want.”

He competed in the mountain bike orienteering nationals and came second in his age group.

He passed his learner licence test on October 15 – his 16th birthday – and had a driving lesson.

“There was no chance prior to the course I could have with my OCD.”

Bailey wanted to dispel a common misconception of OCD as “being tidy”.

“It’s way more than that and it’s really sad to see when people misuse it.”

He wanted to share how “debilitating” OCD could be.

His message to OCD sufferers was that it “doesn’t have to rule your life”.

“You’re not alone and there’s people there to support you and don’t give up.”

Bailey’s mother, Anna Moore, said Bailey was having constant panic attacks and “couldn’t do anything” last year.

“It was hell.”

Bailey could not be in the same room as his father or two sisters, so “our family was really living separate lives”.

Moore gave up work last year to look after Bailey and has only just returned.

She said Bailey’s life had changed “dramatically” post-treatment, including talking in a “normal voice” again.

“Bergen enabled our family to live life again.”

An Open Closed Doors statement said OCD affected about 100,000 New Zealanders and commonly began in childhood or adolescence.

Exposure and response prevention remained the “gold-standard therapy” for OCD, but weekly sessions over many months were difficult to access and many people dropped out, it said.

Bergen condensed a “highly effective treatment” into four days, making it more scalable and accessible.

The charity had received more than 800 expressions of interest from people with OCD and their families, and 176 clinicians registered interest in training.

Dr Marthinus Bekker, a clinical lead for Open Closed Doors, said funding was the “biggest barrier” to getting a treatment like this established in public mental health services.

It costs between $6000 and $7000 per person.

Health New Zealand mental health and addiction national chief Dr Leeanne Fisher said there was growing interest internationally in intensive OCD approaches, including the Bergen treatment.

Reported outcomes were “encouraging” and the “concentrated combination of approaches” may help some engage more effectively with treatment than weekly sessions, she said.

Fisher said Health NZ Bay of Plenty’s child and adolescent mental health services provided OCD treatment, typically cognitive behavioural therapy with a strong focus on exposure and response prevention.

Medication may also be prescribed and monitored by a psychiatrist, she said.

These approaches were the evidence-based standard of care for paediatric OCD, she said.

Fisher said exposure and response prevention was delivered one-on-one and involved gradually confronting situations that triggered obsessive thoughts while reducing the compulsive behaviours that typically followed.

This could be done in clinic settings, at home, school environments or “in other real-world situations” relevant to the person’s symptoms.

Fisher said intensive exposure-based treatment could be challenging to do in routine service models, given the level of coaching, support and time required.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Election 2026: Strong early voter turnout no reasons to shirk a democratic duty – Editorial

New Zealand Herald November 05, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Election eve has arrived in New Zealand and it’s great to see early voter turnout has been strong.

About 1.25 million of the almost 3.8 million Kiwis enrolled to vote had already cast their ballot by Tuesday – a good chunk more than at the same point in the last general election.

But this is no reason for the rest to shirk this democratic duty.

This year, there will also be those who decide to become a voter too late and fall outside the newly curtailed enrolment period.

That goes against the principle that democracy is strongest when participation is broad.

Yet even when you could enrol right up until election day, hundreds of thousands of eligible Kiwi voters would still opt out every time. The enrolment rate at the 2023 election was 94.7%, the turnout was 74.17%. This year’s enrolment rate is 93.6%.

The adage goes that if you do not vote, you cannot complain.

The ratio of voting to complaining about politics in Aotearoa suggests, anecdotally at least, that this is widely ignored.

Griping about the Government means little, however, unless we follow through at the ballot box every three years by making two ticks at a cardboard booth.

The voters who overcome the alarming fatness of the orange pens to pick a party and a local representative decide what happens next in our country.

New Zealand is a representative democracy.

We, the people, rarely get to make the actual decisions; our only real say is in who will make the decisions for us.

That is a somewhat nebulous thing – elected representatives can lie, flip-flop or abandon pre-election commitments to secure a coalition deal – but it’s really all we have.

The polls predict a close and messy election, one that may challenge another tenet of our system of government – the “proportional part” of MMP.

No reader need look far for explainers about what an overhang is and how a perhaps unseemly level of encouragement for vote-splitting may engineer one in this election.

Suffice to say we might be breaking out the folding chairs to accommodate an expanded Parliament.

The polls also suggest that tomorrow night, all eyes may be on who Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong calls first.

It seems like a long time since anyone other than Winston Peters has worn the kingmaker crown.

It’s hard to imagine Wong giving media a ticking off about underestimating her party outside the Duke of Marlborough on Sunday, but perhaps she’ll oblige for tradition’s sake.

We might not know the full picture of the winners and losers in this election for weeks or even months.

The only people guaranteed to lose tomorrow are those who could vote but elect not to.

To quote The West Wing’s White House press secretary C. J. Cregg: “Decisions are made by those who show up.”

Ride Your Trike NZ launches $25,000 fundraiser for Hamilton shop space

New Zealand Herald November 05, 2026

Ride Your Trike NZ founder Liam Carter, 19, sits on an adaptive trike. He hopes to raise $25,000 towards leasing a space in Hamilton where people can try adaptive bikes and trikes.

Hamilton entrepreneur Liam Carter has faced many challenges entering the business world.

Carter lives with cerebral palsy and is seeking $25,000 towards leasing premises for Ride Your Trike NZ, his business specialising in adaptive bikes and trikes.

Adaptive bikes are cycles designed or modified for people who find a standard two-wheeled bike difficult to use, Carter said.

They can include trikes for extra stability, hand-powered cycles, supportive seating, or wheelchair-carrying designs that let someone enjoy a ride as a passenger.

The 19-year-old’s bike business is now outgrowing its current space, his family’s home, with incoming stock spilling into his father’s workout space.

He said sales had picked up after a quiet spell and the business was growing faster than he had expected.

“It’s exciting, but I need more space; my parents cannot even access their garage.”

Setting up shop in Hamilton is the immediate goal. Longer term, Carter dreams of a Tauranga hub with a cafe, showroom and workshop near the coast.

There is a personal pull, too, he said.

His grandparents are from Tauranga, so he has wanted to build a business there for years.

Walking long distances is difficult for him. Before getting his driver’s licence last year, his trike was his main way of getting around.

“From the age of 5, I’ve been on a bike, and it changed my life.”

It’s given him the freedom to get to school, meet friends and undertake that essential childhood business.

“Buying lollies.”

That experience helped shape Ride Your Trike, which grew from cycling advocacy into a business supplying equipment to help others get riding.

He has since expanded into conventional bikes and e-bikes, widening his customer base and shrinking the available floor space.

“If I want to get somewhere, I’ll get there. And it’s about breaking down those barriers as a young, but also disabled entrepreneur,” Carter said.

Carter is clear that the business aims to make a profit, alongside helping people gain independence.

He does not draw a full-time salary and works with a casual mechanic.

During quiet periods, he has initially considered taking a part-time job, but sales picked up again quickly.

In August 2023, Carter started advocating for cycleways at Hamilton City Council and, through discussions with people in his community, “found a real need for adaptive bikes”.

Carter said people had underestimated him because of his age and disability. Online bullying had also made him question continuing.

But helping customers find a new way to get around keeps him going.

For some, finding suitable equipment involves more than choosing a colour and checking for a bell.

Some need time to build confidence. Others require adaptations, with families, occupational therapists and physiotherapists helping find the right fit.

A test ride might take 20 minutes or two hours.

“We’re not a pressured environment.”

Carter said the aim was to make everyday life more accessible, with support continuing after a sale.

He has driven out at night to help with a customer’s battery and answered early morning calls about equipment.

The bikes may have stands. The business rarely seems to stand still.

Permanent premises would provide room to display equipment and repair donated bikes for resale, with a small profit helping cover operating costs.

Further services offered would depend on the space secured. A smaller fundraising result could help with storage, while more money would allow larger premises.

However, no matter the result, he wants somewhere customers feel welcome.

He sees potential in serving older residents and disabled riders.

“Somewhere where people can feel like they can come in and be themselves.”

Carter has launched a Givealittle appeal and is spreading the word through social media.

He is also inviting people considering larger donations to contact him directly.

Those unable to donate can help by sharing the fundraiser, recommending the business or buying something they need.

“Whether it’s $5, $20 or simply spreading the word, every bit of support means something.”

His Givealittle page is givealittle. co. nz/cause/help-us-build-a-home-for-ride-your-trike-nz.

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before he joined the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He previously worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.
