Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell says she is unlikely to run for mayoralty again

New Zealand Herald November 05, 2026

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell says she wants to leave Rotorua in a stronger position than she found it. Photo / Maryana Garcia

Rotorua could be looking for a new mayor after the next council elections in 2028, with Mayor Tania Tapsell indicating her current term could be her last.

Speaking to Local Democracy Reporting to mark the first year of her second term, Tapsell described the past 12 months as a “whirlwind”, saying she had often felt like she was in “the eye in the storm” amid political, financial and community challenges.

Now, after 13 years in local politics, Tapsell says she might step back.

“At this stage, I’m unlikely to stand again,” she said.

“And the reason for that is I would have achieved everything that I came in to do.”

Tapsell said she wanted to leave Rotorua in a stronger position than she found it and was increasingly confident she could deliver on the goals that brought her into office.

“I am quite confident we’ll be able to have achieved a lot of what I promised when I first started.”

Central to that legacy is the restoration of Rotorua Museum, which Tapsell described as “the biggest achievement of my life”.

The construction phase finished on schedule in September, and the city landmark is expected to fully reopen by 2028, aligning with what would be the end of Tapsell’s term.

“Having grown up here and understanding the connection our community has with our museum, it was just such a pleasure to be able to fix that building.”

Tapsell said the project was one of the most complex heritage restorations undertaken in New Zealand, involving extensive earthquake strengthening work. The redevelopment cost about $73 million, $15.5m of which was funded by ratepayers.

“It’s almost unheard of to finish a heritage project on budget, let alone under,” she said. “So that’s something we can be incredibly proud of.”

She also pointed to progress on reducing emergency housing numbers, improving safety in the city centre, boosting tourism and securing government funding for local projects as key pillars of her mayoralty.

While Tapsell spoke positively about Rotorua’s progress, she was candid about the challenges that had come with the job.

In August, the High Court ruled Rotorua Lakes Council acted unlawfully when approving the Tarawera Sewerage Scheme in 2020.

As well as the court case, the scheme sparked protests and abuse that Tapsell described as the “most difficult period” of her mayoralty.

“The circulation of misinformation on social media created significant challenges, millions of dollars in legal and protest costs and, unfortunately, a lot of hurt in our community.”

Tapsell said the project was about protecting the environment while supporting future papakāinga development.

She said threats directed at her, council staff and contractors during the debate had been “really unsettling”.

“It’s been at times unbearably hard,” she said.

Tapsell said the biggest political challenge of her second term so far had been the Government’s local government reform process.

“I almost lost my mind,” she said of the “unreasonably short” three-month timeframe councils were given to consider merger proposals and submit a response.

The experience deepened Tapsell’s concerns about Wellington’s relationship with councils.

Tapsell, a former National Party candidate, said there was “a real sense of disheartenment and even disillusionment” among elected members around the country.

Speaking about the upcoming general election, Tapsell said one of her biggest concerns remained the long-term financial sustainability of local government.

She expressed concerns about the Government’s planned rates-capping regime, saying communities had not been adequately consulted on what limits of 4% or less could mean for council services.

“I don’t know a single elected member that enjoys increasing rates,” she said.

“Delivering everything we do with only 10% of the total rates and tax take compared to 90% that the Government gets just doesn’t add up, and we need a serious conversation and real solutions.”

She said councils needed new funding tools, including greater control over visitor-related revenue streams, to reduce the burden on ratepayers.

Despite the challenges, Tapsell said her motivation remained the same as when she first entered office: leaving Rotorua in a better place than she found it.

“I walk into the mayor’s office every single day grateful that I get to hold this space and do all that I can.”

Tapsell said her focus over the next two years would be ensuring the city continued moving forward.

“When my term ends, Rotorua needs to be confident that whoever the next person is to take up the mantle after me doesn’t let us go backwards to some of the days of doom that are now a distant memory of the past.”

The role had not always been easy, she said, but it had been worth it.

“Rotorua will always be home,” she said.

“This leadership role is only for a limited time, and I just want to make the absolute most of it every single day.

“Even if it burns me out, I’m sure I’ll reflect and understand it was worth it.”

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in the UK for eight years.

Sleepless nights, family tension and bullets in his arm: Bondi hero one year on

Sydney Morning Herald November 06, 2026

Almost a year after the Bondi massacre, Ahmed Al Ahmed reflects on his brave actions on the day – and his struggles in the aftermath.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Article gifting is here

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

For Ahmed Al Ahmed, the scene is still vivid. On a beautiful Sydney summer evening, he is crouching between two cars in a parking area at Bondi Beach. The warm air is full of the sound of gunfire. And screaming. Terrified people are streaming past his hiding spot, running and stumbling. He tries to make sense of what he is seeing and hearing, but his brain seems to have frozen. Even his body is acting strangely. He looks down and registers that the knee he injured in a work accident, the one that hurts like hell to bend, is flexed beneath him. No pain at all. “My god,” he says to his cousin, who is sheltering beside him, “what is happening?”

It is just after 6.40pm on Sunday, December 14, 2025. In a couple of minutes, Al Ahmed will do something remarkable – something that will save many lives and irrevocably change his own. His action will be captured in a grainy video, which will be watched by millions of people around the world. He will be hailed as a hero by everyone from US President Donald Trump to King Charles III. He will be presented with a GoFundMe cheque for more than $2.5 million.

After the fanfare dies down, he will struggle to regain the use of his bullet-riddled left arm. His two brothers will deny charges of trying to extort money from him. His father will accuse him of assault, then retract the allegation. He will write a memoir. Al Ahmed has quite a year ahead of him.

But he doesn’t know any of that yet. For the moment, he is keeping his head down and listening to the shooting, which is getting closer. Heart thudding, he tries to remember the declaration of faith that Muslims are supposed to make to prepare for death. The words won’t come to him. Then a man steps into his line of vision. A man with a gun.

I meet Al Ahmed at Bondi on a day of swirling wind and rain. It is spring, but so cold that no one is swimming. The few walkers on the beachfront are wearing puffer jackets. Al Ahmed, 45, is smartly turned out in a blue sports coat, jeans and black loafers. His manner is reserved and courteous. Though he has lived in Australia for two decades, his English is heavily accented. “No one is going to forget that day,” he says.

At North Bondi RSL Club, he orders a chai latte. This surprises me a little because I know from his book, Light Will Win, that Al Ahmed is a coffee guy. In fact, it was a craving for caffeine that put him into the middle of the worst act of terrorism on Australian soil. The way he tells it, he had driven to Bondi from his home in the Sutherland Shire, in southern Sydney, picking up his cousin, Hothefa Al Kanj, on the way. By the time they arrived, it was after 6pm. At one cafe after another, they were told the coffee machine had been turned off for the day. Al Kanj was all for giving up and getting a Coke. Al Ahmed, though, was a man on a mission.

Music was coming from a lit-up park at the northern end of the beach. Some kind of market or fair, Al Ahmed presumed. He and Al Kanj walked to the entrance, where security guards said it was a Jewish community festival, Chanukah by the Sea. No coffee cart, unfortunately. “They said, ‘If you want to come in, you’re welcome’,” Al Ahmed remembers. “I said, ‘No, thank you. I want to keep going. For the coffee.’ ” He and Al Kanj turned away from the festival. They had gone about 10 metres when they heard a sharp cracking sound. Then another. And another. “I asked my cousin, ‘What is this? It’s fireworks?’ ”

Al Kanj said, “No. Run!” In a parking area overlooked by a pedestrian bridge that gave access to the beach from busy Campbell Parade, they ducked for cover between two vehicles. That’s where Al Ahmed was when the shooter appeared.

Fear was a familiar sensation to Al Ahmed. In news reports of what became known as the Bondi massacre, he was portrayed as an ordinary man who showed extraordinary courage. “I’m a normal guy,” he assures me more than once during our time together. “I’m the same as anyone.” But Al Ahmed had been tested in the course of his life. “For long stretches of my childhood,” he writes in his memoir, “fear was my only friend.”

He grew up in north-western Syria, near the border with Turkey. Wolves prowled in the mountains and, from his village of Al-Nayrab, could sometimes be heard howling in the distance. Most of the men in his family were shepherds, and as a boy he would trek with them into the hills, where they camped under the stars while their sheep grazed in the high pastures. Up there, the wolves sounded very close. He remembers huddling by the campfire, wishing dawn would come.

But the threat that felt biggest to Al Ahmed wasn’t out in the wild. It was inside his home. He claims in his book that his father, a policeman, was a hard and controlling figure who hit him at the slightest provocation. To me, he points out that this wasn’t unusual in the culture of the time. His father may have believed he was doing the right thing: his goal was to make his son tough. “Obviously he wanted me to be a strong man. But, you know, I was a child.” His beloved mother – “She’s the one who was caring” – would sometimes try to defend him, he says.

As the oldest of seven children, Al Ahmed was expected to contribute to the household income. From the age of nine, he fitted his schoolwork around a string of jobs: labouring, delivering groceries, picking olives. At 18, he embarked on two years’ compulsory military service, at his father’s suggestion opting to do his time in the police wing of the army. He writes that the police training academy was run by officers seemingly selected for their sadism: they subjected conscripts to bizarre acts of cruelty, such as forcing them to lie in the icy exercise yard in their underwear on mid-winter nights, then blasting them with near-freezing water from fire hoses. It seemed to Al Ahmed that the brutality of the regime of then-president, Bashar al-Assad, had poisoned Syrian society as a whole, and he decided he would leave his home country. His other resolution: to be a completely different man from his father. He would be gentle, not domineering. He would live and let live.

There were two shooters, Al Ahmed realised. One was on the pedestrian bridge. The other – 50-year-old Sajid Akram – was standing in front of Al Ahmed, but looking the other way, so hadn’t noticed him. Al Ahmed could see Akram’s likely next victims: people who were lying defenceless on the grass, some of them injured. Thinking back on it, he says he didn’t make a conscious decision to charge at Akram. Rather, he saw the opportunity and took it.

“He was a big guy,” he says. “Very muscly. Higher than me.” As Al Ahmed grabbed Akram from behind, he heard himself swearing in what he describes as “the Aussie way”. Something along the lines of, “You motherf---er. You piece of shit.” His right arm was wrapped around Akram’s neck. Al Ahmed’s other arm theoretically wasn’t capable of much: the rotator cuff on his left shoulder had been damaged in a car accident, and recent surgery hadn’t yet restored it to full strength. But as the two men tussled, that arm did everything Al Ahmed asked of it, including seizing Akram’s rifle. Suddenly Akram was lying on the ground and Al Ahmed was aiming the gun at him.

For Al Ahmed, getting out of Syria had felt like a release. He moved first to Dubai, where he and an uncle established a business importing and selling used luxury cars, then came to Australia. He arrived in 2006, aged 25, and says he felt at home from day one. He found employment on construction sites in Canberra and eventually qualified as a carpenter. He married Alsu, an Australian of Russian heritage, and in 2014 set himself up as a subcontractor, supplying teams of carpenters to building projects while continuing to ply his trade himself.

He was busy and happy. But one day on a worksite he ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament, or ACL. He had reconstruction surgery on his knee in 2020, starting the long process of regaining his mobility just as the COVID-19 pandemic hit the construction industry. He reluctantly closed his company and moved with Alsu to Sydney, where he opened a shop selling tobacco and assorted paraphernalia. (After he became famous, it was reported that he had pleaded guilty to a number of minor tobacco offences in 2022, the same year he was granted citizenship.) He says the shop was only ever a stopgap. He sold it late last year, before Bondi, with the intention of returning to carpentry.

When Al Ahmed came to Australia, he was keen to adopt local ways. He tried to learn to ride a surfboard but couldn’t get the hang of it: he kept falling into the water, and he wasn’t a strong swimmer. The waves scared him. He loved beaches, though, Bondi Beach in particular.

During his military service, Al Ahmed learnt how to clean a gun but not how to use it. He didn’t fire a single shot. At Bondi, he didn’t fire, either, which meant that Akram was able to get to his feet and retreat to the bridge. There he picked up another gun and resumed shooting before he was felled by a police bullet.

In the days afterwards, amid the outpouring of admiration for Al Ahmed, some wondered why he didn’t shoot Akram when he had the chance. Among them was Gefen Bitton, an Israeli man who had arrived at his side as he tackled Akram and seized the rifle. In a recent book, Bondi Terror, by Sharri Markson and Alex Ryvchin, Bitton says he yelled at Al Ahmed: “What the f--- are you doing? F---ing shoot him or give me the gun.”

I ask Al Ahmed if he has ever regretted not pulling the trigger. “Never, never, never,” he says. “My target, when I attacked him, was just to disarm him and stop him from killing people. Attempt to shoot him, no. I’m not the one who can do this. Taking the life of someone – it’s not my job.”

The other gunman, Akram’s son, Naveed, kept firing from the bridge, and both Bitton and Al Ahmed were seriously injured. Five bullets entered Al Ahmed’s left arm and shoulder. He says the medics who treated him improvised a way to get him to an ambulance. “They said, ‘Forgive us, but we need to put you on a surfboard.’ ” Lying on his back, looking at the sky as he was carried to the carpark, he reflected that his wife would be amused if she could see him: “Ahmed Al Ahmed, finally on a surfboard.”

The Akrams were supporters of Islamic State. Sajid was shot dead by police. Naveed would be charged with 78 offences, including 15 counts of murder and 43 of attempted murder.

Al Ahmed says Alsu wasn’t entirely pleased when she learnt what he had done. “She asked me, ‘You didn’t think about your kids?’ I told her, ‘I did think about my kids but forgive me, I couldn’t handle it. People crying. Women. And no one there. It was a hard situation.’ ” He says he emphasised to his wife that he hadn’t intended to put himself in danger. “I ran to protect myself, to hide from the firing, like everyone. But when the evil came in front of me, forgive me, I’m not the person who can sit and wait and look.”

Alsu and Al Ahmed have two daughters, Sofia, now aged 6, and Claudia, 3. Al Ahmed says Sofia had a question for him when she visited him in hospital. “She told me, ‘Dad, why didn’t you go to take the gun from the other guy, on the bridge?’ ”

The governor-general, Sam Mostyn, came to his bedside, too, as did Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and the people who started the online appeal that raised more than $2.5 million for him from donors around the world. “He’d become a global story,” says Ian Robertson, a media law specialist and chair of legal firm Holding Redlich, who offered to help Al Ahmed navigate the unfamiliar territory in which he found himself. “He was not only getting inquiries from the Australian media, he was getting them from overseas as well. He was in pain, he wasn’t sleeping at all well, and he had this avalanche of people basically hounding him. So the job was to try to get that under control.”

Al Ahmed was part of a small group of Bondi survivors and first responders honoured at the Sydney Cricket Ground before the final Test of the summer’s Ashes series in January. As the applause of the huge crowd washed over him, he bowed his head and put his right hand over his heart. Soon afterwards, he accepted an invitation to the US, where he visited a holy site of the Jewish movement known as Chabad. He was photographed praying alongside Rabbi Yehoram Ulman, founder of Chabad of Bondi and father-in-law of Rabbi Eli Schlanger, one of the 15 people killed by the terrorists. That Al Ahmed wore a yarmulke, the traditional Jewish skullcap, drew criticism in some quarters. In his book, he explains that he believes in respecting others’ religious beliefs and customs. “If they were to visit my mosque, they would remove their shoes,” he writes. “It’s a matter of basic humanity.”

In New York, he met Democratic mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and was stopped in Times Square by a couple of cops on the beat, who asked if they could have a photo with him. Then it was on to Washington DC, where he was feted by members of the US Congress. They’d all seen the viral video. Most of them gave him medals. “They gave me their business cards as well,” he says. “Nice people. I love America.”

Back in Australia, Ian Robertson watched Al Ahmed get a standing ovation as he was presented with the key to the City of Canterbury-Bankstown, a local government area in south-western Sydney. “He was kind of mobbed by people wanting to shake his hand and pat his back,” Robertson says. “Everywhere I went with him, same reaction. People walked up to him in the street to say, ‘Good on you’.” In March, he was given the key to the City of Waverley, which incorporates Bondi. With the key came a lifetime beach parking permit – a welcome gift for a man who’d collected a few tickets there in his time.

Robertson likes the way Al Ahmed has handled the attention. “Polite, unassuming, humble,” Robertson says. “Obviously, what he’s done is amazing but he hasn’t sought to exaggerate it. Look, in my view he’s an all-round nice guy.”

Tears rolled down Al Ahmed’s cheeks as he sat in the studio of Sydney radio station 2GB on a morning in June. The previous month, his two younger brothers had been arrested and charged after he told police they had threatened to hurt him if he didn’t give them each $100,000 of the GoFundMe money. Both pleaded not guilty (and the case is still before the courts). Now Al Ahmed himself was in trouble. His father, by then living in Australia, had accused him of assaulting him, and Al Ahmed had been charged accordingly. “I’m honest. Innocent,” he told host Ben Fordham, who elicited from him that he believed his father was paying him back for reporting his brothers to the police. “Either I withdraw the case against the brothers or he will go put [a] case against me,” he said to Fordham.

In August, his father retracted his allegation and the charges against Al Ahmed were dropped. He tells me he holds no grudge – “We are human, we have to forgive” – but it is clear that the family conflict has shaken him. Less upsetting but nonetheless unsettling are the attacks online by total strangers. The nastiness of the anonymous critics bewilders him: “Who is this? I don’t know him. He doesn’t know anything about me.”

Al Ahmed still has two bullets in his left arm. Doctors have told him it’s best to leave them there. He hopes to get back the use of the arm and hand, but so far the improvement has been modest. The emotional wounds are still with him, too. He thinks a lot about the people who died at Bondi, especially the youngest of them, 10-year-old Matilda Britvan. He is acutely conscious that while he confronted a gunman and lived to tell the tale, others who did so – Boris and Sofia Gurman, Reuven Morrison – were killed. He takes sleeping tablets and anti-anxiety medication. “It’s a little bit to forget what happened,” he says. “Because the situation was too big. It was horrible.” He knows he isn’t the only one who can’t get the images out of his head. “I’m one of maybe hundreds, or thousands, of people who are struggling from this.”

He is pleased to have had the chance to put everything down in his book (which is a collaboration with the ghostwriter Liam Pieper, whose previous credits include The Happiest Man on Earth, the best-selling memoir of Holocaust survivor Eddie Jaku). Al Ahmed says his next project will be to establish a foundation to help women and children affected by domestic violence. A cause that is close to his heart.

It’s still raining when we leave the RSL club, so Al Ahmed and I share an umbrella. We head for the old palm tree that gave him some cover when shots were being fired at him that day, and he matter-of-factly shows me the marks made by four bullets that hit the thick trunk. Then we walk the short distance to the pedestrian bridge and stand underneath it, sheltering from the weather. Al Ahmed’s leather loafers are dripping wet. “They’re brand new. Just today,” he says as he wipes them with a tissue.

I commiserate. What a shame! “All good,” he says with a smile. “Doesn’t matter. I’m healthy. I’m here. I’m alive.”

Light Will Win: The Bondi Hero’s Story of Humanity, Hope and Courage (Pan Macmillan Australia) is out November 10.

White House event reveals Ukraine and Russia share one goal: flattering Melania

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 20:52:27 GMT

As war rages on in Kyiv and other cities, the first lady celebrates her single-city ceasefire with Russian and Ukrainian envoys

Beaming from a podium in the White House’s Grand Foyer, Melania Trump welcomed senior Russian and Ukrainian officials on Thursday to celebrate a ceasefire in an embattled Ukrainian town for which she has become the unlikeliest broker.

The evacuation from Oleshky, a frontline Ukrainian town now occupied by Russia where 800 people lived through a protracted humanitarian crisis, may seem like a sideshow at this point in the war. Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv and other major cities, and a single Russian strike described as a “double-tap” bombing killed 40 people in Zaporizhzhia on Wednesday.

So it could have been easy to brush the White House meeting off as a chance for Ukraine and Russia to flatter the first lady. And flatter her they did, praising her for her diplomatic acumen, delivering her state awards and even gifting her trinkets of thanks from the residents of Oleshky whom she saved. In case the subtext was not yet clear, a children’s drawing gifted by the Russian side was inscribed: “I love Melania.”

But there was real diplomatic juice in the room as Trump, a former model who has occupied a relatively quiet role in her husband’s second term as president, now played host to one of the highest-level gatherings of Russian and Ukrainian officials in recent months.

Kirill Dmitriev, the sanctioned head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund who regularly negotiates for Moscow, was seated next to Davyd Arakhamia, the head of Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party and a chief negotiator for Ukraine. Next to them were Ukraine’s Dmytro Lubinets and Russia’s Yana Lantratova, the respective human rights ombudspeople who have become an unlikely and respectful double act throughout the evacuation process.

The meeting came after a particularly bitter public feud between Zelenskyy and Trump, as the US cut intelligence sharing and satellite internet in recent weeks in an apparent effort to pressure Kyiv into capitulating. And the Trump administration’s plans with Russia are in peril after the midterms, with triumphant Democrats promising to investigate senior aides to Trump who had pitched Russia on business deals to end the war in Ukraine.

But everyone at the White House on Thursday was focused on feting Melania, whose role in brokering the ceasefire was extensively praised at every opportunity – even if her descriptions of reviewing de-mining plans and assessing evacuation routes strained belief.

As well as the drawing, Dmitriev extended her a personal expression of gratitude from Vladimir Putin, while on the Ukrainian side, Lubinets presented her with the order of Princess Olga, first class – one of the country’s highest honours. He also issued a general request: “Please continue to do your wonderful work and support people.”

Stepping into the role of diplomat and humanitarian, the first lady called for “humanity over war” and said that she hoped the limited ceasefire in the frontline town would “inspire greater peace”.

“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” she said. “Let us see Oleshky as a spark in a world of darkness, capable of illuminating the best in humanity. Build a powerful flame of peace, visible to the world. Ignite hope, foster cooperation and brighten a path toward lasting peace.”

Later, she handed personal letters to Dmitriev and Arakhamia to bring back to Putin and Zelenskyy.

It was an unusual role for Trump, who has not taken part in high-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia before, and is said behind the scenes to have been critical of her husband’s heavy-handed approach to dealing with Ukraine.

But she has increasingly engaged in humanitarian efforts related to the conflict, first by working on a program that reunified more than 30 children displaced from their families during the conflict.

In Oleshky, she also claimed to have been involved in “every stage” of the planning. To do so, she said, she had “reviewed de-mining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles and medical resources”.

Now the White House has cast her as a dark horse diplomat.

“This unprecedented gathering marks the first time in US history that an American first lady has personally brought representatives of two nations actively at war together at the White House to pursue diplomatic and humanitarian objectives,” said Marc Beckman, an aide who is self-described as her exclusive senior adviser.

What’s clear is that at this moment both sides have recognised the need to keep Melania – and the testy Trump administration – onside.

Lewis Hamilton refuses to back down over criticism of teammate Leclerc

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 20:38:12 GMT

Ferrari teammates clashed at Mexico Grand Prix

Hamilton: ‘I’ve worked hard to build a relationship with Charles’

Lewis Hamilton vowed not to be silenced last night as he refused to back down over his criticism of his Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc after a flashpoint between the pair at last weekend’s Mexico Grand Prix.

Leclerc and Hamilton were competing with one another at turn four on the opening lap of the race in Mexico last Sunday, with Leclerc attempting to pass his teammate. He went off in doing so and Hamilton’s defence left him vulnerable to being passed by Max Verstappen who went on to win, costing Ferrari a potential one-two.

Ferrari do not have formal rules of engagement between their drivers and Hamilton said at the time that the team had “big, big problems”, later squarely blaming his teammate for costing them a shot at victory. “The guy is 28 years old, so I don’t think it’s an age thing. I think it’s a mentality thing. It’s like ‘do or die. Either I win or none of us do’,” he said.

Speaking before this weekend’s São Paulo Grand Prix Hamilton was insistent he would not back down from his remarks. “I don’t really care what everyone thinks about what I said, I wear my heart on my sleeve and I say how I feel in the moment,” he said. “Of course there’s sometimes you say things and maybe you might regret it afterwards. I don’t.

“I’m never going to apologise for being authentic and real and I’m not going to be silenced. I have not been asked to not say anything and that’s just the way it is.”

Leclerc did not take part in media commitments on Thursday in São Paulo as he was attending the birth of his first child, so has yet to respond to Hamilton, who maintained that Ferrari needed to address the issue but also noted that the pair have yet to have the chance to speak to Fred Vasseur, the team principal.

Leclerc has been with the Scuderia since 2019 while Hamilton joined in 2025 and the pair enjoyed a good working relationship last year. However, this season, with the Briton enjoying the better form of the two, the incident in Mexico was the third time they have been at odds with one another on track.

The seven-time champion was clear, however, he had no intention of not fighting his corner on or off the track. “He is very much embedded within the team and I knew that it would always be a challenge, I’ve always respected that,” he said. “I’ve really worked hard to build a good relationship with Charles and bridge the gap and make sure that we’re harmonious and work hard together.

“Naturally, it’s not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I’m very outspoken and I push and push and push for so many changes and I’m going to be pushing for more as long as I’m here. That’s how it’s going to be.

“I’m here to win and to be able to win you have to work with everyone around you. I truly believe that this team can be fighting for the championship next year.”

Having secured the drivers’ championship with Kimi Antonelli last weekend, Mercedes can also clinch the constructors’ title in Brazil if they outscore Ferrari by three points.

British Ebola patient evacuated from DR Congo arrives at London hospital

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 20:30:11 GMT

Doctor who was helping response to outbreak in Africa taken to specialist isolation unit at Royal Free hospital

A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment.

The patient, whose identity is unknown, was transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday. They are now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London.

Dr Renu Bindra, the deputy director for all-hazards public health response at the UK Health Security Agency, said: “UKHSA and the NHS have well-established and robust infection prevention and control protocols to limit the risk of onward transmission, and the risk to the wider public remains low.”

A humanitarian organisation sent the doctor to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free's isolation unit has strict protocols in place to prevent the patient coming into contact with any members of the public, and all staff treating the patient are equipped with the necessary personal protective equipment alongside other measures to prevent transmission.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared in May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths. It has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, and last month Nigeria confirmed a case in its capital, Abuja.

People with the disease tend to fall ill two to 21 days after contact with an orthoebolavirus. Initial symptoms include fever, aches, pains, and fatigue, but can then progress to diarrhoea, vomiting and unexplained bleeding.

Jimmy Anderson in talks with Surrey to continue county career after Lancashire exit

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 20:06:24 GMT

Division One side have offered Anderson a contract

Nottinghamshire also monitoring seamer’s situation

Jimmy Anderson has opened talks over signing for Surrey next season with the club growing in confidence that England’s leading wicket-taker will agree to join them for what would be a remarkable swansong.

The 44-year-old has been inundated with expressions of interest since being released by Lancashire last month after 25 years at Old Trafford, with Surrey understood to have made a firm move by offering him a contract.

Anderson had initially contemplated retirement after being left feeling “sadness and shock” at being let go in a meeting with Lancashire’s new director of cricket, Paul Farbrace, but appears increasingly likely to play on despite turning 45 next July.

Unlike many other counties Surrey have the resources to make Anderson an attractive offer and can easily accommodate him within the England and Wales Cricket Board’s £3.2m salary cap, which the club rarely spends in full due to the number of centrally contracted players on their books.

Nine Surrey players were given central contracts by the ECB last month including five seam bowlers in Gus Atkinson, Sam Curran, Matthew Fisher, Jamie Overton and Henry Crocombe, but there are also compelling cricketing reasons for signing Anderson.

Surrey can offer a return to Division One of the County Championship after Anderson took 50 wickets at an average of 17.68 in Division Two last season, as well as a competitive team capable of challenging for the title playing at a Test venue. The club are yet to appoint a head coach for next season after Gareth Batty, who won three successive County Championships between 2022 and 2024, left the Oval to join Chennai Super Kings last month.

Nottinghamshire are also monitoring Anderson’s situation as they are in the market for an experienced seam bowler, but their preference is understood to be signing Ollie Robinson, who has been given permission to talk to other clubs by Sussex as he would command a transfer fee with 12 months left on his contract.

Anderson has already ruled out moving across the Pennines to Yorkshire, telling the Tailenders podcast that he “wouldn’t have thought so” when asked if that was a possibility last month.

Meanwhile, it has emerged that the Northamptonshire and former Australia batter Chris Lynn has served a one-month ban after testing positive for cocaine at the end of the summer’s T20 Blast.

Lynn accepted the charge from the Cricket Regulator, having admitted to taking the drug after the Steelbacks’s quarter-final victory over Gloucestershire at Wantage Road back in July.

The 36-year-old retired hurt during the match but played at Finals Day the following weekend as Northamptonshire lifted the trophy for the third time in their history. Lynn was selected for doping control after the final, with his eventual ban cut from three months to one after agreeing to undergo a “substance of abuse treatment programme”.

Kamada’s late leveller rescues point for 10-man Crystal Palace and denies Hoffenheim

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 19:56:39 GMT

A late, late strike from Daichi Kamada saved Crystal Palace from embarrassment and another round of navel gazing as they snatched a Europa League draw with Hoffenheim against the odds.

After being outplayed by a side currently in the bottom half of the Bundesliga, and a goal down from the seventh minute, Palace looked to have lost all hope in this fixture when Adam Wharton was dismissed with 13 minutes to go. But after Hoffenheim failed to clear a goalmouth scramble in added time, Kamada fired home under the keeper to generate a rare moment of elation at Selhurst Park this season.

After the match, the beleaguered Pierre Sage struggled to put a positive gloss on events. Asked if he thought his team had deserved their point, he said it “depended on the moment of the game” and while he had praise for his side’s attitude he was critical of their tactical performance. “Offensively we did better than our two previous games but we have to continue to improve defensively”, he said. “We gave up too much space to the opponent and sometimes we had difficulty in duels. When we try to attack a little bit we are very quickly open.”

To be fair to Sage this was an accurate call. Palace were in the match throughout without ever dominating, and Hoffenheim created the best chances in the game without ever having to try too hard. Sitting in 20th place in the Europa League, Palace have work to do in this competition, offering no respite from their Premier League travails, with a visit from Liverpool next up on Sunday.

With a tea-time kick-off on Bonfire Night, a family-friendly crowd might have had a right to expect fireworks. Palace set off with intensity but were sloppy too and coughed up an easy opening goal in the game’s early knockings. Wharton gave possession away cheaply about 20 yards from the Hoffenheim goal. There were perhaps just three touches before the ball reached Tim Lemperle wide right, who whipped the ball first time to the advancing Alexander Pass. The winger’s shot was equally immediate and caught Dean Henderson cold, his save too slow, and the ball squirmed through his midriff before rolling over the line.

The Palace support did not moan and got on with supporting their team. Sadly the team on the pitch did not respond in desired fashion and Hoffenheim should have scored again through a Andrej Kramaric volley in the 23rd minute, well saved by Henderson on this occasion, before Palace started to work their way into the game.

Yéremy Pino was the focus of the home side’s hopes and he was both Palace’s brightest spark and their greatest frustration. He could find the gaps that no one else could but his delivery was either inaccurate or overcomplicated.

He did at least find the right weight on a through ball to Kamada on the half hour, only for his fellow number 10 in Pierre Sage’s system to pull a cross shot beyond Oliver Baumann’s far post. Hoffenheim had a better opportunity for themselves just before half-time, Ozan Kabak heading over at a corner when unmarked six yards out.

The second half started with another burst of intensity from Palace, but it duly fizzled out again and within 10 minutes Sage had made a double change, pulling Kamada back into midfield and bringing Eddie Nketiah into the front three to strengthen Palace’s finishing options. In the 66th minute Palace created their best chance of the match, when Wharton faked to shoot from the edge of the box, cut left and slipped in Pino who looked to shoot over the advancing Baumann only for the keeper to stand his ground and deflect the ball to safety.

You might have thought a rally could spring from there, but no. Hoffenheim soon won a couple of corners on the bounce and killed any home side momentum.

Then Wharton got himself sent off, made a poor decision to lead with his elbow in contesting a header. Horatiu Fesnic did not need a second look and despite Wharton’s protestations the referee showed him a second yellow card.

A sense of injustice did at least succeed in inducing some pep into Palace’s performance while Hoffenheim stepped back and sought to run down the clock. Palace created only one opportunity and that was a bit of a mess, but if there was to be respite from Palace’s perilous Premier League condition it was going to need a bit of fortune, and Kamada duly seized upon it when it arrived.

DP World Tour ready to extend olive branch to rebels including DeChambeau after LIV Golf collapse

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 19:24:23 GMT

Bankruptcy proceedings for LIV Golf begin in New Jersey court

DP World Tour expecting an influx of players from LIV Golf

The DP World Tour is expecting an influx of players from LIV Golf next year and is ready to extend an olive branch to all the former rebels, including the face of its doomed revival, Bryson DeChambeau.

The two-time US Open winner had been due to sign for LIV 2.0 next season, saying recently their “business plan made a lot of sense” and that the reborn rebel tour would “last forever,” but instead they began bankruptcy proceedings in a New Jersey court on Thursday following the withdrawal of their primary financiers, BC Partners.

In a 13-minute hearing LIV’s lawyers announced formal plans to liquidate rather than set up a new tour following the decision of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund to withdraw their funding from next season.

PIF spent more than $7bn in five years setting up the rebel tour that split golf in two before protracted talks over merging with the PGA and DP World Tours involving US president Donald Trump that ultimately collapsed.

“The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan,” Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in court. “Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximising wind-down in their business.”

LIV subsequently released a statement confirming their withdrawal from the sport. It read: “Since April 2026, the league’s leadership team, with the support of its independent directors and advisors, has run a disciplined and thorough process to identify the best path forward for the company and its stakeholders.

“Despite extensive discussions, the relevant parties were ultimately unable to reach a consensual resolution of certain outstanding terms of the transaction contemplated by the Restructuring Support Agreement (RSA).

“As a result, the RSA has been terminated, and the transaction is not expected to move forward at this time.”

LIV’s withdrawal just a month after announcing BC Partners’ funding has left their players facing uncertain futures, although many of them will have the option to join the DP World Tour through a variety of means, if not the PGA Tour.

DeChambeau is ineligible to join the PGA Tour, where he has not played for more than four years, due to a blanket ban on LIV players that runs for 12 months from the date of their last tournament appearance on the Saudi Arabia-funded circuit.

The 33-year-old has never been a member of the DP World Tour, but as a former major winner has an option to join that expires next year, with 16 November the deadline for applications.

Under DP World Tour regulations major champions are given a five-year window for joining, but 12 months is taken off for every year the option is not activated, leaving 2027 as the last season open to DeChambeau.

The major champion window has already expired for LIV players Cameron Smith and Dustin Johnson, although the DP World Tour will permit them to play at certain events under their new Invite Policy, which represents an attempt to add value to lesser tournaments.

Such invitations will not be offered to premier events such as the PGA Championship at Wentworth or the Scottish Open, but a tournament victory elsewhere would permit the winner to apply for category three membership of the DP World Tour facilitating a full return.

Other LIV players eligible for invitations include Joaquin Niemann, Thomas Pieters, Charles Howell III and Lucas Herbert.

after newsletter promotion

In addition around 15 LIV players, including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton, still hold DP World Tour membership so are eligible for every event. Although Sergio García resigned his membership in 2022 to join LIV the Spaniard’s career earnings mean he retains a category ranking and is able to reapply, which he has said he will do.

With no indication from the PGA Tour that they are willing to relax their one-year ban following LIV’s implosion many of the rebels appear likely to play at DP World Tour events, following the example set by Patrick Reed. On leaving LIV Golf in August 2025 the American joined the DP World Tour and is currently No 2 in the rankings, earning a PGA Tour card for next season.

While they have not commented publicly, DP World Tour officials are understood to feel that LIV’s imminent liquidation has vindicated their new hardline approach to the tour. Any player who signed up for LIV 2.0 would have been banned from the DP World Tour next year and been ineligible for the 2027 Ryder Cup, with chief executive officer Guy Kinnings saying the players must “make a choice,” a new policy that led to Rahm and Hatton leaving LIV. While LIV 2.0 did have $300m of funding in place from BC Partners they were unable to secure enough players to service the planned 17-tournament global season.

With the two main tours both making clear that the era of conditional releases and “double dipping” was over only 15 players led by DeChambeau agreed to stay on, with the Financial Times reporting that only four of them signed contracts.

BC Partners claimed last month that they had 30 players committed to sign up, with another 10 still deliberating, but proved unable to agree financial terms with enough of them, as they confirmed in a statement following the court hearing.

“BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf,” it read.

“While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders.”

Trump is soothing the midterms loss with what he loves best: interior design

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 19:12:23 GMT

The president seems to accept this is his last White House stint and is focused on renovating whatever he can get his little hands on

As you’d expect, the right is in a shambles right now. Elon Musk is making jokes about his “election-interfering space lasers” and pretending that he really, really doesn’t care that he threw away nearly half a billion dollars trying to influence the midterms. JD Vance is writing long essays on social media about how he agrees the Iran war was a bit of an oopsie.

Donald Trump, meanwhile, seems to be going through his own idiosyncratic grieving process about the Republicans’ historic midterm beating. The president has skipped all the way past shock, denial and anger and landed at the “admiring my beautiful renovations” stage of grief.

In his very first public appearance after the midterms, Trump did not offer a path forward for the Republicans or unpack what went wrong. Instead, he stood at the construction site where the new White House ballroom will be built and waxed lyrical about how incredible the building will be.

“This has been a structure the likes of which has never been seen anywhere,” Trump told the press corps as a building crew prepared to install the final beam in the ballroom. He then spent more than 20 minutes talking about “magnificent columns”, marble floors, cocktail rooms and Corinthian design.

Finally, in great detail, he explained what the public was so desperate to know: why were the ballroom’s kitchens going to be underground? “If I put the kitchen on top, you would lose three walls, because a kitchen takes about 30% of the space,” Trump noted.

“I love construction,” the president added, before signing a beam with a black Sharpie.

The midterms did eventually come up, but only because reporters insisted on asking about all that nasty business. “If I were on the ballot, I would have won,” Trump shrugged. I guess he forgot the part where he told voters: “Just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot.” According to a Washington Post analysis, he repeated variations of this statement 63 times.

Trump’s reaction to the midterm loss this week was noticeably different from what it was in 2018. While Republicans may not have been rebuked quite as badly then as they were this year, they still lost the House of Representatives. In the aftermath of that defeat, Trump reacted with his characteristic conspiracy and anger. He called the results a “tremendous success” and insulted his enemies. “Mia Love gave me no love, but then she lost,” Trump said in the 2018 press conference, referring to a Utah Republican who lost her House re-election bid. “Too bad.”

Then again, Trump 2.0, as we have all come to painfully realize, is a very different beast from the first incarnation. While the president’s reaction to Tuesday’s defeat may seem bizarre, it is in keeping with the priorities of his second term. Despite all his threats about running for president again, Trump seems to have accepted that this will be his last stint in the White House and is focused on leaving a legacy. He wants to slap his name on as many things as possible, renovate whatever he can get his little hands on, and build a bunch of self-aggrandizing monuments.

“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere,” Barack Obama joked at a recent Ohio rally, in reference to Trump’s aesthetics obsession. “He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV.”

Trump did not find this particularly amusing. “I paid for it myself. I fixed it, and now it’s more beautiful and in better shape,” the president said in defence of his White House upgrades. Obama, he added, just didn’t get it because he is a man who “doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the right thing”.

Trump’s construction projects may soon end up being undermined by more than just jokes. Democrats are already scrutinizing the funding of the ballroom. Now that they control the House and Senate, they could even move to block some of Trump’s building plans, arguing that they haven’t been authorized by Congress and are therefore illegal. And they could clamp down on some of the renovation excesses: despite all his guff about bringing jobs back to America, Trump has outsourced the carving of his ballroom’s Corinthian columns to Italy.

But even if the Democrats manage to rein Trump in, he’s still made an indelible mark on Washington. Work on his 250ft “triumphal arch” could get started this week if a judge gives approval. And the president has just wrapped up a $14m project to clean up the “filthy” Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rid of the algae blooms turning it green.

It’s been a long and difficult battle against the algae but, in a press conference on Monday, the eve of election day, Trump declared “mission accomplished”. In the last press conference before polls opened, Trump did not make a final plea to voters – instead he patted himself on the back about how wonderful the pool was looking. Standing in front of a sign that said: “Back, and more beautiful than ever!” Trump declared that the pool project should unite all Americans. As voters, angry about the price of groceries and gas, prepared to register their anger at the voting booth, Trump held up pictures of rusted pipes and explained the virtues of painting the pool “American flag blue”.

And look, I’ve got to give the president his due. The water does look a bit clearer now. And it’s certainly doing more reflecting than the president is.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

US midterm voters responded in a thunderous voice. This is just the beginning

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 19:09:42 GMT

A note from our US editor: A reckoning is coming, but make no mistake: Trump is still president – we’ll need a free press in 2027 as much as we did in darker days. Please help today if you are able

Betsy Reed is US editor of the Guardian

Over the past two years, millions of people all over the world have watched Donald Trump’s destructive reign unfold with one question in their minds: Is there no check on his power?

This week, voters deciding who controls Congress responded in a thunderous voice: there must be a check on the president’s power. From Texas to Ohio to South Carolina, Americans surged to the polls to register their opposition to Donald Trump – and to show their support for the kind of leaders who will look out for the interests of everyday people rather than those of a corrupt ruling elite. And now many people are looking at politics with a new and unfamiliar feeling of hope.

As this new moment dawns, let’s not forget that, before voters had the chance to weigh in, there were precious few powerful institutions willing to take on Trump’s corruption and lies. Major law firms and universities capitulated to his threats and intimidation. Some corporate news outlets bowed to his pressure, too.

But the independent press stood out as one of the only forces for accountability, uncovering the truth at a time when lies are woven into our information ecosystem – and, crucially, making sure the public understood what was at stake in this election.

Now, an emboldened Congress is poised to investigate Trump and interrogate his appointees about their agenda and qualifications. The Guardian’s small but mighty political reporting team will closely examine the evidence behind allegations of corruption and wrongdoing.

So a reckoning is coming, but make no mistake: Trump is still the president of the United States – the single most powerful person on the planet – with all the degraded norms and protections of friendly supreme court justices he had before. He still has staggering power to launch destabilizing wars of choice, to worsen the affordability crisis with tariffs, to sacrifice Ukraine to Russia, to give tech oligarchs free rein over our humanity and our economy, and to weaponize the justice department and other agencies for his political ends.

While I don’t like to engage in the game of political prognosis, it seems highly unlikely, based on past experience with this man, that Trump will respond to a midterm drubbing by moderating his political stances.

When his back is up against the wall – as it surely will be with a Democratic House and Senate – we can expect a maelstrom of fury and desperate deal-making.

We will need a free press in 2027 as much as we relied on one in the darkest days of 2025 and 2026. At its best, a truly free press can speak directly to the public, shedding light on hidden schemes and revealing the whole picture of our flawed world. Yet these are not the best of times: Trump’s crackdown on the press shows no signs of letting up; consolidated ownership means fewer options and less diversity of perspective; and the advent of AI has threatened the entire business model of journalism, resulting in extreme staff layoffs that have gutted newsrooms.

The Guardian is fortunate to have no billionaire owner, no corporate bosses who put profit over mission. We’re accountable to the facts and to our readers. And the Guardian is fortunate to have our readers who are willing to open their wallets, commit month after month, to help sustain our independence.

We have an excellent team of reporters, editors and others who work hard each day to bring you the news. We don’t cut corners on getting our facts right.

From reporting on the ground to fending off legal risks to keeping our reporters safe, journalism is incredibly expensive to do well. To help fund our work in 2027, we are looking to raise $2,000,000 by the end of the year. If you can contribute any amount, please do so. If you can contribute monthly, even better – I need to know we have the resources to report on the final throes of Trump’s presidency in what may be a tumultuous year ahead.

As I’ve reminded you before: journalism sustains democracy. Together, we’ll sustain journalism.

I know the dangers a wounded Trump presents – this is how the UK should deal with him now

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 19:00:31 GMT

Power is draining away at home, but the US president will see a chance to make his mark through foreign policy

Kim Darroch was Britain’s ambassador to the US between January 2016 and December 2019

Election nights are party time in Washington. The bars and restaurants fill up and the city rocks. For diplomats, it’s an opportunity – but it’s also a long night, as you trek across the party scene in search of insight and illumination. Invariably, it has its moments. I recall being at the Washington Post party on the night of the presidential election on 8 November 2016. Washington is an overwhelmingly Democrat city and the atmosphere was raucously optimistic, reflecting Hillary Clinton’s small but consistent lead in the polls. As the first results came in a shocked hush fell across the room. People gathered in small, murmuring groups. Within 30 minutes, half the guests had left.

In contrast, I recall speaking to Nancy Pelosi, the queen of the Democrats, at a watch party on 6 November 2018, for the midterms during Trump’s first presidency. I asked her what I should put in my overnight report to London, given that most results wouldn’t be in. She said, with striking confidence, that I should predict that the Democrats would retake the House of Representatives. She was right: the Democrats flipped 41 Republican seats. It gave Pelosi a second term as speaker of the House and gave the world the enjoyable theatre of her sitting directly behind Trump at his State of the Union speeches, rolling her eyes at the bombast.

So what judgments will the current generation of British diplomats have made about the extraordinary political earthquake of Tuesday night, and its implications for British interests and the handling of our most important bilateral relationship for the next two years?

The starting point has to be the scale of this victory. The blue tsunami has swept the Democrats into ownership of the House, the Senate and the majority of governors’ mansions across the country. To a real estate guy such as Donald Trump, imagine how galling it must be to lose so much property in one night: the Monopoly board almost swept clean. The Democrats ended their lockout from rural states by taking the cornfields of Iowa. After a succession of “close, but no cigar” elections, they finally took a Senate seat in Texas. And they even won in Kansas, which hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. In short, it is beyond the Democrats’ wildest dreams and the most comprehensive rejection conceivable of the president’s policies and actions of the last two years.

Now we are left to wonder how this bloodbath will affect Trump’s behaviour over the remaining 26 months and 14 days of his presidency. The Washington insider gossip after his 2018 defeat was that Trump had taken it badly; he felt humiliated and was casting around for people to blame. Well, this is a much worse beating. So expect the Trump woodchipper to be fired up. Pete Hegseth first in the hopper? Or the chief of staff, Susie Wiles?

But never mind Trump’s hurt feelings: what about the stuff that matters to us? As JD Vance has pointed out – at some risk to his personal relationship with the president – the conflict with Iran and its impact on global energy prices was a big part of this election disaster.

The problem for Trump is that he hasn’t got an obvious exit ramp. Negotiations are taking place with Iran via intermediaries. US demands seem to change every day, but they centre on ending the Iranian nuclear programme and the destruction of what Trump calls the “nuclear dust” – Iran’s stock of 440kg of highly enriched uranium. But the Iranians are demanding a huge amount in return – security guarantees, the end of the US naval blockade, an end to sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets, a reduction of US forces in the region and even, by some accounts, the strategic prize of sovereignty over the strait of Hormuz. And they think they can outlast the Americans: after all, they live there while the Americans are just visiting.

So perhaps there will be a deal with the midterms out of the way. But equally, given how far apart the parties are, this might drag on, compounding the economic damage for all of us. And the bombing might restart: the Israelis clearly want this, and Trump seems to be keeping his options open, moving more military hardware to the region. No one knows which way he will jump – least of all perhaps Trump himself.

As for Ukraine, for whatever reason (and the conspiracy theories abound), Trump has always appeared to blame Volodymyr Zelenskyy rather than Vladimir Putin for the war. I think he will continue to advocate a peace settlement involving Ukraine giving up all of the Donbas (including the territory Putin has failed to capture) and promising never to join Nato or the EU. Zelenskyy will refuse to sign up to this. So, absent some surprise Putin concessions – of which there have been none to date – this too could drag on and on.

Then we have the continuing possibility of new tariffs. Trump has argued for tariffs for more than 40 years. They will remain his instrument of choice for coercion or punishment. He might use them against Europe if we displease him in any way – for example, by refusing to follow US policy on China, by regulating AI, or by raising new taxes on US tech companies.

So there is no shortage of risks. And there may be more in the pipeline. The loss of Congress will mean Trump is heavily constrained on domestic policy: expect endless fights, vetoes and deadlocks. But he will still have a relatively free hand on foreign policy. And he will want to do things: a deal with Putin, conceivably sacrificing Ukraine, to get US hands on Russia’s energy resources and rare earths; a big trade deal with China; perhaps regime change in Cuba. European and British interests will not figure in his calculations, any more than they did in the conflict with Iran.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The UK embassy will be advising how best to handle this badly wounded president; how to influence his moves and steer him away from decisions that impact on the wellbeing of the UK. My advice would be to carry on pretty much as before, with one important qualification. We are seeing the beginning of the end of the Trump era. Power is already draining away from him: the vultures are circling. But this is not a man who will settle for just raging at the dying of the light; he will light bonfires to ward it off.

So we have to be careful not to appear to be distancing ourselves or moving on from Trump. His antennae are finely tuned to pick up signals of disrespect. This doesn’t mean turning up the dial on sucking up. But it does mean talking to him intensively, arguably even more so than at present, about the issues that matter to us – Iran, Ukraine, the future of Nato, the global economy. And we should resist the temptation to be seen to be cultivating possible successors from either side of the US political spectrum. Trump needs to believe that we recognise what is actually the case: that he is the president and will call the shots until 20 January 2029.

Kim Darroch was British ambassador to the US from 2016 to 2019, and is author of Collateral Damage: Britain, America and Europe in the Age of Trump

The Guardian view on the midterms and foreign policy: American voters spoke, and now the world waits anxiously

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:52:33 GMT

The Democrats have gained new powers to constrain Donald Trump. But the drubbing that Republicans received could yet prompt him to new excesses

Donald Trump is a president without parallel, but history can still be instructive. Lame duck presidents often focus on foreign policy to escape domestic discontent and establish a legacy in an area where a hostile Congress offers less of an obstacle. Mr Trump, who was stunningly rebuffed by voters in Tuesday’s midterms, might seek satisfaction in construction projects, the 2028 presidential race and his family’s future. Or, amid the humiliation and with Republican critics growing louder, he could distract attention with fresh adventurism – perhaps escalating against Cuba – or more likely a vengeful new offensive against Iran.

Mr Trump won’t put in the legwork or attention to detail demanded by, say, Bill Clinton’s push for lasting peace in the Middle East. But he loves the glitz of state visits, spectacular military action, hobnobbing with strongmen and (unearned) credit for dubious “peace deals”. With a potential three-way meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping mooted for the Apec summit in China this month, Ukraine, Taiwan and others have reason to be nervous.

“The reason we lost [the midterms] is the war,” wrote JD Vance, the vice-president, on X. Mr Trump himself acknowledged Iran’s impact. Though voters don’t always connect action overseas to consequences at home, the link to higher prices was clear. Resuming the bombing would only deepen the crisis. The president has so far withstood Benjamin Netanyahu’s blandishments to renew their illegal war, and the Israeli prime minister is now fighting for political survival after last month’s election. But a negotiated exit looks more difficult than ever. A more militarised and hardline regime in Iran has seen the advantages of broadening the conflict and is crowing over Tuesday’s results.

Mr Trump has accelerated the expansion of executive authority over war, rejecting congressional constraint, and now says he will be “Mr Veto” if the legislature proves a problem. But Democrats’ seizure of Congress, which controls government spending, nonetheless gives them significant new power. They can increase pressure by tying their goals to “must-pass” legislation, though threatening a government shutdown over foreign policy comes with political risks. Control of appropriations committees will enable closer scrutiny of what is being spent, and where. Anti-interventionist Republicans will be reinvigorated – though the president vetoed a bipartisan resolution to end support for Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen in his first term.

At a minimum, the Democrats can increase transparency and accountability for this administration’s crimes and follies, including its treatment of Ukraine and attacks on alleged drugs boats. Investigating the Trump circle’s links with foreign powers and business people could prove especially powerful: voters are increasingly concerned about corruption now that critics have tied it to the affordability crisis.

The midterms are an unusually powerful reminder that foreign and domestic policy cannot be sundered and that voters as well as the leaders they pick shape a country’s relationship with the world. Mr Vance was also striking in stressing the need to “change our relationship to Israel”. Like Mr Trump’s abrupt claim that the US would end military aid by the end of the year, that is a belated response to a seismic shift in public opinion – with most Americans now holding unfavourable views of their ally thanks to Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, and Mr Netanyahu’s pursuit of permawar in the region.

American voters, and people around the world, must hope that newly elected Democrats will be deft in using their new levers to shape US actions. But when voters’ opinions are so strongly held and expressed, that moulds policy too.

Cancer diagnoses in England hit record high of more than 1,000 people a day

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:49:25 GMT

While NHS is identifying more cases, it is failing to meet timescale targets on diagnosis and treatment, experts say

Cancer diagnoses in England have hit record highs, with more than 1,000 people a day diagnosed, NHS figures show.

But experts warned that although the health service was identifying more cases, it was still failing to meet timescale targets on diagnosis and treatment.

According to the latest cancer registration statistics, more than 373,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in England in 2024, the highest figure on record. On average, NHS England diagnosed 1,021 people a day with cancer in 2024, up from 972 a day in 2023.

Prostate, breast, lung and bowel cancers accounted for half of all new diagnoses.

The figures showed improvements in stage at diagnosis: 56.7% of first new cancers were diagnosed at stage 1 and 2 in 2024 compared with 55.8% in 2023.

Prof Peter Johnson, the NHS national clinical director for cancer, said the figures showed the health service was “moving in the right direction” and were testimony to NHS staff’s hard work.

He said: “NHS teams across the country are taking tests and checks closer to the people who need them, and with new treatments being developed all the time, we will continue to do all we can to get people seen and treated for cancer as early as possible.”

Experts urged caution, however, given the NHS is failing to meet its timescale targets. The latest monthly NHS figures show that 78.6% of patients in England urgently referred for suspected cancer were diagnosed or had cancer ruled out within 28 days in August – below the target of 80%.

The health service is lagging even further behind on treatment. The proportion of patients who began treatment for cancer within 62 days of an urgent referral or consultant upgrade was 71.9%, well below the target of 85%.

Dr Ian Walker, the executive director of policy at Cancer Research UK, said: “While NHS staff are diagnosing more people with cancer every day, too many are still being caught at a late stage.”

The health service needed additional support to reduce the number of cancers diagnosed at a late stage and treat patients on time, he added.

Walker said: “The UK government pledged to improve early diagnosis, cancer waiting times and access to treatment in its national cancer plan for England. It now needs to keep its foot on the pedal to ensure cancer patients aren’t let down. The situation won’t change without focused effort from the government, clear accountability, and a guarantee that the NHS will get the specialist staff and equipment it needs.”

Dr Hilary Williams, the clinical vice-president at the Royal College of Physicians and a consultant in medical oncology, said: “More than 1,000 cancer diagnoses every day is a stark reminder of the growing demand on NHS cancer services.

“An ageing population is an important factor in the increase in diagnoses, but we must also recognise the role of obesity, which is a major and often overlooked risk factor for cancer.” She added that alongside preventing cancer, the NHS needed to continue improving early detection, including through the expansion of targeted lung cancer screening.

Williams said: “As more people are diagnosed and live longer with cancer, we must ensure they can access the specialist care and support they need.”

Steven McIntosh, the chief partnerships officer at Macmillan Cancer Support, said the figures also masked persistent health inequalities. “We know that who you are and where you live can still have a significant impact on how likely you are to get cancer, as well as how quickly you are diagnosed and your chances of survival,” he said.

Rachael Franklin, the deputy chief executive of Breast Cancer Now, said with diagnoses at an all-time high and overall incidence increasing, “breast cancer remains the biggest killer of working-age women in the UK, with one in seven women diagnosed in their lifetime”.

“That’s why it’s so important that people of all ages are breast aware and get anything new or unusual checked by a GP as soon as possible. We also urge all eligible women to attend their screening appointment when invited,” she said.

The Guardian view on cocaine and domestic abuse: new links between drugs and crime need investigating

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:47:24 GMT

Patterns of drug supply and use are changing and the government’s five-year-old drug strategy must evolve too

A slight drop in the number of drug deaths over a year in England and Wales is the first such news since 2012. Over the past decade, the grim trajectory has been upward; the annual figure of 5,519 has more than doubled since the 1990s. Given this trend, any fall is a relief. But the spike in deaths linked to cocaine, which has overtaken heroin for the first time, as well as evidence uncovered by the Guardian of a link with domestic violence, points to the need for a drugs policy that takes account of changing usage.

Nearly six in 10 drug tests on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine in the year to June, while a previous study found that 59% of suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates. Links between domestic violence and alcohol have been highlighted by campaigners since the 19th century. In 2022, a UK government report found that alcohol and drug use featured in around a third of 127 domestic homicides it examined.

But while some of the issues thrown up by substance misuse are similar – increased paranoia and aggression placing partners and other relatives of abusers at risk – there are specific challenges around illegal drug use that ministers need to address. One woman told the Guardian that she had covered up her former partner’s cocaine use because she feared police would find out that she had also taken it. Charities are frustrated by the way that the criminal penalties for drug possession make it difficult to offer and access support.

In Scotland, which has the highest rate of drug deaths in Europe, a pilot treatment room is operating in Glasgow, though a sharp rise in deaths suggests that while such rooms may be a pragmatic harm reduction measure, they are not a panacea. In England and Wales, a drugs strategy was launched in 2021 following a review by Prof Dame Carol Black. But while the then Conservative government accepted her recommendation to invest in addiction treatment and research, funding has since been frozen – while wastewater samples and crime figures show that cocaine use has boomed. In the year to March 2025, the police and Border Force made 269,321 drug seizures – the highest on record.

The spending review next year offers a chance for a reset that ministers should take. While cocaine use has traditionally been associated with higher disposable incomes, there are five times more drug deaths in the most deprived areas compared with the least deprived ones (London has the lowest rate). Liverpool’s Alder Hey children’s hospital recently opened a clinic to treat under-16s who have injured their bladders by taking ketamine.

Police have an important role in tackling traffickers. But ministers must recommit to the “whole-system approach” proposed by Prof Black. Reducing drug deaths should be part of wider efforts at reducing socioeconomic health disparities. Research should focus on effective treatment, and seek to understand the link between cocaine and domestic abuse. The impacts of the illegal drugs market have altered in the past five years. It is time for the authorities to catch up.

US tech shares fall sharply as investors bet on AI slowdown after Democrats’ election triumph

Nasdaq heading for its worst day in 18 months in volatile trading on Wall Street

The Nasdaq share index was on track for its worst day in 18 months after slumping by up to 5% on Thursday amid growing signs that the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because of the midterm election results.

As Wall Street sustained widespread losses, the Nasdaq composite tumbled into ‘correction territory’ – more than 10% below its recent record high. The tech-heavy index was heading for its biggest one-day fall since Donald Trump announced his “liberation day” tariffs on US trading partners in April 2025.

Worries over massive AI spending gripped the New York stock market and rippled out to other bourses worldwide as investors anticipated tougher scrutiny of datacentre expansion plans.

Chip stocks led the slump, with memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 19% and hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 16.5%.

Wall Street’s ‘fear index’, the VIX, jumped by 40% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.

Analysts pointed to expectations that Democratic governors will clamp down on the rollout of new datacentres after the party won a series of gubernatorial races this week. US voters also rejected datacentres in a series of local ballots across the country.

Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK, said a “complete capitulation-level event” was playing out in tech stocks on Thursday.

“The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh datacentre buildout … this looks totally overdone but the nature of ‘sell everything’ in this market means we need to look for some stability first,” Wilson said.

The Dow Jones industrial average (DJIA) of 30 large US companies was down more than 1,500 points in early afternoon trading, a fall of 2.8%, to 51,868 points. The S&P 500 was down 3.7%.

Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom, was the top faller on the DJIA – down 6.7%, followed by Goldman Sachs, which fell 5.7%.

An early stock market rally in Europe had fizzled out by late trading, with Britain’s FTSE 100 closing down 46 points or 0.4% at 10782.66.

The sell-off is a sharp reverse of Wednesday’s rally, when Wall Street stocks had their biggest daily gain in months as investors anticipated that the Democratic party’s success in the US midterm elections could restrain the White House.

That rally prompted Donald Trump to once again boast about the record-breaking highs the stock markets had reached during his second term. The president wrote on Truth Social: “Stock Market just hit another Record High – 91 Days in just a short period of time — Less than two years. Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Tech analyst Dan Ives has warned that the results of the midterms are a clear sign that the pace of datacentre buildout will start to slow down.

“There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next two years,” Ives said.

“The market’s moving from the promise ⁠of AI to the price of AI,” said Ted Parkhill, founder and CEO of Incline ​Investment Management.

“There’s no question that AI is ​going to be transformative for the world in ​the long run. But that doesn’t mean every AI-related stock is currently priced appropriately. There’s going to be ​a lot of turmoil.”
