The Russell Brand verdict is a landmark victory for the understanding of consent

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:33:10 GMT

The conviction of the comedian for rape and sexual assault upholds the vital principle that women can say no, even after they’ve said yes

With all the sanctimony a born-again Christian rapist can muster, Russell Brand paused on his way into court last week to address reporters. Britain was, he told them piously, “blessed” to have a legal system capable of accommodating truth and justice. Well, amen to that: the former comedian learned today that he will now serve a substantial jail sentence, after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, in what looks like a genuinely landmark victory for the understanding of consent.

Back in the days when comedy was the new rock’n’roll, and he would casually cherrypick girls from the crowd at his gigs, Brand could surely have had all the willing sex he wanted. Yet he seemingly got his kicks from the unwilling, who were forced over boundaries they did not want to cross. “You’re dirty and I wanna push you further,” he texted one victim, months after raping her anally and callously saving her number in his phone under T for “Tart”. The woman – who was in her early 20s when she first gave him oral sex backstage after a gig, and had gone a few days later to his house for what began as consensual sex but soon became something very different – responded angrily via text that he’d treated her “like an animal”.

For too long, cases involving young women alleging rape after going initially willingly to the bedrooms of rich or famous men have ended in sour, uneasy acquittals. Well, not any more. This verdict upholds the vital principle that consent to one thing is not consent to absolutely everything; that women still absolutely have the right to say no, even if they have in the past said yes.

Not all of his six accusers – strangers to each other, until this case brought them together in the most wretched of circumstances – got the verdict they wanted. The jury acquitted Brand of two further counts of rape and one of attempted indecent assault. But in the court of public opinion, there will be little mercy for Brand, nor perhaps for the industry that for too long sheltered and indulged him. After his conviction, the police revealed that he is under investigation for two further rape allegations.

How did he get away with it for so long? In exactly the same way as all the other celebrities you have seen belatedly exposed, along with some you haven’t yet: expensive lawyers, corporate tolerance for the excesses of men making big money, the misplaced shame of women worrying that somehow it might have been their fault, and toxic workplaces where junior women knew it was pointless even complaining.

Several of his victims worked in the media in the 2000s, and I remember that era well. The nagging fear wasn’t just that you might not be believed if you complained of sexual harassment, but that you might be, and that then it would be you rather than him who got sacked. One victim, groped in front of four of Brand’s entourage of hangers-on, said none intervened to help her; instead one started laughing, as if to break the tension. I knew precisely what she meant when she explained that she hadn’t reported it to her boss because it was the sort of workplace where they rated the women on how they looked.

His former PA, Helen Berger, told the court he would interrupt work on a deadline to ask if he could “go and have sex now”, like a spoilt child whining for an iPad; yet his behaviour was normalised and dismissed by everyone around him. Think about that when the usual suspects are complaining, as they invariably do, about new laws that came into force at the end of October requiring employers to take all reasonable steps to protect staff from sexual harassment, both by colleagues and clients of the business. That change in the law didn’t just fall out of the sky: it’s the result of years of bitter female experience of just how little some employers care.

As the BBC’s Lorraine Heggessey once said of Brand, his transgressions were always followed by promotion. The outrage he created was the very thing that mainstream media, desperate to seem more louche and edgy, craved: the more he pushed the boundaries, the more he seemed to be professionally in demand, even as he spun obviously out of control.

At the height of a raging heroin addiction, he was sacked by MTV after arriving at work in the aftermath of 9/11 dressed as Osama bin Laden, accompanied by his drug dealer. Hired instead by XFM, he was promptly fired again, this time for reading porn on air. After getting sober, he went on to present Channel 4’s Big Brother spinoff shows, write a football blog for this very newspaper, and present a show for staid old Radio 2 – from which he had to resign after he and his co-star Jonathan Ross made crude prank calls to the actor Andrew Sachs.

When his luck ran out with the mainstream media, Brand simply reinvented himself as a radical-left guru on YouTube, where people who should have known better still paid homage. (Ed Miliband, who as Labour leader went on Brand’s show in 2015, has since stressed that he wouldn’t have done so if he’d known about the rape allegations.)

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Even after Channel 4’s Dispatches aired Russell Brand: In Plain Sight in the autumn of 2023, he moved to Florida and found a new niche on the Maga circuit, seemingly discovering both religion and a range of populist conspiracy theories. Did all those resurrections make him feel untouchable? Only towards the very end of the trial, in a rambling appearance in the dock where he begged the jury’s forgiveness for what he called “reckless philandering” did something seemingly start to unravel.

In court, one of his victims said of being raped by him that, because they had previously had consensual sex, “I didn’t feel I had as much right to feel as bad about it as I did.” Now a jury of her peers has given her that precious right back, along with so many other women down the years who will recognise the feeling she describes. If Russell Brand’s world felt like to him one delightful “amusement park of orgasms”, as he once said, for too many women it must have been more like being trapped in a fairground house of horrors. Now, at last, a jury has set them free.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

Bomb threats disrupt at least 25 flights across Europe, raising hybrid war fears

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:17:36 GMT

Planes forced into emergency landings or diversions two days after hoax alerts affected air travel

Hoax bomb threats have caused at least 25 flights across Europe to be disrupted, with some forced to make emergency landings, as questions mount over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

The series of warnings on Thursday affected flights between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia.

The threats affected flights by Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet, Aegean Airlines, Iberia, Sky Express, Air Serbia and LOT Polish Airlines. All landed safely. Searches of the planes found nothing suspicious.

In the UK, Heathrow, London’s principal airport, and Birmingham airport received threats overnight, but it was determined that they were hoaxes with the help of specialist investigators from the Metropolitan police’s aviation police command.

The Met said threats had been made against four aircraft departing from or arriving at Heathrow. A police spokesperson added that, after an assessment, “no security issues [were] identified”.

The day of hoaxes followed similar threats on Tuesday, when seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted after malicious alerts. On Monday a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that was apparently without substance. In total at least 33 flights have been affected this week.

Investigators said on Thursday there remained no evidence that the hoaxes were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, although inquiries across Europe into the incidents continue.

The global airlines body Iata condemned the disruption and urged authorities to identify the origin of the threats. “Safety is the number one priority for the industry and we take all threats seriously,” said Nick Careen, Iata’s senior vice-president for operations, safety and security, in a statement.

The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said it was too early to know if the incidents were linked but that any threats against civilians were unacceptable.

Bomb threats emailed to airports in Rome and Sofia were signed “fighters of the Male State”, according to sources at Aeroporti di Roma, which manages the city’s two airports, and a text seen by Agence France-Presse.

Male State is a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016 by Vladislav Pozdnyakov. On his Telegram channel Pozdnyakov, a prominent supporter of the war in Ukraine, did not comment on or claim responsibility for the bomb threats.

The emails reportedly read: “We, the fighters of the Male State, will make history with our actions today. Your feminist regime will remember this for ever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today, your skies will turn red.”

A Cork airport spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian that the airport had received an anonymous threat by phone on Thursday morning, causing a flight to be delayed. It was understood to be a Ryanair flight from London Stansted.

A separate Ryanair flight from Pescara in Italy to Brussels-Charleroi was inspected after the word “bomb” was discovered scrawled on the walls of its onboard toilet.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny fraction of the 27,400 flights scheduled in Europe on Thursday, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol.

The pilot of an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that diverted to Évreux was being questioned by French authorities for initially refusing to land at a military base, according to French media reports.

The disruption followed cyber-attacks this week against supermarket refrigeration systems.

A Kremlin spokesperson said on Thursday it was “absurd” to blame Vladimir Putin’s administration for the fridge hacks. “We have ​such baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything,” Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

In Rome, Guido Crosetto, the Italian defence minister, said: “It seems to me that every day now, from refrigerators to blood supplies in France, to these fake alarms, there’s someone who has an interest in stoking tensions.”

Asked if he knew who was behind the hoaxes, he said: “It’s called ‘under-threshold warfare’ because it’s below the attribution threshold. It’s done that way on purpose, so no one can pin the blame.”

Many of the affected flights were operated by low-cost carriers but there was little discernible pattern surrounding the incidents.

Aviation experts say fake threats occur daily but that such a number of credible threats, even if malicious hoaxes, appears to point to coordinated action.

Capt Martin Drake, a former airline pilot and technical adviser to the British Airline Pilots’ Association union, said airlines had security teams who assessed each threat on a traffic-light scale: green to keep going or red to be grounded, with an amber option only for flights yet to take off, allowing tighter checks and searches of the plane before clearing it to fly.

“If you want to deliberately disrupt a flight, then you need to do so once it’s airborne,” said Drake. Pilots have a QRH – a quick response handbook – whose instructions will probably include to descend quickly as well as divert to the nearest airport on receipt of a red alert.

At cruising altitude, “aircraft pressurisation would do a lot of the work of any improvised explosive device”.

While getting a large explosive onboard should be ruled out by multiple layers of security and screening, the effects of any detonation would be multiplied for planes at typical cruising altitude of 35,000ft.

Diversions are expensive as well as highly disruptive, but airlines have little choice in the face of any remotely credible threat.

The ready availability of airline operations information on the internet means that any hoaxer now has a level of detail about the schedules, the type of plane and its technical specifications that would have eluded all but insiders decades ago.

Rhys Jones, an analyst at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation intelligence firm, said the confidence of airlines in European airport security should not mean any change to normal protocols after the hoaxes, but “one of the natural responses will be to see double-downed security, media coverage and public concern about travelling”.

He said the threats seemed linked but “a reasonably chaotic campaign with no particular region targeted”, and while they could weaken future security responses through the normalisation of threats, simply creating disruption could be regarded as a success by those carrying out the hoaxes.

Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer in Amsterdam and Angela Giuffrida in Rome

Failing Grayling double reports for duty as Reform’s armed forces spokesperson

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:09:39 GMT

New recruit Angus MacIntyre bears an unfortunate resemblance to little-missed ex-Tory minister Chris Grayling

You can make a good case for Nigel Farage having been one of the most consequential British politicians of the 21st century. Without him there would have been no Brexit. And yet it is now beginning to look as if his time has come and gone.

The narcissistic qualities that have served him so well now threaten to finish him off. His skin is becoming thinner by the day. All that’s left is reflexive lashing out. A raging against the dying of the light. You’d need to have a heart of stone not to laugh.

On Thursday, Nige was at the old Billingsgate fish market in central London for a press conference – not another one – at which he was to unveil his new armed forces spokesperson. Only this would turn out to be a press conference with a difference. Nige would not be taking any questions for the cameras.

You couldn’t help but think he was struggling to shake off the humiliation of insisting the pollsters were wrong about the Republicans in the US midterms. Trump would not be smashed, he said. The American voters saw it differently. And now The Donald was proving to be a liability.

It’s not just Nige who is suffering. He’s taking his whole team down with him. Not least those former Tory MPs who had thought the Conservatives were dead in the water. Danny Kruger was supposed to be the sensible one. The one who could provide a veneer of intelligence to the Reform project. Yet Nice Danny is rapidly morphing into Desperate Dan: a man now thinking he may have been a bit hasty and made the wrong call.

Desperate Dan had been roped in as the warm-up act. Usually the sort of meaningless gig that is delegated to Dicky Tice. It probably wasn’t in the script for Dan to use his five-minute gig to unload his full existential meltdown, but that was what he got. Angry Dan is a sucker for any conspiracy theory. The polls had been rigged to make it look as if Reform was in third place. And John Healey had only resigned as defence secretary so that he could get the job as chancellor in order to dismantle all the armed forces.

The madness apogee was reached when Desperate Dan declared that no politician in the whole country knew more about defence than Nige. In a war, Nige would be the first person trying to escape the draft with ingrown toenails. Reform have never even got round to naming a defence spokesperson or showing the slightest interest in the subject. Reform’s attendance in parliament for defence-related matters is pitiful.

Nige took centre stage to a standing ovation. There are still a few hardcore believers left. He craves the attention despite the ever-diminishing returns. “The world is more dangerous now than it has been for 80 years,” he said, with his trademark grin. He could be right, though he hadn’t stopped to consider whether Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump – two leaders whom he has openly admired – might have contributed to that. Nige has blamed the Ukraine war on Nato and was all up for joining the US in bombing Iran.

The 3.5% of GDP by 2035 was paltry, he continued. Though he didn’t commit to spending any more or saying how the increase would be funded. But help was at hand. Nige had tracked down the one man in the entire armed services who could save the country from its darkest hour. No matter that the RAF had rather overlooked the talents of the wing commander with 40 years’ service. Meet Angus MacIntyre, who last week resigned from the RAF to become Nige’s official wingman.

Cue a spectacular double take. Because the man who walked on stage was a dead ringer for Chris Grayling, the former Tory minister who had never yet found a job he couldn’t do worse than anyone else. Failing Grayling made a career out of his own incompetence. Mediocrity was a level of achievement to which he could only aspire.

Being Failing Grayling’s double is a cross no man should have to bear but Angus was determined to do his best. He was happy to report for duty as Reform’s shadow minister for the armed forces. This was Angus’s first lie in his new role. Start as you mean to go on. He is not and is never going to be a shadow minister. That role can only ever be done by a Tory as the official opposition. But maybe no one had yet got round to explaining such things to him. Angus was a grunt who operated on a need to know basis.

MacIntyre quickly moved on to his CV, which includes spells in the US and at Nato HQ. More lanyard class than man of action. Nor did he quite explain why he had finished his career only as wing commander despite four decades of service. You couldn’t help thinking Angus might have been passed over for promotion several times and that the RAF hadn’t quite appreciated his talents as much as he would have liked.

Still, Angus looks as if he has landed in the right place, sounding suitably swivel-eyed about net zero and condemning current attitudes towards the armed forces as “Marxist ideology”. However, it was a little weird that Reform’s new man from the military had nothing to say about either Ukraine or Iran. It would have been good to know if he shared Nige’s admiration for Putin and Trump and whether he, too, looks on not joining the Iran war as a missed opportunity. Nor did he say whether he intended to stand as an MP or who was paying him. Questions, questions.

“Have I got the right guy?” Nige asked the audience, as he joined Angus on stage for a last group hug. We will find out soon enough. But my bet would be that Angus may soon be feeling buyer’s remorse. Nige looks as if he is running on empty.

Flashbulbs, lies and victim blaming: how Russell Brand’s trial unfolded

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 18:00:30 GMT

Level of interest in comedian’s case resulted in examination of affairs inside and outside the courtroom

Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court, which ended with him being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, was one of the most obsessively watched criminal cases in recent history. As well as Brand’s own conduct, the case became an examination of his victims’ evidence, the legal strategy his team used to defend him, and the culture within which he committed his crimes.

Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” from charming to nasty as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong.

The comedian’s youngest victim, who was 21 when he targeted her at the height of his fame in 2009, was left traumatised by their encounter.

Brand had stored her name in his phone alongside a series of letters and symbols. The court heard the letter “T” stood for “tart”, while “AP” denoted anal play, and two asterisks meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.”

It was, indeed, an encounter the woman would never forget, she spent years torturing and blaming herself for what happened.

The woman was starstruck when she met Brand after one of his standup performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009. Brand, who was more than a decade her senior, picked the woman from the crowd and invited her to his dressing room. There, she performed oral sex on him and engaged in a threesome with another young fan.

Days later, Brand sent a chauffeur to drive the woman to his three-storey Victorian townhouse in Hampstead, north-west London, where he forced her to shower and brush her teeth before they had consensual sex.

Then, without warning, Brand flipped her over and anally raped her so violently that she struggled to breathe. She begged him to stop but he refused, telling her: “I want you to feel my come.”

He later chastised her for getting blood on his sheets and ordered her to clean up the mess before casually turning on the TV and instructing an assistant to escort her out.

Two dozen witnesses gave evidence in support of the woman’s account. “The way I would describe that event to people after was that it was traumatic and that he hurt me and harmed me. And when I asked him to stop, he didn’t,” she told the court.

The lasting trauma of her experience was far from unique.

Brand met his earliest accuser at a cabaret event during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. The court heard the woman was not attracted to the then unknown performer, whom she assumed was gay. But she found him intelligent and believed they were passionate about the same causes.

She invited him back to her hotel to continue their conversation, but “froze” when she returned from the toilet to find Brand partly naked. She told police he then raped her but on the evidence presented in court, the jury found him not guilty of that offence. “I remember him on me, very heavy. I know I said no. I kind of drifted out of my head. I couldn’t get out of the situation – ‘Do I shout, do I scream?’” she told the court.

After the incident, Brand left his email address. An act, the prosecutor said, which was designed to characterise the encounter as normal. “Today that might be called gaslighting, a technique that defendant used with good effect on some of his other victims,” said the prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC.

Among them was an MTV worker who met Brand in 2004 at a birthday party held at a bar in Soho, London. Here, Brand sexually assaulted her by grabbing her breasts. The woman claimed he also orally raped her in the toilets, but he was cleared by the jury on that allegation.

Brand also faced claims that he preyed on women while they were at work. The second complainant on the indictment was also an MTV worker, who said Brand transformed into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag her into a men’s toilets in 2001. At the conclusion of the trial Brand was cleared of attempting to indecently assault the woman.

Another woman claimed Brand laughed after “mauling” her by squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was at work at the radio station Choice FM in 2004 or 2005. She said Brand “overpowered her” during the “violent” and “frenzied” sexual assault, which took place in front of his entourage. He was found guilty of sexually assaulting her.

Brand’s final victim said she was “repulsed” when Brand lunged at her crotch and put his head so deep into her lap that she could feel his breath on her vagina during a recording session at Channel 4 in 2009.

She said two members of Brand’s entourage had told her Brand would not continue filming unless she gave him a massage. “I thought they were joking because I wouldn’t expect anybody to say that and then I saw by their faces they weren’t,” she recalled. Brand was again found guilty of sexual assault.

In the dock, Brand barely flinched as his accusers recounted harrowing ordeals through tears from behind a screen. In scenes captured by court artists, he sat bolt upright and stared straight ahead, as the women described his “disgusting” serpent-like body, threatening eyes, and how he “wasn’t very well endowed”.

But his composure appeared to falter on 28 October when he was in the witness box for more than four hours. The case had been a “deeply traumatic episode” in his life and he was “innocent” of all the charges, he told the four women and eight men on the jury.

“Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and, indeed, in many ways more important than sex itself,” he said. He denied setting a “goal” to sleep with 5,000 women, but said he had misused his fame and success “very selfishly”.

“As I became more successful and famous, I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong,” he told the prosecutor.

“With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy.”

He blamed his public fall from grace on 2023 media reporting about his alleged sexual misconduct. He had achieved “staggering fame” after his marriage to the singer Katy Perry, but now nobody would touch him “with a bargepole”.

However, the prosecutor noted the Hollywood actor turned influencer still had millions of followers online. “This is not the case of poor Mr Brand being taken apart by the media,” she told jurors.

Karmy-Jones accused Brand of tailoring his recollections to the prosecution evidence, telling jurors his evidence amounted to “a lot of half truths, but spun into lies”.

Brand’s cross-examination was punctuated by long spells of silence and awkward staring at the prosecutor. But he became more animated while his wife, Laura, 39, gave evidence. He appeared to smile, nod and mouth words at her as she talked about his 2024 baptism and said he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”.

Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, ripped into the complainants with a steely determination. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, had to interrupt him during one uncomfortable exchange about consent, saying: “Shush please. I’m the judge, you have to let me talk.”

In another, the judge objected to Winter questioning a woman about why she had not reported that Brand had raped her during the #MeToo movement when “every woman in the world was examining whether she had been sexually assaulted by a famous person”. “I think that’s a bit of a generalisation,” the judge said.

Described online as a “leading white-collar crime silk” specialising in fraud and financial crime, Winter repeatedly questioned why his client’s accusers had not fought back when they were being raped. “Not one of them resisted or screamed or even tried to leave,” he told jurors.

Referring to Brand’s youngest victim, Winter said: “She didn’t just roll over and kick out.” He went on to claim that Brand’s earliest accuser was not a “naive and wilting flower”, declaring: “She was plainly attracted to him.”

He also questioned why an MTV worker, whom he claimed was “perfectly capable of looking after herself”, did not slap Brand, who is 6ft 2in tall, in the face when he grabbed her breasts before he allegedly orally raped her. He suggested she had not “sufficiently” resisted.

Karmy-Jones criticised Winter’s “skilful but quite aggressive” cross-examination of one victim in her closing speech. “Might you have thought she was being blamed for what happened?” she asked jurors.

Brand arrived at court each day with his entourage to a flurry of camera flashes and questions from journalists as the case attracted unprecedented media coverage.

Well-known for his dishevelled fashion choices, Brand had smartened up his appearance for the trial. The unbuttoned animal-print shirt and monogrammed fedora hat combo he wore to a pre-trial hearing was replaced by a series of dark suits and long scarves.

His bright blue Bible, packed with colourful Post-it notes, was also nowhere to be seen as he sat in the dock, but he, or his entourage, carried it into court in the early days of the trial. Occasionally, Brand was spotted clutching prayer beads.

Brand’s wife was by his side on most days, as was his bodyguard Joe McCann, said to be a former sparring partner of the boxer Tyson Fury. Other members of his daily entourage included his manager and producer, Jake Smith, and the American podcaster David Fields. Newspapers have noted that Smith – who bears a passing resemblance to Brand – was abused and praised by members of the public who mistook him for the comedian outside court.

Five daily podcasts tracked the ins and outs of the trial for audiences in Britain and the US, where Brand now lives with his wife and three children. Content creators crossed legal lines as they live-blogged every twist and turn in the case. In a moment of courtroom drama, the judge demanded one blogger be arrested for publishing identifying information about one of the victims, all of whom are entitled to lifelong anonymity. The man was arrested and cautioned.

In another legal blunder, People magazine in the US risked contempt of court by publishing a pre-trial ruling that could have prejudiced the trial. It can now be reported that Brand’s legal team had tried to get the case dropped, arguing that he could not receive a fair trial due to the 2023 media reports.

They said a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and articles in the Times and the Sunday Times had “destroyed” Brand and “turned the world against him”.

At the end of the trial, Winter launched into an extraordinary tirade against a Sunday Times journalist, Rosamund Urwin, who worked on an investigation of allegations against Brand.

Outside the courtroom, he said: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.” Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done,” before Winter replied: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.”

“Congratulations,” he added.

The prosecution successfully argued that Brand had generated extensive publicity himself in high-profile interviews with Tucker Carlson, Megyn Kelly, and Piers Morgan.

Brand continued to offer competing narratives during the trial in two episodes of his Sunday Service podcast in which he and his wife discussed being in the “eye of the storm” and the “aquarium dock” of court 3.

“If you follow empire media you will be aware that, of course, we as a family, and me in particular, are in a situation that requires the authenticity and authority of true justice, and for that reason we will be extremely cautious in any way we refer to the trial,” the former Big Brother’s Big Mouth presenter told his followers after the first week of his trial.

Wearing a loosely tied leopard-print dressing gown and stroking his cat, Jericho, he added: “The worst of all the things I have had said to me or about me this week was do your shirt up.”

Brand’s victims said they did not report his predatory behaviour at the time because he was an A-list star and they feared they would not be believed. “It was a toxic environment,” the Choice FM worker said of the media industry. If she had reported Brand’s assault to a line manager, she said, “they would have said something along the lines of: ‘Oh you’re lucky.’”

But the court heard that two of the victims who worked in the media did raise concerns about Brand’s behaviour. The MTV worker who was sexually assaulted at a Soho bar said she told a colleague that Brand was a “sexual predator” and asked another in 2006 why Brand had been rehired by the music channel.

The Channel 4 worker told two managers about the incident. One recalled how the woman told her two associates of Brand “watched and laughed” as he sexually assaulted her.

“They were turning a blind eye, as others had done,” the prosecutor said.

Brand’s former personal assistant told the court that his bad behaviour was indeed “normalised and dismissed” by those around him.

“Though I’d worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level,” she said in a witness statement. “I do however remember numerous instances where I knew his behaviour was wrong and would turn to someone and say: ‘This is really fucked up’, but would get told: ‘That’s Russell.’”

Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 17:36:43 GMT

With flights disrupted, how concerned should you be about your travel plans?

More than 30 planes have been subjected to security alerts or diversions this week, with at least 25 more bomb threats on Thursday disrupting civil aviation across Europe.

What do we know so far, and how concerned should you be about your travel plans?

At least 33 flights have been disrupted this week, beginning on Monday, when a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia in Bulgaria was diverted to Budapest. Thursday’s threats affected airports in London, Birmingham, Brussels, Madrid, Milan, Prague, Rome, Sofia and Warsaw, among others.

So far all incidents have been confirmed to be false alarms, with nothing suspicious found by relevant security authorities.

There is no clear pattern of airports and airlines targeted, although a significant number have involved Italian airports as an origin or destination. Seven flights this week were to – or from the UK – and four to or from Ireland.

Sofia and Milan each recorded six incidents, followed by Rome (five) and Prague (four). Ryanair was the hardest-hit airline, with eight reported cases.

The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said on Thursday it was “too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked”. He stressed: “Any threats against civilians are unacceptable.”

There is no intelligence yet pointing to any particular group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, amid growing concerns over hybrid incidents targeting Europe.

Aviation experts say fake threats occur daily but the multiplicity of this week’s threats is unusual.

As our transport correspondent, Gwyn Topham, notes on our live blog, the ready availability of airline operations information on the internet means a hoaxer now has a level of detail about schedules and a plane’s type and technical specifications that would have eluded all but insiders decades ago.

Little is known about how these threats were reported to airlines or relevant authorities, though in cases involving Bulgaria, Italy, Poland and Spain they were reportedly sent via email.

The Italian news agency Ansa, citing police sources, said the warning for Helsinki-Rome and Dublin-Rome flights came from an anonymous email written in Italian and sent to the Rome airport company ADR and other affiliated companies early on Thursday.

Another anonymous email in Italian was sent to Milan Malpensa airport, claiming that explosive devices were on flights from Thessaloniki and Porto. The email included the flight numbers, the airline names and their landing times in Milan, Ansa said.

Most authorities issued carefully worded statements confirming their security checks on the affected planes. However, the Czech police – which investigated four planes landing at Václav Havel airport in Prague on Thursday – said they considered the reports of “low relevance”.

Relevant national authorities treat these incidents seriously in line with their safety procedures, with reports of fighter jet escorts in Bulgaria, France, Hungary and Italy.

Diversions are expensive as well as highly disruptive, but airlines have little choice in the face of any remotely credible threat.

Joji Waites, the director of flight safety at the British Airline Pilots’ Association (Balpa), said any threat received by an airline was passed to a team of assessors who would grade it “red”, meaning credible, “amber”, partly credible, or “green”, not credible. If the plane is already in the air, the only rating possible is red or green.

He said: “Usually if a plane is still on the Tarmac that will mean an evacuation, and if it is in the air the priority will be to land the plane as soon and as safely as possible.”

Airlines appear to be concerned about the scale of possible disruptions and worry potential copycat alerts could cause further chaos.

Wizz Air acknowledged “a series of similar bomb threats affecting several airlines across Europe in recent days”. It said: “Wizz Air is not the only airline targeted, with other carriers also experiencing threats resulting in flight diversions and security checks.”

Finnair, which had two planes affected, said: “Unfortunately, air traffic is sometimes subject to threats, as we have seen this week, when also other airlines in Europe have faced hoax bomb threats.” It added: “Threats are almost always unfounded.”

Henry Nowak’s killer has sentence extended by court of appeal

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 17:29:25 GMT

Vickrum Digwa’s ‘unduly lenient’ term for Southampton teenager’s murder increased after attorney general’s appeal

Henry Nowak’s killer has seen his sentence extended by the court of appeal after it ruled that his original sentence was “unduly lenient”.

Vickrum Digwa’s original sentence of life with a minimum term of 21 years was lengthened to a minimum of 24 years and 190 days after a successful appeal by the attorney general, Ellie Reeves.

Digwa, 23, stabbed Nowak several times in an attack in Southampton in December last year.

When police arrived at the murder scene, Digwa falsely claimed Nowak had racially abused him and knocked his turban off, causing officers to arrest and handcuff Nowak before they saw his fatal injuries.

Digwa filmed his victim as he lay dying and lied to emergency services that Nowak, 18, had racially abused him.

The incident led to riots in Southampton.

Lady Chief Justice Carr said the original sentencing judge, William Mousley KC, had materially understated two distinct dimensions of Digwa’s offending.

She said: “First, the circumstances in which a large and immediately available dagger was used repeatedly with an intention to kill an unarmed man, and secondly, the deliberate cruelty, additional suffering, and obstruction [of justice] which followed the stabbing.”

She added: “A minimum term of 21 years did not adequately reflect the overall seriousness of the murder. It was not only lenient, but unduly so.

“Therefore, we quash the minimum term of 21 years. We replace it with a minimum term of 25 years. From that term must be deducted the 175 days spent in custody on remand, producing an operative minimum term of 24 years and 190 days.”

In written submissions on behalf of Reeves, Jonathan Polnay KC said the sentence failed to take into account a series of “significant aggravating factors”, including Digwa’s “false allegation of racism against the deceased” and his “abuse” of the privilege afforded to Sikhs to carry a knife in a public place for religious reasons.

At Digwa’s sentencing hearing, Mousley said that on the night of the murder, Digwa had a small knife hidden from view called a kirpan, which is a strict requirement for Sikhs to carry at all times.

Digwa also had a “large dagger in a sheath” due to his membership of the Nihang, an order of Sikhs which has a tradition of holding a second knife.

Polnay told the court that the attempt to increase the sentence was “not about the lawful possession of a kirpan” and the laws allowing Sikhs to carry blades. “It is about what followed.” He said Digwa’s use of the dagger was “on at least one level, analogous to an abuse of trust”.

He continued: “When a person who has the benefit of that accommodation uses the article protected by law for repeated lethal violence, that is an aggravating factor of particular weight.”

Polnay also cited “the offender’s sustained attempts to pervert the course of justice” and “his procurement of his mother’s assistance in concealing evidence”.

Digwa’s mother, Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three years for assisting an offender by taking the knife from where her son murdered Novak back to the family home.

Polnay said other aggravating factors included Digwa’s “degradation of the dying victim by filming him, and his conduct in misleading responders”.

His submission said: “The minimum term imposed failed adequately to reflect the combined weight of those features.”

In her ruling made alongside Mr Justice Nicklin and Mr Justice Wall, Carr said: “A person who knowingly carries a large knife or other bladed article in public, even if lawfully, and then uses it to kill an unarmed man after only a brief altercation, is highly culpable. His culpability is much closer to that of a person who takes a weapon into the street for offensive use than to that of someone who kills without a weapon, or someone who picks up a weapon of opportunity.”

On the false allegations of racism, Carr said: “It is unnecessary for us to determine whether the allegation of racial abuse was false, for even if that finding is left out of account, it does not affect our assessment of the appropriate minimum term.”

Digwa watched proceedings from HMP Frankland in County Durham, wearing a dark suit, shirt and tie.

Members of Nowak’s family attended the hearing at the Royal Courts of Justice, with one relative wiping their eyes as the ruling was handed down.

Imran Khan KC, for Digwa, said the sentence could be increased only in “exceptional, rather than borderline cases, and directed to gross error by the sentencing judge”. He asked: “Where is the gross error?”

Challenging the length of the sentence, Khan said that while Digwa’s lies to first responders “unquestionably affected the dignity with which Mr Nowak was treated”, his wounds were unsurvivable. “The false account therefore did not worsen the fatal injury or deprive Mr Nowak of the prospect of survival,” he said.

In response to Digwa’s appeal, Carr said: “Having reached the conclusion that the proper minimum term would be at least 25 years, we refuse Digwa leave to appeal against his sentence. It is unarguable that it is manifestly excessive.”

Reeves said: “The brutality and cruelty of this case horrified me, and I know that feeling is shared by the British public. I welcome the court of appeal’s decision to increase the minimum term of Digwa’s life sentence.”

Russell Brand faces ‘significant’ prison term for rape and sexual assault

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 17:03:15 GMT

Actor and comedian, 51, found guilty of raping a woman and assaulting three others

Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women, ending a years-long legal saga that has raised questions about how he was able to commit his crimes at the height of his fame.

Brand, 51, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator. He was convicted of raping a woman at his luxury London townhouse and of sexually assaulting women in front of his entourage at their workplaces, at a radio station and TV studio.

The Hollywood actor turned online influencer was accused of gaslighting his victims after the attacks, and treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.

It can now be revealed that Brand is under investigation for two further rape allegations and that the Metropolitan police have submitted files to the Crown Prosecution Service.

Brand – who will be sentenced on Monday – stood outside the door of the dock shortly before the jury delivered their verdicts and looked at his wife, Laura, saying: “Laura, I love you.”

Wearing a grey three-piece suit, he appeared to be praying in the dock before he was convicted of four offences on Thursday after a four-week trial at Southwark crown court.

He had pleaded not guilty to three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999.

Brand had claimed he could not remember some of the incidents, and that others had been consensual sexual encounters that had been “reimagined” or “unfavourably reframed” after the publication of sexual misconduct allegations against him in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, and Times and Sunday Times reports.

Brand closed his eyes as a jury found him guilty of four offences against four women after eight hours and 30 minutes of deliberations. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, praised the panel of four women and eight men, and told Brand: “You’ve been convicted of a number of offences, including one of rape. The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I have to therefore remand you in custody.”

Brand appeared emotionless as he was led away by the dock officers down to the cells. His wife was visibly upset and left the court soon after.

His barrister, Ian Winter KC, made a plea for Brand to be given bail over the weekend as an “act of humanity” so that he could say goodbye to his children, but the judge refused.

Bennathan said he regretted the “hardship” caused to the children but said: “Whatever the good intentions of the family and the defendant today, I think there are substantial grounds to fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence.”

As the judge remanded him into custody, Brand made “OK” gestures and said: “I’m good, I’m good, I’m good,” before being taken out of the dock.

On Thursday the Met said its investigation into Brand was continuing.

Brand was found guilty of anally raping a young fan at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd after one of his gigs at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009.

She told the court she had begged him to stop but Brand had continued. “I felt like I couldn’t speak or breathe, the amount of pain,” she said.

He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman who worked for MTV by grabbing her breasts at a birthday party in Soho, London in 2004. But he was cleared of orally raping the woman in a toilet afterwards.

He was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman who told the court that Brand had laughed after squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was working at the radio station Choice FM in 2004 or 2005.

Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker, who said she had been “repulsed” when Brand placed his head in her lap so she could feel his breath on her “vagina” during a filming project in 2009.

He was cleared of raping a woman at the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999, and also found not guilty of attempting to indecently assault an MTV worker by trying to drag her into a men’s toilets in 2001.

Brand’s trial heard victims had been haunted by their encounters with the former presenter and that they had bravely come forward to the tell the truth after realising they were not alone.

The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said they described a similar pattern of behaviour from the comedian that started with compliments, flattery and flirting before a “personality change”. “His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty,” she said.

But Brand’s barrister denied the TV personality was a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal”. The barrister also said that the 2023 media reports had “poisoned the well” of justice, and rendered it impossible for Brand to have a fair trial.

Speaking after the trial, in which part of Brand’s defence rested on the claim that “not one of [the victims] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave,” the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, warned against the perpetuaton of rape myths in the legal system.

“The idea that rape victims must scream, physically resist or immediately report an offence is a well-established rape myth, rooted in outdated and harmful assumptions about how victims are expected to behave,” she said. “Justice must be grounded in evidence, not misconceptions.”

Outside the courtroom there was an extraordinary exchange between Winter and the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, who was involved in the 2023 investigation.

He said to Urwin: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.” After she replied: “I’m pleased justice has been done,” Winter said: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.” He then added: “Congratulations.”

Brand’s case has led to difficult questions for the BBC, Channel 4 and the production companies that worked with him. The TV world is again asking itself whether recent efforts to improve safeguarding will stop similar abuses.

In a statement on Thursday, Channel 4 said: “We recognise the profound impact of these crimes and commend the extraordinary courage of all those who gave evidence as prosecution witnesses at trial.”

A BBC spokesperson said that a 2025 report had examined how complaints about Brand’s conduct were handled, looking at eight allegations from his time at the BBC, and added: “It was of great concern to us that some people felt unable to raise concerns about Brand’s behaviour. We apologised to those impacted, for both the culture and failings at the time, and we reiterate that apology again today.”

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

EU presses UK to guarantee discounted university tuition fees for European students

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:58:54 GMT

Failure to agree lower fees for EU citizens studying in UK should delay prized food and drink deal, members say

UK politics live – latest updates

The EU is seeking a firmer pledge from the British government to guarantee European students discounted rates on university tuition fees before a much-anticipated summit this month.

At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Wednesday, at least six member states called for a clear commitment from the UK by the time of the summit that EU students will pay the lower domestic rate of university tuition fees.

These member states oppose deferring agreement for another half-year. Many believe a failure to reach an agreement should delay the highly prized food and drink deal to cut Brexit red tape coming into force.

European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.

Andy Burnham will meet the EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on 20 November in Brussels, with the aim of signing three agreements – on food and drink, carbon markets and youth exchange – as well as pledging a “trusted partnership” on steel and defence industries.

But a longstanding dispute over whether EU students should pay costly international tuition fees at British universities remains unresolved and could delay the implementation of the food and energy deals, which are worth billions to the British economy.

The EU wants a return to the pre-Brexit status quo where European students paid the UK domestic rate of university tuition, rather than international fees, which can be about four to six times higher for an undergraduate degree.

European Commission negotiators have proposed postponing an agreement on tuition fees by six months to ensure the success of the November event, where Burnham is expected to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU.

But at least six member states, including in central and eastern Europe, want the university fees issue settled by the summit, while many are seeking a firmer commitment on the issue from the British government, according to four EU sources.

One EU diplomat told the Guardian: “Having a youth experience scheme without an agreement on tuition fees has very little added value,” noting the much lower cost of university education in many EU countries and therefore potential greater advantage to British students.

A second EU diplomat said there was cautious optimism about the November summit, but “a large majority” wanted “a more convincing British commitment” on tuition fees.

A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on leaks or provide a running commentary on live negotiations. We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”

For the EU, the creation of a youth experience scheme, known as Yes, which will enable those aged 18 to 30 to live, work and study on both sides of the Channel is a high priority. The erosion of people-to-people links is seen as one of the big losses of Brexit, and many European officials studied in the UK, making the issue especially resonant.

EU officials argue the bloc has leverage, saying the food and drink deal – a Labour manifesto pledge estimated to be worth £5.1bn a year to the British economy – would come into force only if there was a satisfactory agreement on tuition fees.

Similarly, the agreement to relink emissions trading systems sundered by Brexit, which would protect British exporters from European carbon taxes, could also be delayed pending agreement on tuition fees.

A leaked version of the summit statement hints at the link between the trio of agreements, looking forward to “their joint and timely entry into force”.

Separately, EU sources have suggested without a deal on tuition fees, the EU could delay talks on British reintegration into the European electricity market that are expected to intensify next year. To secure its return to the market, the UK would have to pledge an “appropriate” contribution to European cohesion funds aimed at boosting economic development in poorer regions.

This week the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.

The EU said there would be no deal on Made in Europe at the November summit because the bloc was still finalising its position on the key draft law, the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).

Targeted at strategic industrial sectors, such as electric cars and renewables, the law would mean public subsidies and contracts would only go towards products made in Europe.

France, supported by many lawmakers in the European parliament, is pushing for a narrow definition of Made in Europe, while Germany leads a larger group of countries that don’t want to exclude trade partners including the UK.

While Britain is keen to resolve the issue, EU lawmakers are not expected to finalise the IAA text until next spring. In a significant milestone, France and Germany struck a compromise on Made in Europe favourable to the UK, but it only applies to cars, not the other industrial sectors in the IAA such as renewables and nuclear technology, or other draft proposals aimed at promoting European preference.

In a win for the UK, the draft summit statement proposes a “trusted partnership” on strategic industries, starting with steel and defence. The aim is to stop either side becoming collateral damage of the other’s trade defence measures targeted at China’s heavily subsidised imports.

Regulation of counsellors and psychotherapists would protect patients

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:35:29 GMT

Readers respond to the recommendation by an independent commission that the profession be regulated

The independent commission established by the professional bodies that represent counsellors and psychotherapists in the UK makes a case for statutory regulation that is long overdue (Report, 2 November). Ella Janneh, who won damages in a civil case against her therapist, is right that most people assume the safeguards already exist, and the commission is right to say that they do not. What happened to her shows what that mistaken assumption can cost.

I write as the chairperson of the Irish Association of Humanistic and Integrative Psychotherapy and as a psychotherapist for more than 20 years. I trained in the UK and have practised in Ireland ever since. In both countries, personal therapy and supervised practice have long been the foundation of training.

Coru, Ireland’s health regulator, has overruled its own counsellors and psychotherapists registration board and published training standards requiring no personal therapy, no clinical supervision and no minimum training duration if it can be believed, despite strong opposition from the main training and accreditation bodies.

Requiring personal therapy and supervision is essential. It helps to screen out those unfit to hold power. Without these standards, abuse survivors risk being failed again. Clients deserve a therapist who has worked through their own pain, rather than bringing it into the room with a vulnerable person. Statutory regulation must safeguard the integrity of the profession and protect the public by placing personal therapy and clinical supervision at its core. A regulated title offers no real protection if the training behind it has been hollowed out. Jacky Grainger Irish Association of Humanistic and Integrative Psychotherapy

At last there is interest in statutory regulation for counsellors and psychotherapists. This is not the first time this idea has been broached. Indeed, the profession previously made great efforts to interest the government in controlling the title. As early as 1991, the UK Council for Psychotherapy was discussing the route to this. The Liberal Democrat peer John Alderdice tried to interest David Cameron’s government, but it was dismissed as not important.

It took me seven years to become a psychotherapist, with personal therapy throughout. We need counsellors and psychotherapists who understand, through their own experience, the emotional difficulty of undertaking therapy, but who also have the intellectual background and ethical integrity to help others to change and move forward with their lives. Lesley Murdin Former director, WPF Therapy

Not all counsellors and psychotherapists want statutory regulation. While many of us share concerns about harmful therapists at work, we also know that legally protecting titles does not eradicate abuse or malpractice – it may even hide abuse behind enhanced professional status. We also need to be cautious of unintended consequences of statutory regulation, which could further restrict access for marginalised groups due to increased costs for training and accreditation.

The current system of therapists accredited by the Professional Standards Authority may be imperfect, but offers potential ways forward that deserve close attention before we rush into the statutory protection of titles. Andy Rogers BACP-registered counsellor and psychotherapist, Basingstoke, Hampshire

Your report on the call for statutory regulation of counsellors and psychotherapists highlights a gap in public protection that should have been addressed years ago.

It’s extraordinary that someone seeking mental healthcare, often at a particularly vulnerable point in their life, cannot necessarily take for granted that the person treating them is appropriately qualified or subject to enforceable professional standards.

As the founder and CEO of an independent mental healthcare organisation, I welcome the call for change from the commission established by the professional bodies, but would argue that regulating individual practitioners is only part of the answer. We also need to examine the ethical conduct of organisations providing mental healthcare, including the transparency of their relationships, whether referrals are always made in patients’ best interests and how conflicts of interest are managed.

Last month, in response to these concerns, we partnered with colleagues across the sector to launch the Independent Mental Healthcare Ethical Practice Charter, establishing shared principles for greater transparency, accountability and ethical practice.

Statutory regulation of practitioners is long overdue, but it should be accompanied by greater scrutiny of the organisations operating within the sector. Maryam Meddin Founder and CEO, the Soke

The case made for statutory regulation of psychotherapists applies equally to sports therapists. People seek sports therapy for injury treatment, pain management and rehabilitation. Yet “sports therapist” is not a legally protected title. Voluntary registers provide some reassurance, but cannot prevent an unregistered, inadequately qualified individual from using the title.

In worst-case scenarios, we have seen individuals struck off from other statutory registers for abusing patients, only to reinvent themselves as “sports therapists” and continue to pose a threat to the public. The Society of Sports Therapists has been seeking statutory regulation for years to ensure that the public can identify who is properly qualified, and for action to be taken against those who present a risk. The Health and Care Professions Council has approved our application on three separate occasions, but the necessary legislative action has still not followed. Significantly, 94% of our members support this change.

It is high time that the government applied the same public protection principle across therapeutic professions and completed the process. Regulation is not a badge of professional status; it is a safeguard for patients and a means of protecting the many responsible practitioners who deserve public confidence. Simon Bowen CEO, the Society of Sports Therapists

Carers deserve a new, fairer social contract

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:33:36 GMT

Academics question the purpose of the carer’s allowance and say we can learn from the Scottish government’s reform process

Your editorial (27 October) is right: serious issues with the Department for Work and Pensions’ administration of carer’s allowance run far deeper than inadequate IT systems. Well-documented systemic failures and flawed design have caused preventable financial and emotional harm. While the abolition of the punitive “cliff edge” is welcome, a taper cannot be the extent of the government’s commitment to carers.

The unacceptably long timeline for implementation prolongs the injustice. How will the government protect carers who are at risk of incurring overpayments debt in the period until 2030-31? Following the revelation that the DWP has completed fewer than 2% of the cases included in its reassessment exercise, this brings into question the urgency given to improving carers’ financial security.

Carer’s allowance, originally intended for unmarried women who were presumed available to care, has barely changed in half a century. It reflects assumptions about gender roles and work that no longer hold true. At £86.45 per week, even with the new taper it limits claimants to low-paid work that does not facilitate a decent standard of living. Its interactions with the state pension, universal credit and disability benefits are unfair.

It is time to ask what the purpose of carer’s allowance is in 2026. We can learn from the Scottish government’s reform process, which resulted in a clear statement of purpose. Its overall aims are: “to provide income for unpaid carers in recognition of their vital role and its impact on their lives”; “to provide stability and support carers to access opportunities outside of caring”; and “to ensure that carers have a positive experience of the social security system, and to maximise carers’ take-up of all support available to them”.

After years of inaction, it’s time for a new social contract that properly values carers. Becky Driscoll, Dr Louise Overton and Dr Maxine Watkins University of Birmingham Prof Kate Hamblin, Prof Nathan Hughes and Fay Benskin University of Sheffield

Charity shops have value in the community

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:33:16 GMT

They help volunteers to develop skills, make friends and find employment, says Antony David Davies

Your article on the declining profitability of charity shops struck a chord with me (UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market, 31 October). Having spent many years managing charity shops and community reuse projects, I feel that something important is being overlooked.

Charity shops were never just about making money. They provided affordable goods for people who needed them and, equally importantly, opportunities to gain confidence, develop skills, make friends and sometimes find their way back into employment. For some, volunteering is their first step back into society after a difficult period in their lives.

Of course, charity shops must pay their way. I spent six years managing a Salvation Army shop, substantially increasing its turnover, only to see it eventually close. So I understand the financial realities only too well. But I wonder whether in the pursuit of profitability and increasingly professional retail operations, parts of the sector have lost sight of their original purpose.

The true value of a charity shop should never be measured solely by what goes through the till, but also by what it gives back to its community. Antony David Davies Shrewsbury, Shropshire

Each gift I’ve featured has been put through its paces by me for the past few months and has made it into this list because it has become something I reach for on a near-daily basis (or, in the case of the AeroPress coffee maker, multiple times a day).

Testing has involved cooking copious amounts of rice, making my home smell like a greenhouse and rolling my sleeves up in the garden (and I don’t think I’ll need to sharpen my knives for a while). Despite the rise in Apple Pay and its Android equivalent, wallets still have their place in a pocket. This neat design from Roka London has three interior compartments for cards, coins and receipts. Made from a durable recycled canvas, it has retained its good looks after months of cut-and-thrust testing, and kept its contents dry in a downpour when my trousers weren’t as lucky.

The company will design a poster based on the memorable kits of any team (from non-league to national sides), and the result is a tasteful piece of art that is a cut above most sporting merch. My Arsenal-mad brother confirmed the early 90s yellow and black JVC away shirt was a particularly accurate representation.

Niwaki golden spade

Don’t be fooled by its colour. This spade might scream bling, but it’s an invaluable addition to any garden shed. It can break up rock-solid borders in no time, and its sharp tip has been great for dividing perennials.

Tomato vine refillable candle starter pack

Brighten up any WFH setting with a candle from Pott. Its collaboration with Isle of Wight Tomatoes is a welcome change from traditional scents and has brought a deep, summery tomato vine smell to my office as the nights have drawn in. Its jazzy pot can be used again with a candle refill, making it a longstanding staple of any desk.

UE Wonderboom 4 portable speaker

Electronics and outdoorsy dads don’t always mix well, but this portable speaker from Ultimate Ears is up to the challenge, including being submerged in water (it has an IP67 rating) and getting dropped in the sand by my toddler during a day trip to the beach. Its sound quality is surprisingly strong and bassy for such a small package (10.4cm high), and the audio doesn’t break up when cranked to the max.

Reusable earplug discovery pack

An earplug is an essential part of my sleep routine, though they rarely stay in until the morning. Happy Ears solved this issue with this discovery pack, helping me find a size that fits. Rather than completely blocking noise, they take an ambient edge off, and their use isn’t limited to the bedroom: they’ve been great for swimming and help at gigs, too.

The North Face wash bag

Although on the small side, this wash bag seems Tardis-like and has managed to fit all the essentials for weekends away and longer stays without taking up loads of room in luggage. Its zipped compartment means you don’t have to rummage for small items like contact lens cases and tweezers, and its integrated hanging loop was helpful when sink space was at a minimum.

Face cleansing bar

Swap out the plastic pump bottle for this face cleansing bar from Lifejacket. The bar itself lasted about three months of daily use and left my face feeling clear, refreshed and ready for bed after a day of sweat from exercising.

Horace mattifying face moisturiser, 75ml

For time-poor dads who aren’t au fait with a solid skincare routine, a moisturiser keeps things simple while soothing dry skin. This pick from French brand Horace packs SPF30 coverage, a matte finish with no glossy sheen, and instant absorption so it takes seconds to apply.

For more, read our guide to the best face moisturisers

Bob body wash bar starter kit

This refillable applicator and bar set from Bob lets you ditch the plastic bottle of shower gel. The applicator’s bristles help get a real lather going, and the bars themselves leave skin feeling clean and smelling subtly of peppermint and lime for the rest of the day.

Clear AeroPress

An AeroPress is the gateway method to making great coffee at home. Relatively mess-free, simple to clean and a fraction of the size of an espresso machine, I have used one daily for more than 10 years.

For more, read our guide to the best coffee machines for every home and budget

Folding knife sharpener

Sharp knives are safe knives – a blunt blade is more likely to slip – and this neat tool from Joseph Joseph has become a great, compact addition to my cutlery drawer. Dull, old knives have been given new life with some swipes on the coarse and fine ceramic sharpening wheels; its non-slip feet mean it feels secure to use.

For more, read our guide on how to look after your kitchen knives

Frying pan, 28cm

Substitute his scratched non-stick and its microplastic particles for stainless steel. I’ve found this tri-ply frying pan brilliant for steaks, stir-fries, scrambled eggs; its high sides mean it can even work for stews. Plus, it will survive contact with metal implements and over-enthusiastic scrubbing.

For more, read our guide to the best frying pans

Yep Kitchen Sichuan chilli crisp, 160g

Sichuan peppercorns are something of an acquired taste, but if you’re buying for a fan of the mouth-numbing spice, this chilli crisp lingers on the tongue and lips. Great in stir-fries, dolloped on dumplings or slathered on scrambled eggs, it adds a tingly sensation to any dish.

Hario cold brew bottle, 550ml

Cold brew isn’t just for summer: this Hario glass brewer is a feature of my fridge long into the depths of winter. The simplicity of brewing is the big draw – stick ground coffee and cold water in before bed and wake to a beautifully balanced cup. Having a batch to hand means it can also be used for cocktails such as carajillo and espresso martini without a coffee machine.

Wüsthof chef’s knife

Spending more than £100 on a knife may seem excessive, but this 8in Wüsthof chef’s knife has left the rest of my block firmly in the shade. Its handle has a satisfying weight that keeps you in control, while the blade is remarkably sharp and adept at everything from deboning chicken thighs to finely chopping garlic.

For more, read our guide to the best (and worst) chef’s knives

Yeti Rambler, 473ml

The Rambler is a rock-solid reusable cup from outdoor specialist Yeti, and its cup-holder compatibility makes it ideal for dad’s taxi. For an extra £8, it’s possible to add a personalised message to create a unique gift for your one-of-a-kind.

For more, read our guide to the best travel mugs

Bruichladdich the classic laddie whisky, 70cl

A contemporary take on a classic, this 10-year-aged single malt scotch is an approachable drop with a sweet nose and warming, biscuity taste that should get the seal of approval from aficionados and newcomers alike.

For more, read our guide to the best whisky

Bird & Blend tea infuser

This infuser makes brewing a mug of loose leaf tea straightforward. Fill with tea, plonk in a mug, pour over water and hey presto, you’ve got the taste of a teapot without the big clean-up operation and the convenience of a teabag minus the microplastics.

Stripes mug

A hot drink instantly tastes better when it’s served in posh crockery, and Villa Bologna’s handmade and handpainted striped number has an artisan feel without the associated price. Dishwasher safe and able to hold 400ml of tea or coffee, it’s a serious upgrade on his faded Sports Direct mug.
