after newsletter promotion

Bombom Korean barbecue sauce, 420g

Whether drenched on tofu, stir-fries and rice, or used as a marinade for chicken or salmon, this Korean soy and garlic barbecue sauce was an instant hit in my household. It’s moreish … so won’t last long.

Black Lines negroni, 500ml

Negroni’s three ingredients – gin, Campari and vermouth – make it one of the most straightforward cocktails to create, but not all serves are made equal. Black Lines’ premixed concoction is better than most, and means aperitivo hour is only the uncorking of a bottle away.

Craft beer gift pack

Gluten-free, vegan and carbon-negative, Jiddler’s Tipple craft beer creations are as guilt-free as they come. Its hoppy core range – which is included in this gift set with a vintage shirt pattern-inspired pint glass – all sit under 3.8% ABV too, so are less likely to leave a headache the next morning.

Rothaus Alkoholfrei pils 0.4%, 8 pack

Low-alcohol doesn’t have to be boring, as this Rothaus brew proves. After sampling a pint of the crisp, smooth 0.4% wheat beer in the summer, I was thrilled to find it came in a bottle for sober sipping at home. The flavour profile is perfect for the festive period, but also a welcome treat in warmer weather.

Forest Feast dark chocolate cashews, 120g

Swerve the chocolate orange stocking filler this year for a packet of these Belgian chocolate-covered salted cashews instead. A luxurious taste that perfectly balances the bitterness of dark chocolate with a hit of salt; buy a pack for yourself too, as they won’t be offered around.

Vina Real Rioja Gran Reserva Especial 2018, 75cl

If your old man knows his way around the wine aisle, then this special rioja is a sure-fire hit. A 2018 vintage that won’t break the bank, it has fruity notes that go well with red meat or manchego. Its ageing potential means it will also be a welcome addition to any burgeoning cellar (if it makes it through the festive period).

Yum Asia Kumo rice cooker

This rice cooker has become an invaluable addition to my kitchen, and a gadget that earns its place on a limited work surface. It’s simple to use – add water and rinsed rice, select the type (white, brown or short grain) – and about 40 minutes later you’re left with fluffy individual grains with no effort. For big families, Yum Asia’s Sakura has a larger capacity and can make up to 16 portions of rice in one go.

For more, read our guide to the best rice cookers

Running socks, per pair

A great stocking filler for the parkrun-obsessed pops, these socks from Hoka have a plush, cushioned feel underfoot when pounding the streets. They stay firmly in place even if you pick up the pace courtesy of an anti-slip silicone strip on the ball of the foot.

Running top

A base layer with fashion credentials, this moisture-wicking short-sleeve from Nike subbrand ACG keeps things cool during a run but won’t look out of place when they’re not working out. A slightly thicker front panel keeps the chill off on colder starts while mesh panels at the rear and armpits handle hotspots with ease.

Crewneck fleece

A fleece for all occasions, this versatile pullover from Arc’teryx has been a brilliant addition to my wardrobe. The organic cotton has a soft touch against bare skin and is great for lazy days around the house. But it’s equally adept when heading out in the cold for a walk or layering as part of a smarter get-up.

Weeknight Vegetarian by Joe Woodhouse

This has become a firm fixture on my cookbook stand, filled with quick fresh recipes that make veg, beans and vegan protein such as tofu sing – from fast-assembly jobs like the WFH-friendly store-cupboard bean salad to the hearty lentil cottage pie that will have him converted from the beef version.

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Elizabeth Strout’s Booker prize-shortlisted novel has a father as its focus and deals with themes inside and outside the home through protagonist Artie Dam’s lens. Funny, sad and at times a real thinker, it’s a refreshing break for anyone caught in the thriller loop.

London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe

An engrossing nonfiction read with the mysterious death of a young man as its focal point, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestseller is a page-turner that sheds light on London’s dark underbelly, complete with lies, deceit and dirty money.

Dressing gown

Warm and luxurious, the recycled polyester fleece hooded dressing gown from Chelsea Peers belies its price. It’s the first thing I reach for in the morning and has even stayed on deep into the afternoon on those video-call-free work-from-home days.

Merino wool socks

Darn Tough is known for its hiking socks, but I feel its lifestyle lineup is a step above any high-street hosiery. Despite their lightweight construction, the cushioning is the sort of support you expect from thicker walking socks, while the merino wool adds warmth in winter without getting sweaty on hotter days.

Flannel pyjama bottoms

Comfortable in a wide range of temperatures and showing no signs of wear after several washes, these posh pyjama bottoms are worth the expense, and you won’t need to replace them in 12 months.

Suede slippers

Slippers are a Christmas gift staple, but these suede M&S mules are an upgrade on any run-of-the-mill moccasins. The shearling lining gives your feet a cosy cuddle, and an antibacterial treatment keeps them smelling fresh, despite hours of wear.

Beanie hat

This soft, stylish beanie from Cornwall-based B Corp Finisterre is minimalist in design and made from merino wool. It keeps the warmth in and the cold at bay without blocking my ears, making it great for ear pod use or staying alert for any impending toddler tantrums.

Retro T-shirt

Brewery merch can often be naff, but this collaboration between Guinness and Manchester-based UN:IK is a legitimate addition to any T-shirt drawer. It pairs the Irish stout’s classic posters with a washed-out design and is a great gift for any G-splitting pros.

Extra virgin olive oil subscription

This small-batch extra virgin olive oil subscription is ideal for foodies who want to add punch to a dish – whether it’s salads, pasta or drizzled on Greek yoghurt. Handpicked and cold pressed in Crete, two bottles come directly from the farmers every two or three months, and for £30 a pop it beats supermarket fodder hands down on taste, price and sustainability.

Workshop Coffee subscription, three months

For adventurous types who are happy to have their taste buds tested, the Workshop single-origin coffee subscription offers a rotating selection of roasts. Available for filter or espresso brewing and as whole beans or ground for various brewing methods, a new brew arrives through the letterbox each month, and can be as varied as a lightly roasted zesty Ethiopian and a dark and deep Colombian cup.

National Trust individual membership, one year

Although you might have to get creative with your presentation of this gift (time to fire up Canva and dust down the printer), for less than two pints of beer a month (£8.40), you can provide free entry (and parking at most properties) to more than 500 National Trust sites around England, Wales and Northern Ireland (with some access to Scottish sites). Whether it’s interesting family days out, short solo walks around some grounds, or interesting ways to break up a long car journey, this pass will have you covered.

Bassvictim: Peace + War review – like a thrillingly chaotic house party that goes on too long

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:30:26 GMT

(VOTB)​On their fourth buzzy project in two years, the gobby and combustible US-Polish pair are best when they’re leaning into the roughness of their sound

Even by the standards of an age in which artists are encouraged to maintain a constant stream of new releases to ensure that they maintain a continual presence in an attention-deficit economy, there’s something pretty startling about Bassvictim’s work rate. Peace + War is the London-based duo’s fourth project in two years: 19 more tracks to add to the 31 they’ve already released since last January.

It’s a lot, but then, reading Bassvictim’s interviews you wonder if they’re simply splurging out material in the knowledge that their time is limited. The duo – Polish singer Maria Manow and Brooklyn-born producer Ike Clateman – really don’t give the impression of a band built for longevity. They have already announced their split on at least two separate occasions and lurid stories of a reportedly turbulent relationship.

At the end of 2025, they gave a tumultuous interview to Pitchfork that began with Manow taking ketamine to calm her down and got progressively more chaotic from there. She kept bursting into tears, threatened to quit yet again and suggested artists who were struggling for ideas “should take ketamine … and if some people die as a result of that, so be it”. (If you incline to the Daily Mail line that gen Z should consider bucking up their ideas a bit, you might note that at least some of her distress was apparently occasioned by losing her lucky hair slide, and that, at one point in the feature, it looks as if the evening’s gig might be derailed because she’d mislaid her vape.)

You hesitate to mention the 00s revivalist tag “indie sleaze”, because the thought of being labelled as such was one of the things that started Manow weeping, but you can see why the label has attached itself to them. The ongoing obsession of teens and twentysomethings with dissolute early 00s alt-rock and electro could be a screw-you reaction to growing up in a climate of constant nitpicking surveillance on social media, pressure to maintain a perfect Instagram-ready outward appearance, and lectures about health and abstinence from wellness influencers. If that’s the case, then Bassvictim, in all their confused, gobby combustibility, might well be its poster children. On Peace + War, Manow’s vocals frequently tend to yelling in the manner of someone in the throes of an implacable end-of-a-long-night meltdown: better that, the suggestion seems to be, than the scenario sketched out in the lyrics of I Don’t Know: “To me your life seems mid … plain girl, plain meals”.

More prosaically, echoes of several micro-genres from the era of Myspace and MP3 blogs gust through their sound. Electroclash is the obvious comparison, but as Peace + War progresses, you also catch distinct hints of witch house in the keening, echoing, atonal synths of Charred Glass, chiptune on Summer Song’s tinny vintage video game soundtrack aesthetic, and the decade’s wholehearted embrace of the kind of indie pop once reviled as irredeemably twee. Manow’s vocals keep slipping from the aforementioned yell into a slurred, childlike and occasionally melodically wayward tone; I Don’t Know’s lyrical bitterness is set to a melody so perkily simplistic it sounds like a nursery rhyme. Elsewhere, their penchant for multi-tracking vocals into faintly chaotic-sounding playground chants has a hint of the Go! Team about it, while a four-to-the-floor powered collaboration with underground rapper Fimiguerrero, inescapably – and not unpleasurably – evokes the period where UK rap briefly turned its attentions to chart-friendly house-fuelled commerciality.

They’re capable of writing nagging pop hooks, and of slipping into a more contemplative space – the beatless electronics of closer The End might glitch, yet there’s a lulling, becalmed quality about them nonetheless – but Peace + War is at its most exciting when the rough demo-like quality of its sound evokes a sense of teeming chaos. When layer after layer of vocals, spoken word and random interjections give you the impression it was recorded in the middle of a particularly messy house party; when huge basslines suddenly appear at a volume that means they drown out everything else; when its songs don’t so much come to a conclusion as collapse in front of you.

The problem is one of abundance. Even if you understand Bassvictim’s desire to splurge out material while they’ve still got the opportunity, this is music that works best in short bursts, and ideas run thin over the course of an hour. “There’s no more words left to say,” sings Manow towards the album’s conclusion, or at least she does eventually. It takes her a few goes to get the lyric right; the mistakes, punctuated by frustrated sighs, are left in. She sounds exhausted by the whole enterprise, and the listener may feel the same way some time before she does.

Piss – How Can You Act Opposite to This Emotion Like a lot of 2026’s best albums, the cocktail of raw-throated punk noise, spoken word and sound collage on the Canadian quartet’s You Made Me/Skin on Linen is a challenging listen. But if you’re in the market for scourging fury, 2026 has produced nothing to compare.

Is that an explosion, an implosion or an orgasm? Pixies bass-player Emma Richardson’s realm-leaping life in painting

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:12:43 GMT

Huge, ecstatic canvases are just one of the vocations of the musician who joined the art rockers in 2024. As her show Hotwire My Heart opens, she talks terror, awe and teabags

Emma Richardson loves to eavesdrop when people look at her paintings and talk about what they see in them. “They turn into these Rorschach inkblot tests,” she grins. Looking at her works, you do stand back in awe wondering. Is that a nebula, a god or a fleshy, baroque orgy? An explosion, an implosion or an orgasm? Richardson implies all of these and more, her paintbrush chasing in vivid oils the hedonism, desire and breadth of human experience.

This fascination with the transcendent has in part been informed by her other life as a musician, formerly in the garage-rock trio Band of Skulls and currently playing bass and singing in Pixies.

“Teabag in or out?” she asks brightly, her studio flooded with natural light, illuminating her canvases, some two metres tall. We are in the far, ungentrified reaches of east London, where a Dickensian-vibes building with a glazed roof and bathroom tiles of architectural salvage dreams can still serve as affordable studios. It’s a muggy afternoon and some of the works remain bubble-wrapped after returning from Richardson’s home town: Southampton City Art Gallery recently underwent a £2m revamp and she was chosen for its grand reopening exhibition, Levitate Me: Desire, Ecstasy and the Sublime. “They did such an incredible job,” she says. “It was celestial.”

But the paintings won’t sit here long and nor will she: these works are destined for a new show across town, while their creator will soon be touring the US with Pixies. While Richardson’s degree was in painting, she has always made music. She was asked to join Pixies in 2024, having had a few years off performing to concentrate on painting. She left Band of Skulls during the pandemic, five albums in. “That experience of playing live definitely feeds into my work,” she says. “There’s an electricity in that connection between audience and performers, then the danger and fear – no one knows what’s going to happen next.”

This is especially true with Pixies because there is never a set list. The next song is always decided on the spur of the moment by Black Francis, lead singer and guitarist. “It’s a real thrill,” she says, “and the show goes so quickly because of that excitement. There’s an element of extreme focus, but you let loose as well. It’s really freeing.”

So she explores these experiences on canvas, “and other ways human beings choose to transcend. It’s fascinating to me how we choose to do that through dancing and raves and festivals, big sporting events, but also solitary meditation and connecting to ourselves a bit more deeply.”

Sex is a big one: “Those ecstatic peak experiences. I’m fascinated by desire and female sexuality, connection with other human beings, and the sublime in the natural world. We see it these days more and more with climate change and the storms and this uncontrollable nature. It’s the contemporary sublime, terror mixed with awe, but it’s all under this umbrella of ways of transcending.” Equally for some, this may involve “intoxication and psychedelics or it could be reading a book and getting lost in it.”

Richardson has a crate of her favourite books right here, fresh from being displayed alongside her exhibition in Southampton. Many focus on female desire, a subject she’s been doubling down on as she enters midlife at 44. Miranda July’s All Fours from 2024, Nell Dunn’s Talking to Women from 1964: “Lots of psychology of desire.” She mentions Audre Lorde’s Your Silence Will Not Protect You, which contains her famous 1978 essay about “the erotic as an inner, driving force, a life force, rather than the pornographic reading of the erotic. That fascinates me. That inner drive and push in women, trusting what brings you joy and what gives you pleasure. What do you want out of life? It’s important to figure out these things.”

There’s Gillian Anderson’s Want, too, the first of two collections of anonymously submitted sexual fantasies from women around the world. Richardson digs out another from the box. “This is an incredible book, Alphabetical Diaries by Sheila Heti. She put every single line of her diary into a spreadsheet and then ordered them alphabetically, but they link and make patterns. It’s brilliant when you get to I – and I am and I love and I hate. I’m intrigued by how other writers or artists or musicians explore what it is to exist in a female body.”

I spot the catalogue from the British surrealist painter Ithell Colquhoun’s 2025 exhibition at Tate Britain, a show that made me feel so seen as a red-blooded woman that I developed a palpable swagger the further I got around it. And a book on Artemisia Gentileschi, “one of the earliest baroque painters”, says Richardson. “She was very sassy and clever about how she painted her self-portrait, using powder pigments and oil.” Part of the power of Richardson’s work is that it’s steeped in the history of art – you can see abstract ghosts of Gentileschi, Rubens and the female surrealists – but takes the discourse somewhere new and peculiar to her.

She’s inspired visually, too, by the Hubble telescope and sci-fi films such as 2001: A Space Odyssey. “There’s a stargate sequence where they’re travelling through time. It’s like loads of flashing, colourful lights going past the helmet of the person in the spacecraft and the energy and colour feels like you’re lifting out of your body – that inspired a painting called I Slipped My Body Completely, which is that sensation that you’re hanging in space, this idea of a transitional state almost.” How to capture that statically in paint is the challenge, she says: “Surprising yourself with what comes out and what you can then work into further. It’s like hunting it down.”

When she talks about oil paints her eyes widen like a toddler investigating its first snail after a downpour. “It’s quite alchemic,” she says. “You can layer it, and you can make it glow and sing like no other medium. There’s something about the consistency, colour and depth you can create, the fact it stays wet so you can work into it and blur and smudge and mix.”

With canvases of this scale, she says, the work “envelops you, it’s wider than your vista”. But while on tour, she paints and draws in more portable dimensions, packing acrylic paint, charcoal and watercolour. “I work in hotel rooms and backstage and make small pieces. I need that outlet on tour.”

It has been 13 years, and two other bass players, since Pixies’ revered original bassist, Kim Deal, left. How has it felt taking on her mantle? “It’s huge shoes to fill and I’ve got nothing but respect for her,” says Richardson, “but all I can do is my best – and know they asked me to do it. But my voice does sound different, and I might have a different playing style. I can’t imitate, but respect.”

She plays the songs how they should be played, “but there’s going to be an element of myself in there. I hope that works with the current lineup. They seem happy, so I’m happy. But it’s an incredible position. And the basslines are so cool.” In fact, learning the songs was a revelation, as a longtime fan. “You realise how cleverly structured they are. They’re really tricky. The time signatures are quite different. There are sections you don’t expect cropping up, and not many repeats.” Richardson played on their 2025 album The Night the Zombies Came. “We’re looking to do some more recording, but it’s all very relaxed.”

The new London show is at the Wolf Collective – a commercial gallery within the curator’s Primrose Hill home. It’s called Hotwire My Heart, borrowed from a 1976 song by a band called Crime, later covered by Sonic Youth. “It has a real frenzied garage rock’n’roll sound like the Stooges,” she says. “I heard it back when I was at Wimbledon School of Art, loved it and titled one of my degree show paintings with the name.” Hotwire was also a name she used when she played solo gigs around Southampton when she was starting out. It feels apt, she says, to reuse the title for these paintings crystallising “the need to be whipped up into another realm”.

Emma Richardson Hotwire My Heart is showing at the Wolf Collective, Primrose Hill, London, until 28 February. Admission is free. For further information on Emma’s work please visit www. emmarichardsonart. com

Tracking the blue wave: how our visual and data journalists helped you navigate the US midterm elections

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:00:28 GMT

Ahead of the Democrats’ ‘Blue-nami’, some of the team behind our epic results page explained the work that goes into preparing for every election night

On millions of screens around the world this week, the colour of the US electoral map digitally transposed. But behind the pixelated blue states and red states there were really 50 shades of purple.

Some midterm races for the Senate and House of Representatives were closer than others. Some swings didn’t represent an actual shift in party allegiance. The shades and nuances in each race were always going to be important this year, with expectations that many Republican supporters wouldn’t turn out for their party because of specific issues, such as inflation, fuel prices, the Iran war, datacentres, or Donald Trump’s toxicity.

That’s why our data and visual journalists spent months working on features that don’t just show you which side won each race, but also what issues might have swung it, and the demographic makeup of the swing voters.

I spoke to some of them ahead of the elections for a newsletter that was sent out to Guardian supporters before Tuesday’s blue wave. This article is adapted from that newsletter to give you a sense of the work and thought that went into the Guardian’s results pages, the main one of which has been viewed nearly 6 million times over a total of more than 100,000 combined hours of our readers’ time.

“It will likely become apparent quite quickly which party has won the Senate and the House,” said Ashley Kirk, the Guardian’s senior editor for visual journalism. “But then the questions will be: Why did they win, and who was significant in swinging the election a certain way?”

As well as a live results page, the team also built an interactive visual analysis feature to illustrate key swings that might be attributable to a specific issue or driven by a particular demographic group. “The only way we can tell these kinds of stories is by having the actual live voting data,” said Ashley, “and then trying to correlate the swings in small geographic areas, such as counties or districts, with demographic data or historical voting patterns for those areas – for instance, people’s educational, income or racial background. So, part of the work of planning and preparing for the midterms involves ensuring that we’ve got all of that live data feeding in.”

The Guardian had a team of 14 data and visual journalists working on our coverage of the midterm elections, alongside dozens of reporters and editors. The team included colleagues in New York and London engaged in a relay effort across different time zones as they monitored and supported our live results page, analysed the data feeds, produced and updated the interactive analysis feature, and worked on the visuals for the Guardian’s print editions.

“We always plan a full rota of editors, journalists and developers on the visuals team to monitor and support the pages because there are always surprises that mean that we have to do live fixes or change things,” said Ashley. “It’s live news – there are always events we need to respond to.”

The live feeds of granular data were essential for establishing the bigger picture. “Having all those live feeds so that we can spot correlations in the data means we can quickly get a finger on the pulse of what has been going on on the ground,” said Ashley. “And that will inform all of our coverage so that we’re not having to wait to see what others are reporting; we can shed our own light on things early on.”

As well as preparing the feeds, the team also prepared analysis for a range of different scenarios. “We have to think about every eventuality and prepare for it so that we can turn things around fast enough on the day,” explained Ashley. “There might be runoffs or unexpected changes in turnout, or challenges to certain race calls. Maybe only half the things we’ve prepared will end up getting published, but we have to do it this way because if we just wait to be reactive on election day, there just won’t be the capacity to publish everything in time.”

Like many other news outlets, the Guardian takes US election vote counts and race calls from the Associated Press (AP). The winners of Senate and House races typically get called well before every single vote has been counted, when it becomes clear that there are no paths for a trailing candidate to catch up. This means there’s always a time lag between a winner being declared and analysable voting data feeding through. Our journalists only published and updated the interactive analysis feature when they were confident there was enough data to bear out a trend, insight or interpretation.

The team had to navigate other time lags. For instance, votes in a state’s more densely-populated cities often take longer to count than votes in rural areas, which can sometimes lead to seemingly sudden surges in votes for the Democrats. However, these kinds of standard vote declaration lags have become highly politicised in today’s post-truth era of election denial. “We know that, in the past, Trump has cast doubt on elections because of a sudden blue surge in the vote count as more urban precincts in a state declare, and so Trump will question where those votes have come from,” explained Ashley. “So we have to make conscious design decisions on how our results page looks when a particular party is leading. So, for example, where Republicans are leading we’ll have a pink shade so it conveys a sense of uncertainty. In a time when people cast doubt on electoral processes, we have a responsibility to present this information in as clear and accessible a way as possible.”

Antonio Voce, an interactive journalist on the team, said the live results page for this year’s midterms had been honed by work on previous contests. “It’s been easier this year because we’ve built on extensive previous experience with live US election results coverage,” he said. “But we decided to introduce some visual changes and to focus on improving the technical infrastructure behind the results page. We also collaborated with our product and engineering colleagues to create new tools to facilitate the election coverage across the newsroom, such as graphics for key races that update live as the votes are counted across our news stories.”

The shape of the US presents particular challenges when it comes to making electoral maps work in different aspect ratios for viewing on a mobile phone as well as a desktop screen. Navigation functions have been developed to make it easier for readers to see the results in geographically smaller states. “That’s why we have things like search boxes, zoom functionality and cartograms that distort geographic shapes into something more meaningful and representative, for instance with every seat having the same area on the map. These functions allow people to surface their results as quickly and as easily as possible,” said Ashley.

“But while we have a tried and tested approach to results pages, it’s never a rinse and repeat process because every election has its own quirks,” he added. “For instance, there might be boundary changes or changes to the electoral voting system.”

Indeed, this year’s House elections had been overshadowed by a spate of politically motivated redistricting attempts. As our journalists explained in this interactive map of what to look out for ahead of the elections, nine states have redrawn congressional boundaries since Trump set off a redistricting war last year.

“As we use the AP live feed to visualise and determine seat flips and incumbents on the maps, decisions on how to treat redistricted seats for those purposes are delegated to them,” explained Antonio.

While the team had prepared for scenarios such as disputed results that have sadly become a feature of US elections, they hoped those aspects of their preparation wouldn’t be needed. “There’s a lot of work that goes in that you might not see – and we hope you don’t see, because it would mean that something bad is happening,” said Ashley. “But, again, we need to be prepared.”

Wallabies’ pay dispute with Rugby Australia overshadows Nations Championship finale

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:00:26 GMT

Australia are preparing for their clash with England under a cloud with RA claiming the players’ union’s proposals ‘threaten the future of the game’

An increasingly ugly pay dispute is threatening to unravel Australian rugby a year from a home World Cup, as the Wallabies prepare for four Nations Championship matches crucial for reversing fortunes smashed by two heavy Bledisloe Cup defeats.

The Wallabies meet England at Allianz Stadium – the sponsor’s name for Twickenham, not its namesake in Sydney – on Sunday afternoon local time (early Monday AEDT). The fixture is critical as the team looks to revive the momentum developed early under new coach Les Kiss before Australia were given a reality check against New Zealand last month.

Those two matches – when they conceded 93 points with alarmingly little resistance – were the last under the previous collective bargaining agreement, struck in 2023. The negotiations for a new one are not going well.

The Wallabies’ first press conference on tour in the UK this week should have been a celebration of the recall of Kurtley Beale, and the return of assistant coach Jonny Fisher to his homeland. Instead, questions about the bargaining process prompted an awkward exchange, with both men unable or unwilling to diagnose what has quickly become a sore.

Rugby Australia (RA) took the unusual step of sending a letter directly to players this week outlining their offer, bypassing the Rugby Union Players’ Association (Rupa) which is responsible for negotiations. A response from Rupa president Tom Robertson expressed disappointment about RA taking the step “particularly while the Wallabies are on tour”. RA chair Daniel Herbert returned with his own statement saying Rupa’s counter-proposals “threaten the future of the game in Australia”.

Bargaining in sport is rarely cordial, but this has come to resemble punch. The immediate tension surrounds RA’s uncomfortable financial situation. Only two years removed from a $37m annual deficit, the governing body hopes to squirrel away much of the near-$100m fee paid by World Rugby for hosting next year’s men’s World Cup to make up for coming leaner years. Although last year’s British & Irish Lions matches allowed the governing body to clear debts, those tours come around just once every 12 years. Officials are well aware they will not see another home men’s World Cup in twice that time, or longer.

There is clearly a need for players to be fairly compensated. Male rugby union players in Australia are already paid less than those in rugby league. The NRL’s $5.3bn, seven-year broadcast deal with Channel Nine and Kayo struck this year is likely to increase player salaries in a rival code that can already offer professional contracts greater in number and average value to promising young footballers.

Although the Wallaroos will host the women’s World Cup in 2029, they are well off the standards set by the likes of England, New Zealand and Canada. This season’s NRLW successes of former sevens players Teagan Levi and Sariah Paki will increase the appetite of league recruiters for union players.

RA’s current offer increases payments to men’s and women’s players, including an expansion of the Wallaroos’ full-time program, but Robertson argued there are still “basic protections” sought, including “proper career-ending injury cover and fair conditions across the men’s and women’s game”. Herbert countered by saying the players have “some of the best working conditions in international rugby”.

The latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewed

after newsletter promotion

As the terms are being haggled over, rugby union faces broader challenges in the region. Rivals in rugby league have been given generous Australian government funding to develop talent in the Pacific, and New Zealand Rugby faces tens of millions of dollars of losses in coming years. With South Africa aligning itself more closely with the northern hemisphere nations and the All Blacks, Australian rugby must save itself.

The negotiations could not come at a more important time. The coming 12 months is an opportunity for rugby union and its players to return the code to the lofty status it enjoyed in 2003 when Australia last hosted the World Cup. The Wallabies realistically have little chance of winning the trophy, given they are already on the outer of the group of contenders. But high profile World Cup failures resembling the thrashings handed to them by the All Blacks last month would not only spurn this generational opportunity, it would send the sport backwards. To have the Wallabies and Rugby Australia united in a year that so much is at stake, and when every ounce of performance must be squeezed from this still-improving playing group, is a basic necessity.

With a lapsed agreement, players are able to pursue industrial action, including media boycotts and protests. The most prominent recent example of a similar dispute in Australian sport was in 2023 rugby league players taped over the logo of the NRL on their shirts and refused to perform their ordinary press obligations. Back then, the NRL used its media partners to put forward its claims. The Australian broadcast of this weekend’s Wallabies match – and three more later this month – will be instructive about just how deep the ill-feeling goes.

Both Robertson and Herbert expressed some positivity in their statements this week that a solution could be found. The match against England is therefore timely: a reminder of the common enemy.

Cristiano Ronaldo merely the latest example of a great player who couldn’t let go

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 13:32:02 GMT

There is no doubt his international career was an incredible one, but it would have been greater still if he had not lingered on the stage so long

Nothing, perhaps, is quite so difficult for an elite sportsperson as timing their exit. It’s not easy for any person in any job to weigh the hope of having more to give with the desire not to linger beyond their usefulness, but it’s perhaps particularly hard for top athletes because unrealistic self-confidence is so essential to their success. It takes an almost unhealthy level of self-belief for anybody to make the sacrifices to get to the top, to dedicate themselves to such a precarious vocation, to overcome all the setbacks and injuries and failures. How can someone – whose whole life has been spent assuring themselves there are no odds they cannot overcome – accept that is it, that the time has come to say goodbye?

The news that Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football brings with it, inevitably, a sadness. Sadness we will no longer see him skipping past a defender, or burying a neck-thrusting header, and sadness in that the end of the career of any great is a reminder of mortality; all things in time must pass. But there is also a sadness he timed his departure so badly. For at least three tournaments, there has been a sense of Ronaldo holding Portugal back.

At the 2022 World Cup, Fernando Santos belatedly took the decision to leave Ronaldo out for the last-16 tie against Switzerland. Portugal suddenly had a fluency and fluidity they had lacked for years and the player who had replaced Ronaldo, Gonçalo Ramos, scored a hat-trick. That seemed incontrovertible evidence the end was upon Ronaldo, or at least his role might become that of an impact substitute.

But even in the final minutes of that game, half the crowd were chanting for Ronaldo. Some, perhaps, were Portuguese fans but many were tourists. They didn’t care much about the result or who went through, they just wanted to see the famous man do the famous thing. Near the end, he scored a goal that was obviously offside. He knew it was offside, but he also knew what his public wanted. So he did the “Siuuuu …” celebration and was rewarded with the biggest cheer of the night. This was like seeing late-period Elvis in Las Vegas: it didn’t matter he was no longer the singer he had been, he was still Elvis. It’s just that Elvis wasn’t also carrying Portugal’s World Cup hopes on his rhinestoned shoulders.

When a player has such celebrity status, when he is still somehow the show no matter how sluggish his movements, making that decision on when to quit must become even harder. And Ronaldo, with his status as Portugal’s greatest soft-power export, also became a political issue. A cabinet minister publicly said he couldn’t be dropped because of how much revenue he generated and what he meant for Portugal’s brand. Portugal is not a country replete with global superstars.

Portuguese Football Federation "Every drop of sweat, every decisive goal, and every captain’s arm-band he wore with honour on the field reflected his unconditional love ⁠for our jersey. His dedication ⁠and his legacy ​transcend the four lines of the field. Ronaldo has raised Portugal’s profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for ⁠many of us, he is the greatest player of all time! …"

Al-Nassr (Ronaldo's current club) "It’s not just a chapter – it’s history you’ve shaped. You’re an icon to the entire world, not ⁠just Portugal. Portugal is in your heart, and you are in the hearts of the world. A page ​has turned, but there is still history left ‌for us to write together at ‌your home, Al-Nassr."

Manchester United (one of Ronaldo's former clubs) "Congratulations on an incredible international career."

Bruno Fernandes (Portugal and Manchester United) "Thank ‌you for the inspiration. It was a privilege to be able to share great moments with our national team alongside my childhood idol."

Diogo Dalot (Portugal and Manchester United) "They don’t know that dreams are a constant in life … Portugal’s history tells us that we are a people who have never accepted limits, unafraid of uncharted seas or weathering storms. We were and are shaped by achievements, sacrifices, tears, and sweat … ‌By dreams that seem impossible – until someone has the courage to make them a reality. You did it. You made us believe, dream, and achieve! A legacy that will be remembered ​not only for the trophies or the goals, but also for the path you paved for all those who came after you. Your passion and determination to represent our country is something I’ll never forget and that will stay with me forever. I’m immensely proud of everything you’ve done for our national team! Thank you, idol."

Pepe (Former Portugal and Real Madrid defender) "It was more than just soccer. Thanks for everything, Cris."

Gianni Infantino, Fifa president "Few players have ever ​touched the heart of football fans ​around the world quite like Cristiano. A career defined by extraordinary talent, relentless determination and ​an unwavering desire to ‌push the boundaries ​of what is possible … Cristiano has ​achieved milestones that may never be matched but his greatest legacy goes far beyond records, trophies and goals … Thank you, Cristiano, for the passion, the unforgettable moments and the immense contribution you have made to our beautiful game proudly wearing the 'Selecao' shirt. Your international career will forever be part of football’s history." Reuters

Ronaldo hung around at Euro 2024, weeping after missing a penalty against Slovenia, the magnitude of his fame and ego warping perception so everything became about him, no matter how many other hugely gifted players were in that squad. And implausibly he was still doing it at the World Cup this summer: gumming the mechanisms, constantly demanding the ball, occasionally drifting out to the left to get in Rafael Leão’s way. At one point against Spain in what turns out to have been his final World Cup game, Ronaldo was released on the break but, lacking pace, ended up having to turn back and play the ball to his full-back, the opportunity gone. There was something almost painful about seeing a player once so explosive reduced to this.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

There needed to be some sort of intervention. This generation of Portuguese players, who really should be challenging for major honours and not just the Nations League, could not continue to struggle on with such an albatross around their necks. It came from Jorge Jesus, the admirably forthright 72-year-old national coach, who was appointed after the World Cup. He didn’t bring Ronaldo off the bench in the second half of a tight game Portugal ended up winning against Norway. Ronaldo insisted he had been promised minutes – but even if there had been an agreement, it would be absurd to refuse a coach the capacity to adapt to circumstance – and stormed out of the camp, an indication perhaps of how his self-regard had come to distort his judgment.

And, assuming this retirement isn’t some sort of power play to force Jesus out, that is where it ended, with a €255 (£212) fine and 30-day ban over a period in which Portugal had no games. Ronaldo will go back to the Saudi Pro League to continue his pursuit of a 1,000th goal. He has been an extraordinary player. He will be remembered as an all-time great, vying with Eusébio as the greatest Portugal player of all time, but his legacy is undoubtedly tainted by this protracted farewell, by the sense that a player who at his best could win games single-handed, came by the end to be a burden to his national team. His has been a great career, but it would have been greater had it been a little shorter.

‘Revenge of the nerds’: US midterms deliver a win for science – and a rebuke of Maha

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 13:00:24 GMT

The wins for Democrats come after years of cuts and upheaval to US health and science infrastructure

A political organization behind a wave of Democratic doctors and scientists winning elections up and down the ballot is calling the stunning rebuke of Trumpism the “Stem swing” and “revenge of the nerds”.

The wins come after years of cuts and upheaval to US health and science infrastructure, as Democrats spent big on health-related ads and as voters rejected the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement.

“It’s clear from the results: 2026 was a healthcare election,” said Erik Polyak, executive director of 3.14 Action, a group that worked to elect Democratic health professionals and scientists across the country. “We’ve heard a lot about affordability. Healthcare affordability is the No 1 piece of that. Our doctors and scientists are certainly well-equipped to lead on those issues.”

Among the history-making lawmakers are Democrats Dr Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Dr Annie Andrews of South Carolina. The last time a Democratic doctor held a seat in the US Senate was in 1969 – the era when Medicare and Medicaid were passed into law. They are far from alone: 3.14 Action is still tallying wins and waiting for results among “hundreds” of obscure state races, some of which are not even reporting results yet.

“The voters’ message is simple and clear: enough,” Dr Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, a philanthropic organization dedicated to improving Americans’ health, said in a statement.

“People across America are frustrated by the high cost of living, exhausted trying to make ends meet, and fed up with a ridiculously expensive and complicated healthcare system,” said Besser. “They want leaders who understand how hard it is and will do something to make their lives better.”

Doctors and scientists have long held leadership roles in Congress, but until this election, the overwhelming majority were Republican. Perhaps unsurprisingly, scientists studied this: from 2011 to 2020, 86% of the physician-members of Congress were Republican and three-quarters were from southern states.

The 2026 election turned that on its head. Republicans like Dr Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa and Senate candidate Dr Roger Marshall – both allies of the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr – lost. Races for three more Republican doctors were too close to call. Meanwhile, all incumbent Democratic doctors won their races.

Galvanizing Americans behind science did not come without a cost. Trump and Kennedy brought upheaval to nearly every American scientific institution and corner of American healthcare, from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to Medicaid, the public health program that insures 72 million Americans.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has lost up to one-third of its staff in the midst of a record-breaking measles outbreak. The National Institutes of Health (NIH), the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research, lost leadership and saw path-breaking research stymied amid disruptions, cancellations and censorship. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) struggled to keep up with a historic outbreak of diarrhea-inducing cyclosporiasis. On election day, New York health authorities announced that a child in the state had died of measles for the first time in 30 years.

Kennedy disrupted and defunded federal work on vaccines to placate a base of zealots, as four in 10 “Maha voters” worried about healthcare prices. He also became a key figure for doctors and scientists to rally against. Before the election, 3.14 Action said that Kennedy was “our No 1 recruitment and fundraising tool – hands down”.

Democrats capitalized on this upheaval. Healthcare was the second-biggest issue in campaign ads, according to the Cook Political Report, with Democrats running more than 158,000 healthcare-related ads versus 61,000 for Republicans. 3.14 Action alone spent $23m on independent ads, most targeting health issues including – as corruption became a defining issue of the race – standing up to pharmaceutical companies and insurers.

High-profile Democratic candidates often spoke about local healthcare challenges. In South Carolina, as a measles outbreak took hold in February, pediatrician Andrews was able to give specific health advice even as federal authorities downplayed the dangers.

“I never in a million years, when I was in medical school, thought that I would be running for the US Senate and also talking about measles nearly every single day,” Andrews told the 19th at the time.

El-Sayed pitched a vision of Medicare for All that would save rural hospitals threatened by the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act. His call and response with the crowd was direct: “Money in your … ” “Pocket!” “Money out of … ” “Politics!” “Medicare for … ” “All!”

In Ohio, where Dr Amy Acton prevailed, her experience as a health director during Covid-19 turned out to be an asset, rather than a liability. In Iowa, Democrat Christina Bohannan, who is not a doctor but a law professor, pledged to spend more on research as rising cancer rates became a bipartisan political issue in the state.

“Americans who believe in science are fired up,” said Polyak. “We’ve flipped at least 10 Republican seats and the final number is the low 30s,. Flipping control of the House in 2026 ran through Democratic doctors and scientists – and we led the charge.”

New Democratic lawmakers face far-reaching challenges when they are sworn in. The most draconian cuts of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act go into effect on New Year’s Day 2027. Among the most emblematic are work requirements for Medicaid. All told, cuts are expected to result in 17 million people losing insurance in the next decade.

They will also be faced with enormous insurers and drug companies, which will seek to push back and influence lawmakers as Democrats hammer out consensus on wide-ranging health proposals pitched during the campaign, from a public option to government-backed single-payer healthcare. And public health political organizations are already calling for Kennedy to be removed from office.

“In a lot of ways, this election represented the beginning of the end of RFK Jr’s disastrous leadership,” said Polyak. “It’s clear Americans want something different – they didn’t elect all these Democratic scientists just to oppose Trump. People want to see an alternative agenda, they want to see what Democratic scientists can deliver for them.”

How did Republicans lose a Senate seat in fireball-red South Carolina?

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 12:00:23 GMT

Bitter postmortem under way as party comes to terms with Darline Graham’s stunning loss to Annie Andrews

It’s not that Shane Brown somehow didn’t know about the US Senate election in South Carolina. Nor was he unaware that the outcome of the race between Senator Darline Graham and her Democratic challenger, Annie Andrews, was shockingly competitive when he refrained from voting on Tuesday.

The campaigns would not let him forget it.

“Oh, text messages, phone calls, TV, you name it: it was everywhere,” Brown said of the onslaught of political advertising he endured. “Like, the joke at work was the first person who stops texting me is the one we’d probably vote for.”

No one stopped texting Brown, who typically votes Republican. By election day, he said: “Nobody really won me over.”

In a stunning upset, Andrews was elected to the seat previously held by the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, after defeating his younger sister, Darline, a political novice encouraged to run by Donald Trump.

The electoral earthquake has left political observers in South Carolina reeling, trying to understand how Graham could have stumbled in a state as fireball red as South Carolina. Looking at who came to vote and who stayed home reveals part of the answer.

“I think there’s one stat of the day,” said Tyson Grinstead, Republican national committeeman for South Carolina. From 2024 to 2026, “there were 500,000 people who voted in the 2024 presidential election who did not come back in the midterm.”

“Of that 500,000, 400,000 were Republicans,” he said.

Midterm elections are historically lower-turnout affairs than presidential elections, and in most midterm elections the dropoff in voting numbers is larger in South Carolina. But more Black voters and other traditionally Democratic voting groups showed up than would otherwise be expected this year, Grinstead said. And more Republicans stayed home.

“The post-mortem really will be: why did that happen, and what can we do about it moving forward?” Grinstead said, adding: “The story of the night isn’t that South Carolina is getting materially bluer; it’s that we weren’t able to turn out the statewide vote we normally do.”

The results of other contests tell part of the story as well. In an election that sent a Democrat to the senate from South Carolina with a comfortable five-point margin, voters also elected a Republican governor and lieutenant governor, secretary of state, treasurer, attorney general and other statewide offices by similar margins.

“South Carolina is not a Democratic or purple state; South Carolinians remain a conservative lot,” said state senator Shane Massey, majority leader of the Republican caucus in the South Carolina senate. “But they were upset with how some elected officials handled their work.”

The 62-year-old Graham was appointed by South Carolina’s Republican governor Henry McMaster to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term after his sudden death in July. Though initially viewed as a caretaker, she was publicly urged to run for office by the president, upending the contentious GOP primary to replace her brother.

“Senator-elect Andrews’s victory shouldn’t be confused with broad ideological support for her platform,” Massey added. “It was primarily a rejection of the alternative and a desire to send a message. Voters expect their officials, Republican or Democrat, to address real problems rather than just screwing around.”

Berkeley county, one of South Carolina’s fastest growing counties in the fastest growing state, voted for Trump by a margin of about 16 points in 2024. On Tuesday, Andrews drew a nine-point victory margin – a shift of 26 points toward a Democrat and among the largest swings in the state.

Some of that can be attributed to the congressional race to fill the seat vacated by former US representative Nancy Mace. The winner, retired admiral Nancy Lacore – fired by defense secretary Pete Hegseth in a purge of female and nonwhite general officers – flipped its partisan control in a race that goosed Democratic turnout across the first congressional district.

And some of that can be attributed to Graham’s weakness as a candidate.

Voters said they felt like Graham had been selected for them, and they had seen that play before.

“I only voted Trump, honestly, because I couldn’t vote for Kamala because she was forced. We didn’t get a choice,” said Brown. “That was my issue with Darline, too. It was the same exact thing to me … They selected her. The powers that be said: ‘This is the person you guys get to vote for.’ And that’s not the way it should be.”

She has had to dig out from under a series of public gaffes that called her competence into question, beginning with her comments during a primary contest debate in August against US congressman Ralph Norman that “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security”.

Norman picked at Graham as the campaign wore on, in an act of sour grapes that makes the conflict between Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan look like a shopping cart collision. A low-key write-in campaign for Norman fueled conservative skepticism about Graham. Party activists remain bitter about it all.

“You know, here’s this woman who was most likely at Belk buying a pocketbook on 10 July, and she gets put in the Senate,” said Randal Wallace, a South Carolina real estate professional, Republican political commentator and former Myrtle Beach city councilman.

“And then they asked her to run. And who’s going to turn the president of the United States down when he asks you to run? And our party couldn’t get behind her to help her through this whole thing?”

Wallace is furious.

“Norman does this little wink and nod, ‘Well, my family’s not going to vote for her,’ and then he called her a fraud,” Wallace said. “He sent a signal to everybody up there and to all of his people not to help her. And they didn’t. And they succeeded. Annie Andrews is your senator. But I promise you, I’ll never forgive this.”

As the campaign became more competitive in the final stretch, Graham’s aides increasingly limited her availability to the press and the public, pulling her abruptly from the spin room after her sole general election debate with Andrews. The Democrat’s campaign pounded Graham with advertising, bought with donated money from around the country.

South Carolinians have weathered a deluge of political ads before: Jaime Harrison lit $130m on fire trying to beat Lindsey Graham in 2020. The result was a 10-point loss. But this time, there was no Lindsey Graham to raise money, Massey noted.

“Following Lindsey Graham’s death, we had a chaotic sprint primary format,” Massey said. “The nominee was selected in mid-September, leaving Darline Graham only six or seven weeks to run as a first-time candidate, compared to nominees in other states who had months. Lindsey had spent most of his campaign funds in the primary under the assumption that he could easily raise whatever general election money he needed.”

Annie Andrews raised $24.2m for her campaign. Graham raised only $1.9m.

The underlying anger of the electorate also contributed.

In the county on Wednesday afternoon, Derek Rosado loaded $450 worth of groceries into the back of his truck at a Publix in Moncks Corner. He found Andrews’s victory last night delightfully surprising.

“I mean, something’s got to change,” Rosado said. “And I think with the Democrats finally taking over again, I think they’ll bring the prices down. They see what’s going on, and it’s not just South Carolina, it’s the world.

“I mean, let’s be real: why are we fighting over in Iran? Why are we in a war there? Still going on with the Middle East stuff, spending trillions of dollars for a war that’s not even ours.”

‘Children were wearing fake life jackets’: one Syrian family’s terrifying, 10-year journey

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 11:39:48 GMT

In 2015, two film-makers first met 11-year-old refugee Israa, forced to abandon Aleppo for a new life in Europe, along with her parents and siblings. None of them imagined what would come next

In 2015, an 11-year-old Syrian girl called Israa matter-of-factly explained how her family would survive if their dinghy sank crossing the sea from Turkey to Greece. Her father would grab her disabled sister; her mother would look after the baby. “And I,” said Israa, a huge smile lighting her face, “I know how to rescue myself.”

Wife-and-husband documentary-makers Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes met Israa while filming a BBC series, Exodus, about refugees trying to reach Europe. Their plan was to follow Israa and her family on their hazardous journey to Germany. But after Israa reached safety, the pair kept filming. Ten years in the making, their documentary, One in a Million, is extraordinary - with echoes of Richard Linklater’s Boyhood and the Up! series. We watch Israa grow up in front of our eyes, from a sunny-natured 11-year-old to a woman, married with a baby of her own.

Azzam and MacInnes first spotted Israa in İzmir, on the Turkish coast, selling cigarettes with her father to raise money to pay the people-smugglers. “This ray of sunshine appeared in front of us,” remembers Azzam, who is also Syrian. “Israa was smiling and started talking to us. It was love at first sight. She was so bubbly, enthusiastic and positive. We were talking to her, then her father. They invited us back to their flat.” The family had fled Aleppo after their home was destroyed by a missile.

Eleven-year-old Israa joked about the dinghy sinking, too young to understand the risks. But her father Tarek agonised: “I’m gambling with the lives of my children,” he says in the documentary. Just a few months earlier, the body of the three-year-old Syrian boy Alan Kurdi washed ashore in Turkey. The image was in Tarek’s mind as he parted from the film-makers on the night of the crossing: “If anything bad happens to us, you have to tell our story.”

McInnes still finds the scene emotional to watch: “At the time we knew there was a chance that we would say goodbye to them, and that would be it.”

Sitting next to him in the restaurant of a London hotel, Azzam brushes aways tears as she remembers filming in İzmir, a hub for the people-smuggling trade. “It was absolutely heartbreaking. You saw lots of families putting life jackets on their children.” McInnes adds: “People were selling fake life jackets as well. Life jackets that didn’t actually work. I’m not sure we could have filmed it if we’d had children at that point.”

The couple met in 2010 while working together. Soon after, McInnes relocated to Damascus where they planned to start a production company. When the Syrian uprising began in 2011, they moved to London, where they now live with their six-year-old son.

In 2015, after Israa’s family landed in Greece on the dinghy, they joined the flow of refugees. It was Europe’s biggest movement of people since the second world war. Israa trudged through mud and freezing rain carrying her baby brother, while her parents pushed her sister in a wheelchair. Azzam and McInnes were there every step of the journey. “We slept in the street with them. We went on refugee trains and buses,” says McInnes. “By the time we arrived in Germany, we just became a family.”

The family’s journey ended in Cologne, where they settled. But the film-makers found it impossible to walk away. Partly it was about the relationship they had built, explains Azzam: “When we got to Germany, Israa was asking: ‘Are you going to visit us?’ We said: ‘Of course.’”

It also didn’t feel like the end of the story, she adds: “When we started, the idea was: let’s document this journey. Then there was a lot of talk about integration: will these people integrate in Europe? So we kept filming to cover that. Then it became a film about a family and love. Part of the emotional rollercoaster of making this film was that it’s about everything.”

In Cologne, Israa learned fluent German in five months flat. She started school, made friends and fell in love with Justin Bieber. Aged 12, she chose not to wear the hijab, a decision she later revisited. Her once close relationship with her father became antagonistic. One in a Million is a portrait of the refugee crisis, but it’s also a coming-of-age story, a tale about growing pains that feels universal in places.

It took Izzam and McInnes three years to get any kind of financial backing. They juggled full-time jobs, whacking the cost of making the documentary on to credit cards. How bad did it get? “I think we were at least 40 grand in debt at a one point,” McInnes replies grinning. “But we were young freelancers.”

In the documentary, we watch the tectonic plates in the family’s dynamics begin to move. When he left Syria, Tarek lost much of his identity. In Aleppo he ran a falafel restaurant: “He was a big character there,” says McInnes. “Everyone knew him. Now here he is in Germany, just another immigrant.”

While Tarek struggled to adjust, the women in his life blossomed. Halfway through the film his wife Nisreen – Israa’s mother – a background figure at the start, steps in front of the camera. Her transformation is one of the joys of the film. “She has a sort of hero’s journey, doesn’t she?” says MacInnes. “It’s so wonderful to see what’s happened to her.”

When Israa was 14, she disclosed to MacInnes that her father had been hitting her, while they were out picking up kebabs. He switched off the camera and into safeguarding mode: “We suddenly realised something much more important was happening than the film,” he remembers. With great sensitivity the film-makers chronicled what happened next in the family.

Their plan was to stop filming when Israa reached 18. But then she met her future husband Mohammed, who also arrived in Germany from Syria as a child refugee. In late 2024, the Assad regime unexpectedly fell. The film is bookended with moving footage of Israa returning to Aleppo to visit.

For those of us who have never experienced being a refugee, the film is a powerful insight into what it might feel like to have to leave your country and the longing for home. Azzam nods: “I went through that. It’s a struggle. Even though I’m settled in the UK and we have a child together and our life is here, there’s something missing. You feel like a guest that overstayed their welcome. And you struggle with identity. Who am I? Am I Syrian? Am I British?” She shrugs as if to say an answer is impossible.

Does anti-immigrant, anti-refugee feeling in the UK upset her? “It is hard, but you get used to it. There’s a lot of negativity, and you learn to block it.” The rhetoric is also a million miles from her her day-to-day life. “I’ve been in this country for 14 years, and I have never experienced any racism. I understand that people have. But honestly, it’s been an absolutely positive experience. And my parents have been here for a year. They are absolutely shocked at how nice people are. They don’t speak English, and when they walk down the street, everyone smiles at them, tries to help them.”

Azzam is from the Druze religious minority in Syria. Months after the fall of the Assad regime, armed tribes reportedly backed by the new government clashed with Druze fighters in southern Syria. Her village was destroyed: “we saw footage of our house, completely black, burned down.” Her parents have been in London for a year and a half.

Back to the film, Azzam admits there were times when they felt they would never finish it: “Honestly, it was really intense to make. It was just out of passion really that carried on for so long.”

She exchanges a glance with MacInnes. He adds: “I remember when Israa was first in Germany, we used to push her on the swings. Now we push our kids together on the swings.”

Over a video call, I speak to Israa, sitting in the kitchen of her home outside Cologne. She smiles easily and often. Now in her early 20s, with two small children, she has returned to education and is training to be a civil servant in local government.

Does she remember meeting the film-makers? “Yes!” she says with one of her biggest, brightest smiles. “I felt a blind trust from the moment I saw Itab, I trusted her straight away. And our relationship over the years turned into a really deep friendship.”

The first time she watched One in a Million, she cried all the way through, she says. How did it feel watching scenes of her family prepare to make the crossing from Turkey? “As a child I wasn’t really aware how dangerous it was. But now, when I remember, when I watch the movie, I can see it was a really dangerous trip.”

I ask if becoming a mother has changed how she feels about the trek she took so young? She nods. “I always say that both of my parents are very brave. Because now as a mother when I look at my children, I say that I would never have the courage to do to take such a trip. I am very proud of them because they took this decision and went on this journey with us.”

One in a Million is in UK and Irish cinemas from 6 November.

Fifa wants talks over restricting women’s Olympic football to under-23s

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:26:54 GMT

IOC open to dialogue and Fifa wants input from others

Fifa concerned about fixture congestion and workload

Fifa wants talks with the International Olympic Committee over restricting the Olympic women’s football tournament to under-23s owing to concerns over fixture congestion and the workload of senior players.

The eligibility criteria for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles has been set, with qualification tournaments having begun in some regions, so no change can be made until Brisbane 2032 at the earliest, but sources at both organisations have said that they are open to dialogue.

Although no formal proposal has been made, Fifa is understood to be interested in examining the matter in talks with the IOC and other key stakeholders, such as the players and leading member associations whose national sides routinely qualify for the Games.

A move to bring in age restrictions would dramatically alter the nature of the event and require careful analysis, consultation and consideration through Fifa and IOC processes.

Such a change would be controversial and could provoke a backlash from leading international players because the Olympics has long been regarded as one of the highlights of the women’s calendar, with Emma Hayes’s United States team securing gold in Paris two years ago. The Olympic title has been contested eight times and the US have won five.

Women’s football also has a major commercial appeal for the IOC, particularly in markets such as the US, Europe and Australia, so it may resist Fifa’s overtures.

Women’s football was introduced to the Olympics at Atlanta in 1996, and as an amateur sport at that time never had eligibility requirements, in contrast to the men’s game.

After admitting football to the Olympic programme in 1908 the IOC did not permit professionals to take part until 1984 owing to Fifa’s insistence on maintaining the primacy of the World Cup, as well as the demands on players from a congested calendar. Under pressure from Fifa the IOC introduced an under-23 age restriction in 1992, although three overage players have also been allowed in each squad since 1996.

The huge growth and professionalisation of the women’s game over the past decade has created increased fixture congestion, with the 2028 calendar the most bloated yet.

after newsletter promotion

Fifa is to a large extent culpable for this because the world governing body has chosen to launch the Women’s Club World Cup in an Olympic year, with the US to stage the 16-team competition between 5 and 30 January, six months before the Games.

The Women’s Club World Cup will cause major disruption to the European club season, with Arsenal and Chelsea or Manchester City likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month if they reach the latter stages, missing four Women’s Super League matches and the FA Cup fourth round. The importance of the sport to the IOC is shown by the fact that the women’s football tournament will be bigger than the men’s for the first time in LA, featuring 16 teams to 12, in a reversal of the numbers at Paris 2024.

Fifa and the IOC declined to comment.
