‘By the time the abuse ended, I was 16, and a husk’: how Johnny Daukes survived his childhood – and fought back

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:00:04 GMT

Daukes was an outgoing 10-year-old when he met boys’ club leader John Phillips. As an adult, he lived through years of chaos and self-sabotage, while repressing his experiences. Then he found out his brother had been abused by Phillips too

In early 2020, Johnny Daukes found an old storage box in his loft with a big black folder inside marked Toxic Hazard. It was stuffed with old sheets of paper: every song he’d written, starting as a teenager, just a boy with a guitar, then for Fin, his 90s indie band, and then his five solo albums.

By that time in his life, Daukes was 55 and deep in turmoil. He and his younger brother were working with the Metropolitan police to build a criminal case against the man who had sexually abused them both as children. Every case of historical abuse can disrupt a family, but this one was truly labyrinthine. Their abuser, John Phillips, had gone on to marry their sister and have 10 children. Every relationship was affected – cousins, siblings, nieces, nephews, aunts, uncles, godchildren and every variety of in-law.

Initially, if Daukes had been asked why the abuse had taken so long to surface, he might have replied that, for years, he hadn’t known it happened, that somehow he’d completely buried it. Now, up in that loft, reading these lyrics, Daukes could see it wasn’t that simple. His song Shadowman was one example of many. (“All he wants is one ambiguous touch / a secret between you that’s never discussed.”) Heaven Is Hell was another. (“I mustn’t let myself relax or fall asleep / Stay still, stay calm, this panic will retreat.”) Then there was Squid. (“Squid’s been abused and his mind is confused in a way that he can’t understand …”)

“I spent weeks sifting through them and I was blindsided by some of the songs,” says Daukes. “I still am now. It’s nuts. When I wrote Squid in 1992, in my brain I thought I was writing about our soundman Phil because he had dark eyes, like a shark. Now it’s obvious that Squid was me, the 12-year-old. How was it possible?”

These songs form the basis of his one-man show Squid: A Victim Impact Statement, which opens shortly at London’s Arcola theatre. Daukes uses them as a route into a childhood, to tell a story that he is still making sense of. He now sees them as cries for help, messages in a bottle.

But the clues weren’t just in his songs. The dark references, the family secrets, hiding under blankets from footsteps on the landing, fumbling in tents – the themes repeat in his scripts and sketches, and much of his life’s work.

Daukes isn’t just a musician. He has written comedy shows for BBC Radio 4 and BBC Three. His film Acts of Godfrey, starring Simon Callow and Celia Imrie, written entirely in rhyming couplets, opened the 2011 Raindance festival and was nominated for a British independent film award. (He calls it a “poem that got out of hand”.) He was the voice of Eurotrash for 16 series, has worked as a motorcycle stuntman and, as his day job, is a film editor. He also published a memoir, Shadowman: Records of a Life Corrupted, in 2022. If all this sounds impressive, Daukes doesn’t see it that way. “I try a lot,” he says. “But at the first sign of difficulty, I jump across and do something different. I cringe at the disasters.”

It’s only recently that Daukes has started to understand what may lie behind so much self-sabotage – splitting his band, firing his agent, the breakdown of two marriages (he’s now on his third). “When I met John Phillips, I was 10, a very confident, funny little kid,” says Daukes. “By the time the abuse ended, I was 16, and I was like a husk, riddled with self-doubt. The most injurious thing he did to me wasn’t physical. Between 10 and 15, you work out so much and I not only didn’t work it out, it got perverted. I didn’t know what to think, I second-guessed myself, and I’ve struggled with this all my life. There’s another song I wrote in the 90s that says it for me: ‘Have you ever been strange, felt like you had been wrongly assembled?’” He takes a long sigh. “You’re just fucked up.”

Daukes grew up in Didcot, Oxfordshire, the fourth of eight children. He remembers his first 10 years as wonderfully ordinary and typically 1970s – the space hoppers, the Raleigh Choppers, jumping from bridges into the River Thames, taking out inflatable dinghies with no adults watching, zero health and safety. His family, he says, was “chaotic and fun”, but for Daukes, the dynamic changed radically when his mother became involved with Opus Dei, an international Catholic organisation whose stated mission is to help people seek Christian perfection through ordinary life. Every member has a spiritual adviser who is also their “confessor”. (Some celibate members also practise self-mortification with metal chains or whips, known as “disciplines”.)

What all this meant for Daukes was firstly that his mother, once the beating heart of the family, now seemed to be focused elsewhere. Opus Dei became her central reference point. Secondly, at 10, Daukes was taken to an Opus Dei boys’ club in Oxford, where fun activities such as camping and football were laced with prayer and confession. It was run by John Phillips, who was 20 – Daukes remembers him then as “ruddy-faced, asthmatic and slightly chubby”. He quickly singled out Daukes and became his spiritual adviser.

Now Daukes can see the sure signs of grooming. Though always obsequious around his parents, Phillips mocked and criticised them behind their backs. “He’d say: ‘Your family have no manners – don’t be like that!’, ‘Your older brother’s a bighead – don’t be like him!’” Daukes says. “As my spiritual adviser, I would have to tell him everything in my head, and of course with him that always came down to an obsession with ‘impure thoughts’. I had to tell him every single occasion on which I had a sexual thought or fantasy, and that went on and on and on.”

Phillips’s trusted role meant that no questions were asked when Daukes stayed the night at the boys’ club, and then later, regularly at Phillips’s home, or when Phillips took him away on trips. In tents, in sleeping bags, in spare rooms, Daukes would wake in the dark, a presence beside him. “I know that I always fought him,” he says. “I say it in Shadowman, ‘He’s an eight-armed beast.’ He was like a bloody octopus.”

Finally, at 16, Daukes was in his bedroom getting changed when Phillips barged in. “He had this sixth sense for when I was vulnerable,” says Daukes. “Closed doors were catnip for him.” He dived towards Daukes and licked his face – and this time, Daukes shoved him hard into a wall and yelled: “Fuck off!”

Five years of sexual abuse stopped there – and for decades, somehow, Daukes gave it no conscious thought. “I’m not a psychoanalyst but I imagine that I just wanted it to go away, so I probably buried it,” he says. “Except ‘buried’ isn’t the word. I think these experiences were hardwired and encoded into me.”

For a long time, in sixth form and beyond, he remained “on the outside” of friendships, gravitating towards solitary pursuits such as playing the guitar or distance running. For years, his only close relationship was with his first wife, whom he met at 18 – but in their entire 18 years together, he never mentioned anything of this. At his core was a truth he couldn’t share.

There were recurring nightmares – in the form of a vague dawning horror of a presence beside him – and there was anger too, a tendency to blow up his life. Fin is one example. The band had success – releasing four EPs to positive reviews, TV and radio coverage, they supported Elastica and the Cranberries and were supported by Supergrass and Catatonia. Still, after less than three years, Daukes split up the band to form a new one, which signed a publishing deal with Chrysalis Music, then also split a year later. Somehow, he believes, he’d imbibed the message that he “wasn’t good enough”. Daukes has since researched the impact of “shame” on victims of child sexual abuse, how it can lead to a deep sense of unworthiness, of “not deserving”. It was, he says, “like looking in a mirror”.

It was after the breakdown of his first marriage, when he was in a new relationship with the woman who would become his second wife, that the abuse surfaced. By then, Daukes was 38. “We were in bed and I had this flashback,” he says. He shivers. “I told Sarah: ‘That was weird.’” As they talked that night, more memories and fragments came out – Daukes says he was “vomiting it up, like a cat throwing up a furball”. By then, Phillips was embedded in his family. Through the years, Daukes had seen him regularly at family events, birthday parties, get-togethers. “There was this unspoken thing that he was a bit weird, a bit handsy,” he says. “To me, he was just this buffoon.”

Days later, while Daukes was still reeling from his new memories, his brother Nick came to stay. “Nick is six years younger and very, very different to me,” says Daukes. “He’d joined the Royal Marines, the Special Boat Service. He’s very bright, very funny. I have so much admiration for him.

“We’d had a load to drink; we were walking to the living room with a bottle of brandy when I stopped and said: ‘I was abused by John Phillips.’ I saw his eyes well up a bit and he just said: ‘Me too.’” For Daukes, it was as if all the air was sucked from the room. “We talked for hours,” he says. “Both of us were crying our eyes out. The only person who truly understood what this felt like was there in front of us.”

Many more years passed before they found any kind of justice. The brothers had quickly called the police child protection unit closest to where Phillips – and their sister, and their 10 nieces and nephews – lived. Shortly after, their home was raided by the Criminal Investigation Department. The wider family’s reaction quickly seemed to morph from shock and sympathy for Daukes and his brother to impatience to minimisation. Daukes says his mum urged them to think of his sister and the children. He remembers an awkward call from his dad, saying: “Look, this business … don’t you think it’s gone far enough?”

Ultimately, a family member hand-delivered a letter from Phillips that carried a full confession. In it, Phillips said that he’d been raised in a loveless family and had “fallen in love” with Daukes and Nick, confusing it for sexual urges. He stated that he’d never abused another child and, should any other victim present themselves, they could take this letter to the police. Daukes eventually withdrew the charges and the case collapsed. “It’s really hard to understand,” he says, “a decision I’ll spend the rest of my life trying to understand.”

It wasn’t until 2019, when they learned there had been not just a third victim but a fourth, that the two brothers went back to the police. Earlier this year, Phillips pleaded guilty to 11 charges of sexual abuse and was sentenced to 10 years in prison.

“For me, what that’s done is remove any doubt,” says Daukes. “In my family, there was always this moral ambiguity and ambivalence, and this has removed any of that. He was tried in a court of law, we all went to the sentencing and heard 32 pages read out, the submission for the prosecution, and it did not spare any detail. A lot of people came away saying: ‘I had no idea.’” Daukes’ two daughters, Pepper, 18, and Betty, 22, were there too. At the end, Daukes apologised for all they’d had to hear. Pepper gave him a huge hug and said: “It was a lot.” “I could have called my bloody book that!” says Daukes. “It was a lot!”

He thinks he’s calmer now, and credits his third wife, Julie, with much of this – they’ve been together for about 16 years. “She has been absolutely essential,” says Daukes. They live in Putney in south-west London, but when we meet it’s a few miles away at the home of Sarah, the mother of his children. Pepper shows me to his studio at the bottom of the garden, where he’s putting the finishing touches to his show. “We all rub along together,” says Daukes. “It’s amicable.”

Recovery is slow but he believes it’s happening. “It’s very, very gentle,” he says. “If what I had was like tar that had hardened on a plate, you can’t go at it with a knife. You have to rub it and rub it and gently, gently, you start to believe it’s coming off. It’s gradually eroding.”

This play, retelling his story before an audience, is part of this process – though, for Daukes, his message goes beyond the personal. “When I finished my book, I sent the manuscript to 70 people – lawyers, agents, friends, editors – and more than one in 10 came back saying that the material was a bit close to them and it wasn’t something they’d ever admitted before. Man, this is widespread,” he says. “In a time where the phrase ‘paedo’ is basically used as a hand grenade to chuck at someone with different cultural or political views, the basic facts are that paedophiles are known, trusted and, in a lot of cases, loved. They’re fathers, grandfathers, uncles, stepfathers. And that’s the truth of it.”

Squid: A Victim Impact Statement is at Arcola theatre, London, from 11 to 14 November

No amount of sliding in the polls can shake Kemi Badenoch’s self-belief – or alter her party’s direction

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:00:04 GMT

Two years in to her leadership, Badenoch continues to take the Tories ever-rightwards, into comfort-zone Conservatism

What happens to a political leader who is too sure of themself? Sometimes, huge confidence is a very useful, self-fulfilling quality: persuading party colleagues, activists, donors and voters that more can be achieved than is usually thought possible. Such utter conviction can keep everyone believing while the actual practicalities of a political project are worked out.

Yet when an air of absolute certainty turns out to be overconfidence, the bubble bursts. The politician may be revealed as disastrously complacent and lacking in judgment, having delusions of grandeur, or being fundamentally in denial. Especially in our era of online mockery and instinctive contempt for politicians, an overconfident leader can end up as a laughing stock.

This week is the second anniversary of the start of Kemi Badenoch’s Conservative leadership. So far, self-assuredness has been her tenure’s central feature, the one aspect that many voters and journalists have noticed. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner … which is all me,” she told GB News last month, after a party conference where activists chanted “Kemi” and her assertive persona pervaded everything, as if the party had found another Margaret Thatcher.

Badenoch’s speeches, interviews and Commons interventions come riskily spiced with contempt, self-congratulation and advice to supposedly lesser political mortals: “I was right”, “let me explain”, “let me tell them [the government] some home truths”. She and her party now present themselves in a similarly self-aggrandising way. Unlike Labour and the other parties, she says: “We live in the real world.” The Conservatives are the party of “common sense”, “the no-nonsense party” that “get stuff done”. A long pamphlet the party recently published, with Badenoch’s name on the cover, about how it would approach governing is a little smugly titled: “The Right Way”.

When she became leader, the Tories were at 26% in Politico’s rolling average of polls: barely above their 24% vote share in the 2024 general election, the worst in their history. After two years of Badenoch’s aggressive leadership, covered ever more approvingly by the rightwing media, accompanied by regular crises inside Labour and Reform UK, the Conservatives have fallen to 21%. The forecaster Electoral Calculus currently predicts they will win 128 seats at the next election, almost three times fewer than Labour – and even this paltry tally depends on the electoral system hugely favouring the Tories over the similarly disliked Reform UK.

During previous periods of defeat and great unpopularity, the Conservatives pored over their mistakes in government, reconsidered policies, reassessed how their party related to society, and changed direction fundamentally. After losing power in 1945 – after 14 years, as in 2024 – they accepted that in office they had not done enough to reduce unemployment, stimulate the economy, or develop the welfare state. After losing power in 1974, they ditched their kinder Conservatism for the ambitious counter-revolution of Thatcherism.

Despite their electoral position now being far worse than in either 1945 or 1974, no such reinventions have taken place under Badenoch. Instead, the Tories have continued to travel rightwards, not in new directions as under Thatcher, but deeper and deeper into a Conservative comfort zone, where they have been loitering most of the time since David Cameron abandoned his government’s brief experiments with liberal Toryism in the early 2010s.

In this comfort zone, traditional Conservative remedies such as deregulating business, building more prisons, cutting taxes for the prosperous and reducing the poor’s welfare benefits are always right – regardless of how society is changing, or whether recent Tory governments have actually applied them, or done so successfully. Brexit’s failure is not to be acknowledged. Net zero’s necessity is to be avoided. Yet according to the Tories, it is Labour, the Greens and Liberal Democrats – who are all trying to develop fresh approaches to the climate crisis, and the outflanking of Brexit by shifts in geopolitics – who are “not serious”, as Badenoch patronisingly puts it.

It’s tempting to ascribe this narrow-mindedness to her character, which seems to lack much capacity for self-criticism. But parts of her life story may also have helped create and maintain her predictable rightwing perspectives. “I was born into a relatively wealthy family,” she told the Nigerian newspaper Peoples Gazette in 2024. Her father “was a doctor who had lots of oil company patients … and got paid very well”. She was educated privately in Nigeria, later worked in London as a director of the elite bank Coutts, and married a Tory activist who was also privately educated and worked in the upper echelons of finance. She represents an affluent rural constituency, North West Essex, with an above-average proportion of wealthy homeowners and retirees, groups that dominate her party’s remaining national support. With the huge exception of racism, it’s not clear she has encountered many social forces during her life which might have made her rethink her outlook.

But the Tories’ complacency extends far beyond Badenoch. Conservatism can be a comfort zone ideology: wanting to conserve the status quo implies that you think things are essentially fine as they are. Only when that status quo, and specifically Tory-aligned interests within it, are seriously threatened does the party switch to its less common iconoclastic mode, as it did under Thatcher in the turbulent, increasingly egalitarian 1970s. One reason the Tories aren’t doing that now is that, for all the rightwing talk about millionaires fleeing the country, the rich, big business and the City of London are still doing well here.

For non-Tories, the party’s long, ongoing holiday from reality may seem something to relish. The Conservatives’ stark decline since the late 1980s – with only one big general election win since, in 2019 – is certainly a great change after centuries of Tory hegemony, and still insufficiently noticed or discussed.

But their stubborn attachment to the same old assumptions also helps keep British politics, and how much of the media cover it, and many voters think about it, skewed to the right, by making traditional Conservative ideas about the economy and society still seem fairly respectable, and therefore realistic. Badenoch’s cocky leadership may be abruptly terminated after the next election. But unless a more open-minded Tory replaces her – which is currently hard to imagine – the “common sense” politics she says she stands for will destructively linger on.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Sports owners bet big on Republicans. What does their defeat mean for US sports?

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 10:00:02 GMT

A Democratic sweep has changed Washington’s balance of power. But from gambling legislation to stadium subsidies, both parties have helped build the system that enriches American sports’ billionaire owners

Before a single vote was cast this election cycle, the technocrats and oligarchs who own American sports had already voted. Pro sports owners put more than $100m into this cycle, according to Front Office Sports. But Tuesday night was a referendum not just on Donald Trump and Maga policies, but on the puppeteers who pull America’s strings. The people voted, and the owners lost.

Before anyone frames this as a rescue, a word about the rescuers. Democrats are the instrument for ending Maga, and they are also the other face of the same coin. Think Republicans are behind all of our ills? Think again. New Jersey’s governor, Phil Murphy, placed his state’s first legal sports bet in 2018. Illinois governor JB Pritzker signed sports betting into law a year later. New York’s mobile sportsbooks went live under Governor Kathy Hochul in 2022, with the state taking 51% of the revenue. Pritzker and Hochul both won Tuesday, and all of them are Democrats. In some of the biggest betting markets in the country, the bookmakers’ most reliable partner has been a Democratic statehouse.

Having said all that, the biggest losers on Tuesday night were Republicans: Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress. That would have made plenty of sports owners disappointed, as they have a habit of backing Republicans. At least 10 sports owners backed Mike Rogers in Michigan, and Abdul El-Sayed beat Rogers. Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones gave $1m to Trump’s super Pac and $250,000 to a committee backing Ken Paxton, and James Talarico beat Paxton in Texas.

The former Mavericks owner Miriam Adelson lapped everyone with at least $67m to Republican committees, in keeping with her history of big spending around elections. What did she get for her money? A House and Senate minority.

So how does all this affect the future of American sports? Let’s count the ways.

The NFL spent a decade teaching its fans to bet, and on 8 October it asked the US supreme court to help protect those fans from prediction markets. The league’s brief makes two arguments: prediction markets are gambling that belongs under state regulation like any sportsbook, and the money is enormous. Football drew $1.8bn in prediction-market trades on the season’s opening Sunday, more than half of everything traded. Kalshi takes customers at 18, three years younger than legal sportsbooks allow in many states.

Here’s the catch: the regulator the NFL is fighting answers to Trump. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has sued at least nine states to stop them from applying their gambling laws to prediction markets, and Donald Trump Jr advises Kalshi. Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, filed 13 felony counts against Kalshi and its two co-founders for taking sports bets from an undercover agent. The league’s owners spent $20m electing the party whose administration filed those suits.

Democrats will control confirmation of the next CFTC commissioners, and they wrote most of the roughly 30 prediction-market bills in this Congress. That’s a turf war over which bookmakers get the money, and the party that built the licensed ones now protects them from the new ones.

Nebraska rejected online sports betting by 54% to 46% after the sportsbooks’ committee outspent the opposition by 20 to one, according to the opposition. Nebraskans saw a casino on every teenager’s phone and voted no. Strip away the branding, and this is straight-up degeneracy with a licensing deal: a league taking a cut of its own fans’ losses and calling it engagement. The industry’s next request to the lame-duck Congress is to restore the full tax write-off for gambling losses that Republicans capped at 90% last year.

The Bears want Illinois taxpayers to help pay for a new stadium, and on 1 October, the NFL commissioner, Roger Goodell, sat across from Pritzker and told him the state had to act now as the team also strongly considers building its new stadium in Indiana. Pritzker, a billionaire Democrat who won a third term on Tuesday, wants the legislature to vote in its autumn veto session, on 17–19 November and 1–3 December.

That session begins two weeks after the election, when voters can no longer take their votes back. In Washington, the president first threatened to scuttle the Commanders’ $3.8bn RFK Stadium deal unless the team brought back their old nickname, then spent the rest of the year trying to get his own name on the building. These deals move money from people who will never afford a club seat to the family that owns the team, and both parties co-sign them.

The WNBA just had the best month in its history. Game 7 of the finals, in which the Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream, drew 3.3 million viewers in the first season under a new seven-year labor deal. Four states also voted on who plays women’s sports. Arizona approved Proposition 318, which requires schools to assign teams by biological sex. Nebraska passed a similar measure with 67% of the vote and put it in the state constitution. Washington’s Initiative 638 held a wide lead on Wednesday morning, and Colorado’s Proposition 134 led narrowly.

The supreme court allowed states to enforce those measures on 30 June, ruling 6–3 that states may bar transgender girls from girls’ teams and that nothing requires them to do so. The 30-year-old league’s own rule is one laconic sentence in that labor deal: “Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA.”

The NBA commissioner, Adam Silver, has spent a year asking Washington to clean up a mess he helped create with the 2014 opinion piece that pushed legal betting into the mainstream. Since federal prosecutors in Brooklyn charged Chauncey Billups and Terry Rozier last October, that office has indicted at least five NBA figures on gambling-related counts. Silver wants Congress to pass a single federal betting law and wants regulators to provide the league with prediction-market trading data.

A league that needs software to monitor its own players’ wagers has already lost the argument over whether wagering belongs near it. Silver gave about $41,000 to Democrats this cycle, Adelson gave $67m to Republicans, and only one of them got what they paid for. The party Silver backed has never met a regulated betting market it wouldn’t tax, so expect it to hand him the framework he wants.

Then there’s Madison Square Garden. The Knicks’ home arena pays no property tax and sits above Penn Station, which is set for an overhaul of around $8bn, much of which the federal government will likely pay for. The Trump administration pushed New York’s Metropolitan Transportation Authority out and handed the project to Amtrak, which chose the plan that leaves Madison Square Garden where it is. James Dolan hosted Trump’s rally there nine days before the 2024 election and put him in his suite for Game 3 of the NBA finals three weeks after the Penn Station decision.

The arena’s 1982 tax break had cost the city nearly $1bn by 2023. Only Albany can repeal it, and Albany belongs to Hochul. She won re-election on Tuesday and has never laid a finger on Dolan’s tax break. This is the governor who put $850m of public money into a Buffalo Bills stadium, the largest stadium subsidy in NFL history, while her husband served as general counsel of the company that runs the Bills’ concessions. Both said he recused himself. The Knicks are defending champions. Dolan is undefeated. Sadly, so is the arrangement.

The Senate’s college sports bill protects women’s programs, but Cory Booker, the Democratic senator from New Jersey, fought it because those protections expire after nine years and the NCAA’s antitrust exemption never does. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, said he would bring it to a vote even if Republicans lost the House, and they did. The House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, now in line to be the first Black speaker, has not said whether he will. How convenient.

The owners, as usual, are less ambivalent than the players. Tilman Fertitta, the Houston Rockets owner and US ambassador to Italy, bought the Connecticut Sun in May and gave $200,000 to the Republican National Committee. Josh Harris gave $255,000, almost all of it to a Republican Senate Pac, and his partner David Blitzer gave more than $150,000, mostly to Democrats. One ownership group covered both parties. Do you see it yet? This is how the donor class always wins. The last time the Atlanta Dream franchise got into a Senate race, their players wore “Vote Warnock” shirts and helped defeat their own co-owner, Kelly Loeffler, who now runs the Small Business Administration for Trump.

Kalshi took more than $1.4bn in bets on the election itself and has hired a lobbyist with ties to the man now in line to be speaker. The owners lost on Tuesday, but they’ll be fine because the people who own your team gave to both parties, and so did the bookmakers. The Democrats who won will investigate what deserves investigating and then go back to signing stadium deals and betting bills. Remember, this is by design.

Was one of the great novels of the Enlightenment written by a man who thought he was a werewolf?

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 09:43:48 GMT

Surreal, mysterious and with an outlandish origin story, Jan Potocki’s The Manuscript Found in Saragossa has amassed a cult following that includes Salman Rushdie and Jerry Garcia. But it’s the book’s global humanism makes it relevant now, say the curators of a new exhibition

A young Walloon officer called Alphonse van Worden travels through the Sierra Morena on his way to Madrid to join the Spanish army. Along the way he has an erotic encounter with two demonic Moorish sisters, falls foul of shape-shifting apparitions and is tested by a Jewish Kabbalist attempting to use mystical formulas to control spirits and decipher the universe.

All these things happen in what might be one of the least-known great novels of the European canon, an encyclopedic roman-monde written more than 200 years ago called The Manuscript Found in Saragossa.

Structured like a Chinese box, with narratives nested within narratives, the book spans a period from the birth of Jesus Christ up to the beginning of the 19th century, and evokes places ranging from the Mediterranean and north Africa to Mexico, Peru and the Philippines. Salman Rushdie once described it in the Guardian as redolent of “the most brilliant modern novels, as if it were written yesterday”, while the curators of a new exhibition in Switzerland hail it as “a western version of One Thousand and One Nights”.

The fact that the book was written (in French) by a Polish count and the first fragments of it were published in 1804 in St Petersburg may explain why it remains relatively little-known in western Europe. That its globalised vision of unfettered human intercourse was dreamed up not in the familiar western European centres of colonial power – Paris and London – but the continent’s eastern reaches, however, may also be the reason why it’s attracting new attention now.

Its author, Jan Potocki (1761-1815), was born in Pików, in the Polish-Lithuanian commonwealth, but educated in Orbe, Switzerland – not far from the small village of Montricher where a newly opened exhibition at the Fondation Jan Michalski explores the books origins.“He was one of the very few Poles with a deep interest in Jewish culture as it was cultivated by rabbis in eastern Poland at the time, in what is now Ukraine,” says François Rosset, one of the two curators of The Manuscript Found in Saragossa: An Investigation into a World Novel. “This fascinated him and led him into the world of esoteric learning, including ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.”

Potocki’s extraordinary life ended in 1815, when he shot himself at the age of 54. After his death, an inventory of his possessions at his Uładówka home revealed a silver sugar bowl with a missing lid. There is some speculation that an ailing Potocki filed down the knob of the lid to cast the bullet that killed him, sparking outlandish theories that he believed he was a werewolf.

The novel he left behind was to have an almost equally extraordinary afterlife. For many years, it circulated in fragmentary and competing versions. Among the most widely read was the English-language Penguin edition, beautifully translated by Ian Maclean, which was based on René Radrizzani’s revised French-language edition of 1990. But the notion that Radrizzani’s version represented the most faithful text was overturned in 2002, when the exhibition’s co-curator Dominique Triaire discovered eight manuscripts that had been miscataloged in Polish archives. “We were able to establish that Potocki had left behind not one but two novels,” Triaire says.

Potocki’s book has fervent admirers among contemporary novelists like the French Prix Goncourt winner Mathias Énard and Poland’s 2018 Nobel prize laureate Olga Tokarczuk, who has described it as part of her “literary first-aid kit”: “I open a page by chance and I draw a good dose of creative energy. All of the vital force of literature is there in its purest state.” But it’s fair to say that because of its inherent weirdness The Manuscript from Saragossa has never managed to establish itself as a classic of the European canon in the way that other roman-mondes such as Don Quixote or Boccaccio’s Decameron have. Yet, precisely because it is so open to interpretation, its influence on visual artists has been incredibly varied.

At the Swiss exhibition, a video screen shows the opening four minutes of Polish director Wojciech Has’s 1965 film adaptation of the novel, which brings all its surreal and comic qualities vividly to life, as soldiers run through the ruins of Saragossa to the strains of Beethoven’s Ode to Joy. The black-and-white film’s cult following helped inspire a restoration in the 1990s, initiated by the Grateful Dead’s Jerry Garcia and subsequently supported by Francis Ford Coppola and Martin Scorsese. Another screen shows excerpts of a four-part 1973 French television adaptation, La Duchesse d’Avila, which leans into a kitsch aesthetic underscoring the extraordinary elasticity of Potocki’s novel. Beyond the screen, the book also inspired 10 dreamlike engravings by Leonor Fini, who was commissioned in Buenos Aires in 1961 to produce illustrations for a rare bibliophiles’ edition.

To contemporary artists, it’s not just the fantastical world-building of Potocki’s book that appeals, but its vision of a globalised, multicultural society. The most recent is a theatrical adaptation directed by Grzegorz Jarzyna, which premiered at the Teatr Polski in Warsaw last year. The Saragossa Manuscript: The Gomelez Legacy is centred on Alex, a young inhabitant of a modern city, who travels back to 18th-century Spain only to be drawn into the machinations of a global secret society led by the Gomelez clan. In Potocki’s novel, the same Moorish family leads Alphonse on a merry dance of self-discovery, from a bumptious young officer steeped in received ideas into a man capable of thinking for himself.

“What Potocki wants Alphonse to acquire, and what makes The Saragossa Manuscript a novel of education, is a new set of values,” Triaire says. “Potocki was fundamentally an heir to the Enlightenment, for whom humanity was universal. There were no separate kinds of human beings divided by race or religion. White people, Black people, Christians, Muslims: these were all members of the same humanity.”

after newsletter promotion

The novel’s principal setting of Spain’s Sierra Morena seems to have been chosen by Potocki to reflect a world without borders where everyone has a place at the table. In the novel, Alphonse encounters a stranger lying between the bodies of two hanged men (a recurring ghoulish motif) and helps revive him. Alphonse brings the man back to his camp where his Spanish hosts have arranged a breakfast. “A place had been kept for me. Another was laid for the stranger and no one asked who he was. Such are the laws of hospitality which are rarely broken in Spain.”

The novel’s treatment of religions is also notably modern. It suggests that the three great monotheistic religions can, in principle, coexist harmoniously, with the main characters often finding ways of understanding one another. The other is not to be feared. When the Spanish geometer Velásquez looks out over the ramparts of Ceuta and sees the vast territories inhabited by the Moors, he does not sense danger but the tranquillity of a pastoral landscape: “the countryside seemed to me to be there only to provide visual pleasure.”

There is, throughout the novel, a celebration of reason, but at the same time an acknowledgment of reason’s fragility. Potocki may have remained firmly committed to the Enlightenment, but its certainties were being shaken by the French Revolution and the Napoleonic wars. “It is through that crack in the edifice that something then described not as the fantastic, but as the supernatural, could enter,” Triaire says. “I think this fragility of reason also speaks to our own age.”

What gives The Manuscript Found in Saragossa such an enduring appeal, adds Rosset, is that its many layers reveal themselves differently to successive generations of readers. “He wrote a book that is outside time, but that belongs to all times.”

The Manuscript Found in Saragossa: An Investigation into a World Novel is at the Fondation Jan Michalski, Montricher, Switzerland, until 14 February

Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 08:00:58 GMT

Some now suggest a monthly dose of art can boost wellbeing. But the last thing we need is another item on our to-do lists

As the long autumn subsides and we finally head into winter, so we hit that point in the calendar when two rival theories of seasonal survival play out: one, the permission-giving invitation to give up and power down, encapsulated by Scandinavian hygge and Katherine May’s 2020 blockbuster Wintering; and two, the exhortation to push through the discomfort and get out there. If the midterm results in the US give us a huge boost this week, still we have to keep going until spring.

The latest contribution to the get-up-and-out-there branch of motivational badgering comes in the form of a report by an arts charity suggesting that, as with exercise and being in nature, our baseline mood may be improved by exposing ourselves to art on a regular basis. According to Art Fund, a national body that promotes access to the arts, a person’s mental and physical wellbeing may be meaningfully affected by abiding by a handy acronym – RDA for recommended dose of art – and attaching it to what appears to be an entirely arbitrary prescription, namely 60 minutes of art ingestion a month. According to Daisy Fancourt, a professor of psychobiology and epidemiology at University College London who wrote the report’s foreword, do this and, “alongside having a balanced diet, regular exercise and spending time outdoors”, your health will thank you.

I don’t mean to sound sceptical. There are excellent reasons for promoting this theory: the ability of art in any form to take us out of ourselves and put us back in a slightly different place. What is fascinating to me is how Art Fund has found it necessary to sell the idea by appealing to a standard that, if not antithetical to art, exactly, seems at the very least to be highly irrelevant. In other words, the key sell for engaging with art in this case is that there is science – a real expertise! – backing it up, to reassure those on the fence that it’s not all a clanging, nebulous waste of time.

There’s probably a way to blame Malcolm Gladwell for this, or take your pick from any number of other narrow-track, extremely literal thinkers who don’t trust any experience of life that can’t be tabulated. And while Art Fund is just conforming to publishing trends, which require measurable takeaways from every single thing we do, I can’t help finding something dispiriting and babyish about the way they’ve gone about it. Not to get too Walter Pater about it all, but the minute you start trying to measure future benefits in relation to standing in front of a painting or reading a book, not only do you wander into upsetting territory where phrases such as “value proposition” and “what’s the unlock on this?” reside, but it risks interfering with the experience itself.

I know, I’m being a snob. The enthusiasm for boiling life down to a series of self-optimising items on an endless, dreary to-do list, however, does get a bit much at times. In this particular case, it is technically true, I suppose, that art belongs in a very broad category with nutrition. And you can hold two apparently contradictory thoughts in your head at the same time, so that the fleeting experience of being immersed in an artwork can live alongside the understanding that there is some future, unspecified benefit to the exercise.

But when so much weight is put on health and welfare as the ultimate goal, it does risk shifting the experience from pleasure to chore. A more accurate presentation of the value of art might be that going to the National Gallery for the afternoon is less like eating a bowl of grains and doing a quick workout than spooning frosting into your mouth, fixing you greedily and indulgently in the thrill of the moment. Only guess what?! Without the cholesterol!

Is the science of art-as-health-benefit a real science? I’ll never find out because, apparently, I have no desire to improve myself by reading the data – although if curiosity or a whimsical need to do something I’m not interested in ever gets the better of me, I’ll certainly look into it.

All of which misses the point, of course, which is about selling a laudable and true idea about how art enriches your life to a possibly sceptical public. I tip my hat to Art Fund for framing this conviction in a publicity-friendly way, which is surely more sensible than wanging on about hard, gemlike flames and watching it dive to the bottom of the news list. Just allow me a quick eyeroll first.

How irrational are Labour’s plans for migrant workers? To find out, read the small print

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:00:55 GMT

Despite the partial U-turn on care worker visas, the staff who keep the system afloat still face a hostile environment

If you want to see the senselessness of Britain’s immigration debate play out in real time, look no further than the crackdown on care workers’ visas that came to a head this week.

As part of its plans to force low-paid migrant workers to wait 15 years before settlement in the UK, the Home Office has been in a battle behind the scenes for the past six months to controversially include care workers in the policy. This is despite the social care system already facing critical staff shortages and the number of British citizens and immigrants taking the jobs dwindling.

After a fierce backlash from health unions and Labour cabinet members, this week the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, announced a partial U-turn: an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents will be exempt and allowed to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years.

It’s a welcome reprieve from a policy that should never have been on the table. But check the fine print and this “watering down” will not protect every care worker. Only carers who earn £25,000 a year and entered or switched on to the care staff visa route before the white paper’s publication in 2025 will be eligible.

Those who don’t meet the strict requirements will have to get another five-year “health and social care” visa before applying for ILR – a move campaigners are warning will leave vulnerable workers open to exploitation from unscrupulous employers.

Ministers have not established what benefit any of this is meant to bestow on the British people, millions of whom rely on migrant carers to help them or their elderly parents wash and dress. Nor has anyone explained how Labour’s upcoming care reforms will work while alienating – rather than actively recruiting – more international staff, as recent tightened immigration rules already have.

Or, to put it another way: the government has simultaneously pledged to fix social care while creating a hostile environment for the migrant staff who keep the system afloat. It sums up not only the nastiness of it all, but the deep-seated irrationality that now plagues almost any mainstream conversation about immigration, with politicians across the spectrum seemingly contractually obliged to ignore basic common sense as well as decency.

Few things demonstrate this more than the obsession with the “contribution v cost” framing that dominates these debates, and which Labour has now threaded through its visa policy. On paper, it appears to many a fair and logical way to allocate visa rights. In practice, it rewards the wealthy and dismisses the value of working-class and predominantly female labour: while care workers will have to wait five or 15 years for ILR, a solicitor on £125,000 can get fast-tracked in only three. It is blatant classism, sure, but also fundamentally misses the very obvious tenet of capitalism that a worker’s “contribution” to a society and economy is not necessarily reflected in their wage packet.

That Mahmood has been doing the rounds in recent months using disputed figures to claim that granting ILR to care staff and their families for the next few years would cost the public purse £10bn over a lifetime suggests how unreliable – and outright ludicrous – the cost v contribution binary is. These are the people keeping our loved ones alive for the minimum wage and we’re still debating whether they’re a burden on the taxpayer.

Of course, evidence shows care workers are, to use that favoured phrase, “net contributors”. The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found this week that skilled migrants – including care workers – and their families due to settle in the UK under current rules are expected to boost the public purse by a staggering £115bn through taxes.

Such a figure doesn’t even include the many other ways care workers save the country money: by enabling family members to keep paying income tax rather than quitting their jobs to be an unpaid carer; supporting younger disabled people to get to the office and stay in work; or keeping older people out of expensive hospital beds by reducing their risk of falls.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And yet we are losing something if we accept the idea that a migrant’s “contribution” is only in economic terms, as if the Home Office can scan a human being at the border and put a price tag round their neck. Anyone who has ever relied on a good carer knows there is value that can’t be measured on a spreadsheet: the security of knowing there is someone to help you get out of bed in the morning; the dignity of having a regular shower; the laughter that comes with a shared joke as you write the shopping list together.

You won’t see many of these people on front pages or hear their voices on radio call-ins. But the people providing care and those who rely on it will “contribute” considerably more to the debate than the non-disabled white contrarians who so persistently dominate it.

If it is a “legitimate concern” for the public to worry about immigration, it is legitimate for a disabled person to be afraid there will be no one to help them cook dinner, or for a migrant to worry about where they’ll live next year.

Because here’s the thing about fears: some are irrational, and others are not. Labour would do well to remember which ones it should listen to and which it should challenge.

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist
