Lab-grown meat was supposed to save the world. What happened?

The Guardian Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:00:54 GMT

We were promised a panacea for the climate crisis and a way to save our food system. So why is nobody firing up the chicken vats? I went to find out

On 5 August 2013, a man and a woman ate a burger. Not just any burger: a world-historic burger, made from cattle cells grown in a laboratory by Mark Post, a professor of vascular physiology at Maastricht University in the Netherlands. The burger had taken two years to produce and cost €250,000 (about £210,000 at the time), money furnished by the Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Now it was being tasted in public for the first time at Riverside Studios in London, at an event attended by 200 members of the press and livestreamed to thousands.

To make this particular burger, Post had extracted stem cells from the shoulder muscle of a living cow, then cultivated them in plastic containers filled with a nutrient-rich supplement called foetal bovine serum, which is derived from cow foetuses. The cells eventually became 20,000 strands of tissue, which in turn became a single 140g patty. Post believed that beef produced this way had the potential to dramatically reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and slow the climate crisis. Raising cattle for consumption requires massive amounts of land and water – and massive amounts of feed grown at a high environmental cost. He projected that global demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it the old-fashioned way, at which point our food systems would become unsustainable. But that didn’t have to mean a mass recalibration of our consumption habits or a global shift away from red meat. Post and his team had found another way.

Standing at a blond-wood island on an otherwise empty soundstage, Post lifted the kind of stainless-steel cloche usually found on a room service cart to reveal his creation. The raw patty sat in a petri dish on a bare plate, where it shone wetly under the studio lights. With the ITV London anchor Nina Hossain presiding, a Cornish chef named Richard McGeown pan-fried the burger in sunflower oil and butter for two volunteer tasters: Josh Schonwald, the Chicago-based author of The Taste of Tomorrow: Dispatches from the Future of Food, and Hanni Rützler, an Austrian nutrition scientist. So precious was this meat that they were given just the one burger to share between them. It was served deconstructed, alongside a sesame-seed bun, lettuce and tomato – showmanship to sell the burger a bit, give it context. The patty itself was reddish brown, flat and perfectly circular. When Schonwald and Rützler cut it, the burger did not bleed.

The two of them ate with forks and knives, passing the plate, sawing off thoughtful bites. Chewing slowly. Afterwards, they rendered their verdicts. “I would say it is somewhere on the spectrum between a Boca Burger and McDonald’s,” Schonwald told a reporter from NBC. “The absence of fat makes a big difference. It has the texture, which I was not expecting. It was like an animal-protein cake.” Rützler noted the burger’s blandness to a reporter from Science. “There is room for improvement here,” she said. At the end of the event, about €113,000 worth of burger remained uneaten. But none of this stopped Post from predicting that meat cultivated in a lab would become a consumer product within the decade.

The event – the theatrical reveal, the PR spectacle – triggered a kind of gold rush. One hundred and forty companies sprang up in six continents, trying to replicate what Post had done with beef across a range of other species: chicken, pork, fish, even quail. Investment to the tune of $3bn (£2.2bn) flooded into the sector. True believers claimed that cellular agriculture would not only fight the climate crisis and global food insecurity but also slow the spread of zoonotic disease and antibiotic resistance. A company called Upside Foods touted its plans to “set the new standard for meat” and to “make meat a force of good in the world”. A company called Vow created an enormous woolly mammoth meatball, though no one was allowed to eat it, since the DNA came from a fossil and the company didn’t know whether it was actually fit for human consumption. The thinktank RethinkX predicted that cultivated meat would decimate the US beef industry by 2030, reducing demand for the conventional variety by a whopping 70%. As the organisation wrote, “We are already on the cusp of the deepest, fastest, most consequential disruption in food and agricultural production since the first domestication of plants and animals 10,000 years ago.”

And yet, despite the frenzy, the meat itself never arrived. The challenges were numerous. There was the exorbitant upfront cost of building manufacturing facilities and the daunting amounts of energy required to run them. There was the difficulty of producing sufficient quantities of the stuff, at a price point low enough for people to buy. There was the lack of a highly skilled workforce trained to operate the new technology. There were rounds and rounds of inspections by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). There was even, occasionally, the unwanted appearance of rodent DNA in research samples, which happened to the companies Upside and Eat Just. After peaking in 2021, investment began to fall off. In 2023, the industry raised a measly $177m globally.

But it wasn’t only venture capitalists who had started to grow sceptical of cultivated meat. The technology soon became a target of conservatives. The state governments of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Indiana, Montana, Nebraska and Texas moved in quick succession to legislate against cultivated meat, passing laws that banned its sale, production, or both. The Florida governor Ron DeSantis made a media event out of signing that state’s law, posing for pictures in front of a blood-stained cutting board piled high with steaks. “Take your fake lab-grown meat elsewhere,” he said. “We’re not doing that in the state of Florida.” In 2024, the industrial biotech consultant Joel Stone told the New York Times that, if he had to put odds on it, the likelihood of the industry producing even 10% of the meat supply in the foreseeable future “would be zero”. Today, cultivated meat is available for purchase at just one store in the world: Huber’s Butchery in Singapore, where customers can buy packages of lab-grown chicken shreds from a manufacturer called GOOD Meat.

These developments were inconvenient for me, a person who became obsessed with the prospect of tasting cell-grown meat just as the possibility of ever doing so seemed to recede before my eyes. I was enthralled by the story of the meat, which seemed to contain so much of what defined this era of American life: dubious techno-optimism, bombastic culture-war posturing, carnival oddities like the mammoth meatball. It presented a snarl of competing motives, a mix of altruism and cold-blooded striving for capital (nothing can ever exist just for the common good; it has to make someone a billionaire). There was also the fact that I had been a vegetarian for almost 20 years.

The last meat I ever ate was a hotdog at Shea Stadium in New York in 2007. I don’t remember how it tasted – probably like every other hotdog I had eaten before. I washed it down with an exorbitantly priced but very cold Budweiser in one of those metal bottles. I quit eating meat after that, not because the hotdog had been disgusting but because I didn’t like the sensation of the inevitable bad bite, the periodic tangle with gristle or tendon or bone. Then my abstention grew into habit, and the habit was reinforced by other concerns: the catastrophic environmental consequences of industrial meat production; the creeping doubt, as I grow older, that I’m necessarily higher in the cosmic order than a chicken or a cow. But cultivated meat raised a compelling question. If you could subtract some of the downsides – make meat less destructive, engineer away its aesthetic flaws – what reason would there be not to eat it?

This question had begun to feel moot as the potential of cultivated meat grew less and less promising. But just when it seemed as though Post’s vision would never be realised, encouraging news emerged from a surprising place: North Carolina. In May 2024, when many of his peers were fleeing the sector, Jeff Bezos granted $30m through his Earth Fund to establish the Bezos Center for Sustainable Protein at North Carolina State University, an initiative dedicated to developing “dietary proteins that are environmentally friendly, healthy, tasty and affordable”. The donation cemented the state’s status as a new global centre of the cultivated-meat industry. The Bezos Center would join the North Carolina Biotechnology Center, an economic development organisation for the life sciences in Research Triangle Park.

On the commercial side of things, Believer Meats, an Israeli company producing cultivated chicken, had recently broken ground on a 200,000 sq ft manufacturing plant in Wilson, North Carolina. The plant would be the largest cultivated-meat facility in the world – capable, the company claimed, of producing 9.5m kilos of engineered chicken per year.

In September 2025, Believer received a “no questions” letter from the FDA, indicating that the agency did not encounter safety concerns in its inspection of the company’s products. “We are proud to be commercialising in this state, creating high-quality manufacturing jobs and enabling us to realise our vision to lead food innovations that care for the planet,” said Believer’s then CEO, a man named (for real) Gustavo Burger, in a press release celebrating the milestone. I got in touch with the company shortly after. In a Zoom meeting with Heather Hudson, Believer’s chief product and growth officer, and Rodrigo Lavall, from sales and marketing, the two dangled the possibility of a ribbon-cutting ceremony. They could tentatively plan something and invite me down to visit.

The whole thing felt a bit Wonka-ish. No one from the press had been allowed inside the factory yet. Only a few professionals in the field had even toured it. Why should I get the golden ticket? But I tried not to question my good fortune. Excited by the prospect of exclusive access, I started planning a trip to the Triangle. If lab-grown meat had a future, I might find it there. Maybe, I thought, I’d even get to taste it.

On a mild day in early December, I arrived at NC State’s sprawling campus, home to about 40,000 students. I expected it to be lively, teeming with kids, but it was eerily dead. Rohan Shirwaiker, the friendly, bespectacled director of the Bezos Center, met me in a pristine building where I didn’t see a single student. Everyone, he explained, had gone home for the holidays.

The Bezos Center aims to address, as its website puts it, the “critical barriers and gaps” still dogging cultivated meat. The process has changed as the industry scales up. It’s no longer Post labouring over a single burger in his lab for years at a time. Cultivation now takes place in sterile factories that look more like breweries, with cells grown not in culture dishes but in giant, stainless-steel bioreactors. Producers have also moved away from feeding the cells with foetal bovine serum, which is expensive and requires harvesting cow blood from slaughterhouses (not exactly a good look for a cruelty-free alternative meat product). The industry now relies on what is referred to as “serum-free media”, or SFM, proprietary compounds that vary from company to company. Still, the basic science remains the same: in one typical version of the process, stem cells are harvested from a living animal via needle biopsy, then nourished in solutions containing glucose, vitamins, fats, minerals, proteins and amino acids, which are swished around inside a reactor to ensure an even diffusion of nutrients. In these conditions, the cells divide, multiply and differentiate just as they would inside an animal. They are ready for harvesting when they reach the desired density: roughly within two to eight weeks, depending on the species being cultivated.

But what also remains is one of the industry’s fundamental challenges. You cannot simply grow a steak – yank it out of the reactor and slap it on the table at a restaurant – because a steak contains multiple kinds of tissue. At the moment, muscle and fat can only be cultivated separately, and typically they do not form solid matter but a semisolid slurry that must be taken from the reactors, washed, combined with other ingredients for flavour and texture, and extruded or 3D-printed into something you would recognise as meat: a burger or a nugget or a meatball or a fillet. Some companies are trying to circumnavigate the slurry stage by building scaffolding inside reactors for cells to cling to, producing a firmer product. (Certain types of cells don’t like floating in a tank all free like that. Tissue, I’m told, wants to adhere to bone.)

The cost of all this has come way down since Schonwald called Post’s burger an “animal-protein cake”, but right now, cultivated meat is far more expensive than the real thing. At Huber’s, in Singapore, the ominously named GOOD Meat 3, which contains only 3% chicken cells, sells for $5.62 (£4.20) per 110g serving. Meanwhile, chicken at my local supermarket, containing 100% animal cells, starts at $3.49 per 450g.

Shirwaiker took me on a tour of the Bezos Center’s brand new protein lab, which was still being set up. It was spacious and filled with light, lined with 3D printers and a humming but empty stainless-steel fridge. The printers, in particular, were huge and impressive. But the lab was still in the early phases of assembly; cables dangled from the ceiling, waiting for equipment that had yet to be delivered.

As Shirwaiker and I walked back to his office, we discussed the day’s shocking headline: while I was travelling to North Carolina from my home in upstate New York, news broke that Believer Meats was being sued for $34m by Gray Construction, the firm that built its hulking factory in Wilson. Believer had recently defaulted on an agreement to pay Gray an instalment of $22m. Maybe I should have seen it coming: after her initial enthusiasm, Hudson, my contact at Believer, had ghosted me in the days leading up to my trip.

I asked Shirwaiker what all this meant. He was as surprised as I was. He thought that the plant was so close to opening that the staff just needed to turn on the lights and boot up the chicken vats. No one knows yet what happened at Believer, he told me. It was unclear whether the company would survive.

Before I left the Bezos Center, Shirwaiker introduced me to the concept of the Gartner Hype Cycle. To me, it had the ring of an old concept, a framework invented in the mid-20th century by an economist or a professor. But no: it was formulated in 1995 by a woman named Jackie Fenn, who worked at the consultancy firm Gartner. Its purpose, according to a YouTube video made by the company, is to help you – a savvy investor, the video assumes – “understand the real risks and opportunities of an innovation so you can avoid adopting something too early, giving up too soon, adopting too late, or hanging on too long”.

Shirwaiker showed me a chart to illustrate. The x-axis was time, and the y-axis was visibility. The cycle begins with an “innovation trigger”, when a new technology is introduced to great fanfare, then arcs upward toward the “peak of inflated expectations” as excitement mounts. But this rise is inevitably followed by a dramatic fall, when investors realise how difficult it’s going to be to actually commercialise the innovation. Later comes a gentler climb up the “slope of enlightenment”, when second- and third-generation products emerge, until, finally, we reach the “plateau of productivity”, the slow, unflashy development of the technology. If Post’s burger was the innovation trigger, I asked Shirwaiker, where were we now? He circled the deep valley in the middle of the chart: the “trough of disillusionment”.

Before leaving campus, I tried Hudson again. I let her know that I was in the area and asked if I should “stop by”, as though the Believer facility were a conveniently located coffee shop rather than a meat factory in a rural area. I immediately received an auto-response that her email account was no longer active. Then I thought, what the hell, and decided to drive out to Wilson, about 45 minutes from Raleigh. I’ll go to see what’s up, I figured. I’ll talk to someone face-to-face, have some sort of confrontation with a person overseeing the plant – maybe even Hudson herself.

Rural North Carolina felt enormous, flat and empty. The landscape was almost featureless; huge swaths of nothing streamed by, and then I hit factories. Believer was located among a loose cluster of manufacturing facilities. To get there, I had to turn off a main strip containing a Chick-fil-A, a Bojangles, a McDonald’s and a Best-N-Burgers. At one point, I yielded to the flashing lights of what I thought was an emergency vehicle, only to find, as it passed, that it was a pickup truck towing a meat smoker. I was surrounded by the stuff. I thought of Post’s prediction that demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it. Sometimes it seems that this will happen tomorrow.

What I found when I got to Believer was grimmer than I expected. Not a chipper-then-confused-then-annoyed desk clerk wondering who this was showing up at a meat factory without an appointment, but no one at all. The facility was deserted, gated: a royal-blue cube under a pale late-autumn sky, millions of dollars of groundbreaking technology locked inside.

There is a widespread feeling in the US that everything is a hoax or a Ponzi scheme, and this feeling is only reinforced by the news. The news that self-driving taxis, when they become confused, are actually operated remotely from the Philippines. The news that the mysterious invention that could scan your blood for any number of disorders was an era-defining scam. The news that the crypto entrepreneur who pledged to secure the longtime survival of the human race was actually stealing $8bn of his customers’ money to fund his polycule in the Bahamas. I became paranoid, standing in front of the abandoned car park, that cultivated meat was just another lie, or a semi-lie, or a bluff. That the reason the meat was so difficult to get my hands on was that it did not exist. The possible implosion of Believer was disappointing not just because it represented a setback in the quest to reduce our carbon emissions and fortify our food systems against climate collapse, but because it seemed to confirm that we live in a cheap, mendacious world, where what passes for progress almost always turns out to be a confidence game.

The morning after my reconnaissance mission, more news broke: Believer was declaring bankruptcy and would shutter the factory in Wilson before it printed a single chicken strip.

I had timed my trip to North Carolina to coincide with the first annual Global Forum for Plant-Based and Alternative Proteins, held at the North Carolina Biotechnology Center. This was how I found myself cloistered among the faithful as their meat dreams unravelled in real time. All the local industry players were in attendance, and more had flown in from around the world. We were sitting together in NCBiotech’s blandly carpeted lecture hall for the opening session, listening to optimistic remarks about international collaboration, an opaque joke about an extruder, a shout-out to “Ian in the back from the insect side”, all the while knowing that the industry’s biggest gambit yet had just failed. With Believer gone bust, I hoped to salvage a glimmer of optimism for the industry from the day’s proceedings – or, at the very least, an honest assessment of what had gone wrong.

During a break in the programme, everyone filed out and congregated in the atrium. We were in the trough of disillusionment, but we were also in the divot of gossip. We were in the furrow of hanging around outside the auditorium talking excitedly. We were in the ravine of wanting to know what the hell had happened. I was surrounded by guys in crisp button-ups and thermal gilets and navy-blue blazers. There were not a ton of women present. All around me, speculation began to fly.

“There was a time about three or four years ago, post-pandemic, the money was so easy to come by. All you had to do was put a pitch deck together, and VCs would throw money at you.”

“They have a pretty star list of investors.”

“Yeah. That doesn’t guarantee a success.”

“They got the building up. The building is ready to, like, turn on.”

“It’s probably gonna be a liquidation. Again, we’re all assuming. We don’t know what the heck’s going on.”

“There’s got to be some news out of Israel.”

Later, we heard from venture capitalists who had no choice but to address the news head on. “I mean, elephant in the room: Believer Meats just down the road basically went out of business,” said Steve Simitzis, from Replicator VC, a firm that invests in early-stage food-tech companies. “I don’t have any information about it, but I would speculate that building factories around technology that isn’t ready at scale is probably a cause.” Well, duh, I thought. The VCs on the panel saw Believer as a cautionary tale. Don’t scale too quickly. Lower costs. Make something consumers actually want to eat. All these observations were sensible, even obvious, and yet wasn’t it also the case that the VCs themselves had put pressure on companies like Believer to expand rapidly in order to provide the returns they sought?

In the afternoon, we all tried to rally for a tasting of products by food startups. At last, I was sampling things. I drank some kind of fizzy peach tea. It was not immediately obvious to me what the innovation was, so I asked the young guy handing out the cans about it. It’s supposed to be refreshing, he said. Like after a run you can drink one and it won’t make you puke. Curiously, though, there was no cultivated meat on offer. The Research Triangle may be an industry hub, but the product did not seem to be available here. The product was still a prototype, or the product was too expensive to give out as samples. The closest thing on hand was plant-based vegan meat. I tried wheat-based turkey and wheat-based pepperoni from a company called The BE Hive. I tried “some kind of pulled meat”, as the person wheeling it out from the kitchen described it, from a company called Delight Soy. It had a stringy texture and was an orangish brown. I tried a fungi-and-soy-based salmon substitute from a company called Juicy Marbles. This one was very close to tasting like salmon. They had got something right, everyone around me agreed. To our wonder and dismay, Juicy Marbles had nailed the fishiness. Probably algae in there, someone remarked. We nodded. Yes, probably algae.

The experience was nauseating, though the cube of salmon tasted good. Or rather, it would have tasted good if you could isolate taste from the other senses. Like, if you didn’t see the morsel of fake fish, or feel it in your mouth, or smell its oily smell. And if you didn’t also know that it was synthetic. The knowing added a layer of queasiness. The idea that they would infuse soy with an unappealing smell for verisimilitude – a cloying, marine smell, like the hold of a fishing boat.

So all it would take for this thing to be palatable would be to experience it in a sensory vacuum and preferably context-free, or immediately after a blow to the head that wipes out everything you know about it. Then it would be pretty nice.

In January, a few weeks after my trip to the Research Triangle, a man ate a chicken sandwich. He ate two, actually: one made with conventional chicken and one made with a cultivated fillet. In a video of his visit to the Upside Foods factory in California, he stands next to a vat of swirling chicken cells. The cells are foamy, the cheerful yellow of Campbell’s broth. The man’s name is Jimmy Donaldson, though he’s known more widely as the YouTube sensation MrBeast, and he thinks that cell-grown meat has a lot of advantages. “These chickens don’t get diseases,” says MrBeast. “So then you don’t have to worry about a disease spreading on the farm and then you eating a sick chicken.” When it’s time to try to guess which sandwich is which, he can’t do it. “I honestly can’t tell,” he says, before guessing wrong.

Watching the video on my phone, it irked me that MrBeast had tasted the meat. That should have been me standing next to the churning chicken water. For months I’d been trying to find cultivated meat on the east coast; I had even considered buying it from Singapore on the grey market. Nothing panned out. Finally, Rohan Shirwaiker sent me details for a public tasting in the Bay Area held by Mission Barns, another partner of the Bezos Center. It would take place at the supermarket Berkeley Bowl West, which had previously sold a limited run of the company’s meatballs.

On a Friday in February, I flew out to San Francisco and got a cab over to the Mission Barns office, which was located in SoMa, on a desolate and unlovely block of warehouses. Not many Waymos swooping by out there, but at least it felt appropriately industrial, with the office upstairs and bioreactors below. Not that I got to see them: when I asked, I was gently rebuffed with the excuse that the company was in the process of moving to a larger facility in Alameda. I felt the ambient paranoia I’d experienced in North Carolina start to kick in again. After the collapse of Believer, Mission Barns seemed like one of the American companies closest to having its products on grocery-store shelves. At the end of last year, it received USDA approval for its cultivated pork fat. At the time of my visit, its products included bacon, pepperoni, meatballs and a couple varieties of sausage.

Bianca Lê, a smiley, put-together Australian and the then head of external affairs at Mission Barns, took me up to the company’s third-floor office, which contained a large kitchen on one side. As we sat at the wooden island, she told me about the origin of the cells for all of the company’s cultivated fat: a single Yorkshire pig named Dawn who was still, according to the company’s marketing materials, “happily roaming free” in an animal sanctuary in upstate New York, not far from where I live. Dawn reminded me of Dolly the sheep – a mascot for something much larger than herself. One wants to picture her soulful.

“Can I ask how Dawn was selected?” I said, hoping to hear something about Dawn as a superior specimen, the fattest, happiest, healthiest, smartest pig in the US.

“Yeah, honestly, it’s not that interesting of a story,” said Lê. “It’s just that she was available.”

The Mission Barns cultivation process takes about two weeks. At the end, they drain the bioreactors until they are left with just the fat slurry. “It’s white, it’s semisolid, it’s really pasty,” Lê said. That slurry is then combined with plant protein to create the final product, which typically contains less than 10% of animal cells per serving. I tried to understand how they got the fat out of one container and into the next, miming a large scoop or shovel, but this part was a secret. The company’s ultimate goal, Lê told me, wasn’t even to sell products but to license the system itself.

Mission Barns’s then CEO, Cecilia Chang, appeared: another smiley, put-together Australian. As she joined us at the counter, I asked her about the biggest challenges the company faces. “The timeline on being able to get costs down fast enough to get to a point of profitability,” she said. “The technology is there, but investors have really aggressive timelines.” Chang also mentioned a newer hurdle: the distrust of food science stoked by Donald Trump’s secretary of health and human services, Robert F Kennedy Jr. Still, the industry was trying to look at Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement as an opportunity rather than as a disaster. After all, MAHA is focused on protein; Kennedy’s new, inverted food pyramid features steak at the very top. And, although the movement broadly disdains processed foods, Chang told me, it may appreciate that cell-cultivated meat is usually organic and antibiotic-free. I recalled the lay wisdom of MrBeast: “These chickens don’t get diseases.”

As we chatted, Zachary Tyndall, Mission Barns’s product-development and culinary manager, prepared some meat for me in a frying pan. Tyndall is a former chef who once worked at the three-Michelin-star restaurant Noma, an apprenticeship that seemed unnecessary for the level of cooking involved here. He used a spatula to roll a single meatball around in a pan. The meat was a pale, pinkish beige, like real pork. It’s not that different from cooking conventional meat, he told me, though maybe a little bit quicker, since the company’s meatballs are precooked and only need reheating. It smelled savoury, like food, and indeed, it was food. I’ll give it that.

I received my meatball on a tastefully speckled earthenware plate. Though nearly delirious with excitement, I tried to zoom out for a second and glimpse the situation with objectivity. I was looking at a single small meatball in the middle of a plate in a chilly, industrial office thousands of miles away from home. This was what I had elected to pursue over the course of months with single-minded determination. With all eyes on me, I used the fork to cut it in half and took a bite.

The taste. The taste was not terrible. It was seasoned, oregano-heavy. It even had a kick. Everyone was watching as I chewed, so I feigned deep consideration, the way you do when the waiter brings you a sample of wine at a restaurant. “Hmm,” I mused. I am contemplating the tasting notes, my face said. I am weighing the mouthfeel. I tasted the salami too, which looked exactly like regular salami. It tasted like salty paper. Salty paper with a kick – they’re good about putting in the kick. I could not find much to say to Chang and Lê about the meat, though I tried. The phrase “blandly inoffensive” came to mind. The word “anticlimax” came to mind. This was what I had come all this way for? To eat something that felt like mushy cardboard in my mouth?

“It’s good,” I managed to tell them. Then, suddenly, the nausea hit, a taste of vomit in the back of my throat. It was the Juicy Marbles effect again. The problem was not the flavour, not the texture, but the knowing. The Knowing. Knowing about the fat tank, about the sticky white substance. The envisioning of the scoop. The knowing about Dawn, an ordinary pig who was available, and the extraction process that took her cells. Earlier, I’d thought this feeling was triggered entirely by Juicy Marbles’s ersatz fish odour, by its inherent artificiality. I hoped it would be different with the cultivated meat, which was, in the end, an actual animal product, at least in part. But no. If anything, it was worse.

The next day at Berkeley Bowl West, a large grocery store across the Bay, I watched a couple of dozen customers line up to taste the meatballs. Lê explained that Mission Barns has a fanbase, people who follow the company’s progress and register for events in advance. Here, a new contingent of the public revealed itself to me: my fellow cultivated-meat-curious. They were young and slightly goth. They were gen-Z vegans with lip rings and huge black trousers that flapped in the wind. Aside from these devotees, the crowd was made up mostly of people who happened to be at the grocery store for other reasons: Saturday shoppers, parents with kids in tow, people in athleisure. It was a warm and sunny February morning, a good day for a free sample. Passersby queued up, mildly interested.

Previous tastings had drawn protesters. In 2024, the week before the Florida cultivated-meat ban went into effect, Upside Foods hosted the Freedom of Food pop-up, a tasting on a Miami rooftop that was pitched as a protest of the new law. A chef from Caja Caliente, a restaurant in Coral Gables, made chicken tostadas with chipotle crema while a group of conventional-meat zealots parked a van in front of the venue’s entrance. The van was affixed with a huge LED screen displaying criticism of lab-grown meat. No long-term health studies, it read. Secret chemical formulas.

But nothing like that happened in Berkeley. Tyndall stood at a hot plate, gamely rolling the meatballs around a pan and placing them into small bamboo trays. As the samples were distributed, I made myself eat another one to see if my reaction would be the same as the day before. Instantly, I was clobbered by the Knowing, but around me, muffled sounds of approval rose from the crowd. A few people told me, shrugging, that the texture seemed right. A child, maybe two years old, accepted a meatball from her dad. She ate it happily, bobbing around like little kids do, with no objection.

A woman in a fleece jacket walked around asking tasters to fill out a survey on an iPad. She was an independent researcher conducting a study on consumer acceptance of cultivated meat for Tufts University. After the science, this is one of the biggest challenges to the product’s long-term success. Do people actually want to try it? Do they want to incorporate it into their diets? According to a report published last year by the Good Food Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to promoting alternative proteins, only 18% of Americans find cell-cultivated meat extremely or very appealing, and almost 60% say they are somewhat or very unlikely to buy it. Interest typically decreases with age and increases with educational attainment, which tracked with my own observations. The goth college students were the most excited by the meatballs, but even they were muted in their praise. No one said “I love it” or “Hell yeah” or declared it a triumph. I did not hear the word “yum”.

The days of cultivated meat as a possible panacea for the climate crisis are long gone. Many of the industry’s biggest players – the ones still in business, anyway – are now embracing a more modest role in our food system. Since I tried its meatballs earlier this year, Mission Barns has announced a new strategy: it is pivoting from retail to wholesale and developing new products that will combine plant protein with conventional pork fat – to be replaced by their own, cultivated fat only once they’ve achieved a certain scale. Elsewhere, cellular agriculture is being used to create exclusive novelty items that could be fairly described as Frankenmeat, whereby their freakiness and limited availability are not liabilities but rather the selling points. Vow, the Australian company behind the mammoth meatball, has also developed a variety of Japanese quail foie gras as part of its objective to craft meats “unconstrained” by “the limits of nature”. Why, one might wonder? No real reason, except that they can. This, at least, feels like a more fitting use for cultivation technology and a more honest reflection of the ecosystem that has financed it.

This isn’t to say that engineered food needs to be virtuous to justify its existence. Before I left Berkeley Bowl West, Dixon gave me a tour of the store’s produce section, which was filled with the inordinate splendour of California. There must have been 20 varieties of crazy-looking mushrooms. She insisted I take two sumo citrus oranges – the ones with the bump on top – back home with me. Sumos aren’t naturally occurring; they were created in the 1970s by Japanese scientists who crossbred two citrus hybrids in a bid to produce a more flavourful, seedless fruit that might sell better than existing varieties.

I peeled a sumo and ate it as I walked through Berkeley. The afternoon was hot and windy, but the orange was sweet, hydrating, refreshing. Enormous and delicious. It was one shade paler than a traffic cone, with a palm-filling heft. It was perfect: a perfect example of an orange. A miracle, really, how it had just been handed to me.

A longer version of this piece appeared in the September edition of Harper’s

Bolsonaro’s Flight to the U. S. Was Aided by a Milei Adviser

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Brazil’s Presidential Election

Advertisement

Supported by

A top adviser to President Javier Milei of Argentina met Flávio Bolsonaro, the defeated Brazilian presidential candidate, at an Argentine airport, three people involved in the operation said.

By Emma BubolaDiego Bogarin and Lucía Cholakian Herrera

Emma Bubola and Lucía Cholakian Herrera reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina, and Diego Bogarin from Puerto Iguazú.

When Flávio Bolsonaro fled Brazil two days after losing last month’s presidential election and arrived at an airport in Argentina, a top adviser to Argentina’s president was waiting for him on the tarmac.

The adviser, Santiago Caputo, a member of President Javier Milei’s inner circle, met Mr. Bolsonaro at the Puerto Iguazú airport on Oct. 27, where he boarded a jet that ultimately took him and his family to Miami, three people involved in the operation said.

Mr. Caputo had traveled about 800 miles from Buenos Aires, Argentina’s capital, to the region the day before and helped coordinate Mr. Bolsonaro’s departure from the airport, including helping fast-track the family’s passport processing and flight paperwork, the people said.

Mr. Bolsonaro faces multiple criminal investigations in Brazil and, according to Brazilian authorities, had not complied with an order to surrender his travel documents.

Like other people interviewed for this article, the three people familiar with the effort to help Mr. Bolsonaro reach the United States requested anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mr. Bolsonaro did not acknowledge receiving any help from the Milei government or any other authority. He said that he did not know Mr. Caputo and that at the airport, “several Argentines were by my side, I don’t know if one of them was this guy.”

Mr. Bolsonaro did not explain how he was able to travel internationally, saying only that he made his way to the United States on his own. But Mr. Bolsonaro’s Brazilian passports had been canceled, and President Trump said that the United States gave him “a pass” to enter the country. The New York Times also reported that a White House official arranged the plane that Mr. Bolsonaro took to Miami.

Mr. Caputo, in a WhatsApp message, said he had “played no role” in Mr. Bolsonaro’s travels and did not respond to questions about his presence at the airport. Argentina’s foreign ministry said the Argentine government “had no involvement whatsoever” in Mr. Bolsonaro’s exit from Brazil. Yet Mr. Bolsonaro publicly thanked the Milei government soon after reaching Miami.

“I would like to thank President Milei for his courage, sense of justice and legality,” Mr. Bolsonaro wrote in a statement.

Likewise, Mr. Milei’s allies also cheered Mr. Bolsonaro’s escape and suggested their government played a role in it.

“Milei’s government is the bravest in history,” Juan Carreira, who oversees Mr. Milei’s digital communications, wrote on social media, adding, “Flávio Bolsonaro is safe from the claws of communism.”

Mr. Caputo holds no official government position but, together with Mr. Milei’s sister, is one of the president’s closest advisers and wields considerable influence over foreign policy and intelligence matters.

Mr. Milei, a political ally of Mr. Bolsonaro and one of the few world leaders who have not recognized the re-election of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Caputo’s role in Mr. Bolsonaro’s escape is another example of how personal and partisan alliances are reshaping Latin American politics. A victory by Mr. Bolsonaro in the presidential election would have given the ascendant right its biggest win in Latin America.

Before the election, Mr. Milei had participated in a campaign event with Mr. Bolsonaro in São Paulo and insulted Mr. Lula, as well as a Brazilian Supreme Court justice who has been targeted by the right in Brazil.

Mr. Lula accused Mr. Milei of interfering in his country’s internal affairs, recalled Brazil’s ambassador to Argentina and asked the Argentine ambassador to leave the country.

Brazil is Argentina’s neighbor and largest trading partner, and experts have warned that a deteriorating relationship between the two countries could have serious economic consequences for Argentina.

Brazil’s foreign ministry last week summoned Argentina’s chargé d’affaires, the highest-ranking Argentine representative still in Brasília, the capital, to ask for an explanation about Mr. Bolsonaro’s escape, according to two Brazilian diplomats.

Pablo Quirno, Argentina’s foreign minister, denied in a post on X that such a request had been made.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s journey has fueled countless conflicting reports and generated many unanswered questions. While Brazilian authorities had barred Mr. Bolsonaro from leaving Brazil, his passage through Argentina does not appear to have broken any Argentine law.

Mr. Bolsonaro has not been charged with any crime.

Despite a court order banning Mr. Bolsonaro from traveling because of investigations linking him to a money laundering scheme, there was no arrest warrant when Mr. Bolsonaro crossed from Brazil into Argentina on the night of Oct. 27 with his wife and two daughters.

Mr. Caputo arrived in Iguazú by private jet on the night of Oct. 26, the day after Brazil’s election, said two of the people involved in Mr. Bolsonaro’s transfer through Argentina.

He spent much of Tuesday waiting for Mr. Bolsonaro in the border town, including at a cafe inside a gas station, one of the people said.

A separate private jet that would transport Mr. Bolsonaro was also waiting at the local airport. The plane is owned by an Argentine company, Baires Fly, whose owner, Luis Grande, said he had been hired by a broker who chartered the plane for $150,000.

Mr. Grande said he had used the same jet to twice transport Mr. Lula, once to visit a former Argentine president and on another occasion to travel to Havana.

The plane had been chartered on Oct. 26 and was initially meant to depart Argentina on the same night, Mr. Grande said. But it was delayed because the passengers “had trouble arriving,” he said.

Mr. Bolsonaro eventually crossed the Argentine border the following night, and then entered the Iguazú airport in a gray van, two of the people said.

Once there, Mr. Bolsonaro had his paperwork to board the plane expedited through immigration by Mr. Caputo and his aides, according to the three people who said they witnessed the interaction. The group with Mr. Caputo included two agents from a joint Argentine-Paraguayan public agency that manages a hydroelectric complex elsewhere along the border (Iguazú is also along Argentina’s border with Paraguay).

Mr. Bolsonaro’s plane finally took off right after midnight on Wednesday.

After the plane took off, Mr. Caputo went to find a junior police officer who was taking videos of the scene on the tarmac. Two of the people involved in the operation said Mr. Caputo told him to delete the videos.

Ana Ionova contributed reporting from Miami.

Emma Bubola is a Times reporter covering Argentina. She is based in Buenos Aires.

U. A. E. Sent ‘Desert Wolves’ to Help Sudanese Militia Accused of Genocide

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Sudan’s Civil War

Advertisement

Supported by

Lana Nusseibeh, one of the Gulf nation’s top diplomats, has led the effort to deny her country’s role in Sudan. Now it’s complicating her bid to become secretary general of the United Nations.

By Declan Walsh

The United Arab Emirates hired Colombian mercenaries to fight alongside a notorious Sudanese paramilitary group that has been accused of genocide, United Nations investigators have found.

A confidential report submitted to the Security Council last week and obtained by The New York Times details how an Emirati security company with close ties to the government moved the Colombians into Sudan through territory controlled by Emirati proxies in Libya and Somalia.

The report is the most detailed accounting yet by the United Nations of the Emirati role in Sudan’s civil war, in which the Emirates is accused of supplying drones, weapons and mercenaries to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or R. S. F., fueling a conflict that has caused hundreds of thousands of deaths.

The U. N. findings come at a sensitive time for the Emirates. One of its top diplomats, Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, who for years has led Emirati efforts to deny her country’s role in Sudan, is a candidate to become the next secretary general of the United Nations.

Cambridge-educated and of Palestinian heritage, Ms. Nusseibeh, 48, has represented the Emirates at the United Nations for over a decade, returning in 2024 to the Emirates, where she was appointed minister of state for foreign affairs last year.

Since emerging in October as a last-minute candidate in the contest to lead the United Nations, Ms. Nusseibeh has shaken up the race while coming under sharp scrutiny for her role in Sudan. She is accused of trying to deny or downplay evidence that the Emirates, in violation of a U. N. arms embargo, has backed the R. S. F., a group accused of countless atrocities.

Critics also say Ms. Nusseibeh has sought to silence, sometimes successfully, the work of U. N. bodies investigating Emirati policy in several Arab countries, where it has been accused of backing warlords and breaking international arms embargoes.

“Lana Nusseibeh has spent over a decade in roles acting for the U. A. E. government and repeatedly whitewashing their abusive role in Yemen and Sudan, presenting Abu Dhabi as a humanitarian actor while dismissing or obscuring mounting evidence of its role in fueling abuses,” Bruno Stagno Ugarte of Human Rights Watch said in a statement.

Ms. Nusseibeh’s candidacy raised questions about whether she would be willing “to defend the independence and integrity of the U. N. and its investigative mechanisms, including those exposing U. A. E. abuses,” Mr. Ugarte said.

A spokesman for the Emirates denied the country supported any side in Sudan’s war or sought to undermine U. N. investigations. The Emirates separately told the U. N. that the security company named in the confidential report had not deployed mercenaries to Sudan or broken any Emirati law.

In an email, Ms. Nusseibeh said that ending the “terrible conflict” in Sudan would be her priority as secretary general. She pledged that if U. N. investigators identified a foreign power fueling the conflict, she would “act on it and engage that state.”

“Sudan will be a litmus test for the next secretary general,” she added.

Ms. Nusseibeh has been on the front lines of Emirati diplomacy on Sudan since the country fell into civil war in 2023.

Within months, the Emirates began supplying weapons, drones and military aid to the R. S. F., hoping to help the paramilitary group defeat Sudan’s military and assure Emirati interests in a country with deep gold deposits and a strategic position on the Red Sea. In 2024, The Times revealed that the Emirates was flying powerful Chinese drones from a base in Chad, under the cover of a Red Cross operation.

Other countries and companies have fueled Sudan’s war as well, including Russia, Iran, Turkey and Ukraine, mostly by sending or selling weapons to Sudan’s military. But none have been as pivotal as the Emirates, which has used its vast resources and close alliances with countries like Ethiopia and Chad in support of the R. S. F.

In interviews, Ms. Nusseibeh has repeatedly said that her country is not backing the R. S. F. “Those allegations are categorically untrue,” she told CNN in 2024, adding that the Emirates sends only humanitarian aid to Sudan.

Behind closed doors, Ms. Nusseibeh has quietly pressed foreign allies to support the Emirati position of professed neutrality on Sudan, according to several former U. S. officials.

But even in private, she has refused to speak candidly about her country’s role in Sudan, complicating efforts to bring the conflict to a negotiated end, the officials added.

In 2024, Emirati leaders, angered that Britain had not defended them from attacks during a Security Council meeting on Sudan, canceled planned meetings with senior British ministers in retaliation, said a senior former U. S. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive deliberations.

More recently, scrutiny of the Emirati role in Sudan has focused on the so-called Desert Wolves, a group of Colombian mercenaries hired to fight alongside the R. S. F. Several news outlets and rights groups have documented how the Colombians flew drones, trained fighters and provided artillery support as the R. S. F. carried out its punishing siege of the Sudanese city of El Fasher last year, one of the most notorious episodes of the war.

While the Emirates has often brushed past negative news reports, it appeared defensive earlier this year when the United Nations also accused the Emirates of providing Colombian mercenaries in Sudan.

In July, a panel of United Nations investigators monitoring an arms embargo on Darfur sent a detailed report to the Security Council that contained a blunt assertion: “The U. A. E. supported the R. S. F. by providing mercenaries,” it wrote.

Colombian mercenaries had been trained at two military bases in Abu Dhabi before being deployed to Sudan, it said. Emirati officials mounted a fierce pushback, and before the report could be made public it was blocked at the Security Council over objections from Bahrain, which currently holds a nonpermanent seat.

A senior U. N. official and a regional diplomat who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters said Bahrain had been acting at the behest of the Emirates.

The Emirates “rejects as unfounded the allegation it is influencing any Security Council member,” its spokesman said. Bahrain’s foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The investigators’ latest report, sent to the Security Council on Friday, said the mercenaries were hired by Global Security Services Group, an Abu Dhabi-based private security company with strong political, business and familial ties to senior figures in the Emirati ruling family.

The company was founded by a senior official in the Emirati presidency, records showed, and on its website it is described as “a preferred security provider” for the Emirati Foreign Ministry and Ministry of Presidential Affairs.

Analysts say the growing scrutiny of Ms. Nusseibeh’s record on Sudan may be hurting her campaign for secretary general. A recent straw poll of eight candidates placed her in the middle of the field.

Cameron Hudson, a former C. I. A. analyst and director for African affairs at the National Security Council, said the continued Emirati denials of support to the R. S. F. “make a mockery” of the investigative mechanisms that Ms. Nusseibeh now seeks to lead.

“She played a significant role in obfuscating her government’s contribution to atrocities in Sudan,” he said. “That ought to disqualify her from any further consideration.”

Under Ms. Nusseibeh, the Emirates has sought to quell U. N. scrutiny of its actions in other countries, too.

In 2011, the Emirates, alongside Saudi Arabia, successfully lobbied to close down a panel of U. N. investigators reporting on rights violations and other abuses in Yemen, where Emirati troops were deployed.

In 2016, Ms. Nusseibeh corresponded with other Emirati officials over U. N. accusations that their country was arming the warlord Khalifa Hifter in Libya. “The fact of the matter is that the U. A. E. violated the Security Council resolution on Libya and continues to do so,” one Emirati official wrote to Ms. Nusseibeh in a chain of emails that were accidentally sent to the U. N.

The U. N. published several of the emails but redacted the name of the official. The Times obtained an unredacted copy of that correspondence this week, identifying the official as Ahmed al Qasimi, a diplomat who worked for Ms. Nusseibeh at the U. N. mission in New York.

In November 2025, Ms. Nusseibeh led a concerted Emirati effort to influence members of the European Parliament over a pending resolution condemning atrocities in Sudan, Politico reported. The Parliament passed the resolution without mentioning the Emirates.

Declan Walsh is the chief Africa correspondent for The Times based in Nairobi, Kenya. He previously reported from Cairo, covering the Middle East, and Islamabad, Pakistan.

Newsom Commutes the Sentences of California’s 548 Death Row Inmates

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is expected to run for president, called capital punishment morally objectionable. Though California hasn’t executed anyone for 20 years, that represents about a quarter of death sentences nationwide.

By Laurel Rosenhall

Reporting from Sacramento

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California moved to spare the lives of all 548 prisoners on the state’s death row on Thursday in the largest mass commutation of death sentences in modern American history.

Mr. Newsom said he made the decision because he finds capital punishment morally objectionable. He reduced every death sentence to life in prison without parole, a sweeping move that will require a review by the state’s highest court in some cases and could draw legal challenges.

“State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us,” Mr. Newsom wrote in an open letter to California residents. “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”

Mr. Newsom is not the first governor to empty a state’s death row, and California has not executed anyone in 20 years. Nor was it likely to soon, given that Mr. Newsom’s successor, Xavier Becerra, has committed to maintaining a moratorium on capital punishment.

But the many people sentenced to death in California makes his decision especially significant. California has more death row inmates than any other state, and Mr. Newsom’s action cancels approximately one-fourth of all death sentences nationwide.

In his letter, the governor described the decision as one of the most difficult of his career, “not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families.”

Mr. Newsom acted just two months before he will leave office and as he considers a run for president. The act could make him a more compelling candidate to liberal voters in a Democratic primary, but likely would open him to attacks in a general election.

Death penalty opponents have planned a national ad campaign praising him for the move. The minute-long commercial casts the governor’s decision as an act of courage and leadership inspired by the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Dolores Huerta and Robert F. Kennedy. It will air on dozens of news and political shows nationwide, said Dan Newman, a Democratic strategist who advises both Mr. Newsom and the anti-death penalty groups sponsoring the ad.

Mr. Newman said that the governor had been motivated by personal conviction. But the ad could also help Mr. Newsom in a 2028 presidential campaign.

“We’ve entered a post-Trump world,” said Mr. Newman, the strategist. “And Democrats have to show what we’re for, and not just what we’re against.”

Mr. Newsom acted after months of lobbying by death penalty opponents and counter arguments from prosecutors and victim advocates. Those against Mr. Newsom’s move are expected to file a challenge arguing that he violated the law with a blanket commutation and that each case must be considered on individual merits.

They recently sent Mr. Newsom a seven-page letter, written by Anne Marie Schubert, a former Sacramento district attorney, that included photos of people killed by prisoners now on death row and detailed descriptions of their crimes. The cases included an 8-year-old boy who was severely abused for months before he died from torture in 2013 and another 8-year-old who disappeared while walking home from school in 1996.

California’s death row includes notorious killers such as Richard Allen Davis, who murdered Polly Klaas, a 12-year-old, after kidnapping her from her home in 1993. It also includes Cary Stayner, who killed four women near Yosemite in 1999, and the 1980s serial killer Charles Ng.

Ms. Schubert said that she had heard from the families of many victims who were distressed at the idea of commutations.

“These are people that have suffered unimaginable losses and were given some sense of finality through the justice system,” Ms. Schubert said in an interview before Mr. Newsom acted. “That is all being reopened and rehashed.”

Ms. Schubert, who leads the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, a victims rights group, said she plans to sue Mr. Newsom. Under California law, a governor can unilaterally grant clemency to offenders convicted in only one felony case. The California Supreme Court, however, must approve a governor’s clemency request for prisoners with convictions in multiple felony cases.

More than half the sentences Mr. Newsom seeks to reduce must now be reviewed. A state Supreme Court spokeswoman declined to comment on how long that could take.

Ms. Schubert contends that the court must review each case individually. Other legal experts have said that the court could consider them en masse if Mr. Newsom sought clemency based on a moral objection to the death penalty.

“When a governor is moved to be merciful, the courts recognize that’s between the governor and the Almighty,” David A. Carrillo, executive director of the California Constitution Center at the University of California, Berkeley law school, and Brandon V. Stracener, a research fellow, wrote in 2024.

Marc Klaas, the father of Polly Klaas, whose kidnapping and murder prompted an era of tough-on-crime policies in California, is livid at the idea of Mr. Newsom granting mercy to his daughter’s killer, or anyone else sentenced to death.

“We’re talking about serial killers, spree killers, cop killers, baby killers,” Mr. Klaas said. “We’re talking about absolutely the worst people in our society, without a doubt. And he’s putting his energy into commuting these characters?”

Mr. Newsom had already placed a moratorium on executions, a decision that upset Mr. Klaas when it was made seven years ago. The idea of a mass commutation revives his fury.

“It regurgitates the horrible emotions,” he said. “It just leaves me feeling raw and angry.”

Mr. Newsom recently met with other family members of Polly Klaas. Jess Nichol, her stepsister, said that she and another sister met with Mr. Newsom in October and encouraged him to commute all death sentences. Ms. Nichol is not the daughter of Mr. Klaas.

“We used to think that having a vengeful death penalty sentence is going to be what gave us justice,” Ms. Nichol said: “We’ve discovered that it doesn’t.”

Their meeting took place at the San Quentin prison that once housed all of California’s death row inmates, including Mr. Davis, who killed Polly.

Ms. Nichol, who was the same age as Polly, at first felt the killer deserved death, she said. But, Ms. Nichol said, she came to think that capital punishment would not help crime victims as much as resources to aid their healing. Ms. Nichol now facilitates rehabilitation programs at San Quentin.

“I want to live in a world where I am well, and not haunted by the hungry ghost of vengeance,” she said.

Mr. Newsom’s action echoes a similar move by President Joseph R. Biden near the end of his term. In December 2024, Mr. Biden commuted the sentences of all but three prisoners on federal death row.

Other Democratic governors have also used their executive power during the 2020s to reduce death sentences, albeit on a much smaller scale. Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina commuted 15, Gov. Kate Brown of Oregon commuted 17 and Gov. Jared S. Polis of Colorado commuted three.

Until now, the largest mass commutation in modern history was in 2003, when Gov. George Ryan of Illinois, a Republican, nullified death sentences for 167 inmates just before he left office.

Celinda Lake, a Democratic pollster who has conducted surveys for anti-death penalty groups, said she sees little political downside for Mr. Newsom because Democratic voters and Black voters who are influential in the party overwhelmingly oppose the death penalty.

“The chattering class will say this makes you vulnerable,” she said. “But I think that sounds like old establishment arguments.”

Laurel Rosenhall is a Sacramento-based reporter covering California politics and government for The Times.

Across the South, Black Voters Help Propel Democratic Wins

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democrats in the South used anger over redistricting, cuts to key federal programs and attacks on Black history to help galvanize a crucial bloc of voters to the polls.

By Emily Cochrane

Emily Cochrane, who is based in Nashville, covers the South.

The Supreme Court ruling in April that weakened the Voting Rights Act set off fears across the South that Black voters would be discouraged from turning out to vote and that gains in Black representation could be reversed.

And so community networks went to work. Elders at Black churches invoked their memories of the civil rights movement. Students at historically Black colleges and universities led marches and set up political events. And organizers who had spent years warning about the threat of disenfranchisement sought to convince a new generation that its vote mattered.

It worked. On Tuesday, Black voters in the South showed up to vote at unusually high levels, and Black voters chose Democrats at higher rates than in 2024, according to Times Voter Trends. They played a pivotal role in elevating Democrats to state office or narrowing the margins in races once thought to be safely enshrined in Republican control.

Georgia became the first state to elect a Black female governor. Alabama re-elected two Black representatives to the House. Mississippi could be on the verge of sending its first Black senator to Washington since the Reconstruction era.

Democratic candidates broadened their already overwhelming advantage with Black voters by successfully tapping into anger over not only the V. R. A. ruling but also high prices that strained budgets and the dismantling of programs aimed at bolstering diversity and Black institutions.

“Voters went above and beyond to come out to say: We’re going to elect a Congress that can begin the repair,” said Ashley Shelton, the executive director of the Power Coalition for Equity and Justice, which has been involved in the yearslong litigation over Louisiana’s congressional maps that led to the Supreme Court ruling. “We have to elect a Congress that’s going to stop this deterioration of our rights.”

In the House, Black voters supported Democratic candidates at a margin of roughly 80 percentage points nationwide, according to Times Voter Trends. That was a return to levels of support among Black voters that Democrats had enjoyed in 2020. But that support dipped in 2024, when Kamala Harris earned a smaller margin, at 70 points.

Representative Troy Carter, Democrat of Louisiana and a front-runner to lead the Congressional Black Caucus in January, said the caucus was on track to see one of its largest memberships in its history.

Early analysis of voter data showed that Black voters made up a larger share of the electorate in many Southern states than in 2024. Republican redistricting after the ruling sliced up districts in Tennessee, Alabama and Louisiana where Black voters had previously wielded significant power in choosing their representative.

Note: Southern states include Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia.

Source: Preliminary data on U. S. House vote shifts from Times Voter Trends as of Nov. 4, 2026 at 6:41 p. m.

Lily Boyce/The New York Times

Even in races where it did not change the outcome, high turnout among Black voters could provide Democrats with a pathway to whittling away at conservative strongholds across the South. About half of Black Americans live in the South, according to a 2025 Pew Research analysis.

The turnout also reflects the community networks that Black candidates and organizers relied on to help reach voters and connect frustrations with federal policy under the Trump administration to the effort to redraw district lines at both the congressional and state level.

In the months before the election, those groups packed campaign events, knocked on doors for long-shot candidates and, perhaps most importantly, rallied first-time or reluctant voters to the polls.

“Anger alone does not build a movement. I think folks being able to really connect the dots is what really mobilizes people,” said Anneshia Hardy, a voting rights organizer who splits her time between Georgia and Alabama. “This has been brewing.”

The Democratic wins were shaped in part by white voters who shifted toward Democrats by 11 points in Mississippi, 16 points in Alabama and 18 points in North Carolina. But Democrats still managed to expand their already dominant margins among Black voters in Southern states, including Mississippi, Georgia, North Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana and South Carolina.

“I think people were just tired,” said Representative Shomari Figures, Democrat of Alabama, who held onto his seat even though Republicans changed his district to include more white, rural conservative voters.

While voters were clearly motivated by a number of factors, including high prices and federal policy, he said, “the redistricting effort was certainly a large piece of that pie.”

For some Black voters, the effort to undercut their vote weighed heavily, particularly in a region still shaped by the legacy of slavery and segregation.

“Permanent protections for voting rights, that’s what has been on my mind,” said Willie Williams Jr., 30, an artist and gallery owner in Birmingham, Ala. “It needs to be permanent and equal for everyone, especially for those who are most marginalized — Black people.”

In Georgia, Black voters helped elevate Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic former mayor of Atlanta, to the governor’s mansion and keep Senator Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent, in office. In Mississippi, Scott Colom, a district attorney, holds a razor-thin lead over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, in a state where around a third of voters in 2026 were Black — one of the largest shares of Black voters in any state.

Both prospects had long seemed elusive.

“Living in Georgia and coming from Mississippi — two historically red states, but also two very Black states — representation matters,” said Conchetta Johnson, 39, who cast her first vote in a midterm election on Tuesday. “Growing up in a state with a complicated political history, a complicated racial history — that is the most important part for me.”

The Democratic wins were not comprehensive. The city of Memphis, where the highest concentration of Black Tennesseans live, is expected to be represented in the House entirely by Republicans after the General Assembly carved the city into three districts. Governor candidates in Tennessee and Alabama fell short, though their margins were narrowed to single digits.

Some Democrats questioned whether earlier or more robust investment in contests like the Mississippi or Louisiana Senate races could have made a difference this year. Representative Julia Letlow, the Republican in Louisiana, narrowly won, holding 50.9 percent of the vote over Jamie Davis, a Black Democrat and farmer.

The turnout, they said, was further proof that the region deserved the same opportunities and attention afforded to other states viewed as more easily winnable for Democrats. Both Mississippi and Louisiana have governor races in 2027.

“This is not going to be a one-and-done,” Mr. Carter said. “Buckle up, America. Our eyes are open.”

Sean Keenan, Bryant K. Oden and Caroline Soler contributed reporting.

Emily Cochrane is a national reporter for The Times covering the American South, based in Nashville.

A Viral Ad and a Trump Rally Visit Helped a Democrat Compete in Mississippi

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Scott Colom, a Democrat, ran a viral ad and courted Republicans at a Trump rally before winning virtually the same number of votes as Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican.

By John Yoon and Jim Beaugez

Jim Beaugez reported from Jackson, Miss.

Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Mississippi, went from a long shot months ago to holding a lead of more than 1,700 votes over the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, leaving the race too close to call on Thursday.

The tiny margin has given Mississippi an unexpected turn in the national spotlight as the only state other than Alaska where the Senate race has not yet been called. With more than 95 percent of the vote counted, it also sets up a nail-biting wait to learn whether Democrats will expand their already large Senate majority through a state that has not elected a Democrat to the chamber in more than 40 years.

Here’s how the race became this close:

In Mississippi, which President Trump won by about 23 points in 2024, Ms. Hyde-Smith was favored to win throughout her campaign. But the deep-red state became an unexpected battleground in October when one of Mr. Colom’s campaign ads went viral.

The roughly 30-second video mocks Ms. Hyde-Smith’s response to a local television anchor’s comment on the rising price of beef: “You have so many proteins to choose from,” she says in a clip.

The video cuts to a man grilling burgers. “Pick another protein?” he says. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.” The message, which aligned with Mr. Colom’s focus on affordability, amplified a gaffe by Ms. Hyde-Smith that turned off voters.

National Democrats noticed. Not long after the ad’s debut, the Senate Majority PAC, the flagship super PAC for Democratic Senate candidates, poured $1.2 million into the race, and later invested another $1 million. The Senate Democrats’ campaign arm also put $500,000 into the state.

High-profile Democrats campaigned for Mr. Colom. Former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad. Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and Senators Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia all campaigned with him in Mississippi.

Republican super PACs invested into the race, and Mr. Trump campaigned with Ms. Hyde-Smith as the race tightened.

Mr. Colom, a Black prosecutor running against a white incumbent senator, appealed to Mississippi’s Black residents, a crucial group that typically leans Democratic and accounts for about 37 percent of the state’s population, the largest share of any state. He had the biggest margins in predominantly Black counties, according to election data compiled by The New York Times.

If Mr. Colom wins, he would be Mississippi’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era, though he downplayed the milestone during his campaign.

He also employed an unusual strategy: He attended Mr. Trump’s rally in Mississippi for Ms. Hyde-Smith the week before the election — not to confront voters but to walk the line and listen to them discuss issues like health care, grocery bills and gas prices.

He posed for selfies with rally-goers and later said he had converted some to his camp. In an interview with CNN last week, he made an appeal to Republican voters.

“I’m going to get you what you were promised in 2024,” he said, citing three issues he brought up with them: lower grocery prices, an end to wars and the full and transparent release of the Epstein files.

The wait could drag on because the deadline for every county to accept mailed ballots is not until next Tuesday. The same deadline applies to affidavit ballots, also known as provisional ballots, which voters can cast if they show up at the polls but are not in the voter rolls or have forgotten to bring a photo ID.

Mr. Colom urged residents to mind the deadline and provide the required documentation, such as a proper ID, to their circuit clerk’s offices to ensure their affidavit ballots are counted.

Counties must process those ballots by Nov. 13, the deadline to submit certified results to the state. After that, the result is virtually fixed. Mississippi’s secretary of state, Michael Watson, will compile each county’s numbers and certify the cumulative total by Dec. 3, said Elizabeth Jonson, a spokeswoman for Mr. Watson. There will not be a runoff, in accordance with state election laws.

A quirk in Mississippi’s statutes — the lack of a mechanism allowing recounts in statewide general elections — means the candidates may have to wait to see every last ballot being tallied. Without an option to contest the results, candidates can file a legal challenge only to include or exclude a specific group of ballots before the vote is certified, said Derek Muller, an election law expert at Notre Dame Law School.

“We have hundreds of volunteers, we’ve got local lawyers that are going to be at the county meetings in each county,” Mr. Colom said in a news conference on Wednesday. “We will protect the process of this election, we will protect the integrity of this election.”

Analysts said they could not remember a Senate race this close in Mississippi. Some supporters of Mr. Colom said they believed that even if Ms. Hyde-Smith wins, the thin margin would diminish her power in Washington.

“I’m pretty amazed,” said Ervin Ricks, 55, who works at a church in Brandon, Miss. “I thought for sure that Cindy Hyde-Smith would retain her office pretty easily.”

Some voters also blamed Ty Pinkins, who is Black and ran in the race as an independent after leaving the Democratic Party last year, for splitting Democratic voters. A lawyer and an Army veteran, Mr. Pinkins disputed this claim, saying that he had not drawn voters away from Mr. Colom and hoped the Democrat would win.

“I didn’t expect it to be this close,” Mr. Pinkins said in an interview. “I am happy that the Democrat is leading.”

An earlier version of this article misattributed a quotation from a voter in Mississippi about Cindy Hyde-Smith. It was Ervin Ricks — not Christi Payton — who said, “I’m pretty amazed. I thought for sure that Cindy Hyde-Smith would retain her office pretty easily.”

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

John Yoon is a Times political reporter based in New York.
