Harmeet Dhillon, Leader of Justice Department’s Civil Rights Unit, Resigns

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The move came after conflicts with Justice Department leaders, including disagreements over legal strategy in the midterm elections, people familiar with the matter said.

By Glenn ThrushMichael C. Bender and Alan Feuer

Glenn Thrush and Michael C. Bender reported from Washington, and Alan Feuer from New York.

Harmeet Dhillon, the chief of the Justice Department’s civil rights division, resigned on Thursday after conflicts with department leaders, including disagreements over legal strategy in the midterm elections, two people familiar with the situation said.

Ms. Dhillon, whose tenure was defined by a successful pressure campaign against universities and unsuccessful efforts to obtain voting data from states, had been telling friends for weeks that she planned to step down to return to her law firm, one of the people said.

In less than two years on the job, Ms. Dhillon repurposed a unit created to address Jim Crow injustices into a battering ram against the left, setting aside its longtime mission of fighting discrimination against Black people to battle campus antisemitism and diversity initiatives.

The announcement came two days after voters handed Republicans a staggering electoral defeat, giving Democrats control of the House and Senate. It is not likely to be the last resignation, as officials in the depleted department face the prospect of intense scrutiny from an antagonistic Congress.

President Trump and other White House officials recently expressed annoyance over a recent appearance Ms. Dhillon made on “60 Minutes,” according to people with knowledge of the situation. In their view, she downplayed the prevalence of voting by undocumented immigrants — a central driver of the department’s aggressive legal strategy in the weeks leading up to the election, even though studies show that such fraud is rare.

Ms. Dhillon, whose law firm was part of Mr. Trump’s campaign legal team, told Fox News she had resigned of her volition and had withheld her announcement at the request of Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, until after Election Day.

“I resigned three weeks ago, and Susie asked me to please wait until after the midterms,” said Ms. Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for civil rights.

It was not immediately clear who would succeed her.

The White House did not address whether Ms. Wiles had played a role in extending Ms. Dhillon’s time at the department, saying Ms. Dhillon had done “a fantastic job” in protecting civil liberties.

Attorney General Todd Blanche praised her work, saying in a social media post on Thursday that she had led the division “with conviction.”

“She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor,” he wrote. “The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors.”

Former department officials welcomed the move, assailing Ms. Dhillon for what they argued was her inversion of the department’s mission. “From Day 1, Harmeet Dhillon abdicated her responsibility to enforce our nation’s federal civil rights laws and destroyed the crown jewel of the Justice Department,” said Kristen Clarke, who served in Ms. Dhillon’s role in the Biden administration and is now the general counsel of the NAACP.

“We know the fight for civil rights long preceded her and will live on long after her,” she added.

Another senior department official, Henry C. Whitaker, is resigning “imminently,” according to a court filing on Thursday. Mr. Whitaker, a former solicitor general of Florida, previously served as the acting head of the Office of Legal Counsel, which provides critical legal guidance to the department’s lawyers.

Mr. Whitaker had handled high-profile cases for the department, including appealing the dismissal of the first criminal case brought against James B. Comey, the former F. B. I. director who was accused of lying to Congress in 2020.

Ms. Dhillon’s hard-line approach, laid out in a series of April 2025 memos declaring her intention to pursue a conservative culture war agenda, prompted the departure of hundreds of career officials in the unit. That left her short-handed to pursue many of her objectives, including the deployment of 1,000 election monitors around the country on Election Day.

She was a central figure in Mr. Trump’s pressure campaign on colleges and public schools, fundamentally reshaping the Justice Department’s approach to education with a sharp pivot toward conservative priorities.

In higher education, she mounted repeated challenges to admissions practices and campus speech policies, opening high-profile investigations and lawsuits against elite institutions.

She sued Harvard twice, once over accusations of antisemitism and another over claims that the school’s admissions policies discriminated against white and Asian people (she lost both times). She also spoke out in support of parent rights groups fueling the administration’s push to pare back protections for transgender students.

Ms. Dhillon drew intense criticism for abandoning longstanding federal efforts to integrate schools. She ended more than 50 school desegregation cases, dismissing them as “onerous and outdated.”

Ms. Dhillon’s resignation was not unexpected. The department’s leadership was frustrated by what they saw as her go-it-alone approach, which included an unwillingness to attend planning meetings with Mr. Blanche’s staff, according to an official who requested anonymity to discuss internal conversations.

Administration officials also expressed concerns that Ms. Dhillon’s highest-profile effort on elections, a monthslong legal campaign to force states to hand over sensitive voter roll data, had failed time after time, the person said.

In June 2025, Ms. Dhillon and her team pushed James E. Ryan, the president of the University of Virginia, into early retirement over his reluctance to adopt Mr. Trump’s anti-diversity policies and narrow view of anti-Semitism.

But White House officials orchestrating the administration’s broader “anti-woke” campaign against academia only learned of Ms. Dhillon’s plot against one of the nation’s most prestigious public universities from a report in The New York Times, according to people familiar with the matter.

Her team helped the department develop the two most significant cases filed before the election. One is an effort to impound 20,000 ballots in California to bolster the administration’s unsubstantiated claim of illegal voting by unauthorized immigrants. The other was a lawsuit seeking to preemptively block certification of the Senate race in Alaska, after Democrats recruited a candidate with the same name as the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, to appear on Tuesday’s ballot.

But neither Ms. Dhillon nor members of her senior staff signed either lawsuit, or represented the department in court. Two top Blanche deputies, Trent McCotter and Stanley E. Woodward Jr., filled in.

It is an ill-kept secret that Ms. Dhillon disdained Mr. Woodward, the associate attorney general, and that she was interested in replacing him as the department’s No. 3 official.

In April, when Mr. Trump fired Pam Bondi as attorney general, Ms. Dhillon made it clear that she believed Mr. Woodward, whom she cast as an overbearing bumbler, needed to go, according to six people familiar with the situation.

Mr. Trump initially appeared to be on board. Time passed. Mr. Woodward stayed put.

Ms. Dhillon is leaving.

Erica L. Green contributed reporting.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Michael C. Bender is a Times correspondent in Washington.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

How Melania Trump Became a Dark-Horse Diplomat on Ukraine

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Both Moscow and Kyiv say Mrs. Trump’s team was the driving force behind an evacuation of a besieged city. It was also in their interest to deliver her a humanitarian win.

By Siobhán O’Grady and Katie Rogers

Siobhán O’Grady reported from Kyiv, Ukraine, and Katie Rogers from Washington.

After nearly five years of war, Russia and Ukraine now agree on at least one thing: They should keep Melania Trump happy.

Last month, Mrs. Trump, the first lady, emerged as a dark-horse diplomat when she announced a local cease-fire that would allow for the evacuation of hundreds of people from Oleshky, a frontline Russian-occupied city facing a starvation crisis.

The six-day truce, the first of its kind since Russia’s all-out invasion in 2022, was the product of an unconventional foreign policy intervention by an American first lady. It was all the more remarkable for a presidential spouse who has at times disappeared from the public eye and rarely comments on international affairs.

And it was in keeping with her recent efforts to construct an image as a humanitarian, including through her association with a campaign to return children from Russia to Ukraine.

Mrs. Trump’s exact role in negotiating the cease-fire has remained murky. On Thursday, during a meeting at the White House with a small delegation of Russian and Ukrainian representatives, she publicly discussed her efforts for the first time.

The first lady said that she had learned about the situation in Oleshky in September. She portrayed herself as having been heavily involved in the evacuation’s details, saying she reviewed mine removal plans, roadways, vehicles and medical resources. Mrs. Trump said she had deputized her adviser Marc Beckman, a film producer with no diplomatic experience, to work with Ukrainian and Russian officials.

After the evacuation last week, Russian and Ukrainian officials insisted that the first lady and her team, including Mr. Beckman, had spent weeks talking to both sides and were pivotal to the final agreement. Ukraine had publicly called for urgent aid to be sent to the city and had sought help from various groups, including the International Committee of the Red Cross, when the first lady intervened.

In the end, the Ukrainian and Russian governments decided that it was in their interest to work with Mrs. Trump and deliver her a humanitarian victory. Doing so would address two challenges: It would resolve the deepening disaster in Oleshky and, presumably, help their dealings with Mrs. Trump’s unpredictable husband, President Trump.

Just as in their interactions with Mr. Trump, the two sides seem to know what is expected in working with his wife, going to great lengths to invoke Mrs. Trump’s name as often as possible. After the evacuation, the Russian and Ukrainian officials who led the efforts praised her effusively, describing her as essential to the mission.

At the White House on Thursday, Kirill Dmitriev, a Kremlin envoy, said that Mrs. Trump had ensured that “agreements became actions and actions stayed wise.” He gave her a painting from an 11-year-old who he said had chosen to depart Oleshky and live in Russia. The painting had three words: “I love Melania.”

As Mrs. Trump delivered her speech, Mr. Dmitriev sat next to David Arakhamia, the head of the governing faction in Ukraine’s Parliament. That brought top emissaries of President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine side by side as the war between their countries intensifies with no end in sight.

Mr. Dmitriev, who runs Russia’s flagship state investment fund, has led the Kremlin’s effort to pitch business deals to the Trump administration and has sought sanctions relief for his fund in those talks.

After Mr. Arakhamia spoke, Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian human rights ombudsman, gave Mrs. Trump a humanitarian award. Mr. Zelensky had awarded Mrs. Trump the Order of Princess Olha, First Class, the highest honor that Ukraine can be bestow upon a woman.

Mr. Putin and his spokesman have also repeatedly thanked Mrs. Trump for her humanitarian work.

Mrs. Trump’s efforts were not the only ones in pursuit of a cease-fire. Pope Leo XIV also sought a truce, including in a call to Mr. Putin from a hospital where the pontiff was recovering from surgery. Ukrainian officials say that much of the work had already been done before the pope intervened.

“With all respect to all other parties — we are very grateful for phone calls personally from the pope to the president of the Russian Federation and separately grateful for the call to our president,” Mr. Lubinets said after the evacuation. “But at that time when all this was happening it was the final stage.”

The White House event demonstrated the lengths that Ukraine and Russia are willing to go to please Mrs. Trump as they both frantically try to curry favor with Washington. Thursday’s event preceded a separate track of meetings that the Trump administration is holding in the United Arab Emirates next week. Those peace negotiations would be the first since February involving all three countries.

Some observers have wondered whether the success of the brief cease-fire around Oleshky could serve as a confidence-building measure as the United States aims to restart talks to end the war.

The Kremlin has cautioned that this was a specific humanitarian operation and that no immediate evacuation plans were in the works for other besieged towns, although efforts to feed and care for people who opted to stay in Oleshky may continue. And Mr. Zelensky has pointed to recent Russian attacks as evidence that Moscow does not see the short truce as a step toward any larger agreement.

Russia in recent days has hammered Ukraine’s energy grid, plunging major cities, including the capital, Kyiv, into darkness. That has intensified fears that the coming winter could be Ukraine’s hardest yet of the war.

Also this week, a Russian glide bomb attack on a school being used as a humanitarian hub in southern Ukraine killed at least 42 people, with another 30 still missing. That attack is shaping up to be one of the deadliest against civilians during the entire war.

Mr. Lubinets has emphasized that “there were no agreements about political steps” in pursuit of a settlement to the war.

While he praised the first lady and Mr. Beckman at the White House, Mr. Lubinets delicately signaled that any negotiations would be complicated and asked for more American support as Mr. Trump has openly favored Russia in recent weeks.

“Sometimes your vision is above the politics,” he told Mrs. Trump. “I have only one request from all Ukrainian nation: Please continue to do your wonderful work and support Ukraine.”

Before Thursday’s event, Mr. Lubinets said, he had first learned of a crisis in Oleshky last February, when pleas poured into his office to help arrange an evacuation or food deliveries. That process began to truly take shape “only when Melania Trump joined,” he said.

The main obstacle was building trust that a cease-fire would hold. Mr. Lubinets offered to be the first Ukrainian official to travel with his Russian counterpart into occupied territory during the war. Joining the mission himself — which he ultimately did — would ensure that Russia understood that Ukraine would hold its fire, he suggested.

“The American side liked this idea,” he said, adding that it was offered as Mrs. Trump received daily briefings on the talks.

Mr. Lubinets and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, signed separate documents, his in Ukrainian and hers in Russian, agreeing to the temporary truce. Washington acted as the guarantor. After the cease-fire took effect early on Oct. 27, Ukrainian and Russian representatives met online to monitor it, and agreed that it was holding. That allowed them to proceed with removing mines that littered the area and later with the evacuation.

Mykola Bilieskov, a political analyst with Come Back Alive, an organization that supports Ukraine’s military, said the evacuation was “a rare case where interests of all aligned.”

He said it was unlikely that the warring sides would be able to “replicate this local success within this big framework of negotiations.”

Still, he added, “We have no choice — we need to dance this dance.”

Ivan Nechepurenko and Valerie Hopkins contributed reporting from Moscow, and Anton Troianovski from Washington.

Siobhán O’Grady is a Ukraine correspondent for The Times, based in Kyiv.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Brazil’s Presidential Election

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

From Miami, Flávio Bolsonaro is making unfounded claims of a stolen election and plotting to sway his nation’s politics from afar, even though his party is not challenging the results.

Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing Brazilian senator who lost last month’s presidential election, in Aventura, Fla., on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil. Credit... Scott McIntyre for The New York Times

Supported by

By Ana Ionova

Reporting from Miami

Flávio Bolsonaro was leaving the gated community where his father is under house arrest, he said, when he decided he’d rather leave Brazil than risk the same fate.

That decision, which Mr. Bolsonaro said he only made the morning after losing Brazil’s presidential election, sent him on a spectacular 5,000-mile escape from criminal investigations, traversing South America to ultimately end up in the United States.

The jet that flew him to Miami was arranged by a White House official, and his entry into the United States was granted directly by President Trump, according to U. S. officials. Much remains murky about the trip, which also took Mr. Bolsonaro through Ecuador and Argentina, where one of the Argentine president’s top advisers met him at an airport.

Yet in his first interview since fleeing last week, Mr. Bolsonaro said he pulled off this stunning and secretive voyage entirely on his own. “It was all me,” he told The New York Times on Wednesday afternoon. “There was help from absolutely no one, from no government.”

“How I got here,” he added, “I’ll take that to the grave with me.”

The plan to leave, he said, was spontaneously decided with his wife, though he knew they had friends abroad: “There may have been cheerleading, but nothing else.”

Mr. Bolsonaro, 45, who faces several investigations in relation to money laundering and corruption in Brazil, fled after the Brazilian authorities ordered him to hand over his passports. On Wednesday, Mr. Bolsonaro reasserted his innocence and insisted that, had he remained, he would have faced almost certain conviction.

“I already know that the final outcome will be my imprisonment,” said Mr. Bolsonaro. He called the judiciary overzealous and politically motivated, singling out the Supreme Court justice who jailed his father for trying to stage a coup after losing the 2022 election to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

In a 75-minute interview, Mr. Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator, at times acknowledged his family’s current predicament — going from the verge of returning to power in Brazil to sudden exile abroad. Not only does his father, Jair, face a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup, his brother Eduardo had also fled to the United States, where he stayed once he was convicted in Brazil for urging the Trump administration to interfere in their father’s trial.

Flávio Bolsonaro has not been charged with any crime; once his term as a senator ends in early 2027, he will lose his parliamentary immunity and could be prosecuted, though.

Even though his own party has accepted the election result, Mr. Bolsonaro was unwavering in rejecting his loss last month to Mr. Lula, which he claimed without evidence was “mathematically impossible.”

“I know it won’t lead to anything,” he said of his frustrations. “I lost to the system.”

He complained at length about government spending during the race, claiming it gave Mr. Lula, a leftist, an unfair advantage. He railed against the digital movement that helped lift his rival. And he drastically expanded his claims of fraud, at times echoing the conspiracy theories his father once peddled about Brazil’s voting machines, a system international experts consider one of the world’s most secure.

“I have my suspicions,” Mr. Bolsonaro said when questioned about his claims. “No one can say with 100 percent certainty that I am right, nor with 100 percent certainty that I am wrong.”

Four years ago, the claims of his father found a captive audience, inspiring supporters to camp outside military barracks across Brazil. Thousands of rioters stormed Brazil’s halls of power on Jan. 8, 2023, demanding that the army overturn the narrow result.

His eldest son faces a starkly different scenario. Mr. Lula won by a wide margin, and key leaders in Mr. Bolsonaro’s party have said there was no evidence of fraud. So far, few Brazilians have taken to the streets over Mr. Bolsonaro’s loss. Even his right-wing Latin American allies have recognized Mr. Lula’s win.

Still, Mr. Bolsonaro said he was cheated out of the presidency.

Until now, Mr. Bolsonaro’s complaints had mostly centered on an extension to voting hours, which he claims was handed down by a politically motivated justice.

In fact, both candidates had requested the change because torrential rains and bus delays had impeded voters in some regions. But the court decision granting the extension came near voting’s end, causing confusion as some stations struggled to stay open.

It ultimately affected only 34,000 votes, though, which Brazil’s electoral authorities said was too small to affect the result; Mr. Lula won by 4.4 million ballots.

But Mr. Bolsonaro, who had until now adopted a more moderate tone than his father on many issues, including the electoral system, widened his accusations.

He spoke of vote tampering and reasserted claims, which have been debunked, of a security breach at the vault room where computers tally the vote. The extension to voting hours, he claimed without offering evidence, could have served as a cover to illicitly add many more votes to his opponent’s scorecard.

Brazil’s electoral court, which oversees the elections, has dismissed his allegations. International independent observers have also certified the election’s integrity and dozens of countries have recognized the result.

Though the United States is not among the countries to recognize Mr. Lula’s victory, Mr. Trump only suggested Brazil’s elections seemed “strange,” declining to say who won.

Mr. Bolsonaro did not fault him. “He didn’t take sides, which is the right thing to do,” he said, thanking Mr. Trump for allowing him to stay in the United States.

And even after Mr. Trump said last week that he has no plans to meet Mr. Bolsonaro, his team is hopeful for an encounter at the Conservative Political Action Conference at Mar-a-Lago over the coming days.

From abroad, Mr. Bolsonaro said he would seek to legally challenge Mr. Lula’s victory, though he acknowledged that has little chance of success. He also plans to champion allies in Brazil pushing his agenda, including lowering the age of criminal responsibility and seeking amnesty for his father and the Jan. 8 rioters.

At the same time, Mr. Bolsonaro sidestepped questions about whether he also plans to lobby the Trump administration for further U. S. actions targeting Brazil.

The State Department this year designated Brazil’s two largest drug gangs as terrorist groups, and Mr. Trump last year used tariffs and sanctions to try to pressure Brazil to drop the case against Mr. Bolsonaro’s father.

The morning after his electoral defeat, Mr. Bolsonaro said, the authorities approached him as he left his father’s house to tell him he had 24 hours to hand over his passports. The older man, tears welling in his eyes, took aside his son before they parted, according to Mr. Bolsonaro.

“He looked me in the eye and said, ‘You already know where they are going with this, right?’” he recalled.

“I said, ‘Dad, I already know,” he added. “‘And I am prepared, I know what I have to do.’ I turned my back and I left.” Neither spoke of a plan to flee, he said.

A few hours later, Mr. Bolsonaro posted a video on social media saying that he planned to surrender his documents as ordered. “I have never thought about leaving ⁠the country,” he said in the video, vowing to lead the opposition after his party achieved major victories in Brazil’s legislature.

Soon after, he vanished — only to turn up in Miami some 42 hours later.

Mr. Bolsonaro, his wife, and two daughters will now be allowed to stay in the United States for at least a year, under an immigration status usually given for humanitarian reasons.

Mr. Bolsonaro said he is not sure yet where his family will settle down. His younger brother, Eduardo, has been living in Texas and was recently granted permanent resident status, known as a green card.

But, after a Democrat flipped Texas’s governorship in this week’s midterm elections, Paulo Figueiredo, one of the Bolsonaros’ close allies, pitched Florida as a natural base for the family.

Mr. Bolsonaro said his family is settling in, though he hopes only temporarily. “I will need to move on with my life from the United States, at least for now,” he said.

Still, he hasn’t ruled out a comeback. “If there are new elections, obviously I will be a candidate again.”

Adam B. Ellick contributed reporting from São Paulo and Lis Moriconi and Isabela Cruz contributed research from Rio de Janeiro.

Ana Ionova is a correspondent for The Times, covering Brazil and neighboring countries.

6 Are Killed in New York City’s Deadliest Fire This Year

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The cause of the fire, at a house in Brooklyn, is not yet clear, but Mayor Zohran Mamdani raised concerns about electric bikes. Fatal fires have soared in New York City this year.

By Emma G. FitzsimmonsAndrea Barnes and Ali Watkins

Flames ripped through a two-story home in Brooklyn early Thursday morning, killing six people in New York City’s deadliest fire this year.

Firefighters rescued people trapped behind window bars and set up a ladder after a staircase partially collapsed. Three hours later, the fire, on the 600 block of 58th Street in the Sunset Park neighborhood, was under control.

As fire officials examined the scene on Thursday, they said it was not yet clear what had caused the fire.

But Mayor Zohran Mamdani raised concerns about electric-bike fires, and fire officials appeared to remove a charred electric device from the home. The deaths also raised fears among New Yorkers about an alarming rise in fire fatalities — there have been 86 this year, compared with 44 during the same period last year, according to the Fire Department.

The community in Sunset Park — a working-class neighborhood with many Asian and Latino immigrants — was shaken and looking for answers. Some called for stronger rules to regulate e-bikes and e-scooters.

Mr. Mamdani held a news conference outside the home on a residential block, standing in front of its scorched black exterior.

“This was a devastating fire,” the mayor said. “It will take a long time for this neighborhood to mourn the neighbors they lost this morning and to recover from this immense grief.”

Xu Yan, a 19-year-old neighbor who is from Fuzhou in China, said he had heard a “loud explosion” and walked outside and saw the fire starting on the second floor. He said he had worried it would spread to his home.

Nine people were injured in the fire: Two people were taken to hospitals; three firefighters had injuries that were not life threatening; two police officers had minor injuries; and two other people were treated at the scene.

Firefighters arrived at the home at around 1:30 a. m. A hazardous materials crew was also called to the scene because of the presence of a lithium-ion battery.

There are several electric-bike shops near the home. David Yin, 50, the owner of a local bike and moped store, said that he had stopped selling e-bike batteries.

“It’s too dangerous — we won’t carry them,” he said.

Mr. Yin said that city inspectors came to his shop once a month to inspect whether he had any nonapproved e-bike batteries. He believes people buy them from an underground network of smaller sellers.

The blaze is at least the city’s second fatal fire in recent weeks. Four members of a family, including an 11-year-old boy, were killed after an electric-bike battery burst into flames on Oct. 28 and engulfed an apartment in the Bronx.

Nine people have died and 70 people have been injured in battery fires so far this year, the Fire Department said on Thursday. During the same period last year, one person died and 42 people were injured in battery fires. There have been 406 fires caused by batteries this year, compared with 241 fires during the same period last year.

E-bikes and e-scooters, embraced by delivery workers and commuters, have flooded the city’s streets in recent years. The batteries inside them have led to a series of dangerous fires.

Lithium batteries, which are also used in laptops and smartphones, can overheat or malfunction and spark explosive, fast-moving fires with little or no warning, leaving people just seconds to escape. In 2024, as deaths rose, the city started a public education campaign to encourage people not to store the batteries inside buildings.

Laura Kavanagh, the city’s former fire commissioner, said the city had brought down deaths and that public education was a key component. But the city also needed to address manufacturers, she said.

“It’s not reasonable to ask delivery workers or consumers to also be battery scientists and fraud detectors,” she said.

Ms. Kavanagh said there should be federal legislation to ban unsafe devices from entering the United States and an investment in outdoor battery-charging infrastructure.

In the summer of 2025, the Department of Buildings received three complaints of illegal construction at the Sunset Park home. The owners had illegally converted the basement into an apartment, and the two apartments on the first and second floors had been divided into three units, one of the complaints said.

All three complaints were closed without the building being inspected because the investigators were not allowed inside. Inspectors made four attempts to gain entry between September 2025 and August 2026, but no one answered.

David Maggiotto, a spokesman for the Buildings Department, said it was standard agency protocol for complaints to be closed after inspectors had made multiple unsuccessful attempts to enter a building. Inspectors do not have the legal authority to force their way into buildings to conduct inspections, he said.

Mr. Mamdani raised concerns about electric bikes in a television interview on Thursday when he was asked about the cause of the Sunset Park fire.

“We are investigating what the cause of this fire is, but I can tell you that e-bike fires as a whole have increased to more than 400 fires this year and they are something that can cause people to lose their lives as well as their livelihoods,” he said in an interview on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe.”

At the mayor’s news conference, fire officials said that firefighters had arrived at the scene within three minutes and 18 seconds after the blaze was reported. Already, the basement, first floor and second floor were under “heavy fire.”

Julie Menin, the City Council speaker, said in a statement that the presence of lithium-ion batteries was a “serious concern.”

“More must be done to encourage and mandate safe storage practices,” she said. “Enough is enough.”

Susan Zhuang, the Council member who represents the district, said in an interview that residents should not charge their lithium batteries at night.

“If they catch fire, it will be explosive,” she said.

Elvin Mata, a fire restoration expert who will help to clean up the debris, said at the scene that he believed that the investigation would point to lithium batteries. He said that the devices were common in the neighborhood and should be banned.

Shortly after Mr. Mamdani’s news conference, his office sent an email announcing the results of a crack down on illegal e-bike and e-scooter sales. Mr. Mamdani has targeted sellers after a rise in fatal electric-bike and scooter crashes, some of which have involved illegal high-speed devices.

The city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection inspected more than 200 shops in the city and issued 136 violations, including 77 summonses, from August to mid-September, the mayor’s office said.

Ashley Southall, Dave Sanders, Maia Coleman, Wesley Parnell, David Cheung, Nate Schweber and Yi Liu contributed reporting. Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

Emma G. Fitzsimmons is a public policy correspondent for The Times, covering New York City.

Ali Watkins covers international news for The Times and is based in Belfast.

Four Kennedy Appointees to Powerful Health Panel Allowed to Keep Drug Stocks

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

New members of the influential U. S. Preventive Services Task Force were given waivers to serve with financial conflicts.

By Maggie Astor

Four of the eight people appointed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to an influential health panel in September own stock in companies that make drugs and other products affected by the group’s decisions, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times.

The investments were described in conflict-of-interest waivers that gave the members permission to serve on the panel, the United States Preventive Services Task Force. The Times obtained the waivers through a public records request.

The task force evaluates evidence for services like colonoscopies, H. I. V. prevention medications, depression screening and more, and its recommendations both inform doctors’ decisions and determine what insurers must pay for. They also affect the popularity, and therefore the profitability, of numerous drugs and medical devices, such as statins for cardiovascular disease prevention and the special X-ray machines used for mammograms.

The type of waiver the members received can be given to employees in various parts of the federal government. But several former task force members and federal officials said that, in the case of the task force, such conflicts could undermine the scientific rigor of the recommendations as well as public trust in them.

Until President Trump and Mr. Kennedy took office last year, and a Supreme Court ruling gave Mr. Kennedy more control over the task force, the panel operated independently of politics, and such financial conflicts were not considered acceptable, according to former members and federal officials.

Among the new appointees, Dr. Patrick K. Hunter, a pediatrician who served on the Florida Board of Medicine; Dr. Ronald P. Karlsberg, a cardiovascular expert; Dr. Venkatesh L. Murthy, another cardiovascular expert; and Dr. Dennis W. Wulfeck, a diagnostic radiologist, all own stock in the pharmaceutical giants Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson, according to the waivers.

Dr. Hunter also owns stock in Bristol Myers Squibb and nine other companies whose work could intersect with the panel’s business. Dr. Karlsberg owns stock or has an unspecified other “financial interest” in Merck and 16 other such companies. Dr. Murthy owns stock in Merck, Pfizer, the insurer Cigna and 16 other companies. And Dr. Wulfeck owns stock in Novo Nordisk, Pfizer, CVS Health and 17 others.

Mr. Kennedy’s other four appointees, as well as seven of the eight members already on the task force, did not receive waivers for any investments specific to the medical industry. The other older appointee, Dr. Sarah Wiehe, received a waiver for such investments, but she said in an email that she no longer owned them and that they had been in a portfolio managed by a third party.

The waivers do not make clear whether the new appointees’ holdings are in portfolios managed by third parties. Dr. Wulfeck declined to comment on his investments, and the other three members did not respond to requests for comment.

Historically, any candidate for the task force would have been asked to sell these stocks, said Dr. Quyen Ngo-Metzger, who evaluated conflicts of interest as the scientific director supporting the task force at its parent agency, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, from 2012 to 2019. If a prospective member had refused to sell, she said, they would not have been appointed.

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

“When you have this much involvement with industry, pharmaceutical stocks and all of these, it really undermines the trust in the process and the trust in the people,” said Dr. Ngo-Metzger, who reviewed the waivers at The Times’s request, in her capacity as a former AHRQ employee.

Emily Hilliard, a spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees AHRQ, said task force members were subject to different ethics requirements now because the Supreme Court’s ruling had made them “special government employees,” a different legal status than they had before.

“Federal law provides that a waiver issued in accordance with the legal standard is an appropriate remedy for a conflict of interest,” Ms. Hilliard said. “AHRQ is updating its procedures and criteria to reflect these changes in member status.”

The waivers say that the members must still consider whether they need to recuse themselves from an individual topic being considered by the task force if it has particular relevance to their financial interests. However, Dr. Michael Silverstein, who led the task force until his term ended this March, said large pharmaceutical companies made such a range of products that the conflicts would touch numerous topics.

The waivers contained an explanation from Dr. Roger D. Klein, the AHRQ director, on why he believed the new members should be allowed to serve, including that each member, as one of 16, individually has “no power to render a final decision on behalf of the United States.”

Dr. Klein added that the medical companies did not account for the members’ full investment portfolios, and that “matters on which you work are not likely to affect the financial interests of all of your assets named in this waiver simultaneously.” (He described the companies as being no more than 15 percent of Dr. Karlsberg’s portfolio, 20 percent of Dr. Murthy’s and Dr. Wulfeck’s and 45 percent of Dr. Hunter’s.)

Dr. Silverstein, the former task force chairman, said those arguments were not persuasive to him.

The percentage thresholds were “something that we never thought about,” he said, noting that the task force had previously taken amounts as small as $1,000 seriously. Every member matters even if they are only one of 16, he added.

“You’re asking someone to join a deliberative body where recommendations are made through discussion, consensus building and a vote,” Dr. Silverstein said. “To say that a certain level of conflict of interest is permissible because you’re only one within a larger group, to me, does not pass the smell test.”

Maggie Astor covers women’s health and the health effects of government policies for The Times.

Justice Dept. Steps Up Criminal Inquiry of Supreme Court Abortion Decision Leak

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Exclusive

Investigators, using subpoenas and other law enforcement powers, are accelerating an inquiry that takes the Trump administration into the inner workings of the court.

By Jodi Kantor and Michael S. Schmidt

Jodi Kantor and Michael Schmidt’s reporting illuminates the Supreme Court and the law. Tips can be sent to them securely via nytimes. com/tips.

The Justice Department is pursuing a criminal investigation into who leaked the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision overturning the right to abortion, examining the inner workings of an institution that has long operated in secrecy and resisted oversight from the other branches of government.

At issue is who provided the draft decision to Politico two months before it was formally released by the court, a seismic breach of confidentiality that led to intense partisan accusations about the motivations of the leaker.

Despite an internal inquiry by the court, no leaker has ever been publicly identified. An F. B. I. official said last year that the Justice Department was exploring the issue.

But prosecutors are now pursuing a criminal case, which has not previously been reported. The investigation has ramped up in recent weeks as prosecutors have sent grand jury subpoenas for testimony and sought information from people who worked at the court at the time of the leaks, according to people familiar with the inquiry.

From the beginning, the question of how to deal with the leak has been complicated by what charge could be brought even if the leaker were identified, as well as by concerns about the constitutional issue of separation of powers between the executive branch and the court.

The U. S. attorney in Washington, Jeanine Pirro, a Trump ally, is overseeing the investigation. Along with several career prosecutors, Ms. Pirro has assigned one of her top lieutenants to the investigation. That prosecutor, Carlton Davis, has led efforts to investigate local fraud and violence and also oversaw a failed effort to indict six Democratic lawmakers for reminding troops they could refuse illegal orders.

It is not clear what law prosecutors believe might have been broken as a result of the leak, or whether investigators have developed new evidence pointing to a potential suspect. Nor is it clear why the investigation has picked up steam now, including if political pressure from the White House may have played a role. Some potentially relevant laws have five-year statutes of limitations that would expire in the spring.

Many conservatives have pushed for a criminal investigation, convinced the culprit was a liberal seeking to derail the abortion decision, a call echoed by President Trump.

“That person should be found,” he said in July.

The Justice Department’s handling of the case echoes a now-familiar pattern. Mr. Trump demands an unorthodox investigation, and then his political appointees try to deliver on his wishes. The dynamics raise questions about whether the inquiry may be another attempt by Mr. Trump and his allies to harness the vast law enforcement powers of the federal government to settle political scores.

But on the long list of Trump administration legal targets, the Supreme Court and its employees stand apart. The investigation comes as the justices consider cases that go to the heart of Mr. Trump’s agenda and his assertions of executive power. The inquiry could expose the court’s inner workings to a kind of scrutiny that it has always worked to deflect, said people familiar with the inquiry.

The justices have repeatedly said they would like the culprit identified. But cooperating with a criminal inquiry could mean providing investigators with access to court employees and highly restricted internal records, like the files showing the justices’ private deliberations in the case — a sharp break with the court’s tradition of maintaining secrecy around its work.

Patricia McCabe, a Supreme Court spokeswoman, did not respond to questions, including about the extent to which the court has cooperated with the inquiry or turned over information.

A spokesman for the U. S. attorney’s office in Washington declined to comment. The people who described the inquiry to The Times did so on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter.

When told of the inquiry, some legal experts said the administration might be again pushing into uncharted territory through its use of its law enforcement powers.

“Once again, the Trump Justice Department has created questions about whether there are precedents when there are no precedents,” said Samuel W. Buell, a professor of law at Duke University and former federal prosecutor.

The Justice Department has the right to investigate any federal crime committed at the court, such as insider trading based on advance knowledge of a case outcome, said Michael C. Dorf, a constitutional law professor at Cornell. But if the leak does not amount to a crime, the investigation could violate the separation of powers that ensures the court’s independence, he said.

That could amount to “the executive branch harassing members of the judicial branch,” he said.

An indictment could end — or extend — the court’s four years of trauma over the leak.

The day after the Politico article was published, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. ordered an internal investigation. Supreme Court clerks, valedictorian types who win a year of apprenticeship and a lifetime of prestige, were pressed for information and required to sign affidavits swearing they had not leaked the document. Staff members did the same. In all, 97 court staff members and clerks were interviewed. In contrast, the justices were treated lightly, consulted but not formally interviewed, The New York Times has reported.

Conflicting theories about who was responsible circulated in legal circles and on the internet. Many conservatives believed that the leaker was a liberal, throwing a desperate grenade before the decision was finalized. On social media, some pointed fingers at clerks for liberal justices, posting their names, photos and unsubstantiated theories.

Many liberals, meanwhile, theorized that a conservative did it to lock in the abortion decision. The Times has reported that at the time of the leak, some of the justices were pursuing compromise efforts that might have preserved some federal right to abortion, efforts that ended with the publication of the leaked draft.

The court’s monthslong investigation led nowhere. In a report published in January 2023, its top security official concluded she could not identify a suspect through a “preponderance” of the evidence. The report called the court’s information systems outdated and security practices lax, and added that the online allegations against liberal clerks remained unsubstantiated.

Months later, Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. told The Wall Street Journal that he had “a pretty good idea who is responsible” but not enough evidence to name anyone publicly.

Meanwhile, Mr. Trump called for jailing the reporters to get them to reveal their source. When he returned to office in 2025, the leak in the case, Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, quickly joined a list of other matters that he and his allies promised to solve. In a May 2025 post on social media, Dan Bongino, the deputy director of the F. B. I. at the time, said the Trump administration was continuing to pursue the leaker.

Members of the court have said in recent months that they remain eager to find the culprit.

“We will pursue it till the end,” Justice Elena Kagan told Congress while testifying in July. Justice Amy Coney Barrett, speaking alongside her, called leaks of some court materials illegal.

The Trump administration has aggressively used the Justice Department to try to punish unauthorized publication of government information, including sending subpoenas to New York Times journalists and raiding a Washington Post reporter’s home in January.

Each of those cases, however, involved the release of information related to national security, which is protected by law. No such law specifically forbids the release the internal records of the Supreme Court.

Some experts have said prosecutors could try to charge the Dobbs leaker with violating a statute that prohibits theft of government property or one intended to protect against the disclosure of confidential government information, though either would be a relatively novel use of the laws.

Another avenue prosecutors could pursue would be to target any false statements that employees made during the court’s initial investigation. During that inquiry, employees were warned that they could be prosecuted for lying to the government.

If prosecutors bring charges, another challenge could be securing an indictment in Washington, where grand jurors and judges have repeatedly thwarted attempts to mount cases that have even a whiff of following through on Mr. Trump’s demands.

The increasing public distrust of the Justice Department by grand juries in Washington has convinced some senior officials there that it may be impossible to bring a politically sensitive case until Mr. Trump is out of office.

In another twist, several clerks who were employed by Republican-appointed members of the court at the time of the Dobbs decision now work at the Justice Department.

T. Elliot Gaiser, for instance, clerked then for Justice Alito, who wrote the Dobbs majority opinion. He now heads the influential Office of Legal Counsel, the Justice Department office responsible for providing legal advice to the president and executive branch agencies.

Asked if Justice Department employees, or any of the justices, are being interviewed, or if the court handed over the records from its initial investigation, the court, the U. S. attorney’s office in Washington and the Justice Department did not respond.

Devlin Barrett contributed reporting. Julie Tate contributed research.

Jodi Kantor is an investigative reporter currently focused on the Supreme Court. Her work has spurred cultural and legal shifts in the United States and across the globe.

Michael S. Schmidt is an investigative reporter for The Times covering Washington. His work focuses on tracking and explaining high-profile federal investigations.

Tech Stocks Plunge, Erasing Post-Election Rally

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The S&P 500 slumped to its worst daily decline in more than a year, dragged down by the technology sector as investors fretted about the durability of the A. I. build-out.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Joe Rennison

Stocks sold off sharply Thursday, erasing all of their post-election rally, as investors’ concerns about weaknesses in the A. I. build-out re-emerged with intensity.

The S&P 500 slumped over 3 percent on Thursday, led lower by the technology sector. The decline, if it persists through the day, would be the most severe since April last year, when President Trump unveiled sweeping global tariffs.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell roughly 5 percent, putting the index into correction, defined as a drop of 10 percent or more from its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a benchmark for the industry, tumbled around 10 percent. That index has fallen roughly 30 percent since the beginning of October and is 35 percent below its peak in June.

The moves reverse the stock market’s gains after the Democrats’ sweeping victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections and rekindle a sell-off that had paused in the immediate run-up to the election.

The moves gathered pace through the day, engulfing all 11 sectors of the S&P 500. The 10-year Treasury yield, seen as a haven during periods of market stress, fell to 4.83 percent, its lowest since September. Yields move inversely to prices.

While gridlock in Washington has broadly been welcomed by investors, curtailing the likelihood of new rules and laws being imposed on businesses, concerns about a backlash against the A. I. industry are compounding fears of runaway spending and rising debt at tech firms.

How the tech-heavy index in the United States is trading

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Qualcomm, a large chipmaker, sank over 10 percent on Thursday after the company dialed down its earnings forecast as a result of high demand for chips raising its own costs faster than it has been able to raise prices. The sharp stock move reflected broader concerns that supply bottlenecks created by the rush to build A. I. infrastructure could slow the industry’s growth, which means slowing the time it takes for investors to realize profits on their A. I. bets.

Arm Holdings, another chipmaker, also fell more than 10 percent after reporting underwhelming revenue from its push into A. I.

Shares of Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX fell sharply for a second day. The two companies are run by the world’s richest person — and Republican megadonor — and have come under particular focus after the elections, with potential investigations and regulatory scrutiny in store.

Some analysts noted that while gridlock in Washington might limit the chances of A. I. regulation, the Democrats flipping key governorships in states that are becoming important hubs for data centers could create a meaningful roadblock to the rapid pace of the A. I. build-out.

“In many ways, what happened in state-level races around the U. S. are arguably just as important” as the Democrats’ success in congressional elections, said Kent Fung, vice president of market intelligence at Fundstrat. “Not just to Americans, but to investors,” he added.

The stocks of some of the large “hyperscalers,” like Alphabet and Microsoft, fell less on Thursday than the broader market. Some analysts have suggested that a slowdown in the race to build A. I infrastructure could favor these large, entrenched players, securing their dominant position and slowing the rapid pace of spending that has put pressure on their businesses.

“The Democrats in this scenario,” Mr. Fung said, “might be a bit like the massive bouncer at a bar who keeps an outwardly belligerent customer from brawling, giving the customer a face-saving way to avoid a fight he didn’t really want and secretly knew was a bad idea.”

Analysts broadly remained sanguine about the outlook for the stock market, expecting major indexes to rally once the current volatility subsides. Many noted that the S&P 500 has risen over the 12 months after every midterm election since the Second World War. The index remains roughly 8 percent higher for the year.

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

Iran is Reviewing ‘Concrete Proposals’ on Nuclear Program, Officials Say

The New York Times November 05, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Iran’s willingness to re-engage on the issue suggests that Qatar-led diplomatic efforts to avert full-blown war between the U. S. and Iran have had some success.

By Adam RasgonVivian NereimTyler Pager and Farnaz Fassihi

Iran is reviewing a set of proposals presented by mediators that could shape the future of its nuclear program, according to five officials briefed on the negotiations, representing a potential breakthrough in stalled diplomatic efforts to end its war with the United States.

Iran’s willingness to re-engage in nuclear talks, after weeks of refusing to budge, suggests recent mediation efforts led by Qatar to prevent a return to full-blown war have had some success, the officials said. They described the terms being reviewed as “concrete proposals,” without elaborating.

The Iranian foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The five officials, including an American and two Iranians, spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details of the talks.

Qatar has spearheaded a diplomatic blitz with Iran in the past week, the officials added, participating in two rounds of talks in Tehran and hosting a third in Doha. Two of them said that the Qataris have also held recent talks with Iranian officials in Armenia.

Vice President JD Vance has emerged as a key proponent of the Qatari-led efforts to avert a military escalation, according to three of the officials. He has also appeared to try and distance himself from President Trump by blaming the war for the Republicans’ heavy losses in the midterm elections this week.

Last month, Mr. Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, proposing to hold direct peace talks that would also cover Iran’s nuclear program. Mr. Rezaei said the letter had shown that the United States had changed its tone toward Iran, which he described as a sign of the “Iranian nation’s strength and victory.”

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, Mr. Vance was the figure in Mr. Trump’s inner circle who was most opposed to a full-scale war. At the time, he warned Mr. Trump that a conflict could cause regional chaos and untold numbers of casualties.

On Monday, Mr. Vance said progress had been made with the Iranians, but he noted that Mr. Trump had both “kinetic” and “non-kinetic” options. “The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” he said.

The flurry of diplomacy comes as Mr. Trump and Israel have been weighing a large-scale attack against Iran. The American and Israeli militaries have drawn up a list of targets to strike, including energy infrastructure and other sites vital to the Iranian economy.

Iran’s nuclear program, which Mr. Trump says is an effort to develop a bomb while the regime insists it is for peaceful purposes, has bedeviled efforts to find a long-term solution to end the war.

In June, the United States and Iran agreed to a cease-fire. The deal was intended to pave the way for talks about the nuclear issue, and lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil and gas shipments that Iran effectively closed early in the war. But the agreement collapsed, sparking months of intermittent clashes before the conflict settled into a tense stalemate.

Both Iran and the United States have used increasingly bellicose rhetoric in recent weeks, propelling Qatari mediators to try and broker a last-ditch deal between the two countries.

Mr. Rezaei suggested in a televised address on Saturday that Iran would not hold nuclear talks until the United States accepted the country’s demands. Those include releasing frozen Iranian assets, and lifting sanctions on the country’s oil and the U. S. naval blockade on Iran’s ports.

Privately, however, Mr. Rezaei has shown more openness to discussing the nuclear issue, according to the two Iranian officials and the American official. He has been negotiating with the Qataris alongside senior Iranian officials, including Abbas Araghchi, the foreign minister, and Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s Parliament.

The future of Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium has been one of the key sticking points in the talks. Mr. Trump has said Iran must give up the stockpile, which he has referred to as “nuclear dust.”

Iranian officials have been adamant that they will not ship the uranium outside the country. In previous rounds of talks, Iran has discussed diluting the stockpile on its own soil under the supervision of international inspectors.

The International Atomic Energy Agency, the U. N. nuclear watchdog, estimated in a report published this year that, as of June 2025, Iran had about 440 kilograms, or roughly 970 pounds, of highly enriched uranium. Experts say that it could be used to develop a small number of nuclear bombs.

As of Thursday morning, Iran and the United States were reviewing the latest suggestions from mediators to bridge any remaining gaps, two of the officials said.

Mr. Trump has vacillated between making bellicose threats to return to all-out war and saying he wants to give diplomacy a chance. On Wednesday, he said Mr. Vance’s assertion that the war with Iran was to blame for the midterm defeat was “largely true,” but he also defended his decision to attack the country.

Oil prices fell sharply after the midterm results, as some observers thought it could encourage Mr. Trump to end the war.

Iranian leaders have warned that its forces would expand their range of targets if the country is attacked again. Senior Iranian officials and clerics are also debating whether Iran should withdraw from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, which prohibits the development of a nuclear weapon.

Gulf Arab officials have expressed growing concerns that a renewed U. S.-Israeli attack on Iran could lead to devastating retaliatory strikes on their own countries, further straining their already bruised economies.

“From the perspective of the U. A. E., and I would also say Gulf countries, we don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region,” said Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the president of the United Arab Emirates, at the Manama Dialogue security conference in Bahrain over the weekend. “We want to see a diplomatic and political resolution of this protracted crisis.”

Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting to this article.

How Democrats Won Across the South

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

They won Senate races in North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia, with a Mississippi race still too close to call. Their wins lifted down-ballot candidates too.

By Patricia Mazzei

Reporting from Charleston, S. C.

A new wall of blue states emerged from the midterm election map. It was not along the edges of the Great Lakes but along the Atlantic Ocean, from Virginia to Georgia.

Democrats won competitive races in North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia on Tuesday, gaining ground across the South.

In North Carolina, Roy Cooper, the popular former governor, won the Senate race by nearly 20 percentage points, a resounding victory that appeared to make waves down-ballot, helping flip control of the state’s congressional delegation and State House.

In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff won re-election by 18 points, helping to lift Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the nation’s first elected female Black governor. Democrats won every statewide race in Georgia and flipped the State House.

Even in South Carolina, which had hardly been on the battleground Senate map, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, upset Senator Darline Graham, the interim Republican incumbent, by more than four points. Democrats also flipped a House seat and 10 state legislative seats in a traditionally Republican state.

And Democrats’ power in the South could expand even further: The Mississippi Senate race remained too close to call on Thursday, with the Democratic nominee, Scott Colom, a district attorney, leading Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, by a razor-thin margin.

Democratic Senate nominees in the South benefited from the national mood punishing President Trump and his party over high prices and the unpopular war in Iran. They also harnessed anger from Black voters over redistricting efforts that diluted some Black representation in Congress.

The winning nominees made key decisions at pivotal campaign moments that contributed to their victories. Here are some of them:

In North Carolina, Mr. Cooper knew that voters knew him and mostly liked him. But he also knew that Republicans would spend vast sums to defend the Senate seat in North Carolina, a state that Mr. Trump won three times. So he raised money knowing that national Republican political groups would be able to outspend Democratic ones.

His campaign went on television early, reminding voters who he was and defining Michael Whatley, his Republican rival, who was little-known to most voters, as a Washington lobbyist for energy companies. When Mr. Whatley’s campaign attacked the former governor as soft on crime, Mr. Cooper’s team pushed back with fact-checking ads — and tied Mr. Whatley to a convicted sex offender who held roles with the state Republican Party.

Mr. Cooper wanted a short and direct campaign slogan that could cut across party lines and demographic groups, and he found it: “Make Stuff Cost Less.”

By the time October arrived, Mr. Cooper was so consistently ahead that Republicans pulled their advertising money from the state. Then, so did Democrats, allowing them to spend in competitive races elsewhere.

In Georgia, Mr. Ossoff laid the foundation to win a second term during his first. He built a robust constituent services operation. He maintained strong relationships with Black communities and churches. He befriended local Republican officials, including mayors and county commissioners, and tried to fulfill their federal needs. Some of them later endorsed him.

The senator’s fund-raising prowess helped scare off potential opponents. When Representative Mike Collins won the Republican primary, Mr. Ossoff tagged him as a bigot, an attack that resurfaced following several news reports connecting his aides and his son-in-law to white nationalism and racism. (Mr. Collins said in a debate last month that he had “condemned racism, antisemitism, hate.”)

Mr. Ossoff’s message was an aggressive critique against President Trump and his administration — not only on tariffs and the war in Iran but also on corruption. When he started delivering it, some Democrats worried he might be going too far. By the end of the campaign, corruption was a motivating issue for many voters.

In South Carolina, Ms. Andrews’s original opponent, Lindsey Graham, died in July. That gave her an opening to run not against a four-term incumbent but against his sister, an inexperienced candidate.

Ms. Andrews campaigned with well-known Black Democrats, such as Representative James Clyburn of South Carolina and Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia. She gave interviews to conservative media outlets. She held town hall-style events in rural and Republican parts of the state. She leaned into a message of rejecting family dynasties in politics.

Ms. Andrews saw a way to win over independents and Republicans after Representative Ralph Norman lost to Ms. Graham in a bitter Republican primary. Mr. Norman’s son, Warren, said he was leaning toward voting for Ms. Andrews. They spoke; in her final rallies, she referred to the support she was getting from her “new friend” — Warren Norman.

Democrats in the South hope that their wins will persuade national Democratic leaders to run year-round organizing and voter registration in states that had previously been seen as unwinnable.

Back in April, some Democratic donors laughed when Mr. Warnock, who campaigned for candidates across the South, suggested they consider investing in Mississippi, according to an audio recording of a private fund-raiser obtained by The New York Times.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mr. Warnock said that he hoped donors would now see “a multiracial coalition” rising in the region. Democratic wins in Georgia, he noted, came after a decade of work organizing, educating and registering voters.

“It felt like it happened all of a sudden,” he said. “It wasn’t sudden.”

“We know the formula,” he added. “We need to enact it in Mississippi, in South Carolina, in North Carolina, in Florida, in Texas.”

Patricia Mazzei is a national political correspondent for The Times, based in Miami.

MAGA Finally Gets What It Deserves

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

By David French

Opinion Columnist

There is one number that stands out above all others as I think through the meaning of the midterms: 13.

As I type this, Democrats are on track to achieve a 13-point margin in the total popular vote for the House of Representatives. If you put that in presidential terms, our nation hasn’t seen a margin like that since 1984, when Ronald Reagan swept the popular vote and won 49 states.

If you compare that margin to previous midterms, the American people haven’t spoken that clearly since 1974, the first midterm after Watergate.

That’s not the only important number, of course. There’s 81, the projected Democratic margin in the House. There’s 56, the possible number of Democratic senators (if Mississippi and Alaska go blue). And there’s 26, the potential percentage of the statewide swing (from Trump plus-14 in 2024 to Talarico plus-12 in 2026) that turned Texas blue.

I’m going to say that again — that turned Texas blue.

The Democrats hadn’t won a statewide race there since 1994, and then James Talarico led an epic rout. Republicans lost every single significant statewide race. Even the Republican State Supreme Court justices lost their races.

Over the last quarter-century of tight races and extreme partisan polarization, we’ve grown used to election analysis that requires poring over exit polls, agonizing over messaging mistakes, and parsing the impact of different issues and scandals.

Perhaps the paradigmatic example is the 2016 presidential election.

Did Donald Trump win because Antonin Scalia died and Republicans held their nose and voted for him to save Scalia’s seat? Maybe. Did Trump also win because the James Comey letter reopening the Hillary Clinton email investigation chased the “Access Hollywood” tape out of the headlines? Possibly.

Or did Hillary Clinton lose because she didn’t spend enough time in Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania? Perhaps. Or did she lose simply because 2016 was a change election, and she represented the establishment? That could be, too.

But that kind of analysis is completely inappropriate in an election this decisive. In the aftermath of a wipeout of biblical proportions, it’s better to begin our analysis with one of my favorite biblical passages: “Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall.”

Or, put another way, it’s as if we pulled away the algae from Trump’s filthy Reflecting Pool, and found an inscription that read, “My name is Trump, king of kings: Look on my renovations, ye Mighty, and despair!”

That’s right: It’s the Ozymandias election.

It is difficult to overstate the sheer arrogance of Trump and his remaining MAGA base. They treated the rest of the people of this country as if they were of no consequence.

Actually, it’s worse than that. They treated the rest of the country as if they were enemies.

To the voters who longed for peace, he gave them a unilateral, undeclared war.

To the families seeking relief from high prices, he gave tariffs.

To the voters alarmed about corruption in Washington, he made the swamp so corrupt that barons of the Gilded Age are regretting that they were born in the wrong era.

To the new Hispanic Republican voters who helped Trump win and transformed the Republican coalition, he gave brutal racial profiling and pogroms in the streets of Chicago, Minneapolis, Los Angeles and other cities.

To voters who were weary of intolerance and cancel culture, he delivered a wave of censorship unseen since Woodrow Wilson imprisoned his political opponents by the hundreds.

To voters who wanted stability in the world, he gave fractured alliances and embraced Vladimir Putin, the world’s deadliest and most dangerous dictator.

And then, when dissenting Americans — including dissenting conservatives — condemned these outrages and cried out for relief, they were treated with contempt and rage.

The cancel culture of the MAGA right inflicted immense cruelty on its enemies, and MAGA relished their pain.

It would be a grave mistake to lay the blame for all this pride and arrogance on Trump alone. Last month I wrote that every institution eventually takes on the character of its leader, and so it is with Trump’s Republican Party.

The cult of Trump was so comprehensive, so all-consuming, that it became virtually impossible to succeed anywhere, at any level of Republican politics, without explicitly swearing fealty to Trump — and not just once but again and again, whenever you were asked to do so.

There was no better way to pledge loyalty to Trump than by acting like Trump.

That’s why a loathsome politician like Vivek Ramaswamy runs an ad exploiting the rape of a child. That’s why an equally loathsome politician like JD Vance spreads gross lies about immigrants far and wide even as innocent people suffer from the pain and shame that he caused.

That’s why grotesque racists like Bo French felt that they had a home in the Republican Party. After all, if the president can condemn entire groups of immigrants based on their countries of origin, then why can’t every other Republican who wants to broadcast his own bigotry do so? That’s why hundreds of thousands of Texas primary voters could look at Ken Paxton — and all of his adultery and corruption — and say, “Yep. That’s exactly the man we need in the Senate.”

If a MAGA voter is bewildered today, perhaps he should stop making a meme calling his opponents “fake and gay,” delete the post declaring that Indian Americans worship demons, turn off the podcast that’s shrieking at him that every person who votes Democratic is a heretic, and take a very long and thoughtful look in the mirror.

A guy can dream.

Donald Trump is to blame, but no one — absolutely no one — made you imitate him.

One thing that struck me when I traveled down to Texas to report on the Talarico-Paxton race was the combination of anger and fear emanating from Paxton’s Republican opponents.

They weren’t just angry at Paxton for challenging and beating the longtime incumbent, John Cornyn. They were furious at Paxton’s supporters, the people who’d insulted them, mocked them and hounded them out of Republican politics. They wouldn’t go on the record with their support for Talarico, but it was easy to see where they stood.

Midterm wipeouts don’t have to be fatal to parties (though they can signal a party’s demise). The Republicans almost held the White House in 1976, just two years after the 1974 election I mentioned earlier nearly wiped out the Nixon-era G. O. P. Bill Clinton was re-elected two years after the Republican revolution of 1994, and Barack Obama won after the Tea Party movement erupted in 2010.

But in those previous elections, the parties that experienced serious losses in the midterms were ultimately led by responsible adults who could react and respond to voters’ concerns, adjust policies and tactics, and revitalize their parties’ fortunes.

But Donald Trump is not Bill Clinton. He’s not Barack Obama. He’s not even Gerald Ford, who had the dignity and integrity to salvage the Republican brand after Watergate.

At least when Ford was trying to rebuild the Republican Party, the “crook” wasn’t still in the White House. In 2027, the Republicans will be trying to pick up the pieces with a crook in control of the Oval Office and his own cult of personality.

Trump is an erratic, egomaniac tinpot tyrant in decline who will blame everyone but himself for the loss. In fact, that’s already started. In a Truth Social post Tuesday night, he said that Fox News “bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse.”

There you have it. The problem with the 2026 midterms was that Fox News wasn’t sycophantic enough.

And there’s another thing — as a practical matter, every faction of the Republican Party has a reason to blame a different faction for its defeat. The circular firing squad has started, and every part of it has plenty of ammunition.

Free-trade Republicans are blaming the tariffs. America first Republicans are blaming the Iran war. (In an X post on Wednesday morning, Vance wrote, “The reason we lost is the war.”) Hispanic Republicans can blame ICE. South Asian Republicans can blame Bo French. Anti-woke Republicans can blame Trump’s crackdown on free speech.

They would all be correct, at least to some degree. They made the conscious decision to follow, defend and pledge allegiance to an unstable, hateful man, and now — at long last — they’re experiencing the inevitable consequences of their inexcusable moral compromises.

The next few days and weeks will be filled with conversation and debate over what the Democrats should do next. The easiest possible advice is to focus like a laser on the voters’ overwhelming concerns — corruption and the cost of living — but it’s now quite possible that our nation could be looking at a generational realignment.

That’s a conversation for another day. For now, we can sum up everything that happened in the midterms in three words, words that the MAGA movement has scorned for 10 years: Character is destiny.

Speaking of character, my Sunday column was about Todd Blanche, Trump’s attorney general, and the damage he’s doing to the Department of Justice:

In case after case after case, the Department of Justice is targeting Trump opponents, making frivolous arguments and engaging in vindictive, meritless prosecutions.

I blame Trump, but I also blame Blanche. He doesn’t understand his own job.

We all know that Trump has an extreme view of executive power that renders him a virtual elected monarch. His administration’s actions extend well beyond conventional unitary executive theory, which puts a premium on presidential control over the executive branch. He treats the law as his plaything, deciding on his own whim which laws will be enforced and which ones will not.

It is true that the president is the boss of every cabinet official. He can fire them at will. But it is also true that the attorney general is different from every other member of the cabinet.

Unlike, say, Pete Hegseth, Blanche has three masters, not one. The attorney general and all the lawyers working for him also answer to the judiciary, which not only decides the cases he brings; it also governs the conduct of D. O. J. officials in court. And he also answers to the bar — rules of ethics are binding on every attorney, including government attorneys.

Thanks for reading. You will soon start to get my columns emailed to you too.
