Infant Bleeding Surged as Parents Rejected Vitamin K Shots, Studies Find

The New York Times November 05, 2026

U. S. Health Policy

Advertisement

Supported by

One study found a 347 percent increase in cases as fewer babies received the shot, which helps blood clot.

By Maggie Astor

A growing number of infants in the United States are experiencing potentially life-threatening bleeding as more parents decline a vitamin K shot that has long been recommended for newborns, according to two new studies.

One of the studies found a 347 percent increase in these bleeding cases since 2017.

For decades, the American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended that every newborn receive an injection of vitamin K, which helps blood clot and can protect against sudden and catastrophic bleeding that can occur even in otherwise healthy babies. The injection is not a vaccine, but as mistrust in medicine has grown and as Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other prominent health figures have cast doubt on the importance of childhood vaccinations, more parents have started forgoing it.

With fewer babies getting these injections, doctors had already begun to see more infants with serious hemorrhages. The new studies, published Thursday in the journals JAMA and JAMA Pediatrics, provide some of the first concrete data on this pattern. One found an especially sharp increase from 2024 to 2025, with cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding roughly doubling in that time.

“How do we help people understand what danger awaits?” said Dr. Steven Woolf, a professor of family medicine and population health at Virginia Commonwealth University and a co-author of that study.

The JAMA study looked at more than five million infants. In 2017, 3.1 percent of these newborns went without a vitamin K shot; by 2025, it was 6.8 percent. The infants who had not received the shot had significantly higher rates of bleeding in their first six months, including more than double the risk of brain bleeds, which are especially deadly: 33 brain bleeds per 10,000 births, compared with 13.2 per 10,000 for babies who received vitamin K.

The JAMA Pediatrics study, on which Dr. Woolf was a co-author, looked at more than 11 million infants and found similarly that the rate of infants going without vitamin K more than doubled from 2017 to 2025. The overall rate of vitamin K deficiency bleeding rose nearly 350 percent, to 107.4 cases per 100,000.

This study looked only at bleeding that medical records attributed to vitamin K deficiency, which can require extensive blood work to confirm; that doesn’t always happen even when it is suspected. The other study looked at all bleeding in the first six months of life, which is often but not always caused by vitamin K deficiency.

The huge number of births the researchers looked at, and the fact that the trend was the same in both studies, made the results compelling, said Dr. Steven Abrams, a professor of pediatrics at the University of Texas at Austin’s Dell Medical School who co-wrote a review of the evidence for the newborn vitamin K injection but was not involved with the new studies.

The studies do have limitations. For example, the databases they relied on exclude many home births, where vitamin K refusal rates tend to be higher. And doctors might be more likely to diagnose vitamin K deficiency bleeding when they see that a baby didn’t receive the injection.

But they add significantly to the understanding of the problem in the United States. Before, said Dr. Jaspreet Loyal, an associate professor of pediatrics at Yale School of Medicine and a co-author of the JAMA study, most data on rates of vitamin K deficiency bleeding came from other countries.

The vitamin K injection is very safe, but more parents started declining it in the 2010s, citing, among other things, a belief that the shot was unnatural or unnecessary. Some have seen misinformation — widespread on social media — about a preservative called benzyl alcohol, though there is no evidence of harm from it in the small quantity in the vitamin K shot, and preservative-free shots are available. Others cite an old study suggesting a link to leukemia, which multiple larger studies have debunked.

Dr. Elizabeth Wolf, an author of the JAMA Pediatrics study and an associate professor of pediatrics at Virginia Commonwealth University, said she hoped the results would break through to parents who may not realize the severity of the risk of going without vitamin K.

“People just don’t realize how important it is,” Dr. Wolf said. As pediatricians, she added, “it sometimes feels like we’re on the front lines of this.”

When public health interventions decline, there is often a lag before the impact becomes clear, as was the case with measles skyrocketing recently after years of declining vaccination rates, said Dr. Woolf, the professor of family medicine and population health. With the new studies, he said, hard evidence is beginning “to shed some light on what consequences these trends are having on actual health outcomes.”

Maggie Astor covers women’s health and the health effects of government policies for The Times.

Up in the Clouds With the Pope, It’s Still Commercial

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Unlike American presidents, Pope Leo XIV has no private jet, so he travels on commercial airlines, like the rest of us. Well, almost.

By Motoko Rich

Motoko Rich, the Rome bureau chief, has traveled with the pope on three international trips.

A day before Pope Leo XIV departed for France in September, on the fourth major international trip of his papacy, the crew of the plane he was to use, known colloquially as “Shepherd One,” gathered to learn the inviolable rules of the flight.

No selfies with the pope, said Gennaro Anastasio, the senior cabin manager, as he reeled off a list of dos and don’ts.

If the Holy Father offers his hand, shake it, don’t kiss it. Make no personal requests of the pontiff, such as asking that he pray for family members. Check the bathroom at the front of the plane — the one used by the pope — several times throughout the flight and keep it spotless. Don’t speak directly to the pope, but talk to his personal secretaries.

And mind your language. The men wearing black robes with red sashes and skullcaps should be addressed as “eminenza,” the salutation for cardinals, the highest-ranking clergy except for the pope. The men in purple caps and sashes are bishops and should be greeted as “eccellenza.”

“Don’t mess up,” said Mr. Anastasio, an impish 67-year-old. “If, though, you call a bishop ‘eminenza,’ he’ll say, ‘No I’m not an eminenza,’” he added with a chuckle. “And you can say, ‘You’ll become one!’”

Above all, he said, the crew should deliver anything the papal passengers ask for. “There’s never the need to say, ‘I’m sorry, it’s not possible, that’s not allowed, it can’t be done,’” Mr. Anastasio said. “Here, it’s done. Always.”

The Vatican, unlike the United States government, owns no dedicated planes and has no equivalent to Air Force One. Instead, the pope always flies commercial — in business class on charter flights operated by regular airlines.

For more than six decades, ITA Airways — and its predecessor, Alitalia — has been the preferred airline for the first leg of the pope’s foreign journeys, and sometimes more. Mr. Anastasio has led crews on more than 80 of those flights, but many members of those crews do it only once. Mr. Anastasio is preparing for the pope’s trip to Latin America, a 12-day journey through three countries starting Friday.

Last month, Pope Leo underwent surgery for lung cancer, but his doctors have cleared him to travel.

For ITA, being the pope’s preferred carrier is a clear bragging right. The pope’s international trips are among the most public events of any papacy, allowing the pontiff to meet with the faithful in their home countries and demonstrate the reach of the Roman Catholic Church.

Joerg Eberhart, ITA’s chief executive, said the role was not guaranteed. The airline regularly competes in Vatican tenders for the main papal flights, he said, and the airline loses money operating them.

These are no ordinary flights. For starters, they are almost always perfectly on time, unlike over half of ITA’s other flights last year. The papal plane’s call sign — AZ4000 — is instantly recognizable to air traffic control towers across the world, allowing them to clear routes to ensure the flights take off and land according to schedule.

That means the plane can push back and head for the runway as soon as the pope steps aboard and sits in his usual front-row seat on the left side of the plane.

The typical limits for carry-on baggage are overlooked. During the taxi to the runway, the cabin crew skips the usual announcements and safety videos to allow the Vatican news corps to work without background noise. All the seat backs — including in economy class, where the journalists sit — are topped by a small cloth, known as an antimacassar, that is embroidered with the pope’s coat of arms. (They make for nice souvenirs.)

In Rome, the planes take off from a terminal reserved for V. I. P. charter flights at Fiumicino Airport. Officers from Italy’s military police force and the Swiss Guard, the Vatican security service, patrol the aisles. Bishops and cardinals are driven directly to the tarmac and board shortly before the pope, who arrives by black car or papal helicopter just before takeoff and climbs the staircase to the front door, news cameras flashing.

On rare occasions, the papal flights cannot be cleared for on-time takeoff. When Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, was departing for Cuba in 2015, another jet stalled on the runway, Mr. Anastasio recalled. Francis suggested the pilot simply fly over the beached plane, and Mr. Anastasio had to explain that was not possible, he said. The flight departed 63 minutes late, but the pilot made up the lost time in the air so that Francis still made his first appointment in Havana.

Mishaps can arise on arrival, too.

When Pope Leo landed in Cameroon in April, Mr. Anastasio noticed that a ruby-red carpet with gold trim, laid out by local officials on the passenger staircase, was twisted in places. Mr. Anastasio ran down to straighten it to ensure the pope would not trip, he said.

Perhaps the most important detail for any flight is getting the onboard meals right. On a recent trip to France, Mr. Anastasio said, he needed to figure out how to cram in a breakfast service around the pope’s traditional one-on-one greetings with journalists on a flight lasting less than two hours.

He calculated that the crew would have no more than 30 minutes to get from the front of the cabin to the back, which meant that the passengers would need a meal that they could scarf in 10 minutes or less.

After consulting with ITA’s chefs, the Vatican opted for a tray with a scrambled-egg-and-bacon sandwich, slices of prosciutto, pecorino and primo sale cheese, fruit, petit fours, a twisted roll and a croissant.

For many journalists, it’s a rare chance to experience business-class service with meals served on ceramic plates with cloth napkins, drinks served in real glass, cutlery made from silverware and a menu printed on a thick card.

Mr. Anastasio said he liked to add local touches for meals — hence the croissants for France and the Turkish chocolates he bought in Istanbul to serve in gift boxes on the return flight.

During the eras of John Paul II and Benedict XVI, Mr. Anastasio said, the popes and their entourages ate premium meals while journalists and lay staff from the Vatican ate economy-class fare.

Then Francis boarded a papal flight, observed the formal meal service for the clergy — and asked Mr. Anastasio what the journalists ate. When the cabin manager showed the pope the economy-class trays, Francis told him, “I am not a king,” Mr. Anastasio recalled. From then on, the journalists ate the same meals as clergy.

Mr. Anastasio, nevertheless, made sure to offer some special treats to Francis. Once he learned the pope liked Havanna lemon cookies from Argentina, Mr. Anastasio started bringing the biscuits on every flight. And Francis occasionally asked for customized meals, including rice with Parmigiano-Reggiano and Amalfi lemons that Mr. Anastasio personally prepared on board.

Benedict once asked for some premium mortadella — sliced pork sausage — from Campotosto in central Italy, recalled Giovanni Bernardi, a chef for ITA’s main meal supplier. Mr. Anastasio joked that the meal almost caused “a diplomatic incident” because the flight was on its way to a Muslim country that he would not name.

And what about Leo? Mr. Anastasio said the new pope has made no special requests so far.

“He’s really simple,” he said.

Josephine de La Bruyère contributed reporting.

I have now traveled three times with Pope Leo on major international trips. Flying with the pope is a unique experience, and in some ways rather more prosaic than one would expect. The planes are simply chartered commercial jets, with the same layouts you might find on any international flight. (Not a lot of legroom or elbow room at the back.) But there are protocols and rituals, and it was fun to learn from the inside what the crew is expected to do when up in the air with the leader of the Roman Catholic Church.

Motoko Rich is the Times bureau chief in Rome, where she covers Italy, the Vatican and Greece.

Tech Billionaires Face Tricky Political Waters After Democratic Sweep

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Many donated money to President Trump’s favored causes and became his allies. Now that political alignment may be a liability.

By Eli TanTheodore Schleifer and Erin Griffith

Eli Tan and Erin Griffith reported from San Francisco, and Theodore Schleifer from New York.

In September, President Trump hosted a White House luncheon to discuss artificial intelligence, flanked by some of the world’s wealthiest tech executives: Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and others. They had the president’s ear to pitch an A. I. future uninhibited by regulation or guardrails.

For two years, it had been that easy to get what they wanted. Tech billionaires and their companies donated money to Mr. Trump’s favored causes, including the White House ballroom. The moguls posed for photos and lavished him with praise and gifts. Amazon heavily promoted a movie about Melania Trump.

Then on Tuesday, the American public delivered a rebuke of the tech industry’s agenda. Overnight, the billionaires’ political alignment with the president may have become a liability.

Democrats, riding a wave of anti-tech sentiment, including distrust of tech leaders, opposition to data centers and fears of job loss fueled by A. I., will soon control Congress and prominent state governments. In victory speeches around the country, they made tech titans avatars of inequality and corruption that plagued the Republican Party in the election cycle.

That puts some tech executives in a trickier position. It may be harder for them to make progress on their goals of A. I. dominance. And some may even find themselves under investigation.

“You guys aren’t the actual leaders of the Valley. You’re the mis-leaders of the Valley,” said Reid Hoffman, a founder of LinkedIn who is one of the country’s top Democratic donors and a leader of the tech industry’s progressive wing. “It will no longer be that these MAGA voices in the Valley are in charge.”

Silicon Valley’s shift to the right began in 2024, when Mr. Musk and others went all-in on Mr. Trump, visiting Mar-a-Lago and taking up powerful positions in his administration. New political groups supporting niche interests like cryptocurrency spent enormous sums to promote their agendas.

This time, the money was even bigger. Among the 20 biggest donors in the midterms were tech billionaires, including the venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz.

An Andreessen-backed cryptocurrency group, Fairshake, spent tens of millions on a mission to defeat Sherrod Brown, the Democrat running for Senate in Ohio. Mr. Musk poured over $474 million into Republican super PACs, including hundreds of millions to support Ken Paxton, the Texas Republican nominee for the Senate. And a Musk-endorsed billionaire ran for governor in Ohio.

All three efforts failed.

Mr. Musk’s results, said Rohan Patel, a former Tesla vice president reporting to Mr. Musk who now works in Democratic politics, are a “total repudiation of his ugly brand of politics.”

Neil Malhotra, a professor of political economy at Stanford’s Graduate School of Business, said tech leaders had mostly been acting out of self-preservation.

“They understand when you have a president who is willing to use the state to intervene in the economy, it’s smart business practice to be on good terms with the administration,” he said.

Dr. Malhotra noted that most business leaders would rather that the government not move too far from the center in either direction. After the 2024 election, “Republicans overinterpreted their mandate,” he said.

Now, tech leaders may find their business dealings under investigation. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Senator Edward J. Markey, Democrat of Massachusetts, posted on social media on Tuesday.

The tech titans appeared triumphant in one race: A proposed billionaire tax in California is on the cusp of being defeated. Sergey Brin, a co-founder of Google, and other tech investors and founders poured about $330 million into efforts to vanquish the measure, which called for a one-time 5 percent tax. A companion measure that would effectively ban all future wealth taxes also appeared likely to pass.

Still, anti-billionaire and anti-tech sentiment was prominent in victory speeches around the country. Mr. Paxton’s opponent in Texas, James Talarico, whom Mr. Hoffman backed with nearly $17 million, compared his race to David versus Goliath.

“We just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor,” he said. He called out “the billionaires who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians.” This election was a referendum on their power, too, he said.

Roy Cooper, a Democrat who won a Senate seat in North Carolina, said in his victory speech on Tuesday that “we told Washington loud and clear that North Carolinians will always matter more than the billionaires and the insiders.”

The left-wing victor in Michigan’s Senate race, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, said he would be “taking on the corporations and the billionaires, special interests who’ve rigged the system against us for far too long.”

And Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat who won re-election in Georgia, called out “the titans of Silicon Valley,” who “dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.”

Late Tuesday, as the results of the election rolled in, the hosts of the tech podcast “All-In,” who are tech investors, expressed surprise and disappointment in a livestream at the possibility that Texas’ Republican governor, Greg Abbott, could lose his bid for a fourth term.

The tech industry had assumed that after Mr. Abbott won, he would lift a moratorium on data centers in Texas and that construction would begin again, the “All-In” hosts said. Pro-business Texas is the second-largest state for data center projects, representing roughly 30 percent of the planned capacity for 2028, according to SemiAnalysis, a research group.

Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who beat Mr. Abbott, has said she would keep the moratorium going until the state could pass legislation around data centers, delaying projects from coming online for many months.

Chamath Palihapitiya, an “All-In” host, connected the slowdown or halt of data center projects to the performance of A. I.-related stocks and, ultimately, the fate of the U. S. economy. He warned of a recession, noting that losing the computing power of new data centers was the “single most effective way to tank the market.”

Mr. Musk, who donated $5 million to Mr. Abbott’s campaign, posted on social media after the results: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Eli Tan covers the technology industry for The Times from San Francisco.

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.

Erin Griffith covers tech companies, start-ups and the culture of Silicon Valley from San Francisco.

Justice Alito Will Not Retire Immediately, Despite Election Outcome

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The conservative justice has told friends he does not plan to step down before the end of the court’s term, even as Democrats are set to seize the Senate in January.

By Ann E. Marimow

Reporting from Washington

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. has told people close to him that he does not intend to retire immediately from the Supreme Court, despite Democrats’ commanding win in Senate contests on Tuesday, which means Republicans will hold the chamber for only a short time longer.

As a result, Republicans may have missed the window for President Trump to name a fourth or even a fifth justice to the Supreme Court in the final two years of his presidency.

Justice Alito shared his plans with friends after the election results were clear this week, according to two people close to the justice who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

As recently as last month, Justice Alito, a forceful conservative and reliable vote in favor of Mr. Trump’s policies, had rejected the idea that he would step down if Democrats took control of the Senate.

“I intend to stick around through this term,” he told Bloomberg News, in an interview published in early October.

But the state of the electoral map after Tuesday’s election generated speculation that he or Justice Clarence Thomas — the court’s two oldest justices — could quickly announce their retirements and give the president a brief window to push through a successor during the Senate’s lame-duck session.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Over the years, Justice Thomas has ruled out retiring, suggesting he would serve for decades more. With 35 years on the bench, if Justice Thomas were to stay through May 2028, he would set the record as the longest-serving justice in Supreme Court history.

Justice Thomas, who is 78, and Justice Alito, who is 76, did not respond to requests for comment about their plans.

Despite the public conversation, legal experts were largely agreed on Wednesday that a speedy retirement would be a potentially dicey and problematic proposition that was not guaranteed to secure a seat.

A nominee would have faced the newfound independence of departing Republican senators such as John Cornyn of Texas and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who were defeated in primaries by Trump-backed challengers, in addition to Susan Collins of Maine, a moderate who lost on Tuesday. The group may have had little appetite to help Mr. Trump ram through a nominee of his choice.

After Mr. Trump won re-election in 2024, the conservative legal analyst Ed Whelan said that he expected Justice Alito to announce his retirement the next spring and predicted that Justice Thomas would step down in 2026. The moves, he had believed, would allow Mr. Trump to replace the justices with younger jurists who might secure the court’s conservative supermajority for a generation.

Of course, an unexpected vacancy due to health concerns, for instance, could arise at any time during the remainder of Mr. Trump’s tenure. But after Tuesday’s election, in which the scale of the Democrats’ win in Congress was larger than expected, Mr. Whelan said the two conservative justices now may not be able to retire before 2033 if they want to be succeeded by a nominee with a similar judicial philosophy.

“No justice is going to announce in the next few days that he will be stepping down,” Mr. Whelan wrote, adding, “Justices don’t make snap decisions about retiring.”

Robert Luther III, a professor at Antonin Scalia Law School who helped choose Mr. Trump’s judicial nominees during his first term, agreed.

“I don’t anticipate any retirements before January, and frankly, I wouldn’t advise it,” he said.

Both justices were on the bench when Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg decided not to retire before the 2016 election, a decision many court observers consider a cautionary tale. Instead of allowing President Barack Obama to pick her successor, Justice Ginsburg died while in office in 2020, creating an opening for Mr. Trump to replace the liberal icon with a conservative, Justice Amy Coney Barrett.

But now, conservatives fret that both men may be in danger of following Justice Ginsburg’s example. If a Democrat were elected to succeed Mr. Trump as president in 2028, both Justices Alito and Thomas would be in their 80s before a Republican could regain the White House and be in position to nominate a successor. Forecasts for when the G. O. P. might regain control of the Senate are even cloudier.

At the end of the Supreme Court’s last term in June, speculation had intensified about Justice Alito’s future and whether Mr. Trump would have an opening to continue to remake a Supreme Court that already includes three of his first-term nominees.

Because of Justice Thomas’s previous statements, attention centered on Justice Alito. It reached a fever pitch on the last day of the term when NPR erroneously reported, and then retracted, his retirement.

In a series of interviews published in October, Justice Alito acknowledged that he had “thought about” retiring at the end of the term, but said he had ruled it out, thinking he could still make a “valuable contribution,” as he told CBS News.

Meanwhile, a newly empowered Democratic Congress will have other implications for the Supreme Court beyond vacancies and nominations. Democrats unhappy with rulings from the conservative bench have repeatedly called for changing the structure of the court. Recent polls show bipartisan support for enacting an enforcement mechanism for the ethics code the justices adopted in 2023, and for eliminating life tenure for justices.

Gabe Roth of Fix the Court, which advocates judicial accountability, predicted on Wednesday that House and Senate committees overseeing the courts would also revive judicial ethics investigations that were largely paused two years ago.

Justice Thomas, for one, could face renewed questions surrounding gifts he accepted, but initially did not report, from his friend Harlan Crow, a Texas billionaire and Republican donor. The justice has said he was not required to report such gifts at the time.

Abbie VanSickle and Michael Gold contributed reporting.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

The Machine, and the Messaging, That Won Texas for Democrats

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Years of organizing met a moment of voter discontent, as James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa offered Texans a vision of economic relief and political change.

Years of organizing met a moment of voter discontent, as James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa offered Texans a vision of economic relief and political change.

James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa at a campaign rally in Austin, Texas, a day before the midterm election. Credit... Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

Supported by

By J. David Goodman

Reporting from Austin, Texas

The Democratic Party’s stunning domination in Texas on Tuesday began with the promise of one candidate, James Talarico.

After decades of Republican rule, his well-funded, disciplined and scandal-free U. S. Senate campaign helped convince voters that winning was possible this time. He soon had help.

Gina Hinojosa, a little-known state lawmaker who had appeared destined for defeat when she challenged Gov. Greg Abbott, emphasized the issue of data centers, sitting in the living rooms of conservatives angry about the massive, noisy, energy-guzzling facilities. She promised a halt.

Behind them both was the deepest bench of Democratic candidates assembled in decades in Texas. Transcending any single person, the party built quiet momentum with voters fed up with rising prices and unmoved by Republican warnings that voting for Democrats would signal the end of Texas as they knew it.

With Democrats poised to occupy nearly every statewide office — a tectonic shift — top campaign advisers, newly elected leaders, party operatives and strategists described in interviews how Mr. Talarico’s campaign had galvanized voters and fueled improbable triumphs.

They also credited a yearslong organizing effort and the party’s success at fielding candidates for nearly every race — all 150 state House districts, every statewide office, every state board of education position and every major judicial race. The Republican Party in Texas did not do the same, leaving some Democrats with uncontested seats.

“This is the first year where we really had a machine built,” said Katherine Fischer, the executive director of the Texas Majority PAC, which worked with the Texas Democratic Party to run and train candidates. “We filled every single state and federal seat for the first time in state history of either party.”

By Wednesday, the scale of Democratic success was so great that it appeared likely to propel a legislative candidate in Fort Worth’s conservative suburbs to victory despite having suspended her campaign over questions about whether a conviction could disqualify her.

The results surprised even winning candidates, who were in a state of elated shock on Tuesday night.

“I had no idea what was going to happen. Frankly, none of us did,” said Sarah Eckhardt, the comptroller-elect, as she stood in a Whataburger restaurant in Austin packed with jubilant Democrats.

Mr. Talarico and Ms. Hinojosa, who will be the state’s first Latina governor, sat at a table and toasted with orange-and-white soda cups as giddy supporters cheered and snapped photos.

“We’re in a realignment that goes beyond party,” Ms. Eckhardt added. “That’s what’s happening here.”

Republican Party leaders had long assumed that the only threats to their power were from the right, even as Texas became a landing pad for transplants and immigrants, its cosmopolitan urban centers ballooning to include five of the nation’s 15 largest cities.

That assumption that moving right was always the right move led Ken Paxton, a scandal-scarred attorney general, to challenge and defeat Senator John Cornyn in the primary. It also allowed Bo French, a brazenly anti-Muslim candidate, to become the party’s nominee for oil and gas regulator. He complained publicly about the number of South Asians at the University of Texas. He lost.

The long rightward lurch had not been a problem for Republican officials. Then, on Tuesday, the lurch back swept most of them away.

The Democratic Party’s candidates, especially in statewide races, stuck to a consistent middle-of-the-road message, promising to address cost-of-living concerns and to curtail cultural battles that have consumed Texas politics for years.

For many, including Ms. Hinojosa, the biggest challenge was being taken seriously, especially by major donors.

“It was really hard to get people to believe in this race,” said Amy Friedman, her campaign manager. “It was a slog to get our first million. It was a slog to get the next two.”

By contrast, Republicans leaned into culture wars that had seemed potent just two years before. They believed they had easy targets in Ms. Hinojosa and Mr. Talarico, who had spoken publicly about gender, race and equity.

“Some people know him as ‘Tofu Talarico.’ Some people call him ‘Six Gender Jimmy,’” said Mr. Paxton on the night of his primary victory in March. “I’ve even heard some people even call him James Talafreako.”

That nickname stuck, but not as Mr. Paxton expected.

At a Houston rally the next day, Mr. Talarico told supporters that they could buy a T-shirt declaring “I’m a Talafreako.” More than 43,000 did, netting his campaign more than $1 million.

The nimble response — parrying rather than counterpunching — captured the instincts of his campaign. Mr. Talarico stuck relentlessly to a core message: Texas politics was dominated by billionaires and politicians like Mr. Paxton who had served their own interests at the expense of ordinary Texans.

Mr. Talarico navigated fraught moments in his speeches, often germinating in iPhone notes shared with his 26-year-old speechwriter, Antonio Esparza.

On Sept. 10, 2025, the day after Mr. Talarico announced his Senate run, he learned that Charlie Kirk, the conservative activist, had been assassinated. He was at his Austin home with Mr. Esparza when they decided to directly address the killing at a planned rally that night, “instead of running from it,” Mr. Esparza said.

They wrote a speech as they drove to a San Antonio rally in Mr. Talarico’s pickup, driven by another aide, each on his own laptop in a shared document, typing as they headed down Interstate 35.

“I disagreed with Charlie Kirk on almost every political issue, but Charlie Kirk was a child of God,” Mr. Talarico, a former seminarian, said in the speech. “He was our sibling, our brother. He was a human being.”

A video of the remarks, clipped and shared on social media, spread widely.

“I’ll never forget being in that truck,” Mr. Esparza said.

The approach underscored what Mr. Talarico presented in his campaign as a commitment to bipartisanship, to faith and to getting beyond divisions. He hammered home that message to audiences listening to hourlong podcasts. He delivered it in person around the state, first with town halls where he took questions and then in speeches to thousands.

The message of ending division and transcending partisanship united the ticket in 2026. It was repeated by candidates like Taylor Rehmet, a union machinist uncomfortable with party labels, who flipped a State Senate seat in a deep-red district in Tarrant County in a January special election and held onto the seat on Tuesday. It was also part of Ms. Hinojosa’s victory speech in Austin.

“Whether you’re a Democrat, a Republican or neither,” Ms. Hinojosa said, “hear what Texas said today, loud and clear: Your government belongs to you.”

Ms. Hinojosa at first struggled to gain attention, but she often met with individual voters, and spent time trying to understand issues like data centers before becoming among the most prominent Texas politicians to support a moratorium.

“We had months of meetings before that rollout,” said Ms. Friedman, the campaign manager. Ms. Hinojosa wanted to talk to people directly affected and to know where labor organizations stood.

Democrats also had to regain support from Latino voters. They did so by not taking it for granted, said Regina Montoya, a board member of the Latino Victory Fund political action committee. She recalled Mr. Talarico visiting her at home in Dallas last year as he embarked on his campaign. They shared breakfast tacos.

“He was there to listen,” Ms. Montoya said. “He promised then that he would work hard to earn the votes of Latinos.”

Mr. Talarico accomplished that also through deft use of social media, courting influencers while he was running in a tough Democratic primary.

“His skill is being genuine, and this is not like an ideology thing. It’s like a personality thing,” said Carlos Espina, a Texas-based progressive influencer who makes videos in Spanish. Mr. Espina, who has said he was not paid by the campaign for his videos backing Mr. Talarico, also said the bipartisan message resonated with Latinos.

“We don’t say, ‘Oh, it’s Democrat and Republican,’” he said. “This is a right or wrong thing. Like, should you be treating people this way as human beings?”

The Democrats at the top of the ticket also magnified each other through joint appearances, introducing one another to new audiences. Mr. Talarico teamed up for events with Ms. Hinojosa and with Bobby Pulido, a well-known Tejano singer who flipped a congressional district in the Rio Grande Valley on Tuesday.

And Democrats also had one major, if unintentional, benefactor: President Trump, who visited the state repeatedly, reminding voters of why he was unpopular.

“The biggest thanks have to go to Donald Trump,” said Cristóbal Alex, who helped advise a super PAC supporting Mr. Talarico.

He said the president’s endorsement of Mr. Paxton could have made them a powerful Republican force. Instead, he said, it backfired.

“It’s like the two of them are part of this political A team,” Mr. Alex said. “Except the A team was the C team.”

J. David Goodman is the Texas bureau chief for The Times, based in Houston.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

A Bronx native who’d spent his whole life in the city left on foot in May.

Credit...

Supported by

By Dodai Stewart

Visuals by Mark Abramson

Reporting from Mound House, Nev.

In the minutes before sunrise in Mound House, Nev., Chantz Rivera, bundled in a high-visibility yellow-green coat, climbed out of the blue tent where he’d spent the night, just off the shoulder of U. S. Route 50.

It was a chilly morning in the high desert. The sky lightened and mountains appeared on the horizon. He would soon be crossing through the Sierra Nevada foothills, walking with his shopping cart full of belongings.

Rivera, 29, is slight of build, bearded and handsome, with a Bronx accent. He was born and raised in the Gun Hill Houses, a New York City Housing Authority complex in the Williamsbridge neighborhood of the Bronx.

He had spent his whole life in the city, and earlier this year, he had been feeling stuck. So he’d started walking. That was four and a half months ago.

On this day, his destination was Carson City, just seven miles away and downhill — light work for Rivera, who had been walking 20 to 25 miles a day. He would sleep in a motel for the first time in a few nights.

He held up his phone and filmed himself, the tent and the busy road.

“Day 135!” he said with a grin, speaking to his online following, which had grown to around 60,000 since hitting the road. “We out here!”

He ducked back into the tent and gathered his bedding, camera and pillow. He retrieved the cart from where he had parked it, near a reflector post on the roadside.

Then he put on his headphones, cued up Meek Mill and headed west along the shoulder of Route 50 as cars and trucks flew past.

The American phrase “Go West, young man” is almost 200 years old — credited to the famed newspaper man Horace Greeley — and there is a long history, from John Steinbeck’s Tom Joad to Jack Kerouac, of young men heading out to the frontier, to discover the country and themselves.

For Rivera, it was a way to turn things around.

He tries his best to see silver linings. Growing up, his father worked, and his mother used drugs, but he considered himself lucky to have two parents. He wasn’t great at basketball, but he still played every day, even when there was snow on the ground.

But as he entered the work force after graduating from high school in 2015, it was harder for him to find upsides.

He worked at a warehouse. Then as a door-to-door salesman. Then as a dishwasher for a catering company — $20 an hour, no benefits, no path up the ladder.

“I’m working and I’m paying the bills and then I still can’t afford much,” he remembers thinking. “I can’t do nothing. I’m just stuck here.”

He thought joining the Army could be a way to leave. See the world a bit, get paid for it. But he knew he had a record — “weed charges, disorderly conduct, a bunch of misdemeanors.” The military recruiter denied him, he said. By April, Rivera was wandering around New York, unemployed and wondering what to do.

If you don’t have a job in this country, he said in a video on Instagram, “You might as well be dead.”

“Because what are we living for?” he continued. “To keep struggling and striving and working so the next man can have money?”

Rivera had about $500 to his name. He spent it on a tent, a sleeping bag and a backpack, and filled it with supplies — water, granola bars, a big jar of peanut butter, portable chargers and a survival kit complete with first-aid supplies. And bear spray and a machete, for protection.

His bag was too heavy, so he bought a foldable grocery cart.

His parents gave him $250. It was all the money he had.

“The hardest part was definitely leaving,” he said. “Even when I was leaving, I was hesitating,” he continued. “I’m walking around with the bag on, everything in the bag, walking back and forth down my hallway — like, am I gonna be walking like this?”

He left a few days after his 29th birthday.

That first day, not far past Tarrytown, the grocery cart broke. Rivera replaced it and kept going. He slept on a bench in a railway station that night. The next day, he said, a man saw him and asked if he was homeless.

“No,” he replied, “I’m walking across America.”

Rivera had never hiked before. He’d never been camping. For his trip across the United States, he chose the most direct route the map showed — which mostly meant walking on highway shoulders, drowning out the car traffic with his big headphones on. (His playlist included a lot of rap — Future, A Boogie, Lil Durk, Young Thug, Kodak Black — but for motivation he also liked to play Kate Bush’s “Running Up That Hill.”)

“In the beginning, everything was hurting,” Rivera said. “I was so cramped and sore and my knees hurt,” he added. “I was literally limping for like a week.”

In New Jersey, his tent fell out of the cart he was pulling without him noticing, and he had to backtrack to find it.

In Pennsylvania, it was too hot to sleep with the rain tarp on, and the forecast looked clear, but it ended up raining and he got soaked.

During those first few days, he did think about turning back. But he’d talk himself out of it.

His second cart broke — then his third, then his fourth.

He would replace them at supermarkets or big box stores, which — along with gas stations — is where Rivera would use the bathroom and resupply. Powerade was a staple, as were 15-count boxes of individually wrapped peanut butter and jelly Uncrustables sandwiches. Those could be breakfast for two weeks.

He began to develop routines. When possible, he would line up his walking schedule so that sundown corresponded with his arrival in a town, where he’d find a cheap motel to stay for the night. If he arrived early enough, he would take in whatever sights there were to see — statues, monuments, museums, rivers, railroad tracks. If he slept in a motel, he’d stay in the room until the very last minute before checkout, maximizing his bed and bathroom time.

Sometimes he would find himself between towns at sunset. On those nights he would sleep on a bench or at a bus stop, or set up his tent in a field or a park — or in a liminal space behind a church, gas station, fast-food joint or a Walmart.

“You doing all right?” a law enforcement officer in Indiana asked.

“We got a call that you were pulling a cart and looked exhausted,” the officer continued. “Just wanted to make sure you were all right.”

“Yeah, I’m good,” Rivera said. “I’m walking across America.”

Getting stopped by police officers or state troopers also became routine. It happened in almost every state, he said, often multiple times a day. Sometimes the officers would drive him to the next county, or to a road they deemed safer for pedestrians.

Because of his brown skin, people commenting on his posts warned him about racism and sundown towns, but Rivera found warmth and hospitality instead. “I went through a lot of small towns that was nothing but white people,” he said. “And I got love — like, they showed me love.”

In Ohio, a pastor picked him up and gave him a lift to a motel. (Unlike some extreme walkers, Rivera was not a purist; he accepted a few short rides when offered.)

In Indiana, a woman gave him a bottle of water and some beef jerky, and a man brought him ice, water and iced tea.

In Missouri, two guys noticed the wheel of his cart was wobbling. The men drove Rivera and his cart to their garage. “We’ll put a Band-Aid on this thing,” one of the men said as he repaired the wheel with thick black tape.

In Colorado, a reporter at a radio station interviewed Rivera and gifted him a pair of white and red Nike Cortez sneakers — the same ones Tom Hanks had worn in the movie “Forrest Gump.”

Unlike Forrest Gump, Rivera did not inspire people to actually join him on the road, but more and more people began to follow him online. Some of the hospitality he encountered was surely spontaneous, but other times it came from people who had seen what he was trying to do and wanted to help him succeed.

When he hit Nevada, a woman named Jennifer commented on one of his posts: “You near Fallon yet? Got a home-cooked meal for you.” Rivera wrote back: “I NEED THAT!” Sure enough, Jennifer and her husband, Matt, let Rivera pitch his tent on their property, he said, and fed him mac and cheese, steak, ribs and potatoes.

Usually, people go to New York to find fame — for Rivera, leaving town is what did it.

Back home, his journey became news: He did a phone interview with Hell Gate, the New York news site. And he told the Bronx Times about how the kindness he’d encountered had surprised him: “Being in the city, you think everybody’s just, like, for himself.”

His followers prodded him to work out a way to let people send him money. Rivera waved away that suggestion at first, but he eventually relented and set up a GoFundMe account that raised more than $10,000.

Mitchell Hulse, a researcher in New York, gave $10 after reading Rivera’s interview on Hell Gate. “I think when somebody pulls something like this off,” Hulse said, “it can show you your own capability.”

Nev Schulman, one of the hosts of the MTV show “Catfish,” donated $300.

“He’s a young Black man from the Bronx taking on something incredibly ambitious,” Schulman said. “And I think there’s real value in helping people from communities that have historically had to work harder to have their stories heard.”

“What he’s doing,” he added, “is bigger than just walking across the country.”

For those not accustomed to traveling major roadways on foot: The trek from Mound House to Carson City is far from peaceful. The traffic whizzed by on the multilane Lincoln Highway, so loud it made talking impossible. Gusts of brisk desert wind blew this way and that, and the whole situation felt, frankly, dangerous.

But Rivera seemed unperturbed. He just kept pushing his cart — past an auto body shop, a self-storage business, and then gas stations, thrift stores, pizza places. Before long he spotted the Nevada State Capitol Building.

He parked his cart on a path, and entered the grand wooden doors.

“Is the governor here?” he asked a woman behind a desk in the office. “I want to meet him. I’m walking across America!”

The governor was not available. Rivera went upstairs and browsed the small museum, which featured exhibits about Nevada’s mining history and Native American heritage. “Oh, that’s the ram!” he said when he saw a taxidermy bighorn sheep kneeling in the corner of the museum. “I seen one of these in person! In real life.”

Before embarking on the walk, he had left New York only twice — once to Florida, for a week, and another time to Washington, D. C., for a weekend.

Now he had seen Amish people with buggies. He had seen sheep, cows, horses, an attraction described as the world’s largest Czech egg. He had seen incredible desert sunsets, snow-capped mountain landscapes, the most stars he’d ever seen in his life. He had discovered that true happiness could be found alone beneath the stars in Colorado.

“People are like, What are you doing?” Rivera said. “What are you doing it for? When I tell them I’m walking across America — ‘Oh, what’s your reason?’ You need to have a reason?

“I just want to be free. I’m just walking because I’m using my free will. That’s it.”

After lunch, he went back to the Capitol building to check again if the governor was available.

“He’s in Vegas,” an officer posted in the lobby said.

“Oh, he’s at the craps table, huh? He’s gambling it all away?”

The officer laughed.

Afterward, Rivera made his way to a Motel 6. He had prepaid for a room that was on the ground floor, so he could wheel his cart inside. He hadn’t let the motel know he had a cart.

“Sometimes they say ‘no carts,’” he said. “The motel lady in Kansas was actually saying, ‘Homeless people come all the time’ and this and that.” That had upset him a bit. He couldn’t believe some places would turn people away because of a shopping cart. “I’m not homeless, you know? Why are you discriminating? Judging me.”

And so he tried to keep a low profile as he pushed the rattling shopping cart through the door of his room. The next day he would be walking uphill to his final state.

Two weeks later, Mr. Rivera stood on a rocky shore and pointed his camera across the bay at a distant skyline.

“I ain’t gonna lie, I think that’s San Francisco, bro,” he said in a video he posted to social media.

Just shy of the Golden Gate Bridge, he stood on his cart and filmed a mailing label stuck to a road sign. In the “to” field, in black marker, it said: “WALK ACROSS AMERICA COMPLETE DAY 149!!”

The next day, in San Francisco, someone stole his portable chargers and survival kit from his cart while he was using the restroom at a McDonald’s on Fillmore Street.

Rivera didn’t care about the kit, but he’d stored a memory card and a flash drive in a pocket of that bag. Some videos he’d filmed were now lost.

Perhaps the greater loss was that his walk was over. Over the phone, he sighed but said he felt relatively calm about everything, even the missing belongings. “In a way, I feel more free than I’ve felt, ever,” he said.

The plan now was to spend a few weeks in California before flying home to New York.

But he was already thinking about his next big walk. Europe, maybe. The language barrier would be a new challenge, but he felt he could figure it out.

“You know, even if I do feel stuck, I’m more comfortable leaving now,” Rivera said.

“I’m not scared or nervous or anything to just up and go — because I did that.”

When photographer Mark Abramson and I spent the day with Chantz Rivera, I was struck by his humor, his persistence, and how naturally he took the kindness of strangers in stride. “I think people are just nice,” he told me. “People actually want to see somebody succeed.”

An earlier version of this article misspelled the name of a rap artist that Chantz Rivera listened to during his trip across the United States. He is Lil Durk, not Lil Dirk.

Dodai Stewart is a Times reporter who writes about living in New York City, with a focus on how, and where, we gather.

Elon Musk’s Very Bad Night

The New York Times November 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Michelle Goldberg

By Michelle Goldberg

Opinion Columnist

Will Lawrence, one of the founders of the Sunrise Movement, a progressive environmentalist group, was supposed to be unelectable in the purple House district in Michigan held by a Republican, Tom Barrett. When he pulled ahead in his primary, a headline on the influential political site Punchbowl said, “Democrats’ Nightmare in Michigan.” Representative Hillary Scholten, a centrist Michigan Democrat, told Axios, “He can’t win.” During the general election, Republicans gloated when Lawrence’s old social media posts emerged, including one calling nuclear family homes an “isolating, individualistic, violent way of organizing society” and another dreaming of a world of “free and open migration.” I worried that the left might have cost Democrats a swing seat.

But when I met Lawrence last summer in the Seventh District — a largely white middle-class place with lots of rural and exurban areas — he insisted that outsiders were misreading the environment. “People are tired of these corporate-funded Republicans and corporate-funded Democrats,” he said. He would win people over, he argued, with opposition to the war in Iran and, crucially, to the spread of data centers. “Stopping these A. I. data centers has been a huge uniting issue across people of all political persuasions,” he said.

Republican PACs, flush with tech money, spent more against Lawrence than any other Democratic House candidate. Mailers called him “the most radical Democratic candidate in America” and warned of the socialist menace. (He’d been a member of the Democratic Socialists of America until July.) It didn’t matter: Lawrence won by just over 3 points.

Tuesday night’s blue tsunami carried so many Democrats to victory that we can’t attribute every win to candidate skill or strategy, especially a relatively narrow one like Lawrence’s. (In Iowa, a Democrat who’d suspended his statehouse campaign because of health problems was elected anyway.) But many of the triumphant Democratic underdogs were united by their opposition to Silicon Valley’s priorities. They promised to stand up to the domineering tech titans who’ve clustered around Donald Trump, arrogating to themselves the right to define America’s future. The election was an epic repudiation of the president, but it was also a democratic rebuke of Silicon Valley by voters who felt their ability to write their own destinies slipping away.

After Trump, there was no bigger loser on Tuesday than Elon Musk, who spent over $400 million backing Republicans. He poured more than half of that sum into Texas, his home since 2020, when he left California out of anger at regulation and Covid restrictions. He later moved most of his business empire to Texas and even built his own town, Starbase, there. Musk almost single-handedly funded the Senate campaign of Texas’ widely despised attorney general, Ken Paxton. He tweeted obsessively about James Talarico, Paxton’s opponent, amplifying conspiracy theories that Talarico was in a mental hospital when he was really sick with the flu.

Talarico, in turn, sometimes seemed to be running as much against Musk as against Paxton. Even before he won the Democratic nomination, he railed against Musk’s greed, saying: “The reason poverty exists in the wealthiest country on earth is not because we can’t feed the poor. It’s because we can’t satisfy the rich. But what we can do is tax trillionaires out of existence.” Last month he told a packed rally in Austin — until recently a tech bro Valhalla — that Musk was trying to buy himself the state. “Elon Musk wants our land,” said Talarico. “He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.”

It wasn’t just Talarico. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic state representative who stunned the political world by unseating Texas’ governor, Greg Abbott, made opposition to data centers and the power of tech barons a centerpiece of her campaign. She took aim at Abbott’s relationship with Musk, whose companies have received more than $1.6 billion in tax incentives and over $100 million in government grants from Texas. In October, Hinojosa sued to force Abbott to release his office’s communications with Musk and his companies. At one of her final rallies she said, of Abbott’s relationship with Musk, “I think Greg Abbott is embarrassed that he sold us out.”

After Tuesday’s blue wave, shares in SpaceX and Tesla plunged even as the broader stock market soared. The stocks of data center operators also fell as investors sized up a hostile political climate. Across the country, there were more than 40 ballot initiatives that would either restrict or allow data center development. Data center opponents are on track to win all but one of them. (The facilities are apparently still welcome in Harwood, N. D.) Meanwhile, Congress is preparing investigations into the tech overlords who’ve spent the past two years sucking up to the president — and, more important, paying him off. On X, in response to a call for “live televised trials of Big Tech executives,” Senator Ed Markey, the Massachusetts Democrat, wrote, “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

On Wednesday, I spoke to Lawrence again and asked what he’d say to Democrats who I expect will soon be receiving overtures from a newly conciliatory tech industry.

“I’d say, ‘beware,’ because these tech oligarchs are dramatically unpopular,” he said. “If we want to be a party of the working class, these are the Rockefellers and Carnegies of our day. These are the richest and most powerful people who are accustomed to operating with complete impunity, and they need to be brought to heel.”

Democrats emerged from the midterms with a mandate to do just that.

Michelle Goldberg has been an Opinion columnist since 2017. She is the author of several books about politics, religion and women’s rights and was part of a team that won a Pulitzer Prize for public service in 2018 for reporting on workplace sexual harassment.

Political Losses Deepen the Stakes as Trump Contemplates Renewed Iran Attack

The New York Times November 05, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

The midterm results laid bare the deep unpopularity of the war of choice that President Trump started and is now struggling to end.

By David E. Sanger

David E. Sanger has covered five American presidents over more than four decades at the Times, often focusing on nuclear competition and the revival of superpower conflict, the subject of his latest book.

President Trump’s loss of the House and Senate intersects with one of the most consequential decisions of his presidency: whether to resume intense combat operations against Iran, in a war that Mr. Trump’s vice president said Wednesday was the primary reason for the Republican Party’s crushing defeat.

The results across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections drove home how deeply unpopular the war was among Americans — and how much backlash Mr. Trump could face if he renewed major strikes against the country, which the United States and Israel jointly attacked in February.

The political blow deepened the challenge Mr. Trump faces in ending a war of his choosing.

He has already hinted that he is in no rush to resume bombing, despite a major naval and air power buildup that has been underway for weeks as he has mulled whether to launch an intense, short attack on Iran’s surviving nuclear-related sites, along with energy and infrastructure targets.

It may yet happen: Past presidents, suddenly plunged into lame-duck status, have often reached for their military options, partly to demonstrate that their role as commander in chief is undiminished. George W. Bush accelerated in Iraq after his historic midterm defeat in 2006, though only after replacing his defense secretary, Donald H. Rumsfeld, and radically changing his strategy. Within limits, it worked.

But Mr. Trump’s choices in Iran are far more complex.

If the president has a new strategy for prosecuting the war, he and his aides have been silent about it. The rifts in his administration over his decision to go to war, barely hidden from the beginning, broke out into the open as soon as election results were in. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance wrote in a social media post, claiming the president had made a similar assessment. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”

Mr. Trump immediately did so. “I can tell you as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” the president said a few hours later, as he gave reporters a tour of his under-construction White House ballroom.

If Mr. Vance’s logic wins the day, Mr. Trump will now resume negotiations, hoping to get some kind of agreement tougher than the cease-fire pact he signed in June, only to see it fall apart within weeks.

If Mr. Trump truly believes force will make a difference, he could order a resumption of bombing, though it is unclear why he might expect the outcome to be different than it was in the spring. Thirty-eight days of continuous attacks failed to collapse the regime, recover Iran’s vast stockpile of nuclear fuel, eliminate its missile stores or lead to what he once insisted would be “unconditional surrender.”

Now he is negotiating from a weaker hand, and the Iranians know it. “The elections decided the fate of the war,” Danny Citrinowicz, a former Israeli intelligence officer who focused on Iran for two decades, said on Wednesday. “The only question is how it will end: with a bang, a peaceful, negotiated but likely unsatisfactory solution, or Trump saying, ‘JD Vance was right, and goodbye.’”

Time is not on Mr. Trump’s side. From the war’s start on Feb. 28, the Iranians have been betting that they can frustrate Mr. Trump’s efforts at regime change; protect the deeply buried nuclear stockpile or hold onto it until the end game of any negotiation; and ramp up the pain by restricting shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Along the way, they have so devastated several American bases in the region that, Pentagon officials concede, they will probably never be rebuilt.

The cost of the war so far has hit $47 billion, the Pentagon told Congress recently. That does not including damage to the bases — or the huge cost consumers have had to absorb in increased prices for gas, diesel and heating oil.

Mr. Trump and his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, could well run out of money before the conflict is resolved. Congress has never passed additional funding for the war in Iran, and the chances that the new, Democrat-controlled House and Senate would pay for it seem remote.

And Mr. Hegseth does not have much political currency in Congress: Democrats have indicated they plan to investigate and potentially impeach him.

All of that suggests that if Mr. Trump truly believes that an additional round of bombing will make Iran more likely to make concessions at the negotiating table, waiting will not help him. Moreover, he may be concerned that his powers appear undiminished to other world leaders, especially as he heads to the Philippines and China in less than two weeks for back-to-back summit meetings.

Former State Department diplomats, Pentagon officials and military commanders with long experience in the Middle East said that it was difficult to predict Mr. Trump’s decision, but that he may have boxed himself in.

“It makes little sense to resume attacks on Iran, since even the Republicans acknowledge that the war is why they lost,” Daniel Shapiro, the Pentagon’s top Middle East policy official in the Biden administration, said on Wednesday, referring to Mr. Vance’s remarks. “But Trump is erratic, unstable and hates to be seen as a loser.”

Mr. Shapiro, a former U. S. ambassador to Israel, added, “Iran has little incentive to give him a good deal that would allow him to claim victory, so his choices are to escalate and then claim victory — with the risk that he cannot control the escalation — or essentially walk away.”

The Pentagon has made no secret of its military buildup, perhaps hoping that the appearance of so much American firepower in the Gulf would push the Iranians to concessions.

Pentagon officials and military commanders said on Wednesday that thousands of American air and naval forces on more than a dozen ships and at bases around the Middle East and in the U. S. were poised to resume major combat operations against Iran on Mr. Trump’s orders.

The U. S. and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for a short but intensive operation whose targets were likely to include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal, officials said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.

Mr. Trump himself has frequently suggested as a possible target Pickaxe Mountain, the name the United States has given an underground facility that they believe holds advanced centrifuges to produce uranium — but, as far as anyone can tell, little or no nuclear fuel.

The U. S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers. The Pentagon and State Department have withdrawn personnel from bases and facilities in the region as a precautionary measure. And remaining forces have rehearsed responding to mass-casualty incidents in case Iran retaliates against any American attack.

Ryan Crocker, a six-time U. S. ambassador in the Middle East and South Asia, said on Wednesday that the war’s role in the Republicans’ midterm losses should validate Mr. Trump’s long-stated reluctance to avoid forever wars.

“I would hope that this midterm result will reinforce the president’s gut instincts toward caution in military conflict,” Mr. Crocker said at a briefing held by the Middle East Institute.

Mr. Crocker said that Iran’s leadership has long shown a high tolerance for pain and suffering, and would not be fazed by several more days of heavy bombing. “We will be playing into their strong suit if we restart kinetic activity,” he said, referring to military operations.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

The Blue Wave Has Tech Bros Scrambling for Data Centers in Space

Wired November 04, 2026

A wave of Democratic candidates across the country—and notably in Texas, a national data center hot spot and home to Elon Musk’s SpaceX—won their state and congressional races on Tuesday, including many candidates who voiced opposition to the data center industry. The results have sent some corners of the tech industry looking to the heavens for answers.

In recent hours, data center enthusiasts have proclaimed on social media that they’re still “bullish” on building data centers—just not necessarily in Texas, or even on Earth at all. Instead, they say, it’s time to focus on data centers in space.

Elon Musk—who spent more than $400 million of his fortune supporting Republican candidates who all went on to lose their midterms races—has been among those leading the charge. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk posted on X in the early hours of Wednesday, after it was clear that Democrats had taken the House and Senate.

Jordan Lasker—the man behind the X account "Crémieux,” which is a popular follow in the tech world and is known for posting race-based pseudoscience—also weighed in, saying, “Data centers in space are an incredible idea and anyone who doubted them didn't think enough about tonight's election results.”

Throughout the day, Musk employees, tech investors, AI researchers, venture capitalists, and industry fans joined the chorus of support for space-based data centers. Soham Mehta, a research fellow at the techno-optimist think tank Foundation for American Innovation, argued that underwater data centers should also be considered. (In June, China began operating what it claims is the world’s first underwater data center.)

Some companies are already trying to put compute in orbit. Among them are Google, which launched a satellite that it says contains “data center class TPU,” and SpaceX, which says it aims to deploy “thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027.” Blue Origin is also in the mix, having filed for a Federal Communications Commission permit to launch 50,000 satellites that will constitute an “orbital data center system.”

There are also a few startups aiming to build data centers in space, including Starcloud, which claims to have carried "the first Nvidia H100 GPU into orbit" in November 2025.

Despite being technically possible, the realities of in-orbit data centers are difficult. Among other things, space-based data centers are much more expensive than land-based ones, can’t grow to hyperscale size, and are subject to the risks and whims of satellite launches.

When it comes to Texas data centers, the concerns of tech bros aren’t completely unfounded. Experts tell WIRED that the change in leadership could translate to some concrete changes in the industry—albeit with limits.

Although Democrats will have control of the Texas House of Representatives, Republicans still have control over the state’s senate. Robert Paterson, professor of land use and environmental planning at the University of Texas at Austin, tells WIRED that the split means that some immediate attempts at change “will probably be stymied a bit.”

Adrian Shelley, director of nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen’s Texas office, tells WIRED that the legislature would be a likely place to hash out high-impact policies like the reallocation of state agency resources. However, he adds that the governor could effect more immediate changes by issuing executive orders, or requesting the resignation of politically appointed officials in state agencies.

Shelley says that these oversight agencies—such as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Public Utility Commission, and the Texas Water Development Board—have the authority to charge fines for breaking state law, or in extreme cases to revoke permits for projects like data centers. But Paterson notes that Texas developers have particularly strong “vested rights,” which protects the terms of their projects from the moment their permits are approved, even if construction hasn’t begun.

Another medium-term route to reshaping Texas’ data center industry could be to give more power to its counties. Paterson noted that nearly half of the state’s data centers exist in unincorporated territory, which puts them outside the jurisdiction of city zoning laws.

Unlike other states, Paterson says, Texas counties have relatively limited enforcement abilities. Under the state's so-called Dillon’s Rule, counties only have powers that are “specifically allotted to it by the state.” So while they have authority over things like access and egress to county roads or construction on floodplains, he says they don't have the zoning authority that would help closely regulate projects like data centers.

Paterson says that the new attorney general could theoretically adjust the terms in the state’s biannual handbook, which establishes the limits of county authority. He also argues that even in a split legislature, especially since anti-data-center sentiment crosses party lines, state lawmakers could propose a viable bill giving counties “limited zoning authority over data centers."

Shelley tells WIRED that since “data centers were a decisive factor in this blue wave,” the upcoming legislative season will be “very interesting.”

“I will say the data center industry hasn't shown a lot of interest in working with state lawmakers or local leaders,” Shelley says, “and I will be interested to see if that changes.”

If not, there’s always low Earth orbit.

‘We Have No Shared Reality’: Two Political Influencers on the Future of Politics Online

Wired November 04, 2026

A voter going to the polls Tuesday night was more likely than not to use information from their favorite influencer than traditional news when casting their vote. According to a recent YouGov survey, nearly 65 percent of 2,000 adults surveyed say they receive their political information from digital creators.

Given that that statistic jumps to 77 percent when you isolate Gen Z, it’s unlikely to change anytime soon. On the heels of a historic Democratic wave capturing the House and Senate Tuesday, Kat Abughazaleh, who ran for an Illinois House seat earlier this year as a Democrat, and Republican strategist CJ Pearson talked about the future of influencers and algorithms at the WIRED World Fair in Miami on Wednesday.

The Trump administration has been particularly aggressive in welcoming right-wing creators into the White House. Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt opened formal press briefings to digital creators last year and hosted influencer-specific briefings during her tenure. (Leavitt’s move garnered hefty criticism for favoring softball questions, especially as the administration cracked down on the presence of more traditional media in press briefings.)

Pearson, who previously served on the RNC’s Youth Advisory Council, has been directly involved in these efforts, and points out that multiple federal agencies are now copying the White House’s playbook. He said that it’s simply the cost of getting people’s attention in the digital age.

“It’s a very chronically online administration,” he said. “With how short people’s attention spans are, you have to make [things] interesting.” Not all of the White House’s efforts have been received smoothly on the right: Pearson believes the administration’s decision to distribute portions of the Epstein files to 15 right-wing creators last year was “a misstep.”

For Abughazaleh, a former Media Matters reporter, the administration’s embrace of the internet signals something far more nefarious. Abughazaleh brought up the Department of Education’s recent use of the “Malfoid” meme—a gender-bent Harry Potter fascist figurehead—which, she said, was being promoted for a too-online audience of “incels.” And the White House’s embrace of “AI slop and brutality,” seen in ads about ICE actions, was turning “cruelty into content” rather than informing people, she says.

“They’re trying to ruin your attention span,” she said.

Abughazaleh and Pearson are pretty far apart on the political spectrum. The WIRED forum included some testy exchanges, including whether or not ICE facilities can be called “concentration camps”—a term Abughazaleh, who was arrested for protesting outside an ICE facility last year, used consistently. (The charges were dropped after allegations of misconduct by prosecutors before a grand jury.) They also skirmished over Pearson’s claim that Elon Musk had turned X into a “bastion of free speech.”

But both agreed that reliance on algorithms is increasingly creating echo chambers with young Americans of both parties.

“Algorithms show us what you want to see,” Pearson said, mentioning that his friends on the left will sometimes send him articles on political topics he simply hasn’t seen before. “The deeper question is, is that good for society or for democracy?”

On this, Abughazaleh agrees. “We have no shared reality,” she added.
